New Delhi, Nov 3: The National Investigation Agency on Tuesday opposed a plea by Baramulla MP Abdul Rashid Sheikh alias Engineer Rashid in the Delhi High Court for bail in a terror funding case, alleging that he has influenced some of the prosecution witnesses.
The probe agency contended that two of the prosecution witnesses, who are also protected witnesses, have turned hostile.
The submissions were made before a bench of Justices Prathiba M Singh and Vikas Mahajan, which reserved its order on the bail plea.
Senior advocate Sidharth Luthra, representing the National Investigation Agency (NIA), said the testimony of the witnesses, examined so far, would show that three particular witnesses have been influenced by Rashid.
He contended that at least two protected witnesses have turned hostile.
Luthra submitted that Rashid has given specific speeches against India and has been supporting anti-India activities.
"In view of the influence that the appellant (Rashid) wields, he does not deserve to be granted bail," he contended while giving details of bail orders passed against Rashid.
He added that when Rashid was granted bail to meet his ailing father, he met certain witnesses.
In his rejoinder submissions, Rashid's counsel said the argument that Rashid influenced witnesses is completely untenable as during most of the period he was in custody.
The witnesses who Rashid is alleged to have influenced are extremely closely attached to him; that is, one is a driver and two others are personal assistants and they have been continuously working for Rashid for years, the counsel said.
He added that the appellant is a member of Parliament and has sworn his allegiance to the Constitution of India, and therefore this is a fit case for grant of bail.
The court had earlier noted that Rashid has been in custody for almost seven years and there are a total of 240 witnesses in the case and the trial would take a long time to conclude.
The court was hearing arguments on Rashid’s plea seeking bail in the terror case lodged under the provisions of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.
Rashid was earlier granted interim bail to attend the ceremonies related to his father’s demise.
He faces allegations that he funded separatists and terror groups in Jammu and Kashmir. He has been lodged in Delhi's Tihar Jail since 2019 after the NIA arrested him in the 2017 case.
After he was named in a chargesheet in October 2019, a special NIA court framed charges against Rashid and others in March 2022 under sections 120B (criminal conspiracy), 121 (waging war against the government), and 124A (sedition) of the Indian Penal Code and under relevant provisions of the stringent UAPA.

China state broadcaster pulls Real Madrid match over Mbappé joke
- Published
China's state broadcaster CCTV did not air a Real Madrid match on Sunday, despite the club's star striker Kylian Mbappé's apology for his "ill-judged" remarks on the late Chinese leader Mao Zedong.
Mbappé drew huge backlash after saying the meme "that makes [him] laugh the most" was the one in which his face is superimposed on a "Chinese dictator" resembling Mao.
China Media Group, CCTV's parent organisation, said last Tuesday it would suspend broadcasts of Spanish football La Liga matches following the furore, which also led to Mbappé being dropped by several Chinese brands.
China's foreign ministry had said it took Mbappé's apology "seriously". Real Madrid and La Liga have also apologised.
China Media Group had earlier demanded apologies from the three parties, calling them "an absolute prerequisite" for moving past the incident.
It has acknowledged the apologies, but has not commented on how long the broadcast blackout will last.
Mbappé, who reportedly made his remark about the meme on French talk show The Bridge, apologised later on Tuesday.
"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," he had said.
The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his having overseen one of the bloodiest chapters in the country's past.
Mao, who led the Chinese Communist Party to victory in the civil war and founded the People's Republic of China, died in 1976.
During his rule he oversaw the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which led to a famine that killed tens of millions and unleashed violent purges across Chinese society.
This is not the first time Beijing has suspended sports broadcasts over political sensitivities.
It pulled NBA games for a year from October 2019 after Daryl Morey, the general manager of Houston Rockets, tweeted in support of Hong Kong protesters during widespread pro-democracy protests in the city.
Morey backtracked on his comment after fierce criticism from Chinese fans, sponsors and commercial partners.
"I have had a lot of opportunity since that tweet to hear and consider other perspectives," Morey later wrote.
"I have always appreciated the significant support our Chinese fans and sponsors...I would hope that those who are upset will know that offending or misunderstanding them was not my intention."
Real Madrid beat Racing Santander 3-0 in Sunday's match, with goals from Mbappé, Jude Bellingham and Yan Diomande.

Yes, as long as your card is still recognized, you may be able to recover deleted files, but you need to ensure the memory card is readable and the data hasn’t been overwritten.
2. Can Recoverit Recover RAW Photos and Camera Video Files?
Yes, Recoverit supports recovering various photo, video, and camera file formats from memory cards, including RAW images and different wide formats. However, results may depend on the file’s condition and supported formats.
3. What if a Recovered Video or Photo Still Won’t Open?
The recovered file may still be damaged, fragmented, or corrupted, preventing it from opening. In such cases, you can use file recovery and file repair services separately and try repairing the file after recovery.
4. Can Overwritten Files Be Recovered?
No, overwritten files are generally not recoverable because a new file replaces the deleted file’s data. That’s why we highly recommend stopping use of the SD card as soon as you notice the missing content and starting your recovery process immediately. And once you have successfully recovered files using software like Recoverit, there are a few steps we would like to recommend to prevent future data loss:
- Verify the recovered files and back up the recovered data immediately.
- Maintain two copies in two different storage locations.
- Verify the data completely before formatting your memory card.
- If the memory card has an issue, we highly recommend replacing it with a newer one, since you still risk losing data on future shoots.

Steve Yedlin is a certified color nerd. He almost immediately starts explaining “the math” behind his passion for color science.
But I didn’t call to chat about psychophysics or color theory. I called to talk to Yedlin about his Chromagraph Camera app, newly released, virally popular, and available only on the iPhone.
Yedlin is a longtime collaborator with director Rian Johnson, shooting his films like Knives Out and Star Wars: The Last Jedi. The duo teamed up again for this launch. “I write all of my own image processing that we use on the movies,” he says. The Chromagraph Camera app brings a taste of Yedlin’s special sauce to your smartphone camera.
Instead of the iPhone’s built-in image processing, this app shoots RAW image data and processes it with a similar formula to what he uses in film production. After Johnson promoted Chromagraph Camera on social media in late October, it quickly became the top paid download in the iOS store. The app costs a one-time fee of $13 and only shoots still photos. (There’s no video support yet.)
I am far from the resident photography nerd on WIRED’s gear team. (That award goes, in part, to my wonderful editor, Julian.) I’m often just whipping out my iPhone and snapping a picture with the default settings. Even so, I really enjoyed capturing some of San Francisco’s fall vibes using the Chromagraph Camera. Although Apple gives iPhone owners plenty of built-in tools for adjusting the color on your own images, I loved this app’s ability to capture highly stylized shots without me needing to fiddle with anything at all.
When you open the app, what you see in the viewfinder before snapping the shot is not what the Chromagraph Camera will spit out. The photo is essentially “developed” in the app after you capture the image. This is because the app needs a moment to run its unique processing for the specific tone, color, and grain effects. You can also alter how an image looks in the app after it’s processed, if you want to tweak the overall exposure or texture of an image.
Yedlin is adamant that he’s not attempting to replace your iPhone camera app or release a professional tool for editing everything. It’s all about that color, man. “It's just this curated app that takes the pictures the way we like,” he says. Yedlin and Johnson teamed up with programmer Eric Cameron to build the app centered around their color tastes, experimenting with it for a couple of months before launch.
Even after all of this custom image processing, Yedlin still sees the iPhone as a fundamentally limited device. “This idea that you can actually have the control that a professional camera would have is not really true anyhow,” he says. Software can only do so much to change how hardware works, especially when developing an app within Apple’s parameters that limit how far the software can push the phone’s hardware.
As advances in computational photography and generative AI have renewed discussions about what a smartphone photo even is anymore, Yedlin’s approach isn't an attempt to find a sense of neutrality. He doesn’t see any image as a literal rendering of what exists. It’s always an interpretation, whether that's a stylized, artful depiction or a more stagnant shot. He says that the look of the Chromagraph Camera app is consciously “opinionated” and specific.
“You can describe how the different rendering looks in words, but you just have to look at it,” he says. The color speaks for itself.

A mock-up of an astronaut on a spacewalk welcomes visitors into "At Home in Space," the last of the space-themed galleries to open at the renovated National Air and Space Museum.
Credit:
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
After seven years of work and nearly $1 billion, the Smithsonian has completed the renovation of the National Air and Space Museum’s flagship building in Washington, DC.
On October 30, the museum debuted its last-to-open spaceflight exhibition, returning “home” with a gallery devoted to establishing a spacefaring civilization.
“Welcome to ‘At Home in Space’!” said curator Jennifer Levasseur, who guided us through a virtual tour of the gallery. “This is the story of long-duration spaceflight in the last few decades. We generally call it ‘reaching orbit.’”
“It’s the prep story, the space shuttle story. It’s what allows us to end up at a place where we have 25-plus years of long-duration spaceflight experience, the capacity for humans to be living in space on the International Space Station (ISS), and then it carries that story forward. So the middle of our story then becomes the ISS, and the end of the story are the next steps,” said Levasseur.
“At Home in Space” takes visitors on a 50-plus-year journey of learning how humans can live and work in space continuously and venture beyond Earth orbit.
Credit:
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
“At Home in Space” takes visitors on a 50-plus-year journey of learning how humans can live and work in space continuously and venture beyond Earth orbit.
Credit:
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
Entering “At Home”
Over the past several years, the National Air and Space Museum has introduced new galleries showcasing how US astronauts first entered space and landed on the Moon (“Destination Moon”); how robotic probes have explored every planet in our solar system (“Kenneth C. Griffin Exploring the Planets”); how technologies and infrastructure impact our daily lives (“RTX Living in the Space Age Hall”) and what approaches spaceflight will take in the years to come (“Futures in Space”).
“At Home in Space,” which follows the similarly themed “Moving Beyond Earth,” immerses guests in the equipment, spacecraft, and orbital platforms that have enabled humanity from simply visiting space to living there, setting up the near future for bases on the Moon and Mars.
“We have a great way to attract people into the gallery, which is this overhead mock-up of an astronaut on the end of the robotic arm, and then the backdrop to that is this photo mural—a full-size photo print—of the ISS,” said Levasseur. “Our astronaut up here is intended to be [an actual] person, but I’m not going to share who that is. They are wearing an Expedition 60 patch, so that’ll give you a little clue.”
Outer space outfits
Some of the gallery’s artifacts include a space shuttle main engine, Robonaut 1A (a prototype humanoid robot), and an extravehicular mobility unit (EMU) spacesuit.
“It’s pretty damn special,” said Levasseur of the EMU. “This, as far as I know, is the first and potentially only public display of a fully flown set of EMU equipment in the world. I know NASA has one in its EVA office, but it is not on public display.”
NASA astronaut Chris Williams and curator Jennifer Levasseur view the only fully flown extravehicular mobility unit spacesuit on public display in “At Home in Space.”
Credit:
NASA/Aubrey Gemignani
NASA astronaut Chris Williams and curator Jennifer Levasseur view the only fully flown extravehicular mobility unit spacesuit on public display in “At Home in Space.”
Credit:
NASA/Aubrey Gemignani
Unlike Apollo-era spacesuits sized to each astronaut, the EMU was designed to be reused, so its components can be swapped out to fit astronauts of different sizes. Introduced during the early years of the space shuttle program, the same EMU suits are still used on the International Space Station for US spacewalks.
The museum’s example is only missing a functioning portable life support system (PLSS), as all the backpacks are still needed for use. So the suit on display only has a PLSS shell for now, according to Levasseur.
The gallery also features Guy Bluford’s and Sally Ride’s in-flight suits, the “shirt-sleeve” outfits the first African American and first US woman wore on the space shuttle (on separate missions).
“Sally is notably missing her jacket, which was a late change to our plan. We were given a drawing of this, a 3D mockup of its display case, and our designers then put it in this way without the jacket on. And we thought, ‘Hey, that’s actually kind of a nice contrast. Let’s keep the jacket out,’” Levasseur told collectSPACE.
Flight clothes worn by the first African American astronaut, Guion “Guy” Bluford, and the first US woman, Sally Ride, on board the space shuttle, as on display in “At Home in Space.”
Credit:
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
Flight clothes worn by the first African American astronaut, Guion “Guy” Bluford, and the first US woman, Sally Ride, on board the space shuttle, as on display in “At Home in Space.”
Credit:
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
The gallery also includes recovered components from the Challenger and Columbia tragedies. It is only the second public display of fallen orbiter debris after a Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex exhibit that opened in Florida in 2015.
“We wanted to honor the individuals who were lost during the shuttle program,” said Levasseur. “So we have an elevon hinge from Challenger that washed up on the beach a few years ago and a little wiring panel fragment from inside the payload bay. And then from Columbia we thought it was appropriate to help tell that story with a piece of RCC [reinforced carbon-carbon]. This is a T-panel from the starboard wing. We also have a CD [compact disc] on a long-term loan from David Brown’s family.”
Inside ISS
Visitors can also walk through a full-size mock-up of the space station’s Destiny module, the US national laboratory on the station, and view its equipment on both sides, as well as above and below.
“Originally, the detailing on the floor was going to be a mosaic of real images, but we found that for accessibility reasons people might come in and see the cables and worry that they were real, creating a tripping hazard,” said Levasseur. “On the flip side, and I had to fight to get these, we had to have labels to indicate activity happens on the floor and happens on the overhead. People need to see this is a literally three-dimensional space.”
The module has interactive elements on one side and showcases some of the crew equipment-related artifacts, including coffee cups engineered for use in microgravity.
Visitors to “At Home in Space” at the National Air and Space Museum can walk through a full-scale mockup of the International Space Station’s US Destiny laboratory, the US National Laboratory, which includes interactive elements and artifact displays.
Credit:
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
Visitors to “At Home in Space” at the National Air and Space Museum can walk through a full-scale mockup of the International Space Station’s US Destiny laboratory, the US National Laboratory, which includes interactive elements and artifact displays.
Credit:
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
“This is probably the best section in my mind because it has fun stuff,” said Levasseur, pointing out the flown miniPCR biotech toolkit and MinION portable device used to sequence DNA in space for the first time.
“My absolute favorite thing to work on in this gallery answers the questions: What does space smell like, and what does the ISS smell like? We have little scent oils inside each of these that allow people to smell them,” she said.
Nearby, the first 3D printer used in space is also on display. In 2014, Made In Space (now part of Redwire) and NASA flew the printer, which produced hundreds of objects, from astronaut tools to space station repair parts.
Awaiting Artemis
The gallery concludes with a space reserved to exhibit the Artemis I capsule, the spacecraft that flew without astronauts to the Moon in 2022. A Lockheed Martin scale model of Orion holds the place until NASA delivers the real spacecraft to the Smithsonian, which is expected later this year.
“This is the piece of Wright Flyer fabric that went to the moon with Artemis II, so that’s on display here, too,” Levasseur said, concluding the tour.
“At Home in Space” displays a scale model of the Orion spacecraft as a placeholder for Artemis I that flew to the moon.
Credit:
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
“At Home in Space” displays a scale model of the Orion spacecraft as a placeholder for Artemis I that flew to the moon.
Credit:
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
The renovation of the National Air and Space Museum also included refacing the exterior cladding, replacing mechanical systems, and other improvements. The first half of the museum reopened in 2022 with eight new or reimagined galleries, the Northrop Grumman Planetarium, museum store, and the Mars Café. The second phase opened in 2025 with five new galleries, and five additional galleries opened July 1.
Following “At Home in Space,” “Modern Military Aviation” will open on November 11.
“We are thrilled to complete the most extensive project the museum has ever undergone,” Chris Browne, John and Adrienne Mars Director of the museum, said in a statement. “With the opening of these last two galleries, the public will once again be able to visit the entirety of the museum and learn from and engage with the nation’s world-class aerospace collection.”
Admission to all of the National Air and Space Museum galleries remains free, but timed-entry passes for the building are required to visit.
Robert Pearlman is a space historian, journalist and the founder and editor of collectSPACE, a daily news publication and online community focused on where space exploration intersects with pop culture. He is also a contributing writer for Space.com and co-author of "Space Stations: The Art, Science, and Reality of Working in Space” published by Smithsonian Books in 2018. He is on the leadership board for For All Moonkind and is a member of the American Astronautical Society's history committee.

Wage protests force hundreds of Bangladesh garment factories to close
- Published
Hundreds of garment factories in Bangladesh have been forced to closed after days-long protests by workers demanding higher wages.
On Sunday, protests in the capital Dhaka turned violent with protesters blocking roads, vandalising factories and setting vehicles on fire. They also clashed with police, who fired tear gas to disperse them. Police later said that dozens of protesters had been arrested.
Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($242; £180), more than double the current standard, citing rising costs of living.
Bangladesh's textile industry employs around four million workers and manufactures garments for major global brands including H&M, Primark and Uniqlo.
There are fears in the industry that the prolonged unrest could disrupt production and affect international buyers, state news agency BSS reported.
The garment industry generates nearly $40bn every year for Bangladesh, accounting for around 10% of its GDP.
The South Asian nation is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China - but its workers are among the lowest-paid in the world, taking home around 13,000 taka ($105; £78) a month.
"We want the government to accept our demands and increase our wages. [And] they need to instruct landlords and homeowners not to raise rent and ensure that the prices of essential commodities remain affordable," one female worker told BBC Bangla.
"Food prices, cooking gas and electricity bills have all gone up," Mamun, a 28-year-old factory worker, told AFP. "The government must either bring down the prices of essential commodities or raise our wages."
The government announced on Sunday that it had established a board to review workers' wages, and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman held an emergency meeting with ministers to address the unrest.
But demonstrations continued on Monday in Dhaka and nearby manufacturing hubs including Ashulia, Gazipur and Narayanganj.
Around 670 factories suspended operations on Monday, according to reports by Reuters and AFP, and hundreds in these areas will remain shut on Tuesday.
At least 29 protesters were arrested as of Monday, according to Dhaka police Deputy Commissioner Mohidul Islam, who said that those who created an "unstable environment in the garment factories" would come under the law.
Authorities have accused the Awami League, the banned political party of former leader Sheikh Hasina, for taking advantage of the protest movement to instigate violence - though they did not provide any evidence of this.
Home minister Salahuddin Ahmed threatened punitive action against protesters who were trying to "destabilise the country" "under the guise of labour protests".
Babul Akhter, a workers' representative on the wage board, urged protesters to go back to work on Monday, promising to "fight for [their] fair wages".
"I tell my fellow workers, return to work. Don't give in to anyone's incitement."

He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
- Published
Even before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.
The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.
One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.
This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.
On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lèse majesté law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.
This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending.
"To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."
The past six years have seen the most extensive use of lèse majesté in Thai history, in response to unprecedented student protests in 2020 which for the first time called for a public discussion of the role of the monarchy. Two hundred and ninety-four people, including 20 under the age of 18, have been prosecuted, receiving prison sentences of up to 50 years. Dozens of them are still on trial.
Most of those charged under this law are denied bail and kept in jail, even though their court cases can last several years. The standard defence of the law given by Thai officials is that it "reflects the culture and history of Thailand, where the monarchy is one of the main pillars of the nation, highly revered by the majority of Thai people".
Article 112 of the Thai criminal code simply reads, "Whoever defames, insults or threatens the King, the Queen, the Heir-apparent or the Regent, shall be punished with imprisonment of three to 15 years."
In practice, though, the law has been interpreted to cover a much wider range of comment about the monarchy, and a much wider range of figures. Saying anything negative about any member of the royal family, about the institution of the monarchy, even about long deceased kings, or in one case, the king's dog, has resulted in prosecutions.
"If you ask me what the text of the law says, I can tell you," says Akarachai Chaimaneekarakate, assistant director of Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, which helps defend those accused of breaking it. "If you ask me how the courts interpret the words "defame" or "insult", I don't think I can give you a definition, because it's so ambiguous, it's so vague. Even questioning the law itself, for example, can constitute lèse majesté under Section 112."
From his cell in the Bangkok Remand Prison, where he has been for the last three years, Arnon has been writing to his young daughter and son.
"Dear Pran and Karl, my beloved children," one of his letters reads, "The winter wind has not only brought us cool weather, but also brings back stories from the past. I miss the time we travelled outside Bangkok that first winter after Karl came into this world. It was such a magical time for me. I shall miss it every winter I spend here until I regain my freedom."
Hearings like the one Arnon attended weeks before Friday's verdict are the only times he has seen Karl since he was a baby.
Karl is shy at first, but soon he's happy to be picked up and shown off to the other prisoners. His 10-year-old sister Pran sometimes visits their father in prison, and often draws and paints him.
But Arnon and Lookwa, his partner, think Karl is too young to visit. For now, Karl thinks the court is just where his dad works. A group of supporters has come too, filling the little courtroom. They mingle cheerfully with the prisoners, laughing and exchanging gossip before the judges walk in to start the hearing. It is an improbably informal setting for men facing one of the most feared charges in Thailand.
The effect of the law has been to smother any public discussion about the monarchy. Until six years ago, opinions on it were only ever whispered in private. In one notorious case a taxi driver was jailed because a passenger reported what he had said while riding in his cab.
That changed on 3 August 2020.
That year younger Thais had become increasingly frustrated with the conservative government led by coup-leader Gen Prayuth Chan-ocha. The year before millions had given their votes to a new party, Future Forward, which promised sweeping reforms, but in February 2020, the Constitutional Court dissolved the party on a technicality. The arrival of the Covid pandemic prevented any protests for three months, but as infections in Thailand started to fall, students began holding rallies calling for an end to the military's role in politics. Arnon Nampa argued this did not go far enough.
In the garb of Harry Potter, he gave a speech saying it was time to talk about the opaque power and wealth of the monarchy. He criticised King Vajiralongkorn's decision to take personal control of the vast assets held by the Crown Property Bureau, and over important units of the army.
In a single speech Arnon shattered a taboo which had hung over Thai society for the whole of its modern history. For the rest of that year the student-led protests continued, with increasingly bold demands for changes to the monarchy.
At the time, the use of the lèse majesté law had been suspended for three years. Sources close to the palace have in the past acknowledged that the negative publicity generated by lèse majesté convictions might do more harm than good.
But the protests forced a hasty reassessment. From the end of 2020 prosecutions under the law restarted and accelerated. Dozens of young activists have fled into exile to avoid being jailed.
One of them is Supitcha "Melinn" Chailom. The 24-year-old from Chiang Mai in northern Thailand lives in Montreal, a fugitive from four 112 charges which have been filed against her.
She was an 18-year-old school girl when she stood up and made a speech at a protest in Chiang Mai University, just three weeks after Arnon Nampa's call for reform of the monarchy.
A local photographer captured the moment she raised her hand in the three-finger Hunger Games salute, eliciting loud cheers from the crowd. It became one of the defining images of the protests, and propelled Melinn to nationwide fame.
She travelled up and down the country as one of the leading voices in the movement, demanding changes to Thailand's old-fashioned education system, conducting polls on what people thought of the monarchy.
"I love playing games, and I dreamed of being a game designer," she told me from Canada. But her parents did not approve.
"I felt that, as a young person, I could not question, or have a discussion with people older than me. The monarchy gave me the same vibe."
In November 2020 Melinn joined a protest in the southern city of Hat Yai, where she gave a speech comparing the royal treatment given to the king's dog with that of ordinary people. Nine months later the police delivered a summons to her home charging her with lèse majesté.
"It was a shock. I wasn't expecting it because I only talked about the dog. It was during Covid when the police came to my home with the summons, so they knew my parents would be there with me. They tried to stay calm, but I nearly lost my mind."
Her family tried to persuade her to co-operate with the authorities, to admit her wrongdoing. But Melinn refused.
She joined a movement calling itself Thalu Wang, which translates as "breaking through the palace". Instead of giving speeches, they came up with stunts like holding polls on the street, asking people what they thought of royal motorcades holding up the traffic, or whether they believed the monarchy had too much power.
"We knew the risks, but we thought it would be safer just conducting a poll. It turns out it was not."
She was given two more lèse majesté charges in 2022, and detained before being released on bail. She had to wear an electronic monitor on her ankle and was barred from leaving her home between 4pm and 6am. Her parents were forced to sign a document promising to inform on her. She was facing decades in jail.
Melinn decided she had no choice. With a friend she fled Thailand and eventually got asylum in Canada.
Article 112 is on paper just a law, like any other, passed by the Thai parliament, which can, theoretically, be amended by elected MPs. In fact it has been amended in the past, notably in 1976 when the punishment for breaking it was increased to between three and 15 years in prison.
But today the Constitutional Court has decreed that the law itself, like the institution it protects, is untouchable. The reformist Move Forward party - the successor of Future Forward - was dissolved in 2024, and its leader banned from politics, merely for proposing that the punishments be less harsh. And the courts make it very difficult for those charged under it to defend themselves.
"In many cases, like the one against Arnon Nampa, prosecutors accuse the defendant of lying about the monarchy," says Chaimaneekarakate, the lawyer. "But when we ask the judge to subpoena documents or witnesses who could show the truth of what the defendant says, the judge refuses to do it. When one lawyer protested against the court deciding that the trial would be held in secret, she was warned by the judge to be quiet or face a contempt of court charge."
He says judges sometimes criticise the young activists over their alleged actions even before the trial has started.
As the one who ignited the debate about the monarchy Arnon appears to be getting the harshest punishment. Despite the formidable odds stacked against him he still prepares carefully for every court appearance, taking part in his own defence and helping other inmates with theirs.
This isn't easy; he is not allowed to bring any of his written notes, and must memorise all his arguments.
The judges object to him playing the part of a lawyer in his regulation-brown prison shorts, his feet bare and shackled. But it does give him an opportunity to see his family.
The letters he writes are the only other way he stays in touch with them. He may spend his entire life in prison. He wants his children to know him, and to understand, when they are older, why he chose to challenge the system and lose his freedom.
"Since the first day that we made up our mind to take up this mission, we knew of the dangers. Speaking the truth is not difficult. What is difficult is speaking a forbidden truth. I remember well that on the evening of 3 August 2020, after speaking at the Harry Potter event, I felt very good, content, and relieved to have finally begun speaking about the truth, in public," he wrote to his family last year.
Earlier this year, he wrote: "Living here is a struggle. But it is just a dot in the bigger picture of our movement's struggle. We must play a part in writing our own history. Become a drop of water that will one day become an ocean."

Fireside Ventures’ cofounder and partner Vinay Singh is stepping down from the investment firm after a nearly decade-long stint. In a statement, the venture capital (VC) firm said that Singh would “transition out of the firm”. The consumer-focused fund has so far not named his successor. On his future course of action, Singh said that he now plans to explore the “frontiers of agentic commerce and its implications for the future of consumption”. “... As AI reshapes commerce faster than most of us expected, I want to spend more time exploring the frontiers of agentic commerce and its implications for the future of consumption. I am excited for this next chapter, and deeply grateful to the Fireside family, and to every founder and LP (limited partner) who trusted us on this journey,” said Singh. An alumnus of IIM Bangalore, Singh counts nearly two decades of experience under his belt. He previously worked at companies like Hindustan Unilever and Bankbazaar. He earlier also cofounded car servicing platform Stepni, which was later acquired by Quikr. He eventually cofounded Fireside Ventures alongside Kanwaljit Singh, Kannan Sitaram and Dipanjan Basu in 2017. Over the past decade, the VC firm has emerged as one of India’s biggest consumer-focused venture funds and counts more than 65 startups in its portfolio. It currently claims to oversee more than $650 Mn in assets under management across four funds. The VC firm last closed its fourth fund at about $253 Mn in December last year. The investment firm currently claims to be helmed by a team of 12 principals and vice presidents. The development comes as a host of seasoned fund managers depart major VC firms to set up their own funds. Earlier this year, Ashish Agrawal, Ishaan Mittal and Tejeshwi Sharma quit Peak XV Partners to establish their own fund, Mettle Capital. Private equity (PE) firm L Catterton’s partner and co-head of India investments, Anjana Sasidharan, also stepped down from the company in March this year to set up Asthrum Capital. Another former Peak XV trio, comprising Shailesh Lakhani, Harshjit Sethi and Mayank Porwal, has launched Ambition Capital and is looking to raise $250 Mn for the maiden fund.

Bengaluru-based wealthtech startup PowerUp Money has raised $10 Mn (₹95 Cr) in a fresh funding round led by Flourish Ventures, with participation from existing investors Peak XV Partners, Accel, Blume Ventures, Kae Capital, 8i Ventures and DeVC. The startup plans to use the capital to expand its AI-led wealth management offerings, scale its managed advisory business and develop personalised financial planning solutions for Indian investors. “We started by making high-quality investment advice accessible to every Indian. A video of Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows him in an intoxicated state. In the video, Mann is seen sitting on a chair in a hall, making noises and appearing to hoot. Social media users have mocked and criticised Mann and the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP)-led government in Punjab. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann in an intoxicated state.
Fact: The video is AI-generated and does not show Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann in an intoxicated state. It was created using a 2017 video featuring a different individual making the same gestures and utterances in an identical setting, with AI tools used to replace the person with a lookalike of Mann. AI detection tools, including Hive Moderation and NVIDIA’s Synthetic Video Detector, also flagged the viral footage as synthetic media. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
Upon closely examining the viral video, we noticed several visual inconsistencies that raised doubts about its authenticity. For instance, the hands of the person standing behind Mann appear distorted at one point in the video. Additionally, the people in the background appear unusually blurred and lack clear visual definition. These visual anomalies suggest that the video may have been AI-generated.
To further verify the video’s authenticity, we analysed it using multiple AI detection tools. Hive Moderation’s AI-generated content detector gave an aggregate score of 81.8%, indicating that the media likely contained AI-generated or deepfake content. Similarly, NVIDIA’s Synthetic Video Detector classified the footage as synthetic media.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple social media posts (here, here, here, and here) from 2017 featuring the same visuals. In the original video, a different individual can be seen seated in the same manner as Mann in the viral clip, making identical gestures and utterances. We also observed that the positions of people in the background and other elements of the setting are identical in both videos. This suggests that the viral clip may have been created using the 2017 video as a reference, with AI tools used to generate a version featuring a person resembling Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann.
The person seen in the original video is Jassi Deol, whose video went viral in 2017. An interview with Jassi Deol can be seen below.
To sum up, this viral video showing Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann in an intoxicated state is a deepfake.

How infant deaths in Keralam’s Attappady expose a deep-rooted health, social crisis
12 infants, including 10 tribals, have died in Attappady this year, sparking a political row as the State government orders an expert probe. Tribal activists say the crisis demands action beyond healthcare, addressing malnutrition, anaemia and deep-rooted social issues
Published - October 31, 2026 01:25 pm IST - PALAKKAD
In Attappady, maternal health remains a major concern. Anaemia among pregnant women continues to be widespread, while underweight mothers and low birth weight among newborns add to the risks (file image)
| Photo Credit: The Hindu
The deaths of 12 infants, 10 of them from tribal communities, in Attappady in Keralam in recent months have once again cast a spotlight on a child health crisis that has defied solutions for over a decade. While the State government has set an expert assessment in motion, tribal organisations maintain that the roots of the crisis run deeper than healthcare, demanding sustained action on nutrition, maternal health, landlessness and the wider socio-economic conditions of the community.
Figures cited by tribal activists show that 124 infants have died in the region since 2011. Since 2012, Attappady has also recorded around 300 abortions, 90 intrauterine deaths and two dozen stillbirths. The region came under particular scrutiny in 2013, when 47 tribal infants died. Tribal observers estimate that around 10 children have died annually over the years.

New Delhi: The Union health ministry has proposed making pharmaceutical companies formally designate a qualified person to authorise the release of every batch of drugs into the market, tightening accountability for drug quality, the government said on Tuesday. Under the draft amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, every drugmaker will have to appoint an expert specifically responsible for batch release. Companies will also be required to issue a “Batch Release Certificate” in a prescribed format and keep records for every lot produced. At present, drugmakers are required to declare the technical personnel overseeing manufacturing and testing, but there is no specific provision for identifying the individual authorised to release a batch for sale, the ministry said. Mint first reported on the government’s plan to tighten these norms in February 2025. According to the health ministry, batch release is a critical stage in the pharmaceutical manufacturing process, involving an overall review of the relevant quality parameters and documentation before a batch is released for distribution. The health ministry added that the proposed amendments are expected to support manufacturers in strengthening their compliance with applicable good manufacturing practices (GMP) and reinforce the regulatory framework governing the quality assurance of drugs. "The proposed amendments aim to strengthen accountability in the drug manufacturing process by introducing an explicit regulatory requirement for the authorisation of personnel responsible for batch release,” the health ministry stated. Under the revised structure, “applicants seeking manufacturing licences under the relevant provisions of the Drugs Rules, 1945, would be required to designate a suitably qualified and experienced person for batch release and maintain batch-release records in accordance with the prescribed requirements.” “The proposed requirements are intended to establish clear responsibility for this function, ensure traceability of batch-release decisions and provide an additional level of oversight of product quality,” the statement said. The development assumes significance for India's $60-billion pharmaceutical industry amid concerns over the quality of drugs manufactured in the country. The drug regulator has stepped up risk-based inspections of domestic pharmaceutical units following cases involving contaminated cough syrups manufactured in India that were linked to the deaths of children in Gambia and Uzbekistan in 2022 and 2023. Last year, contaminated medicines also led to the deaths of at least 24 children in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, respectively. The government has invited objections and suggestions on the draft amendments within 30 days to finalize the regulations. Priyanka Sharma is a journalist at Mint, where she covers the Union Ministry of Health and the pharmaceutical industry. Her work focuses on explaining government policies and how they impact healthcare and the medicine market in India. With 12 years of experience in journalism, she has built a reputation for providing clear and honest news on important health topics that affect the entire country.

Her educational background includes a journalism degree from the prestigious Indian Institute of Mass Communication (IIMC) and specialized training in public health from the Public Health Foundation of India. Before her current role at Mint, Priyanka worked with India Today, The Pioneer, and ANI. She also served as a lead consultant for the National Health Authority, which gave her firsthand knowledge of how the government manages large-scale health programmes.

Nearly 2 out of 3 teens and tweens use AI chatbots, new research shows
Artificial intelligence chatbots are increasingly becoming a regular part of life for American youth. Two new surveys show that nearly two-thirds of tweens and teens use AI chatbots. While most kids use the technology for help with school work, and for companionship and emotional support, certain uses were linked with worse mental health symptoms.
One survey, done by the online safety advocacy group, Common Sense Media, found that AI use starts early – years before kids hit the minimum age of 13 on most popular chatbots. Nearly half 9-to-12-year-olds have used an AI chatbot or companion. By the time kids are 13 years old, nearly three-quarters of them have used chatbots.
The other survey, done by the mental health advocacy group JED Foundation, found that 90% of the 5,500 9-to-17-year-olds in schools across the country have used an AI chatbot. Nearly two-thirds use it both for schoolwork and as companions, or when they are stressed, lonely, anxious or overwhelmed.
The findings are "remarkable" in showing how dramatically AI use by children and teens has changed in a short time, says developmental psychologist Anne Maheux at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, who wasn't involved in the surveys.
"It seems like just a few years ago, no one was using" the technology, she says. "And now it seems like roughly the same number of kids using it for homework are using it to get emotional support or help with coping."
"I use it to make myself practice sample questions – sample test questions that I will answer with my own work," says 15-year-old Arjun Sharda, in Round Rock, Texas. "I use it to understand concepts outside of the classroom."
He uses both OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini, he says, although he prefers the latter lately.
In Raynham, Mass., McKenzie Craig, 17, has been using chatbots since she was in eighth grade. "I use it typically if I'm overwhelmed with a bunch of tasks I have," she says. "I'll have it help me prioritize the tasks."
She also uses it for help with assignments. "If I write an essay, I'll run it through either Grammarly or ChatGPT and have it graded, so to speak," says Craig. "It gives me feedback, and then I can edit accordingly."
Sharda says he and his friends also turn to chatbots when they are stressed and anxious.
"With tests, for example," he says, "I was so scared of failing one of my first chemistry tests on conversions and moles that I kept asking ChatGPT 'Will I be OK? Will my GPA still be fine?'"
Some chatbot uses are linked to worse mental health
Researchers at the JED Foundation also surveyed students on symptoms of overall well-being and mental health.
"We were able to look at how young people are using AI and then how that correlates separately with indicators of well-being, history of suicidal ideation and attempts, and poor mental health," says psychologist Kayla Anderson, vice president of research and evaluation at the JED Foundation.
"When young people are using AI, when they're in emotional distress," she adds, "they're more likely to report poor mental health and well-being outcomes." They also report a greater history of suicidal thoughts and attempts.
But the data don't suggest a causal link, cautions Anderson.
"It's unclear, based on these data, whether AI use is contributing to poor mental health and well-being, or whether students who are already in distress in certain ways are more likely to turn to AI," she explains.
But preliminary data collected by other researchers suggests that the link between chatbots and poorer mental health symptoms in young people might go both ways, says Maheux.
"So kids who do have worse mental health are seeking out AI to help them," she says. "But that AI use may be exacerbating those mental health challenges instead of helping."
In a soon-to-be-published study of middle schoolers in one state, Maheux and her colleagues at UNC found that students who use chatbots for companionship grew lonelier over time.
They found similar results in another study of young adults. "We see that people who are using AI more for companionship or feeling like they're overreliant on AI to solve various emotional or cognitive problems, are developing worse mental health over time."
One potential explanation for this effect, she says, is that AI is easing people's emotional distress — loneliness, anxiety, stress — in the immediate moment, but that reliance on the technology is preventing young people from developing the skills to tolerate and navigate normal daily stresses.
That, she explains, "can lead to worse mental health."

Legal challenge to Australia's social media ban to start in High Court
- Published
Two days of hearings on a challenge to Australia's landmark social media ban for children will begin at the country's highest court on Tuesday.
In a major test of the world-leading policy, a digital rights group will argue that the ban for under-16s robs children of their right to free communication. A separate challenge launched by platform Reddit will be jointly heard.
Introduced last December, the ban is a key part of sweeping changes the Australian government has spearheaded in recent years on online safety.
Supporters say the ban protects children from harmful content but critics say it is too blunt an instrument and efforts should focus on improving online safety.
The constitutional challenge in Australia's High Court was filed by the Digital Freedom Project a few weeks before the ban started on 10 December last year. The group is lead by New South Wales parliamentarian John Ruddick.
Two teens who originally spearheaded the case, Noah Jones and Macy Neyland, have since withdrawn as plaintiffs though Jones is still expected to attend Tuesday's hearing.
Speaking about the legal challenge last November, Jones told the BBC that there were bad things online but a blanket ban for under-16s was not the right answer.
"We shouldn't be using the resources and money of these social media platforms to try to avoid fines from our government," he said.
"They should be using this money and resources to try to get rid of the predators and harmful content out there."
Reddit also launched a High Court challenge to the ban, arguing the policy has serious implications for privacy and political rights.
The company said it shared Australia's goal of protecting young people online "but there are better and more effective ways" than a ban.
"As we challenge this law in court, we'll continue to comply with it and advocate for more effective youth safety measures," said Reddit's chief communications officer Adam Collins.
Communications Minister Anika Wells last year said the government would not be "intimidated by legal threats."
"We will not be intimidated by big tech. On behalf of Australian parents, we will stand firm," she said last November.
Under the ban, ten platforms - Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, Snapchat, X, Kick, Threads and Twitch - must take "reasonable steps" to ensure no one under 16 years old can access its site.
Platforms risk fines of up to A$99m (US$70m, £52m) for serious or repeated breaches, but since the ban started, no company has been fined.
The eSafety Commissioner - the body tasked with enforcing the ban - has launched several investigations into alleged non-compliance by Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube.
WhatsApp and online gaming sites like Roblox and Discord were not included in the ban, nor were educational platforms like YouTube Kids and Google Classroom.
In the first few days of the ban, Meta - which owns three of the banned platforms - said it had closed about half a million accounts.
Some children said they were booted off their accounts in the days before and when the ban started - but many have said they were able to easily circumvent the age checks which included uploading credit card details, photo IDs or a selfie.

Greenland approves security deal with Denmark and US
Greenlandic lawmakers have approved an agreement with Denmark and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic
ILULISSAT, Greenland -- ILULISSAT, Greenland (AP) — Greenlandic lawmakers on Tuesday voted to approve an agreement between the Arctic island, Denmark and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic after months of pressure by U.S. President Donald Trump seeking to control the semiautonomous territory of a NATO ally.
The trilateral deal paves the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and eases tensions over Trump's repeated calls for the vast island to become part of the United States. The agreement's goal is to bolster the U.S. military presence on Greenland but keep the self-governing island under Danish control. It would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.
Greenlandic lawmakers voted 16-0 for the agreement, with seven abstentions.
Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed the agreement in September on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York.
Danish lawmakers are set to debate it later this month. The deal will “enter into force” once the “necessary parliamentary processes of the Kingdom of Denmark, in conjunction with Greenland, have been completed.”

NTSB says crucial plane parts found three miles from Florida crash site
- Published
Crucial components of a private jet that crashed in Palm Beach, Florida - including a part that controlled the up-and-down movements of the nose of the plane - were found 1.3 (2 km) to 3.8 miles away from the crash site, an investigator said on Tuesday.
National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigators said they believed parts of the jet may have broken off before the Sunday crash, which killed all nine on board.
The NTSB found "the majority" of the Learjet's left elevator - a control surface on the tail - in three pieces, NTSB board member Tom Chapman said.
Chapman said because the parts were "quite some distance away" from the site, investigators determined they fell off before impact.
"Knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us towards other things to investigate," he said.
Chapman said officials were still working out whether losing the left elevator caused the plane to nosedive or whether the part fell off because "forces on the aircraft caused that to separate".
He said the part of the plane that controls upward and downward movement may not have been "effective" at the speed the plane was travelling.
The Learjet 60 was bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas, when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.
In air traffic control audio recordings, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".
They are then heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.
An emergency was declared and the pilots can be heard yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".
NTSB plans to investigate the role weather played in the crash. Officials were struggling to access the wreckage due to the huge crater created by the jet on a road in Palm Beach.
Chapman said on Tuesday that the force of the impact severely damaged the wreckage.
Seven passengers died on board, named in a joint statement as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - as well as friends of the family Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and Anita Maria Cetina, a nanny.
The pilot was named in media reports as 55-year-old Jeffrey Gregory. Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the co-pilot.

The NFL is America's favorite league, and a New York Giants co-owner says there are ways to keep it growing.
Carolyn Tisch Blodgett, whose family owns a 45% stake in the Giants, said flag football and international games are the two biggest avenues for the NFL to build on its massive audience.
"There just isn't enough room to continue to grow in the US only. You have to be thinking about international growth too," Tisch Blodgett said at Business Insider's The Long Play event.
Tisch Blodgett, who runs sports-focused venture capital firm Next 3 and Gotham FC in the National Women's Soccer League, said that playing games abroad is crucial to the league's long-term success, as it helps build a younger, more diverse audience.
"A sports fan today in 2026 looks different than a sports fan did maybe 100 years ago," Tisch Blodgett said.
NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has made international contests a key cornerstone of his tenure for the last two decades. The league has played games abroad every year since 2007 (except for 2020), going from one game a year in London to nine this season across the globe in places like Melbourne, Rio de Janeiro, Paris, Madrid, Munich, and Mexico City.
Flag football, which will be an Olympic sport in 2028, is another way for the NFL to connect with new fans abroad and in the US, Tisch Blodgett said. That includes girls who may not have the opportunity to play tackle football.
Playing a sport is correlated with fandom, Tisch Blodgett said. She's bullish that kids who try flag football will develop a lifelong affinity for the NFL.
"If we know we need people to be playing to be a fan, we're going to invest in flag so that we continue to grow that fandom," Tisch Blodgett said.
Flag football participation among high school girls surged 49% last year to over 100,000 — making it one of the 10 most popular sports for that demographic, according to a recent survey by the National Federation of State High School Associations. The NFHS said that four years ago, fewer than 16,000 high school girls played flag football, making it the fastest-growing high school sport in the years since.
Tackle-free football leagues are also open to boys whose parents may not want them to risk getting concussions, which have been an area of focus for the NFL in the last decade.
The NFL is investing in flag football, and its efforts include launching Premier Flag — a new pro flag football league that will start next summer.
"As tackle football has declined, they didn't just sit back," Tisch Blodgett said of the NFL.

On 01 November 2026, the INDIA bloc organised a mega rally at Delhi’s Ramlila Maidan to protest alleged electoral irregularities and demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Congress MP Rahul Gandhi led a ‘Chalo Dilli’ march from the Minto Road-Connaught Place junction towards Ramlila Maidan, where the rally witnessed a large gathering of supporters and party workers from several Opposition parties, including the Congress, Samajwadi Party, TMC and RJD (here, here, and here).
Amid this, several videos and Images are being shared on social media (here, here, and here) claiming to show a massive gathering at the INDIA bloc-led rally held at Ramlila Maidan in Delhi on 01 November 2026. Let’s verify the claims made in these posts in this article.
Claim: The visuals show a massive gathering of supporters at the INDIA bloc-led rally held at Ramlila Maidan in Delhi on 01 November 2026.
Fact: The visuals are unrelated to the INDIA bloc-led rally held at Ramlila Maidan on 1 November 2026. Video 1 predates the event and was shared by Congress leaders in connection with the party’s 14 December 2025 ‘Vote Chor, Gaddi Chhod’ rally at the same venue. Video 2 shows celebrations in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on 20 December 2022, following Argentina’s FIFA World Cup victory. The image is AI-generated, as indicated by AI detection tools.Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
During our investigation, we found social media posts dated 14 December 2025 featuring the same video, shared by Congress leaders Deepender Singh Hooda and Harish Rawat. Both posts criticised the Election Commission over allegations of vote theft. This establishes that the video has been circulating online since at least 14 December 2025 and predates the INDIA bloc’s ‘Chalo Dilli’ march held on 01 November 2026.
Notably, the Congress had organised (here, here) a ‘Vote Chor, Gaddi Chhod’ rally at Delhi’s Ramlila Maidan on 14 December 2025, protesting alleged vote theft and demanding accountability from the Election Commission.
Video 2
During our investigation, we found that Factly had previously debunked the same video when it went viral. Our earlier investigation established that the video shows celebrations in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on 20 December 2022, when millions of people gathered to welcome the FIFA World Cup-winning Argentine national football team.
Image 1
Upon examining the viral image, we noticed distorted facial features of Rahul Gandhi and Sonia Gandhi on the posters. Suspecting that the image might have been AI-generated, we analysed it using AI detection tools such as SynthID and AI or Not. Both tools indicated that the viral image was AI-generated.
To sum up, these visuals do not show the INDIA bloc rally held at Ramlila Maidan on 01 November 2026.

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."
