North Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut off from the world’s economic system – but when it comes to generating foreign earnings it relies on some of the world’s most sophisticated hacking.
Experts, such as TRM Labs, quickly attributed the extraordinary $6.3bn (£4.7bn) Binance cryptocurrency theft to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit that has also been known as the Lazarus Group. Though the link may not be proven yet, the pattern of behaviour is familiar.
North Korea has a history of cryptocurrency theft dating back to 2017, focusing on the sector’s relatively lax security controls as a way of stealing money and generating revenues for its military, including its nuclear weapons programme.
Kim Jong-un, its dictatorial ruler, controls a stockpile of about 50 nuclear warheads, and has been supplying troops and weapons to help Russia in its war in Ukraine. But North Korea is also extremely poor: 40% of the population are undernourished according to the UN and nearly one in five of its children are stunted.
A UN panel of experts, reporting to the security council, said in the spring of 2024 that it was reviewing “58 suspected cyber-attacks” by North Korea “on cryptocurrency-related companies between 2017 and 2023” worth $3bn.
The panel said the cash was estimated to generate half of North Korea’s foreign currency income. One unnamed country went further with its estimate: the stolen billions fund “40% of the weapons of mass destruction programmes”.
The suspected crypto hacks amounted to as many as 17 in 2023 alone: thefts valued at $750m, and disturbingly, the sums involved are only increasing. The world’s largest previous crypto hack took place in February 2025, when $1.5bn was stolen from the Bybit exchange – the work, the FBI said, of TraderTraitor.
Ciaran Martin, a former head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, argues that North Korea appears to have targeted crypto because traditional banks have developed sophisticated defences that the fast-growing and lightly regulated sector has yet to match.
“Over the last decade, hackers have walked off with nine- or 10-figure sums from crypto hacks on more than 30 occasions. The number of traditional banks who have suffered a loss of more than $100m as a result of a cyber-attack in the same period is zero or one,” Martin said.
North Korea was behind one of the last large cyber thefts on a traditional bank – an attack on Bangladesh Bank in February 2016, where North Korean hackers tried to illicitly move $951m from an account the bank had with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, taking advantage of time differences between the two.
A piece of luck prevented most of the money from being sent to an intermediate account in the Philippines. The corresponding bank was based on Jupiter Street, which shares its first word with the name of a sanctioned Iranian ship, so most of the transfers were held up. In the end, $81m was stolen.
The isolated state has long been accused of engaging in criminal activities to survive, including the forgery of high-quality $100 bills, known as “supernotes” in the 1990s, and the production and trafficking of crystal meth for export in the 2000s.
The UK has been rarely targeted. In 2019, North Korean hackers did try to take control of cash machines linked to 56 financial institutions to make them pay out sums well in excess of normal. British officials spotted what was afoot, alerted the banks and the hack was quietly suppressed with no media coverage.
The irony is that the internet in North Korea is severely restricted, with access denied to the general population. Maths and science are pushed at school, however, and at university some of the best students are recruited into hacker groups, such as Lazarus, operating under the auspices of the country’s Reconnaissance General Bureau spy agency.
Hacking is closely tied to the all-powerful state. In December 2014, it emerged, to the embarrassment of Sony Pictures, that film stars Jennifer Lawrence and Amy Adams were paid less than their male counterparts in American Hustle. It was one of thousands of embarrassing emails leaked from the Hollywood studio through a hack.
The attack, by North Korea’s Lazarus Group, was conducted because Sony had funded a film, The Interview: a Seth Rogen comedy that depicted the assassination of Kim Jong-un. Amid the chaos of the revelations, Sony tried to cancel the movie, then had to U-turn on its retreat, releasing it online and to a handful of cinemas, after being criticised for caving in to North Korean pressure.

Quick Answer
To optimize WhatsApp privacy, hide your Last Seen, Online status, profile info, and status sharing under Settings > Privacy. Turn off read receipts, silence unknown callers, restrict group invites, disable link previews, and enable disappearing messages, passkeys, two-step verification, biometric locks, and end-to-end encrypted backups.
I don’t need to specifically tell you about WhatsApp’s popularity. It has billions of users worldwide, and it is the go-to messaging app for many people. Thanks to the network effect, most popular messaging apps haven’t replaced WhatsApp, even with better features and privacy.
One of the biggest reasons most people use WhatsApp, besides the fact that their friends or family are already on it, is that it is free to use. And since Meta owns it, free usually comes with a caveat. And that’s your data and how Meta tracks your WhatsApp chats. Although your chats are encrypted and Meta openly says it won’t use your data for advertising, you can talk to a friend on WhatsApp and still see relevant ads on other Meta platforms like Instagram instantly. Don’t you believe me? Just try it once.
Fortunately, WhatsApp also offers various privacy settings to keep your conversations private, prevent scams, and more. In this ultimate guide, we’ll cover all the privacy settings you need to enable on WhatsApp for maximum privacy. This guide includes all the methods, and I update it frequently and make changes if the features or flow change. Bookmark this page and revisit it anytime to keep your WhatsApp privacy settings up to date.
Table of Contents
WhatsApp Privacy Settings You Should Enable
Hide your Last Seen and Online status
If you care about your privacy and don’t want your people to know when you were online and when you last used the app, WhatsApp allows you to hide the last seen and online status completely
By default, WhatsApp shows the exact time when you last used the app and shows users when you are actually using the app
While these two features let others know when you use WhatsApp, they can also be a downside, especially if others are expecting an immediate reply when they see you online
Fortunately, WhatsApp lets you disable your last seen and completely hide your status. It also gives you more flexibility by letting you hide these from specific contacts, from your contacts, or disable them entirely for everyone.
Here is how to hide your last seen and online status on WhatsApp:
Open WhatsApp on your Android or iPhone and tap the You tab in the bottom-right corner, then tap Privacy.
Now scroll down and, under Who can see your personal info, tap Last seen and online. To hide it from everyone, select Nobody. To show it only to my contacts, select My contacts; to show it only to specific contacts, tap My contacts except.
Hide your profile photo, About, and Links from strangers
Like Last Seen and online status, WhatsApp also shows your profile picture and About to contacts. This also applies to contacts you have outside your network.
Fortunately, like Last Seen and Online Status, WhatsApp also lets you hide your profile photo and About info from strangers, specific contacts, or no one.
How to hide your profile and About from strangers
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture in the bottom right corner of the screen, then tap on Privacy, and then tap on the Profile Picture option
Now you can hide your profile picture, About, and links. To hide it from everyone, set it to Nobody.
If you want to share with all your contacts, select My contacts. To share your profile picture only with specific contacts, tap My contacts except and select the contacts you want to hide your profile picture, About, and links from.
Control who can see and reshare your Status
WhatsApp’s status feature is slowly turning into Instagram Stories. You can now also reshare statuses on WhatsApp. However, unlike Last Seen, this feature is disabled by default.
If you accidentally enabled it and don’t want others to share your status, you can turn off sharing in the status privacy settings. From there, you can also turn off Facebook Stories and Instagram Stories to prevent your WhatsApp status from being shared on other platforms.
How to turn off status sharing on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture, and from here tap on the privacy option
Scroll down, tap Status, then turn off Allow sharing and set your status to be visible only to my contacts. You can also remove specific people by setting up exceptions for contacts, or you can share only with specific contacts. From the bottom, also disable Facebook Stories and Instagram Stories to prevent your status from automatically sharing to Facebook and Instagram Stories.
Turn off read receipts
Even if you hide your online status and last seen on WhatsApp, read receipts can still show blue checkmarks when you read their messages. However, if you don’t want them to know you have read their messages and feel pressured to reply instantly, or if you want better privacy and to balance work and personal WhatsApp chats, you can disable read receipts.
Remember, if you disable it, you also cannot see whether they have read your messages. WhatsApp only shows grey ticks even if you read their messages.
Here is how to turn off read receipts on WhatsApp
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture. Scroll down and tap Privacy. Scroll down again and turn off Read Receipts.
Stop strangers from adding you to groups
Another feature that WhatsApp turns on by default is the ability to let your contacts add you to any groups. This includes the number you have temporarily shared with users you don’t know, and once you add it to the group, your number will be shared with everyone in that group, which is a total privacy nightmare.
Fortunately, WhatsApp allows you to stop random people from adding you to groups.
How to stop people from adding you to random groups
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture, then tap on the privacy option
Scroll down and tap on Groups, then select who can add you to groups. However, WhatsApp doesn’t let you set nobody as an option, but you can still do it by selecting My contacts except and selecting all contacts.
Silence calls from unknown numbers
Since WhatsApp primarily requires your phone number to create an account, once your number is exposed, anyone can contact you on WhatsApp. This is why many of us often receive spam business calls.
However, you can silence unknown calls so that you won’t get notified of random spam calls.
How to silence unknown callers on WhatsApp
To do that, open WhatsApp, tap on your profile picture, and tap on the privacy option
Now scroll down, tap on Calls, and enable the Silence unknown callers option
Make new chats disappear automatically
WhatsApp now supports disappearing messages, which deletes chats from both the sender and receiver after a set time. WhatsApp allows you to enable disappearing messages for individual chats or for the entire WhatsApp for up to 90 days
This is especially useful if you don’t want the other person to save your chats.
Since WhatsApp keeps your messages forever even if you delete your own copy, the other person’s phone still has everything.
When you turn on disappearing messages, WhatsApp also prevents the other person from taking a screenshot and reminds you when they try to save a specific chat.
How to enable disappearing messages on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp, tap your profile picture, then tap Privacy. From here, tap on Default message timer and select how many days you want to set for WhatsApp. You can select up to 90 days or even 24 hours.
If you want to turn on disappearing messages for individual chats, open the new chat and tap on the three-dot menu on the top right corner of the screen, select disappearing messages, and select the timer
Keep WhatsApp photos out of your gallery
By default, WhatsApp saves all photos you receive to your media gallery, including sensitive and personal ones. Even if you lock WhatsApp, anyone can see the photos you received by opening your phone gallery. This also uses your data to automatically download them and increases your storage usage.
WhatsApp allows you to turn off automatic media download and also lets you stop showing media directly from your photos app
How to stop WhatsApp from automatically saving media
First, you can turn off automatic media downloads. To do that, open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner, then scroll down and tap Storage and data.
From there, scroll down and tap Media auto-download, then select all three: when you are using mobile data, when you are connected to Wi-Fi, and when roaming. Then disable all download options, including photos, audio, video, and documents. This prevents files from auto-downloading on Wi-Fi, mobile data, or while roaming.
How to stop WhatsApp from showing media in your device gallery
Open WhatsApp, tap your profile picture, scroll down, tap Chats, then under Chat settings, disable Media visibility.
Turn on two-step verification with a password
WhatsApp also supports two-step verification to prevent your account from getting hacked. While WhatsApp sends a six-digit SMS code for verification, someone with access to that code can log in to your WhatsApp account. However, you can set a second verification method, such as a password, to prevent anyone from accessing your WhatsApp.
Here is how having two-factor authentication adds better security for your WhatsApp account.
Here is how to set two-step verification with a password on WhatsApp
First, open your profile picture in the bottom right corner of the screen, tap on account option, and tap on Password
Now create a new password. Tap Create password and create a new password.
Once you add two-factor authentication, remember to add a recovery email. This is especially useful if you lose your network; your email acts as a secondary verification method, where WhatsApp sends a code to your email instead of sending a verification SMS.
Create a passkey for phishing-proof login
WhatsApp also added support for passkeys; if you’re not sure what a passkey is, we have explained it in a detailed guide.
Passkeys use your fingerprint or Face ID for authentication instead of depending on SMS or passwords. Setting up passkeys lets you log in to your WhatsApp account using your device ID, which is unique to you.
But it also comes with downsides: if someone else has registered a Face ID or fingerprint, they can also log in to your WhatsApp account, so keep note of it.
How to enable passkeys for your WhatsApp account
To enable passkeys, open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner, then tap Account. From here, under the Login and Security section, tap on Passkeys. Then follow the on-screen instructions to create a passkey.
Turn on security notifications
Next, enable security notifications on your WhatsApp account so WhatsApp notifies you if someone switches phones, reinstalls WhatsApp, or changes linked devices. This could also mean someone else accessed their WhatsApp account and signed in on a new device. Turn on security notifications and confirm with the other person why the security key changed.
How to enable security notifications on WhatsApp
To do that, open WhatsApp on your phone. Tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen, then tap Account. Scroll down, tap Security notifications, and turn on the option that says Show security notifications on this device.
Check linked devices and log out unknown sessions
WhatsApp lets you link and use your account on multiple devices. However, this could also mean someone could link your account to their device without you knowing. So, if you are suspicious about your account activity, you can check linked devices and sign out of any you don’t recognize.
How to check linked devices and log out of unknown devices on your WhatsApp account
Lock WhatsApp with your Biometrics
WhatsApp includes a native app lock feature that lets you lock it with your fingerprint or a pattern. WhatsApp also lets you lock immediately or after a set time. WhatsApp also recently rolled out a new feature to lock WhatsApp Web chats. So, I have made a detailed guide on how to lock WhatsApp on WhatsApp Web. You can watch the video below or follow the detailed steps in this guide.
How to lock your WhatsApp account with your fingerprint or Face ID
Lock and hide your most private chats
WhatsApp also lets you lock individual chats, not just the app. This way, you can lock or hide your most private chats. Here is how.
However, Locked Chat uses your device’s biometrics to lock chats. And if you cannot unlock the chat for any reason, you cannot get those messages back. Your only option is to clear the messages and unlock the chat, which you can do by going to Settings > Privacy, tapping Chat Lock, and tapping Clear Chat Lock. To lock the chats, follow the guide below.
Open WhatsApp on your device and, if you want to lock multiple chats on the home screen, select the chats you want to lock, tap the three-dot menu, and tap Lock chat. You can also do it for individual chats right here only.
Turn on Advanced chat privacy for sensitive chats
While disappearing messages remove your chat after a set period, you can turn on Advanced Chat Privacy for chats with sensitive content. This stops the other user from sharing or exporting your chats, and the media used in the chat won’t be saved in that person’s gallery. It also blocks the new Meta AI used in the chat itself.
Here is how to turn on Advanced Chat Privacy on WhatsApp
Hide your IP address in calls
WhatsApp also supports voice calls. Direct calls can connect your phone to another person’s phone, which can reveal your IP address and, in turn, your location. However, WhatsApp allows you to hide your IP during calls. Here is how.
How to protect your IP address in calls
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen, then tap Privacy. Then scroll down, tap on Advanced, and enable the option that says ” Protect IP address in calls.
Disable link previews
WhatsApp also supports link previews, which show a preview of the website content. However, to do that, your phone connects to your website and sends a request from your IP address.
So it can easily reveal your phone’s IP address to the website, along with your location. You can also turn off link previews, which prevents those fancy images websites use for spam calls.
How to disable link previews on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen. Scroll down and tap on Privacy. From here, scroll down again, tap Advanced, and enable Disable link previews.
Block floods of messages from unknown accounts
WhatsApp also introduced a new feature that blocks messages from unknown accounts. It blocks unknown accounts that send you high volumes of messages, which is especially useful if you receive frequent spam texts or your WhatsApp is being bombed with multiple messages.
How to block a flood of messages from unknown accounts
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen. Tap Privacy, then tap Advanced again, and turn on the option that says Block unknown account messages.
Encrypt your chat backup
WhatsApp relies on Google Drive for your WhatsApp backup and iCloud on iPhone. However, by default, your chat backup isn’t encrypted.
You can turn on end-to-end encrypted backup with a passkey, password, or 64-digit key so third-party servers, including Google, can’t read your backup.
Here is how to encrypt your chat backup on WhatsApp
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen, then tap Chats. From here, scroll down and tap Chat backup, then scroll down again and tap End-to-end encrypted backup.
Here, you can turn it on and then use your passkey. Remember, you’ll need this passkey whenever you back up your WhatsApp with this data. You can also use a password or a 64-digit key.
Limit what Meta AI can do with your data
Like any other app, Meta also offers AI features that let you summarise and read messages and also chat with Meta AI. However, because these AI chatbots can’t use your data publicly, Meta uses Private Processing features, which it says process your data privately for those AI features.
However, both of the AI features, including Private Processing features and web search, where Meta AI can search the web based on your queries, are turned off by default. If you turn them on, you can turn them off by default to prevent Meta AI from using your data, even though it is processed privately.
Here is how to turn off the private messaging feature and that switch on WhatsApp
Reserve a username to keep your number private
Recently, WhatsApp introduced usernames on the platform, so instead of your phone number, you can create and share a username and let others contact you through it.
However, your phone number still verifies your account, but for better privacy, you don’t need to reveal it when sharing your WhatsApp account with others. You can also restrict who can message you using your username through a secondary verification method. I have covered in detail how to find your WhatsApp username.
How to reserve a username on WhatsApp?
Use Strict account settings if you’re a high-risk target
If you are a journalist, activist, or public figure, Meta offers Strict Account Settings to help protect your account’s security and privacy. Here is a clear breakdown of the difference between standard settings and Strict Account Settings and how to enable strict account settings for your WhatsApp account.
How to enable Strict Account Settings on WhatsApp?
Run the built-in Privacy Checkup
WhatsApp privacy settings can be confusing for beginners since the platform is used by people of all ages. However, WhatsApp also offers a built-in Privacy Checkup tool that provides a step-by-step process to help you enhance your WhatsApp account’s privacy.
It includes details such as choosing who can contact you, controlling your personal info, the ability to add more privacy to your chats, adding more protection to your account, and much more
This privacy checkup offers detailed, step-by-step instructions to help you enable important privacy settings. If you find any steps in this guide confusing, you can use this tool.

A day after running over a police officer in Madhya Pradesh’s Dewas district, the accused driver, Gajendra Rawat, was arrested from Alirajpur district and suffered a bullet injury in a brief encounter with the police in an attempt to flee while being brought to Dewas, a senior police officer said.
Special DG Upendra Jain said that the accused suffered injuries in his right leg in the encounter that took place in Dewas’s Barothha police station area, and is currently admitted at the district hospital.
Inspector Dilip Puri, in charge of Dewas’s Khategaon police station, had died in the wee hours of Monday (November 2, 2026) after he was allegedly mowed down by a truck carrying illicit liquor to Gujarat that he had stopped for checking. A constable was also injured in the incident and the accused driver had been identified as Gajendra Rawat, a resident of Alirajpur district.
Mr. Rawat had fled the scene by crossing over a road divider and abandoned the truck after some distance to escape. The police had seized about 1,800 litres of illicit liquor hidden in the truck.
Following the death, the police had uncovered an inter-state bootlegging network illegally supplying liquor from Harda district to Alirajpur and further smuggling it across the State border into Gujarat.
Three persons, including key accused Rahul Jaiswal who allegedly ran the entire racket from Harda, his associate Vijay Rao in Indore and the truck owner Kairam Singh Changod, a resident of Alirajpur, have been arrested in the case so far, while search is on for three of Mr. Rahul’s alleged business partners and Mr. Rawat.
The police have said that Mr. Rahul has admitted to be a Congress functionary in Dewas. The Opposition party, that has launched scathing attacks on the BJP government over illicit liquor trade over the past few weeks, is yet to respond to Mr. Rahul’s arrest.
“The main person on the supply side was Rahul Jaiswal and on the execution side, it was Kairam Singh and this driver. We have two of them in custody. We have teams working in various districts, including border areas like Alirajpur where they would smuggle liquor into Gujarat from. The remaining people will be arrested soon,” he said.
Mr. Jain also said that the accused would avoid crossing the truck into Gujarat and supply liquor in small quantities from the border areas of Alirajpur and sell in the neighbouring State.
“They [Mr. Rawat and Mr. Changod] would stock the illicit liquor with them in Alirajpur and then smuggle it into Gujarat on motorbike or other smaller vehicles through porous border in forest areas to avoid checking on state borders,” he added.
The police are yet to make an estimate of the total amount of liquor smuggled from Harda.
“Our priority at the moment is arresting all persons. The specific amount is not relevant at this point because it does not change the offence and what we seized from the truck was anyway a large amount,” he added.
Meanwhile, the Dewas Police have also arrested Madhya Pradesh Congress spokesperson Anand Kasliwal in connection with a separate ongoing investigation into a counterfeit liquor manufacturing and selling racket, that allegedly has claimed 13 lives in Dewas in October.
Mr. Anand’s son, Aman Kasliwal, an Indore-based businessman, had been arrested on October 28 for allegedly selling chemicals used to make the fake liquor. Mr. Aman was among the 11 persons arrested in the case for manufacturing and selling the liquor in Dewas’s villages.
Officers said that Mr. Anand was arrested for allegedly tempering with evidence and sale records at his son’s shop.
Mr. Anand had earlier, in a statement, claimed innocence for his son saying that his company had legally sold paint thinner with proper billing and denying any connection with those involved in manufacturing counterfeit liquor.

Google Dreambeans is a bespoke AI visual feed built from your own context
From forgotten reading lists to uncanny dinner picks pulled from emails, Google’s new app tests the balance between proactive utility and deep context
In an attempt to create a “handcrafted visual journey” of a user’s life, Google has added a new app called Dreambeans to its portfolio, which will be available for Android users as well as the Apple iPhone. The basis for the feed curation, which will heavily rely on a bespoke watercolour style for visuals and not generic artificial intelligence (AI) generated images, will be the context from Google Gemini’s Personal Intelligence capabilities across a number of other Google apps.
“Our product’s vision is simple: we wanted to solve the frustration caused by siloed digital information across the apps that you use every day and build something proactive that does not require prompting,” says Gozde Oznur, Product Manager at Google Labs, in a briefing of which HT was part. Dreambeans uses the latest generative models from Google DeepMind, including Veo video generation for bespoke style visuals that can also include hints of the user, if allowed access to that content (such as caricatures of family members, if there is Google Photos album context).
Dreambeans, which now rolls out for Android and iPhone, will connect with personal Gmail accounts, and not business as well as enterprise accounts at this time. The Personal Intelligence connections are optional. Users have complete flexibility to choose from Google Workspace apps including Gmail and Drive, as well as Google Photos, YouTube, Search services and the Gemini app. This choice selection screen is part of the setup flow, leaving little confusion in the setup process or having to navigate the settings menu later.
Dreambeans currently supports 14 languages including Hindi, English, Bengali, Telugu, Marathi, Tamil, Urdu, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Odia, Punjabi, Assamese, and Nepali.
The India focus, Oznur says, is because India has continually delivered some of the highest global usage for Google’s apps including Gemini, Gmail and Google Photos. “No other country really ranks on all three,” she says, adding, “We thought that India, connecting around family, food, travel, and festivals like Diwali, was a natural place to bring Dreambeans first.” India is Dreambeans’ first international expansion, outside the US.
The Search services integration in particular will be relevant for those who want their curated updates, stories and suggestions feed to include elements based on past searches across Google Search, Maps, Shopping, Flights, Hotels, Translate and News. Similarly, if you connect Google Dreambeans with your Gemini app, that will allow it to create context based on chat history and specifics of conversations with Gemini.
Google insists that the idea is not to create a feed that scrolls endlessly, but instead has pinpointed recommendations, across updates, recommendations, upcoming travel, and weekend suggestions—the key being that many of them will reflect people you interact with most and places you have previously visited or there are hints to Dreambeans that you intend to visit them at some stage.
HT got early access to the Dreambeans app. After setting it up, I only unlocked context from my Google Workspace to curate content based on what it can find in Gmail and Calendar. With Google Photos specifically kept out of the loop, the watercolour style visual artwork didn’t have any personalised elements such as people, which would be the case if you enabled Photos access. The feed updates thrice a day, with the morning digest getting additions in the afternoon and then later in the day.
Suggestions that Dreambeans sent my way included a book that I intended to read and recommendations for weekend dinner spots (some choices were perplexing initially and the title specifically mentioned my wife, which I later realised it gained context from Eazydiner and Eternal’s District emails for the restaurant suggestion; good way to discover new places?) and very interesting suggestions to read Donella Meadows’ Systems Framework for Finding Real Leverage Points as well as the METR Autonomy Benchmarks for Tracking Enterprise Model Safety results.
Each suggestion integrates a Gemini-esque chatbot, and you can ask further questions and context there. Every piece in the feed can be saved for reading later, liked to give Dreambeans a better sense of what you really liked, and even a thumbs down which should effectively move similar recommendations out of the scope of the AI curation. You also have the option to ‘tune your feed’ with specific topics, either to show more of, or to show less of. It understood what I wanted, and the next day, it gave me a piece of content that explained Lewis Hamilton’s high-altitude brake management at the Mexico City Grand Prix.
“When you delete one of the source facts, we have a deletion propagation where the system understands that it is no longer valid, and we then take that information out,” says Oznur. The true magic, if it emerges eventually, will begin after a few weeks of Dreambeans understanding which suggestions and curations you interact with most—apart from manual guidance on topics.
For now, Dreambeans’ development is focusing on a more action-based menu for the feed, and also specific features for Google’s own Pixel phones. It will be interesting to see how Dreambeans develops, with two clear paths, of which one must be chosen—a more social timeline or feed that begins to add context and content from more sources, or a personal journal with a hint of sharing certain articles or recommendations with contacts. On the actionable aspect, restaurant recommendations could link with booking apps that may be installed on the phone already, saving a step for the user.
Eventually, on Android phones, Google must evolve Dreambeans from being an app into a feed that meets the user where they are at different points of time in the day. That means, Android phone users can perhaps be given an option to choose between the standard Discover feed and Dreambeans on the Android home screen. That will remove the one step Dreambeans entails at this time, as an app, which is for a user to open it every time.

It’s widely acknowledged that it’s nearly impossible to publish negative results in scientific journals. “We didn’t see anything” is a much harder sell than finding that a hypothesis is clearly right. Findings of no effect tend to either be shuffled off to low-profile journals or left behind as unpublished lab lore.
The high-profile journal Nature, however, made a notable exception this week, publishing a study that tells us that a bunch of methods we have been using to try to measure a key emotional ability don’t seem to be measuring the same thing. The results mean that we don’t have a good way to measure the impact of a concept that is the basis of a key method in therapy.
Inconsistencies
One of the most successful forms of therapy is cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT. In part, CBT is based on getting people to step back and engage in “cognitive reappraisal.” This requires people to think over a situation that has caused a negative emotional response and find ways to reinterpret it so that it has less impact on them. The ability to engage in this process has been linked to emotional resilience.
Given its importance, a lot of studies have looked at what’s going on in the brain when people engage in cognitive reappraisal. There are also a number of questionnaires that are thought to measure a person’s capacity to engage in the process. So, a large international collaboration of researchers decided to look at these more carefully. “We focused on three widely used indices that are often assumed to reflect related facets of reappraisal capacity: trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings following reappraisal, and amygdala down-regulation during reappraisal,” they wrote.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): The High Court has directed the Special Police Establishment (SPE) to register an FIR against the Chhindwara collector, the chief medical and health officer (CMHO) and the other concerned beneficiaries, interested persons instrumental in grant of illegal compassionate appointments.
Justice Vivek Agrawal said enquiry is required to be conducted in the conduct of the concerned CMHO and the collector who had given benefit of compassionate appointments to ineligible candidates.
The court found there is non-compliance of the order dated Sept 29, 2026, related to action in this matter.
Government advocate Manas Mani Verma submitted that all those who were given compassionate appointments illegally, have been removed.
'But, in my opinion, removal of those employees is not sufficient', the court said.
'Enquiry is required to be conducted into the conduct of the concerned CMHO and the collector who had given benefit of compassionate appointments to ineligible candidates', the court order said of Nov 2.
'Let an FIR be registered by the Special Police Establishment and preliminary enquiry be conducted and enquiry report be furnished within 30 days', the court order said.
Let copy of this order be supplied to the Lokayukta (SPE), State of Madhya Pradesh, for taking necessary action against the delinquents, the court order said.
The court issued the directive during the hearing of a petition filed after the petitioner Nitin Malvi was denied compassionate appointment in 2010.
The court fixed the hearing for December 15, 2026.

A video showing a man attacking a street vendor over allegations that he mixed contraceptive pills into sugarcane juice is going viral on social media. The incident is being shared with claims of ‘food jihad’ and as a warning to people to be cautious when buying food from street vendors. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video shows a customer attacking a Muslim street vendor for allegedly mixing contraceptive pills into sugarcane juice.
Fact: The viral video is scripted and was created by Mohammad Ruhul, a content creator from Bangladesh, for social awareness. It does not depict a real incident. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
First, a reverse image search of the viral footage led us to the original video (archive), which was uploaded on 24 September 2026 on a Bangladeshi Facebook page called ‘Ruhul Vlog’. The page is run by Mohammad Ruhul, who also has a YouTube channel where he regularly posts scripted videos for social awareness and entertainment.
In the viral video, Mohammad Ruhul is seen arguing with a street vendor and attacking him, alleging that he is making people sick by mixing an artificial sweetener called saccharin into sugarcane juice. However, towards the end of the video, Ruhul clarifies that the incident is scripted and was created solely to raise awareness. He also mentions that they will continue making similar videos on social issues. This confirms that the viral video does not depict a real incident but is a scripted video created for social awareness.
However, opinions differ regarding the safety of saccharin in food and beverages. Experts suggest that further research is needed to understand its potential health effects. The FSSAI permits its use only within prescribed limits. However, several media reports (here and here) have raised concerns about the use of saccharin in food and beverages in India and Bangladesh, including instances of its alleged use beyond permissible limits without adequate quality testing.
To sum up, this viral video being circulated with the ‘food jihad’ narrative is scripted.

- The claim that emergency preparation guidelines that multiple countries released in and around October 2026 signal a catastrophic event is about to occur is unfounded.
- The rumor stems from social media posts that circulated in October 2026.
- It's true that countries including the United Kingdom, the United States and Japan released new or updated emergency preparedness campaigns or programs in 2026. However, such announcements are nothing new.
- The European Union released a new emergency preparedness strategy in 2025, and many European countries were simply falling in line with the new EU guidance by releasing new messaging.
In October 2026, posts appeared on social media claiming that governments around the world were suddenly recommending their citizens to prepare emergency kits with enough supplies for at least three days, and that the release of such guidelines was both coordinated and a sign that some unspecified catastrophic, life-changing event was about to happen. 
"What on earth is about to begin?" read one Japanese-language post spreading the rumor.
Several Snopes readers contacted us and asked for an investigation into the claim.
The claim is based in some truth, but the implication that these recommendations mean a catastrophic or destabilizing global event is looming is unfounded. The risk of a catastrophic or destabilizing global event is ever present and governments have urged their citizens for decades to be prepared for emergencies.
The emergency preparedness campaigns
Announcements in several countries — primarily the United Kingdom, Japan and the United States — appear to have been the basis for the claims.
In the United Kingdom, the Cabinet Office announced a new campaign in August 2026 requesting citizens to "stock up on tinned food and take steps to ensure they are prepared for national emergencies," according to The Guardian. Details of the campaign, called "Be Ready," were officially announced in October. The website asks everyone to ensure they stock enough water, food, cash, first aid supplies and more for at least three days.
According to The Guardian, Defense Minister Wes Streeting did explicitly cite "state-sponsored terrorism" against critical infrastructure as a reason to be prepared.
In Japan, according to the Library of Congress, the government passed a law in August establishing a new disaster management agency. The agency, which will report directly to the prime minister and will be led by Goshi Hosono, is expected to help centralize disaster management in the country when it becomes official on Nov. 2.
In an October interview with Fuji TV, Hosono said his first action once the agency is officially established will be to issue an "emergency request" to all citizens to ensure they are prepared for disasters. Similarly to the British campaign, Hosono asked the general public to be stock supplies for at least three days, and ideally up to a week. However, Hosono's public comments seemed to focus exclusively natural disasters — primarily earthquakes, which are common in Japan.
Finally, in the United States, reporting from Fortune covered a new Department of Defense initiative called "FORTRESS" that aims to ensure military bases can operate fully autonomously for at 90 days. The initiative, announced by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in his Sept. 30 "State of the Force" address, involves ensuring that U.S. military bases can generate their own electricity without relying on the civilian grid.
"Power is combat now," Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell reportedly told Fox News Digital. "Without electricity, you lose communications, water, logistics, assembly lines and just basic military command structures."
The initiative also involves making sure military bases have access to water, fuel and outside communications for that 90-day time period, according to that Fox News Digital story.
(On the civilian side, the Federal Emergency Management Agency last updated its guidance on emergency preparedness in July 2026, according to its website.)
The posts also claimed the emergency preparedness messaging was not limited to just the U.S., U.K. and Japan. Lists also named Belgium, Ireland, Germany, Poland, France, Netherlands, Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Switzerland, Taiwan and the European Union as issuing similar stockpiling recommendations.
Snopes found news reporting from Belgium and Ireland showing both countries had also issued new emergency guidelines in September and October 2026, while most of the other countries named had done so in the past two years, as had the European Union.
However, the fact the European Union released a new preparedness strategy in March 2025 makes the list look much less dramatic: European countries were simply falling in line with the new EU guidance. Searching the EU's Civil Protection Knowledge Network website helped confirm this: we found brochures on emergency preparedness tagged under "population preparedness," aimed at citizens of almost all the previously named EU countries (all but Ireland), plus several more — Slovakia, Croatia, Romania, Czechia and Greece.
So why now?
Of course, just issuing a warning about preparedness does not mean an emergency is imminent — the whole concept is to be prepared because you never know when an emergency might strike, and that's why governments have issued such warnings for decades. In the U.S., for instance, the government has maintained a civil defense office in some form since 1941, and Snopes found the recommendation to stockpile at least some supplies is quite common across guidelines.
In this case, there were likely several factors influencing the guidelines issued across Europe.
First, while natural disasters remain a threat across the entire world, Europe has recently faced more powerful storms in the winter and extreme heat waves and wildfires in the summer due to climate change. The more severe an event, the harder it is for emergency services to immediately respond to everyone.
Second, the European continent has become increasingly concerned about war following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. "[War] no longer feels quite so far-fetched," a German pamphlet issued in November 2025 reads. While direct war itself might still be unlikely, the methods of waging war have changed dramatically as the world has become more interconnected.
Countries like Russia and China are known to run sophisticated cyber warfare operations, and some worry that sensitive infrastructure, including basic utilities, could be threatened via direct or indirect sabotage. The governments are absolutely concerned about any holes in their system. In October, the Danish, Dutch, French and Finnish governments briefly took their websites offline after a group of intelligence agencies released a statement announcing critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely-used coding language, according to Reuters. (The vulnerabilities were quickly fixed.)

Executives at the troubled Snowy Hydro company collectively banked bonuses worth a combined $751,925 in the last financial year, despite its renewable energy project blowing out to 12 times its original cost.
But Guardian Australia can reveal chief executive, Dennis Barnes, who has a base salary of $1,845,126, opted not to accept the extra cash.
The company’s chief financial officer, Kim Josling, who has a pay packet worth $828,839, received a $215,440 bonus, according to the company’s annual report for the 2025-2026 financial year.
Its chief operating officer, Maia Schweizer, received a base salary of $1,050,503, and pocketed a $255,570 bonus, while chief commercial officer, Gordon Wymer, who has a base salary of $1,142,268, took home a $280,915 bonus.
The company’s long-delayed renewable energy project, Snowy Hydro 2.0, will not be completed until the end of the decade and is expected to cost taxpayers as much as $25bn.
It was first put forward in 2017 by the Turnbull government and came with an original price tag of $2bn, but the project in the Kosciuszko national park has climbed in cost.
The project was revised to almost $13bn in 2023, and construction was expected to completed by the end of 2028.
Snowy 2.0 now won’t be completed and fully commissioned until 2029.
A Snowy Hydro spokesperson said “short term incentives are based on a range of performance outcomes across these parts of Snowy Hydro’s business”.
“Mr Barnes recommended to Snowy Hydro’s Board that he receive no short term incentive payment for FY26,” the statement reads.
At Australia’s national science agency, the CSIRO, its chief executive, Doug Hilton, received a bonus of $198,517 on top of his $789,391 base salary, according to its 2025-2026 annual report.
He was the only one of the organisation’s senior executives to receive a bonus classed as a “salary at risk” payment.
The cash was awarded the same year the agency made a number of painful cuts, shrinking its workforce by several hundred people.
More than 1,100 jobs have been cut from CSIRO in the last two years, according to the Community and Public Sector Union.
Separation and redundancy payments cost the agency more than $27m.
A CSIRO spokesperson said the agency’s board determined the annual value of the “at risk payment” which was assessed on key performance indicators.
Bonus payments to other senior executives were removed in the 2021-2022 financial year to align the agency with the public service, where such payments were also being removed.
“The size of CSIRO’s workforce is now expected to remain stable, supported by additional funding from the Australian Government in this year’s federal budget,” the spokesperson said.
“CSIRO acknowledges that change can create uncertainty for affected staff, and we do not underestimate the impact of that.”

Don't throw away your old AirPods — do this instead
Instead of getting rid of your old AirPods, replace the battery and give them a new purpose.
AirPods are built to last, and they usually work for years before they stop functioning completely. You'll likely buy new AirPods before your old ones stop working, though they may no longer sound brand-new.
So what should you do with your old AirPods? Throwing them in the trash is something you certainly shouldn't do; Apple discourages this because of the lithium-ion batteries inside them. The good news is that, depending on the problem, Apple can fix your buds for a reasonable fee. Your old AirPods can become good backup earbuds, or even a gift for a friend or family member.
Taking your AirPods to Apple for a repair
If battery performance is the only real problem, it's likely worth getting a replacement before buying new AirPods. Even if you've already bought a new pair, replacing the batteries in your old earbuds will make them better for someone else.
But unlike an iPhone or iPad, Apple won't open AirPods to replace their batteries. Instead, the company recycles your old AirPods and gives you new ones, charging you a lower price per earbud. For most AirPods, a battery replacement costs $49 per earbud, so $98 if you need to replace the battery in both. That's much cheaper than buying new AirPods Pro, for example, which cost $249. For the higher-end AirPods Max, a battery replacement costs $79, which is also much cheaper than paying $549 for new headphones.
If you have AppleCare, you may be eligible for a free battery replacement if any battery falls below 80 percent of its original capacity. And if any battery in your AirPods fails while they're still under warranty, Apple will replace them for free. Some independent repair shops can replace the battery inside AirPods, but this requires cutting them open and gluing them back together. You might end up saving some money, but they won't look as good as new — not to mention that they'll also lose their water and sweat resistance.
If you've lost one of your earbuds or the charging case, Apple offers replacements for them. Prices vary depending on the model; for the Pro line, a new earbud costs $89 and a new case costs $99. For standard AirPods, it's $69 to replace one bud and between $59 and $79 to replace the case.
It's thus usually worth it for the more expensive AirPods Pro, but not so much for the base AirPods. The latest AirPods 5 cost $129 from Apple, and it's not hard to find them for a little less at other stores.
Giving your old AirPods a new purpose
Instead of tossing your old AirPods into a drawer, there are plenty of other ways to put them to good use. Earbuds that still hold a decent charge could be worth something. Apple doesn't offer trade-in credit for AirPods, but buyback services like Back Market will give you some money for them. Selling them directly on places like eBay or Facebook Marketplace usually pays more.
Or you can simply give them to a friend or family member, so they'll only have to pay for a battery replacement if needed. If you pass them on, be sure to clean the AirPods and remove them from your Apple account — new ear tips will be much appreciated.
Keeping them around is also suitable if they still work fine. Have your old AirPods ready as backup earbuds in case you lose your new ones, leave them somewhere or simply need another set when your usual pair runs out of battery. Some people prefer to use old AirPods as gym earbuds so their new ones don't get covered in sweat. If you like to sleep with your AirPods in, using your old ones can avoid draining the battery on the new ones. Or you might devote them for listening to your Roku at night via Bluetooth.
In case your old AirPods are truly dead and you don't want to spend money on them, Apple will recycle them for free. You don't even need to take them to an Apple Store, since Apple provides a prepaid shipping label in certain regions. You won't get paid for them, but at least your earbuds will be disposed of properly.

Days before his retirement as Chief of Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal AP Singh wrote to Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, urging him to intervene in the sealing of the Indian Air Force's (IAF) sports complex at the Race Course Air Force Station in New Delhi.
In a letter dated October 26, Singh sought to ensure that the approximately 40-acre land parcel housing the Air Force Sports Complex (AFSC) remained under the IAF's control, citing operational requirements and the facilities located within the premises, Hindustan Times reported, quoting officials familiar with the matter.
The former Air Chief Marshal also raised the issue during an in-person meeting with Rajnath Singh on October 29, two days before his retirement on October 31, as per the HT report.
He reportedly urged the defence minister to direct the concerned authorities to reconsider the decision and hand over the land to the Air Force.
The intervention came after the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) reclaimed the sports complex, triggering concerns within defence circles.
The closure also led to the cancellation of a farewell event planned for the outgoing Air Chief, as per reports.
In his communication, AP Singh argued that it would be prudent for the land housing the AFSC to remain under the Air Force's control, citing its importance to the overall functioning of the Race Course Air Force Station, according to officials cited by PTI.
He also referred to a joint survey of the land conducted in 2014 by the then Ministry of Urban Development, the Defence Estates Department and the Air Force.
The IAF has separately conveyed its objections to the Defence Ministry and sought the cancellation of the sealing process, officials said.
A key concern relates to the strategic location of the air station, which lies in the high-security zone surrounding the Prime Minister's residence at Lok Kalyan Marg. The Air Force has highlighted the station's role in addressing potential aerial security threats in the area.
Singh also referred to the station's history and existing land arrangements, stressing that its various facilities should continue to function without disruption.
According to officials cited in the report, the station provides administrative support to Air Headquarters and more than 5,000 Air Force personnel.
Its premises house accommodation for married and unmarried personnel, training facilities for airmen and Agniveervayus, security infrastructure, recreational facilities, a medical centre, a school and a unit-run canteen.
The Air Force Sports Complex itself includes a golf course, guest cottages, a swimming pool, a fitness centre and restaurants.
The facility's closure reportedly disrupted regular activities and forced the cancellation of a farewell golf event scheduled for October 28 for the outgoing Air Chief Marshal.
The development also drew attention because of the timing of the reclamation, coming days before AP Singh's retirement.
The sealing of the Air Force Sports Complex is part of a wider exercise by the Centre to reclaim high-value land parcels in the vicinity of Lok Kalyan Marg.
The Land and Development Office (L&DO), which functions under MoHUA, has been reviewing land parcels used for defence-related golf courses and sports facilities in the area.
The ministry had earlier reportedly asked the authorities concerned to hand over the land housing the Air Force Golf Course.
The L&DO subsequently issued eviction notices to the sports complex's management, seeking the return of the property.
Other prominent establishments have also faced action as part of the reclamation drive.
In August this year, the government evicted the Delhi Race Club from its 53-acre premises on Lok Kalyan Marg, citing the requirement of the land for an unspecified public purpose.
The Centre also reclaimed the Jaipur Polo Ground from the India Polo Association, citing broader public purposes, governance and defence infrastructure projects.
The government has not publicly specified the exact purpose for reclaiming the approximately 40-acre Air Force Sports Complex land parcel.
The controversy also triggered a political response, with the Congress criticising the Centre over the reclamation of the Air Force Sports Complex.
Congress general secretary in-charge of communications Jairam Ramesh shared a media report about AP Singh's letter to Rajnath Singh on X, accusing the government of showing "utter disrespect" to the IAF community.
Ramesh said the sports complex had a long history and had served several public purposes over the decades, while also remaining an integral part of the Indian Air Force's social infrastructure.

'We grew up around this historic Delhi mosque - now we have been forced out'
- Published
In the heart of Delhi, a short distance from the Indian prime minister's residence, a small mosque stands amid piles of rubble. Its pale walls and pointed arches remain intact, its courtyard still lined with green-and-white tiles.
But the people who gave life to the place are gone.
Mohammad Wasim, 50, points across the rubble to the spot where his house once stood.
"My father was married there, and, decades later, so was my daughter," says Wasim, a driver.
Wasim and his family were among hundreds of people who lived around the mosque in a patchwork of modest homes tucked between military compounds, exclusive clubs and sprawling bungalows in Race Course, one of the Indian capital's wealthiest and most heavily guarded neighbourhoods. Many of them had lived here for generations, working as drivers, cleaners and gardeners in the wealthy houses around them.
On 7 October, the authorities demolished their houses across three settlements, saying they had been built illegally on government land. They also raised security concerns because of the houses' proximity to military installations. Some 717 families were relocated to Savda Ghevra, a colony nearly 31 miles away, on the city's outskirts.
Residents had challenged the evictions in the Delhi High Court, arguing that moving so far from their jobs, schools and communities would upend their lives. But in August, the court allowed the relocation, accepting the government's security concerns and noting that alternative housing had been provided.
Only the mosque and a nearby Hindu temple were left standing. But their water and electricity supplies were cut off that day, and access to the compound has since been restricted. Worshippers are generally turned away at the gates, though some are occasionally allowed through after pleading with guards.
The government says it owns the land on which the mosque stands, but mosque authorities say it was registered in 1977 as waqf property - land or buildings set aside under Islamic law for religious or charitable purposes - and is listed, external as a heritage structure. The Delhi Waqf Board says it is nearly 300 years old, though other estimates put its age at 125-150 years.
The board has written to the authorities seeking restoration of the mosque's water and electricity and raising concerns about its future. Separately, a worshipper has petitioned the high court over restrictions on prayers and fears that the mosque could be demolished.
1 of 5
On 29 October, the government told the court it would take no action against the mosque for four weeks while considering the board's objections. It opposed restoring access for prayers, citing safety concerns during demolition work, a position disputed by the worshippers' lawyer. The court declined to intervene and scheduled another hearing for 16 December.
While the mosque's future remains uncertain, for those who once lived around it, the question now is what can be salvaged of the lives they built there.
Wasim still returns to the mosque to pray when he can, though guards sometimes turn him away. On a recent afternoon, he was among just four or five worshippers inside. A generator chugged loudly outside, supplying electricity after the power had been cut off.
"Our hearts and entire lives are tied to this place," he says. "How can we let it go, when our childhood was spent playing here?"
Rekha, a widow, remembers the colony with longing. She washed dishes in nearby homes, raised her family and performed seva (voluntary service) at the local temple.
To her, the word rehabilitation seems painfully inadequate: "How can a life built over decades be uprooted and planted somewhere else?" she asks.
Since the move, she has lost the work she depended on. Her 19-year-old son is struggling to find a job. She has been allotted a third-floor apartment but climbing stairs is painful because of a metal rod in her leg after an operation.
"I may have a house but my home was snatched away."
Critics say these experiences are part of a longer history of displacement in Delhi, where working-class communities have repeatedly been pushed, external to the city's distant edges because they lack documents proving legal ownership of land they have lived on for decades.
"Relocation disconnects them from both jobs and networks, resulting in livelihood and income loss," urban researcher Mukta Naik told the BBC.
As families scatter in search of work, she says, the informal support systems they once relied on become harder to rebuild.
"This leaves families to fend for themselves," she says.
The Delhi government's housing agency, the local municipal council and the central government's land office did not respond to requests for comment.
Savda Ghevra was established in 2006 on farmland near Delhi's border with Haryana state, to house families displaced from elsewhere in the city.
The first arrivals found little more than bare plots, without roads, running water or electricity. Over time, they built homes, opened shops and fought for basic services. By the early 2020s, an estimated 50,000 people lived here, external, having made a neighbourhood out of a place they had little choice but to inhabit.
Now the families from Race Course have begun the same slow work.
They have traded the lush tree-lined avenues of central Delhi for rows of nearly identical concrete blocks, with open fields stretching beyond. Life is going on, but much of what sustained these families remains on the other side of the city.
Every day, Babloo leaves home at 5am to take his children by metro to their old school in central Delhi, changing trains three times along the way. He waits out the six hours until classes finish at a tea stall outside his former neighbourhood. When he has work his wife makes the journey.
Their new home is too far away, he says, to return between the school runs. By the time the family reaches Savda Ghevra, it is around 4pm.
Babloo once worked at a club in Race Course. He has now found work in Meerut, a town to the north-east of Delhi. Residents knew they might have to leave, he says, but they hoped they would be relocated somewhere close enough to continue their jobs and their children's schooling.
The government says suitable apartments were unavailable closer to Race Course. In court, it cited Savda Ghevra's schools, dispensaries and transport links as evidence that the area could accommodate the displaced families.
But the presence of these facilities offers little reassurance to Naeem Khan, 63. His two grandsons have hearing and speech disabilities and need specialised care and schooling that he says are unavailable in the area.
The move has also scattered Naeem's family. One son and a divorced daughter share his tiny one-room apartment, while his two other sons had to move elsewhere due to lack of space.
"We have been thrown 20 years backward," he says.
The distance has been especially costly for women. Naik says childcare responsibilities, transport costs and safety concerns make long commutes to work particularly difficult for them.
At Race Course, the wealth surrounding the settlements offered small but vital ways to earn money - dishes to wash, gardens to tend, discarded bottles to collect and sell.
Akhtari, an elderly widow, collected mineral-water bottles for about 100 rupees (about $1.05; £0.80) a day and dried leftover rotis, or flatbreads, to sell as cattle feed.
Now even these modest sources of income have disappeared.
"Everyone living here was evicted; everyone is poor, broken, and struggling themselves," Akhtari says. "Who will hire someone else for housework?"
At Race Course, when she had nothing, the mosque's imam or a neighbour might give her money for flour. Her neighbours checked on her. In the new apartment, she has a roof over her head, but few people to fall back on.
She has begun to worry about what will happen if she falls ill.
"If I collapse and die inside, no one will even know," she says. " Hopefully someone will break down the door and find me."

The French pharma Servier said Tuesday that an experimental drug it purchased in June for $1.55 billion in cash, plus about $1 billion more in potential milestones, failed to slow a rare form of muscular dystrophy in a long placebo-controlled trial.
It’s a surprising setback for both Servier and the patients with Becker muscular dystrophy, who currently have no approved treatments. The drug, called sevasemten and originally developed by Edgewise Therapeutics, had previously shown promising results in a smaller, randomized study.
“The results of the pivotal GRAND CANYON study are not aligned with certain findings observed in prior clinical studies,” Servier said in a statement, using the company’s name for the Phase 3 trial. “Servier is conducting a comprehensive analysis of the GRAND CANYON study dataset, together with relevant prior clinical data, to better understand and further characterize the study findings.”

NMC gives in-principle approval to replace percentile-based NEET-PG and NEET-SS counselling with a rank-based system, under which only candidate ranks would be declared
NEW DELHI: Medical postgraduate admissions could see a major change, with the National Medical Commission (NMC) giving in-principle approval to replace the existing percentile-based system with a rank-based system for NEET-PG and NEET-Super Speciality (SS) counselling.A 12-member expert committee constituted to review the NEET-PG admission and counselling process told Supreme Court in its report on Tuesday that the commission is working on a new regulation under which only ranks would be declared and percentile marks would no longer be specified.The proposal received in-principle approval at the NMC's meeting on Sept 23, according to a letter dated Oct 1, 2026, from the NMC secretary to the director general of health services (DGHS).
The commission is yet to finalise the regulation.SC is examining various petitions challenging Centre's decision to drastically reduce the qualifying cut-off percentiles for NEET-PG 2025. Under revised criteria, the qualifying score for general category was reduced from 276 to 103, while that for SC/ST/OBC categories was brought down from 235 to minus 40.The report was filed after detailed deliberations and consideration of suggestions made by senior advocate Maninder Singh, who is assisting the Supreme Court as amicus curiae.
"NMC is in process of issuing new regulations, which are yet to be finalised wherein only rank-based system for NEET PG & SS counselling will be adopted; no percentile marks will be declared in results; only ranks will be given to candidates. A letter dated Oct 1 has been written by secretary, NMC to DGHS informing proposal for changing existing percentile-based system to a rank-based merit system for NEET-PG and NEET-SS which is under consideration by the Commission.
The panel has accorded in-principle approval for proposed change with a view to address the issues arising from the existing system," the report said.On reduction of minimum qualification, the report said, "sanctity of NEET examinations should be maintained and minimum qualifying standards in postgraduate medical education is not diluted to the extent of permitting candidates with grossly inadequate or negative performance to become eligible for admission; the significance of competitive examinations should not be reduced to an administrative formality."It also suggested that there should be no salary discrimination between residents of clinical and non-clinical branches and incentives should be given to doctors to work in rural areas.

How Antonelli 'blew everyone away' to make Formula 1 history
- Published
Just after Kimi Antonelli clinched his first title to become the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history, Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen were united in their assessment of his achievement.
"Incredible," they both said. Coming from the two most successful champions on the current grid, the men who are first and third in the all-time list of F1 record-holders, it meant something.
That Antonelli shared the Mexico City Grand Prix podium with these two titans meant something, too.
To Antonelli, firstly, who said: "I will definitely frame the picture and put it in my house because it's just an incredible moment. And as well to see so much respect from two incredible drivers who have done the history of the sport is truly special and a moment that will live and will always be remembered."
So, too, though, for its symbolism. Antonelli seems destined to join them among the list of all-time greats of the sport, judging by the scale of his achievement this year.
"There are going to be others," said 1996 world champion Damon Hill, commentating for BBC Radio 5 live.
"I don't see anything else other than him getting better and better. He's going to have to go through hard times as well, but no one is going to doubt his incredible talent."
No one indeed. Not any more, anyway.
- Antonelli - the boy 'born in a garage' who became world champion 
  - Published4 hours ago
- Antonelli heads list of F1's youngest champions 
  - Published4 hours ago
- How much do you know about F1 champion Antonelli? 
  - Published4 hours ago
Antonelli's first title comes at the end of only his second season in F1. When he was drafted into Mercedes last year - to replace Hamilton, no less - there were those who said he was too inexperienced.
For some of last year, he looked it. There were flashes of promise, but by and large it was a shaky debut season, one that did not live up to Antonelli's billing as potentially the next generational talent.
So when it became clear that Mercedes would start this season with the best car, it was his team-mate George Russell, who had comfortably beaten him in 2025, who was favourite for the championship.
But that was without reckoning on the remarkable step forward Antonelli made in his development over last winter.
He finished the first race on Russell's tail. He took his maiden victory in the second, the first of five consecutive wins with which he took control of the championship. Since then, he has never looked like losing it.
Even when Mercedes' early season advantage was wiped out by their rivals, Antonelli was always there, always a factor. Which is more than can be said for Russell.
In that sense, it is important to see his achievement in context. Had the comparative performance between Russell and Antonelli carried on as it did last year, this championship may well have had a different complexion.
It could have been a season during which Russell and Hamilton were neck and neck in the title fight for most of the year - indeed, Russell has now slipped behind both Verstappen and Hamilton in the points table.
Instead, it has been a story of one driver's domination. His performances have been so strong that he has removed pretty much all jeopardy from the title fight.
That has not made it the most exciting season to watch, but it speaks volumes for the level at which Antonelli has performed. All because of the progress he has made - and his remarkable consistency.
"At his age," said Verstappen, "to be so solid, not make big mistakes, and of course also beat your experienced team-mate, he's just driven incredible, and I'm very proud of him, how he has handled himself this whole season."
Lando Norris, the outgoing world champion, was also effusive in his praise.
"It couldn't have gone to a better person," he said. "He's a genuine guy, very, very kind, and he has driven unbelievably well this year, better that what everyone was expecting of him.
"He's certainly not had an easy season in terms of his competition being incredibly high. He has gone up against the best drivers in the world, all in very good cars, and he's blown everyone away.
"I hope everyone gives him enough credit for what he's achieved this year. He's made everyone else look silly. He's driven that well and he's been able to click with his car, he's worked hard to understand how to drive this car and he's exploited it better than anyone else.
"So he should be very proud. He has achieved history and I am very, very happy for him."
For Antonelli, the difficulties of last year were formative, and critical in what he has been able to achieve this.
"The fact that some people said that I wasn't belonging to F1," he said, "or I wasn't ready for it - which at some point last year I probably looked like I wasn't - being able to experience those moments made me much more ready ahead of this year.
"Experiencing really low and difficult situations, high-pressure moments, really helped me to face certain situations this year and definitely they made me mature a lot as a driver, as a person.
"Still this year I've had moments where I could have done better, a lot better, so it's just a constant learning process.
"Last year being able to race straight into Mercedes, obviously straight under the spotlight, made me grow much faster than if I would have gone to a smaller team, for example."
One of those moments was this weekend.
He admitted after qualifying that he had been "tight", not driving as well as he could have, a result of the pressure of the moment.
"Austin, I was much more aggressive, much more present in the moment," said Antonelli, "while in Mexico, yesterday in qualifying, I was a bit more tense in a way because I also wasn't as intense in the way I was driving.
"So definitely, it hasn't been easy on that side. But now finally, we clinched it and now we can just enjoy the rest of the season."
The potency of the moment was clear to see after the race.
Antonelli admitted he was so emotional on the last lap as he followed Verstappen and Hamilton home that he was struggling to see.
"I lost probably two seconds because I was already crying basically and I couldn't see clearly ahead," he said. "I could see two Ferraris somehow with the tears.
"It was very special and a lot of memories went through my mind in that moment."
Then his father Marco and mother Veronica, who have been so important in his rise to F1, were there to greet him at the end.
Marco has been virtually ever-present this season, providing quiet support for his son whenever needed.
"To have my dad during the whole season was very important," said Antonelli, "because, first of all, he was the one keeping me grounded, especially after very high moments, but as well he was the one that was always there when I was facing a difficult situation or I wasn't feeling the best ahead of a session."
Then, in the champions' news conference, he became so emotional at one point as he remembered his late grandfather that he could not talk, and had to take a minute to compose himself.
"Oh my god," he said, after he had collected himself. "I cried way too much today. But it's good."
