Hard to believe, but smart bird feeders have been around for six years.
The idea started with Birdbuddy (then styled Bird Buddy), which launched a Kickstarter campaign in November 2020 for the world’s first app-connected, AI-powered smart bird feeder. Birdfy followed in 2021 with its first camera-equipped feeder, and today the two companies remain the most popular brands in the smart bird-feeder space, with a sizable catalog of offerings, including smart bird baths and smart nesting boxes.
Thanks to two new releases from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, you can now get a premium smart bird feeder experience for under $100—something that just a year or two ago would have cost $200 or more.
I tested both Birdfy’s Rookie and Birdbuddy’s Nook in my backyard for four weeks each, noting annoyances, especially helpful features, and which features were available without a subscription.
While both have a significant number of pluses and minuses, Birdbuddy’s Nook, despite costing $20 more and failing to capture every visit, came out just slightly ahead due to its more premium hardware experience.
Birdfy Rookie
Released in October of last year, Birdfy’s Rookie was positioned as a smart feeder for beginners, with USB-C charging only, no solar (though you can buy a more expensive model that has it), and no complicated assembly process. It functions basically as a lightweight gravity pet feeder with a 1.3-liter seed capacity and a camera on the side—just snap the three main pieces together, charge the camera, and you’re good to go. It can only be pole- or wall-mounted, not hung.
While I loved the simplicity of the Rookie and appreciated that it uses the same excellent app as the pricier Birdfy feeders, the 1080p camera’s picture quality was noticeably lower than the Nook’s, and while it did capture every bird that visited, there were also plenty of false-alarm motion detections.
I also found some significant drawbacks to the design over my four-week test. First, though the feeder itself is IP66 rated for water resistance, there’s no overhang on the roof, which means water is going to get into the seed if it rains (as it did off and on throughout my testing period).
Second, the lid just sits loosely on the top, so it kept blowing off whenever there was a big gust of wind. And third, perhaps most frustratingly, because the camera is on the side, it didn’t do the greatest job capturing larger birds, though the camera lens stayed relatively clean, being farther away from the action, and small-bird shots were well framed. Birdfy advertises the battery charge as lasting seven weeks, but my test unit lasted less than two.
One big advantage the Rookie has, however, is its seed capacity. At 1.3 liters, it’s only slightly less voluminous than Birdfy’s popular original feeder, which packs 1.5 liters. (Though note that this still pales in comparison to Birdfy’s Bamboo feeder, a top pick in our guide to the Best Smart Bird Feeders, which holds 3.5 liters.)
Feeder capacity aside, Birdfy’s app is well designed and simple, and it makes it easy to see which birds visited that day. You can even watch your feeder on TV if you have Roku—the Birdfy app is available on devices running Roku OS 15.1 or higher. Best of all, as of November 1, Birdfy offers unlimited automatic AI-based identification without a subscription, which is a rarity among smart bird feeders. Birdfy’s ID is pretty decent, with nearly no mistakes during my test.
If you want to spring for more storage or longer video recording (free tier is limited to 5 GB and 20 seconds), you can opt for Birdfy Plus for $80/year or Birdfy Pro for $150/year.
Birdbuddy Nook
Birdbuddy’s Nook launched in late October this year and is also aimed at beginners and budget-conscious shoppers. It looks a lot like Birdbuddy’s flagship Home (previously the 2 Pro), just smaller and squatter. It has the same thick plastic construction with a roof to keep out rain, but the Nook’s hinged lid makes filling a breeze. (Note that the $99 version does not come with the extended perch or solar roof, as pictured.)
Like the Home, the camera is a half-sphere about the size of a ping-pong ball that pops in and out with a magnet; you can position it vertically or horizontally depending on which style of photos you prefer. My test unit came with the solar panel, so I was not able to test the battery life of the camera, but know that the Nook’s battery only delivers 3,900 mAh compared to the Rookie’s 5,200 mAh.
The Nook shoots in 2K HDR, resulting in noticeably crisper imagery and sound. Unlike the Rookie’s side camera, the Nook’s is centered on the feeder—which makes for better full-bird shots, but its close proximity means it tends to get dirtier and smudged more easily than the Rookie’s side camera. I was also surprised by how fast the seed disappeared—within a day in some cases. Birdbuddy states that its seed hopper holds 0.9 liters, or 3.8 cups, which is only slightly less than the Rookie, but the difference in empty rates was noticeable.
My test unit also came with the optional Extended Perch for bigger birds like Steller’s jays and crows, though the big birds in my yard have always managed to find a way to visit the Birdbuddy Home, which has Birdbuddy’s usual tiny perch, so I’m not entirely convinced this is worth the extra $40. However, I do like that I can hang the IP67-rated Nook, especially since its pole-mount option doesn’t have a fastener. This means it tends to swing around when it’s mounted on a 1-inch-diameter pole, especially when larger birds land and take off.
Birdbuddy’s strength has always been its app, which remains easy to use and presents a library of shareable photos from each bird visit, though its interface is quickly being bested by newer brands like Kiwibit and even Birdfy, which just began offering AI ID for free with all its feeders. (Birdbuddy’s app also offers free AI ID, which is excellent, but you have to manually engage it for each photo, making it harder to see at a glance which species visited that day.)
Birdbuddy cameras have also historically struggled to capture all bird visits, and while the Nook was advertised to have a faster wake time, it still missed many bird visits I saw, though I did notice more captures than previous models, with no false alarms.
One new feature of the Birdbuddy app—and one I have not seen before—is the ability to ID other birds from sounds in the background, à la Cornell Lab of Ornithology’s Merlin ID app. It currently states it’s a “free preview,” though, so I suspect it will ultimately be locked behind a subscription tier. Still, I found it to be a neat complement to the Nook’s superior onboard microphone. Other features requiring a subscription (Birdbuddy Premium for $70/year or Birdbuddy Family for $99/year) include Ultra resolution, guest access to the livestream, and the ability to name individual birds.
Rookie vs. Nook
| Specs | Birdbuddy Nook | Birdfy Rookie | 
|---|---|---|
| Base-model price | $99 | $80 | 
| Camera | 2K HDR | 1080p | 
| Orientation | Horizontal or vertical | Vertical | 
| Battery | 3,900 mAh rechargeable | 5,200 mAh rechargeable | 
| Camera location | Front | Side | 
| Standard solar charging? | No (available for extra) | No (available for extra) | 
| Seed capacity | 0.9 liters | 1.3 liters | 
| Subscription cost | $70–$99/year | $80–$150/year | 
| AI ID without subscription? | Yes, manual | Yes | 
| Mounting options | Hang, wall, pole | Wall, pole | 
| Supported Wi-Fi networks | 2.4 GHz | 2.4 GHz | 
| Color options | Blue | Tan, blue | 
The Winner: Birdbuddy Nook
If you’re looking to spend under $100, the Rookie is a perfectly respectable smart bird feeder, with excellent free AI ID. However, if you want the whole package, I have to give the edge to the Nook. It won’t show you every bird that visits, which is disappointing, but you’ll get great shots of the ones that do, and its sturdy housing and versatile camera make it a great value that will hold up well in inclement weather.

Iran's senior security official Mohsen Rezaei has claimed that Pakistan Army chief Asim Munir warned of growing ties between Hindus and Jews, alleging that the emerging partnership posed a threat to Pakistan and the wider Muslim world.
In an interview with Iranian state media, Rezaei said Munir raised concerns over growing India-Israel ties during a four-nation security meeting in Tehran on October 26. The meeting was attended by Munir, Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Rezaei, who represented Iran.
Rezaei also claimed that the leaders shared concerns that Israel could target other countries in the region after Iran.
"They spoke very strongly against Israel. Mr Khalid bin Salman said that after you (Iran), Israel would target Turkey, and then come after Saudi Arabia," Rezaei said during the interview.
"Mr Ibrahim Kalin, the head of Turkish intelligence, shared the same view. Mr Asim Munir also spoke about the threat posed by Israel and the emerging bond between Hindus and Jews against Muslims and even Pakistan. These remarks reflect their information and concerns about how Israel may act towards them in the future," he added.
Munir has repeatedly invoked religious differences between Hindus and Muslims, describing the two communities as fundamentally distinct.
Days before the Pakistan-backed Pahalgam terror attack in April 2025, Munir had spoken about the differences between Hindus and Muslims in their religion, customs, traditions, thoughts and ambitions. He had also invoked the Two-Nation Theory.
While Rezaei's latest account of Munir's remarks remains unverified, the reported comments are consistent with the Pakistani army chief's earlier rhetoric.
Meanwhile, India and Israel have steadily expanded cooperation across defence, intelligence, counterterrorism, trade, agriculture, water management and emerging technologies. The two countries elevated their relationship to a Special Strategic Partnership during PM Narendra Modi's visit to Israel in February 2026.
Israel had also openly backed India's right to self-defence during Operation Sindoor against Pakistan in May 2025. Israeli Ambassador to India Reuven Azar had said that terrorists had nowhere to hide.
In February this year, Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu proposed a "hexagon of alliances" involving India, Israel, Greece, Cyprus and other countries to counter what he described as radical Shia and Sunni axes.
In October, Netanyahu again named India as a key partner in his plans to build alternative alliances. He also warned that Israel could face a hostile US administration after President Donald Trump leaves the White House.

Trump is going to get ‘trounced’ in the midterms, Anthony Scaramucci predicts
Former White House aide compares elections to a customer relations survey and concludes the president’s public ‘are not happy’ over his failure to deliver on his campaign promises

President Donald Trump and his Republicans are about to get “trounced” in Tuesday’s midterm elections, former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci has predicted.
Guesting on CNBC’s Squawk Box Europe, Scaramucci, 62, who served for just 11 days in Trump’s first White House administration before being fired, said the U.S. is currently at a crossroads with the two main parties offering “two different visions of where the country should go.”
“I think the president’s going to get trounced, by the way, and I think he knows he’s going to get trounced,” the former financier turned podcaster and pundit said.
“You have one vote. You have one customer relations survey that you can do on the American president – that’s at the midterms, and people are not happy,” Scaramucci added.
“He promised affordability, he promised no more ‘forever wars,’ he promised transparency on the Epstein files. He didn’t deliver on any of that stuff, and so there’s a lot of people inside MAGA that are now also breaking from him.”
Polling heading into Election Day suggested the Democrats will win back the House of Representatives and perhaps the Senate amid widespread voter unhappiness about the Iran war and the high cost of living. If Democrats take control of one or both chambers of Congress it could stall Trump’s agenda for his last two years in office.
Trump has spent the last month touring red states and giving rallies in the hope of encouraging turnout but has continued to dismiss the issues voters tell pollsters they care most about, spending Monday at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool discussing its renovation rather than offering a convincing closing argument for the still-undecided voters.
Scaramucci, whose famously short stint in Trump’s service was recently eclipsed by that of Katie Zachariah, looked ahead to what will happen if the much-talked-about “blue wave” does materialize.
“If he gets trounced here, there will be bicameral investigations that will be the main show because there’s a lot of things that’s going on in the administration that the Democrats are going to want to uncover,” he said.
“The Republicans, in my mind, I think there’ll be a great intellectual civil war. The Republicans are going to have to reconcile where do they want to go. It’s no longer the party of Ronald Reagan, certainly not the party of George W Bush, but is it the party of Donald Trump after he leaves the stage?”
Scaramucci said he foresaw only a gradual break with Trump over time, however, explaining: “There’ll be DNA elements of MAGA in the next presidential candidate for sure, because looming large over that presidential candidate will be Donald Trump and several hundred million dollars of his PAC money, and so they’re not going to want to get too far away from him in 2028.
“So there will be elements of MAGA, but I also think there’ll be a civil war in that party.”
Asked his view of the Iran war, the former adviser said: “I don’t see any alignment between the Iranians, the Israelis, and the Americans for a potential negotiated solution right now.
“If the Americans are going to ramp up the military strikes alongside of the Israelis... I don’t really understand how that’s going to necessarily help the region either.”
The U.S. launched new airstrikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island late Monday, which Trump did not address when he spoke to Sean Hannity on Fox News shortly after, discussing other potential targets and quibbling over whether or not the conflict really amounted to a war as there had been no physical fighting.
“Wars are very bad for business,” Scaramucci warned. “They’re not great for the stock market. So I would like to have a negotiated settlement, but there’s nothing on the matrix where you see the concentric circles lining up, where these three groups would say, ‘OK, that’s a deal that all three of us are willing to accept.’”

For the first time in a dozen years, a leading OB-GYN group has updated its guidance on managing hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and other disruptive symptoms that often come with menopause.
Doctors stressed the importance of hormone therapies, which many women are considering again after the removal of federal safety warnings. On Friday, federal officials said the Food and Drug Administration has been taking steps to ensure there's an adequate supply.
Doctors also described various nonhormonal options in the new advice released this month by the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists, or ACOG.
“We would love our patients to go to their OB-GYNs regarding questions about menopause and really advocate for getting the treatment that they need,” said Camille Clare, the group’s president.
Menopause occurs when a woman has gone 12 consecutive months without a menstrual period. In the U.S., it usually happens around age 50. The time leading up to it is called perimenopause, during which the body’s production of the hormones estrogen and progesterone declines sharply.
Problems commonly arise. More than half of women in menopause report having “vasomotor” issues such as hot flashes and night sweats, said ACOG. As many as two-thirds report menopause-related sleep disruption. And more than a third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal women worldwide report depressive symptoms.
In the past, doctors said, many women quietly suffered.
There's growing consensus that "these symptoms should be treated,” said JoAnn Manson, a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School. “This should help to empower women to discuss their symptoms with their healthcare provider.”
Manson said ACOG’s new guidelines are similar to those put out by other medical organizations.
"Moderate to severe or bothersome menopausal symptoms should be treated with hormone therapy as the first line of treatment,” she said. While it's not appropriate for all women, she added, it’s a good option for many.
But some have been wary.
In 2002, a landmark study in women taking a pill-based combination of estrogen and progestin was stopped early because of links to breast cancer, blood clots and other serious issues. Concerns lingered even though later studies showed the benefits of today’s hormone therapies outweigh the risks for many women. For more than 22 years, all hormone-based menopause treatments carried a government warning, which Manson said discouraged patients and doctors from using them.
But last year, the FDA announced it would remove the boxed warning from more than 20 pills, patches and creams containing the hormones estrogen and progestin. On Friday, the FDA approved updated labeling for three additional estrogen-based patches.
Removing the boxed warning has helped revive interest in and demand for the treatments.
Since the FDA labeling change, some women have reported difficulty obtaining estrogen patches in certain doses and formulations.
FDA officials said Friday that despite such reports, they are unaware of “an imminent risk of a nationwide shortage.” Officials also noted that drug manufacturers have doubled their output of the products over the last year by adding extra manufacturing shifts and production capacity.
Stephanie Faubion, medical director at The Menopause Society, said she’s glad to see ACOG’s guidelines stress the importance of these treatments. “It’s undisputed that hormone therapy is the first line and most effective therapy for hot flashes,” she said.
ACOG reviews the latest evidence on hormone therapy and includes detailed information about the various types. Whole-body therapies, which come in pills, patches, sprays, gels and a vaginal ring, deliver doses of hormones into the bloodstream at levels high enough to have significant effects on symptoms like hot flashes. Low-dose vaginal estrogen therapy is applied directly with very little circulating in the blood. It’s often prescribed to women whose biggest complaint is vaginal dryness.
ACOG recommends that decisions about hormone therapy should be made jointly by doctors and patients, and take into account the benefits and risks given a patient's age and medical history. If it’s appropriate, the group advises starting it before age 60, or within 10 years of menopause.
Some patients choose not to take full-body hormonal medications or are advised by their doctors to avoid them because of their medical histories or conditions.
For them, doctors pointed to different medicines. One is fezolinetant, which works in the area of the brain that controls body temperature and blocks a source of hot flashes and night sweats. Another is elinzanetant, which works similarly.
Doctors also said certain antidepressants can help manage symptoms like hot flashes and depression in patients with either or both of these problems.
There’s also evidence supporting some non-drug treatments for hot flashes, night sweats and sleep or mood problems, ACOG said. These include cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness, exercise, clinical hypnosis and acupuncture. Such approaches can be used alone or alongside medications.
Clare said women may see misinformation and disinformation about menopause treatments online, and urged patients to come to their doctors with any questions. ACOG offers advice on sorting out truth from false claims as well as overall information on menopause.
“Women have options. They have lots of options, hormonal and nonhormonal,” Faubion said. “They shouldn’t be told that nothing can be done about their symptoms. Because again, we have evidence for many different things that can help.”

Lionesses to face France and Portugal in Nations League
- Published
England have been drawn to face France, Austria and Portugal in next year's Women's Nations League.
In Nyon, Switzerland, Sarina Wiegman's side were drawn alongside familiar opponents, having faced Portugal in the previous Nations League campaign, while France and Austria have both been recent rivals in major tournament qualifying campaigns.
The Lionesses will begin their campaign in Group A2 across three international windows in February-March, April and June 2027, with each team playing home and away fixtures.
"[France are] a world-class team," said Wiegman. "They have so much quality, they have power, they have technique and they have some players, of course, also playing in the WSL [Women's Super League] and at other top clubs.
"So it's exciting to play them because you will be challenged in the highest possible way and that's what makes us better.
"We played Portugal before the last Euros, when we tied with them away and at home we beat them.
"They're a team who can change their style from playing a possession game to being a little more direct, and they have some players that bring lots of quality on the pitch, but are also powerful in duels."
Now in its third edition, the Nations League also forms part of the qualification pathway for the 2028 Olympic Games and Euro 2029.
The four League A group winners will progress to the semi-finals in October 2027, before the final is played to decide the Nations League champions.
Scotland will face Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden, while the Republic of Ireland were drawn against Spain, Norway and Switzerland.
Wales will play Denmark, Italy and Iceland while Northern Ireland, in Group B3, will play Poland, Finland and Belarus.
Fixture dates and venues will be confirmed in due course.

Jet may have broken apart before Florida crash, officials say, as family named among victims
- Published
Investigators believe parts of a private jet that crashed in Florida and killed all nine onboard may have broken off while it was in the air.
The Learjet 60 had been bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.
A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old co-pilot, were among those who died on Sunday.
The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said weather conditions would be a major focus of the investigation but that it was struggling to access the wreckage due to the huge crater created by the jet on the road in Palm Beach.
The plane crashed on Military Trail, a six-lane road that features businesses and restaurants, at around 12:50 local time (17:50 GMT).
"The biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway," lead investigator Tim Monville said at a news conference on Monday.
The NTSB said the crater, near the entrance to a mobile home park, had become partially filled with water because of severe storms. Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash.
Debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area.
"We do have some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact," the NTSB's Tom Chapman said.
"We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site."
Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was onboard at the time of the crash and whether it can be recovered.
Flight analysis indicates that the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before it crashed.
In air traffic control audio recordings, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".
They can then be heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.
An emergency was declared and they can be heard yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".
Seven passengers died on board, named in a joint statement as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - as well as friends of the family Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and nanny Anita Maria Cetina.
The pilot was named in media reports as 55-year-old Jeffrey Gregory, while Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the co-pilot.
One man in a car on the ground sustained a leg injury.
Who are the victims?
Robinson and Sharp's family described them as "devoted parents" and said their children were "the light of their lives".
"Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever. Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives," the statement read.
Robinson described himself on his LinkedIn page as the founder and CEO of RB2B and Retention.com, and the CEO of Moltsets - all technology companies. Helen Sharp was an artist, according to media reports.
Robinson previously worked at the global financial services business Lehman Brothers and the banking group Barclays. The BBC has contacted the companies.
The joint statement also named nanny Anita Maria Cetina and said she "cared for Emma and Charlie with tenderness and devotion, and she was truly part of the family".
It added: "She showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion."
Rachel Reed and Charmi Fehr were described in the joint family statement as "full of joy and adventure".
"They loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation. From the moment they met, they were all in on each other and the life they were building."
Nathalia Filgueiras's mother, Camila Corteleti, confirmed to US media that her daughter had died in the crash.
Corteleti told the New York Times: "She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top."
Filgueiras had spoken of her pride at receiving her pilot's licence while still a senior in high school in an interview with a local affiliate of CBS News in 2023.
"I like being different than everyone," she said. "Some people think that it's weird that I can fly planes but I can't drive a car - I mean, I can, but a lot of people think it's funny."
A spokesperson for East Coast Jets, where pilot Jeff Gregory used to work, said: "We are deeply saddened to learn that Capt Jeff Gregory was among those who lost their lives in yesterday's tragic aviation accident in Palm Beach."
He was married with two children, US media report.

Calculated, intentional act: Police file chargesheet in Gurugram biker collision case
Gurugram Police charge-sheeted two men for allegedly ramming a woman biker. Video evidence transformed an apparent accident into an attempted murder prosecution.
Police have filed a charge sheet against two men on charges of attempted murder and other offences for allegedly deliberately ramming a car into a motorcycle ridden by a woman on September 13, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
The charge sheet was filed against Kalyan Baisla and Lavnish in a Gurugram court, which took note of it on Monday, officials said on Tuesday.
The incident was recorded by a helmet-mounted camera worn by the motorcyclist, Shivani Chauhan, and a camera belonging to another rider. It sparked outrage after she shared the video on social media.
Shivani, also known as Siya, is a 27-year-old resident of Kalkaji in Delhi. She was travelling with friends from Golf Course Road towards Extension Road when the accused, who were in a white car, allegedly followed the group and made obscene gestures.
The car then allegedly rammed her motorcycle from the side before fleeing. The impact knocked her off the motorcycle and sent her skidding on the road.
After his arrest, Kalyan admitted that the collision was his fault but denied hitting Shivani deliberately. He claimed that he had "lost control near a U-turn".
However, a Special Investigation Team report concluded that "this was not an accident, but a calculated, intentional act".
A senior investigating officer told PTI that police examined CCTV footage from more than 15 locations and included it in the charge sheet.
"This includes footage from GMDA and DLF cameras, as well as footage from a dashcam mounted on the complainant (female biker) and from a camera belonging to a club," the officer said.
There were four people in the car, with Kalyan and his cousin Lavnish seated in the front. Police booked the accused under provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita relating to physical and digital stalking, insulting the modesty of a woman, attempted murder and common intention.
Police Commissioner Sibash Kaviraj formed the special investigation team after receiving a notice from the Haryana Commission for Women.
Gurugram Police arrested Kalyan and Lavnish from Rajgarh in Rajasthan's Dausa district on September 15. Both are lodged in Bhondsi Jail in Gurugram after their bail pleas were rejected.
"Initially, this incident appeared to be a routine accident, but the footage and facts that emerged during the investigation changed the entire narrative. The footage clearly shows that the collision was not accidental, but deliberate. Based on other evidence gathered during the investigation, the police also invoked relevant legal provisions in the case," a senior police officer told PTI.
The two men, who remain in jail after being denied bail, now face charges including attempted murder after investigators concluded that the collision was deliberate and submitted footage and other evidence to the court.

When Sarojini Nadimpally was diagnosed with HER2-positive breast cancer in June 2025, the Delhi-based public health researcher was staring at a hidden reality as daunting as the tumour. One dose of the targeted combination drug she had been prescribed would cost around ₹2.7 lakh — and she needed 18 doses.
As someone who works on access to medicines, she closely followed the government’s recent decision to cap trade margins on 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs at 30%, extending a 2019 cap that covered 42. The government claims that the cap, which takes effect on November 9, can save patients about ₹2,500 crore a year.
“Any intervention to lower the prices of cancer drugs is a welcome step,” says Ms. Nadimpally. “But it remains to be seen how this cap will actually reduce what patients pay.”
Survival versus solvency
Cancer is said to be India’s leading cause of catastrophic health spending. India’s out-of-pocket share for cancer care — estimated by various studies to be 50%-80% of direct treatment costs — is far higher than in most high-income systems, where insurance or tax-funded care generally absorbs the bulk of these expenses.
Experts say that drugs make up around over half the costs of cancer care. “High costs of treatments such as targeted therapies and immunotherapy can lead many patients to defer treatment, opt for cheaper but less effective alternatives or give up altogether,” says Vedant Kabra, principal director, surgical oncology, Fortis Memorial Research Institute, Gurugram.
When pills threaten to outrun savings, the standard of care is down to a cruel trade-off between effectiveness and affordability. For example, at about ₹1.25 lakh a month, a lifetime course of osimertinib, the drug of choice in fighting EGFR-mutated lung cancer while reducing the risk of brain metastases, is beyond the reach of many. “These patients switch to gefitinib, which costs only about ₹2,500 a month, but return with brain secondaries and disease progression,” says Narayanankutty Warrier, senior consultant oncologist, MVR Cancer Centre and Research Institute, Kozhikode. “About 30% new-generation drugs are really good,” he says. “The rest are mostly claims. But even a slight improvement in survival means they become monopoly drugs.”
The pricing conundrum
With its latest order, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) is setting a common trade-margin ceiling on a broad range of cancer medicines, including patented, chemotherapy, targeted, immunotherapy, hormonal and blood cancer drugs. Manufacturers are required to report formulation-level information, including brand name, composition, pack size, PTS (price to stockist) and revised MRP.
The order spells out that a drug with a PTS of ₹70 and an MRP of ₹300 can have an MRP of no more than ₹100, excluding GST. Experts argue that the permitted margin — which amounts to 42.8% of the PTS — is a sizeable mark-up, especially for expensive drugs.
In effect, the government is putting a ceiling on the profit, not the underlying price. For example, the actual prices at which hospitals buy drugs, often after steep discounts negotiated for bulk purchases, are hidden from sight. “A cap on trade margins means little to patients if hospitals and dealers do not pass those savings on, and there is no way of knowing whether they do,” says Ms. Nadimpally.
On October 28, the NPPA published a revised price list for the 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs based on data submitted by companies. The MRPs of 37 drugs remain unchanged, offering an early indication of what the final list may look like. The list also reveals margins that manufacturers, including some Indian generic makers, have had. For instance, palbociclib’s MRP for one brand is down from about ₹40,421 to ₹2,720 a pack, and thiotepa’s from about ₹80,072 to ₹7,150 a vial — drops of more than 90%.
The latest order also counts the cap from the PTS, not from the ex-factory price or the landed cost (price paid after discounts and freight), leaving out upstream additions. The mark-up for cancer medicines is unjustified, says Malini Aisola, co-convener, All India Drug Action Network. “With few middlemen involved in the distribution of these high-value, low-volume products, a hospital or distributor gets to keep nearly all the margin. That legitimises profiteering.”
When it comes to patented, mostly imported medicines, we are price-takers, insists Ms. Aisola. “The government is averse to using its legal powers under the Indian Patent Act and TRIPS (Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights) — such as government use and compulsory licensing — to increase competition.”
The government, she adds, monitors and controls medicine prices based on a proprietary dataset owned by pharmaceutical companies. “This data,” she argues, “underrepresents or completely excludes institutional sales of cancer medicines because of the way the data are gathered and modelled.”
Besides, freebies under patient assistance programmes (PAPs) are now excluded from the calculation. “Including all PAP volumes would expose the true trade mark-ups to hospitals and force a bigger MRP cut,” says Ms. Aisola.
Beyond medicines
Medicines are only a part of the bill. Cut the margin, and the cost could mimic the cancer in finding another site. Other expensive components of treatment —diagnostic tests, surgery, radiotherapy, hospital accommodation, consumables, consultations, drug administration and associated clinical services — also need to be addressed. “Hospitals have several avenues to recoup the shortfall,” says a healthcare activist.
Running a hospital today is highly capital- and cost-intensive. Industry estimates suggest that each bed can cost ₹30 lakh to ₹1.5 crore, and a hospital needs around two-thirds of its beds occupied just to break even. The bills keep coming even when patients are not, says the COO of a Mumbai hospital. . “Hospitals have long relied on margins because they are legally allowed to,” notes Dr. Warrier.
Optimisation, Dr. Kabra avers, needs to go beyond drugs. “Hospitals and doctors get paid progressively less for the same procedure or disease depending on whether a self-paying patient, an insurer or a government health scheme is footing the bill. This squeeze can make care financially unviable, especially in complex interventions,” he points out. He also asks why caps have not yet been applied to manufacturers. “It seems unfair that manufacturers profit several times their production costs while everyone else is held to 30%,” he says. “Yes, manufacturers take greater risks and often only one of the dozens of drugs they research makes it to the market. But the profits they earn cannot be disproportionate forever.”
The price of exclusivity
Drug patents are another issue, point out experts. While many cancer therapies in India now have multiple generic manufacturers despite patents, generics in India are required to demonstrate bioequivalence — the degree to which they match the reference drug — before they can be marketed, says S. Srinivasan, co-founder of LOCOST, a not-for-profit maker of affordable generic medicines. “Affordability of cancer medicines depends not only on patent expiry, but also on whether generic firms can bear the exorbitant costs of bioequivalence testing,” he says.
Hospitals can add to their troubles. For instance, multinational brands of a targeted cancer medication like palbociclib can cost many times more than their generic equivalents, says a healthcare activist, giving hospitals a significantly bigger margin and thereby, an incentive to push the pricier option. “This only undermines affordable generics and entrenches multinationals,” he rues.
Limits of control
Murali Neelakantan, principal lawyer at advisory firm, amicus, calls price controls a “terrible” solution to a demand-supply mismatch. “It has second order, unintended consequences that are difficult to fix,” he says. “Price control can only be an emergency short-term measure to deal with market failure and catastrophic events that cannot be easily mitigated by market interventions.”
Mr. Neelakantan suggests treating drugs like food grains — not subject to price controls — and releasing government-procured drug stocks to stabilise prices whenever supplies fall short. The government, he says, can intervene by building more government hospitals and by procuring goods and services from private healthcare providers in an efficient manner rather than through fragmented schemes. The scale of procurement gives the government immense economic power to influence demand and facilitate price discovery and stabilisation, he points out. “Coercive regulation of prices will further distort the market and incentivise unethical practices, including evasive tactics by market participants,” he warns.
Trade margin caps are, at best, tokenistic, says Mr. Srinivasan. MRPs of anti-cancer drugs are high even after trade margins. “A better approach,” he suggests, “could be to base the MRP on API (active pharmaceutical ingredient) cost plus manufacturing and marketing expenses, with a 100–200% mark-up to recoup post-manufacturing expenses and trade margins.
The best solution for poor or middle-class cancer patients in India, however, would be free medicines provided by the government.” For now, though, a ‘cheaper’ cancer drug is no cure for exorbitant treatment.
(Harsh Kabra is an independent journalist and commentator. harshkabra@gmail.com)

Hot Springs, Arkansas is known for many things – as the childhood home of Bill Clinton, as the former site of Major League Baseball’s spring training (in the era of Babe Ruth), for its beautiful national park, and for its mineral springs and the splendid early 20th century bathhouses built to accommodate legions of spa-goers.
It’s also known as the home of the Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival, the longest-running nonfiction cinematic event in North America. HSDFF celebrated its 35th edition last month, hosting a selection of world premieres and leading contenders in the Oscar race including Once Upon a Time in Harlem, NAZA, American Doctor, Closure, To Hold a Mountain and more.
On the latest edition of Deadline’s Doc Talk podcast, we’re joined by the man in charge of the festival, Hot Springs Documentary Film Institute executive director Ken Jacobson. He tells us how the festival originally began in collaboration with the Motion Picture Academy as a way to showcase Oscar-nominated and Oscar-winning films. This year, HSDFF returned to those roots in a sense by partnering with Deadline for its first ever Documentary Roundtable of distinguished filmmakers in the awards race, a panel that included directors Biljana Tutorov, Poh Si Teng and Michał Marczak, and producer Liani Greaves.
Watch on Deadline
Hot Springs once again presented its Forum, but with a twist this year: it took place without the usual support of the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, because that important entity was defunded under pressure from the Trump administration.
Jacobson, who has long experience in documentary festival programming, tells us about the biggest challenge he faces putting on a nine-day event and how he makes sure the festival attracts filmmakers from around the world while simultaneously showcasing work from the South and mid-South. He also shares insights on how the Academy Awards competition is shaping up as we near next month’s voting for the documentary shortlists.
That’s on the new episode of Doc Talk hosted by Oscar winner John Ridley (12 Years a Slave, Shirley) and Matt Carey, Deadline’s senior documentary editor. The pod is a production of Deadline and Ridley’s Nō Studios.

Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries
- Published
A spate of cyber-attacks that hit supermarket chains across at least 10 European countries on Monday has prompted European Union officials to warn of a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.
Supermarkets have reported problems in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Germany and Sweden, and the significant increase in freezer temperatures has forced retailers to discard food.
Temperatures in chains across Europe reportedly rose as high as 50C (122F).
No-one has yet admitted carrying out the cyber-attacks.
The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores, causing food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.
The security of refrigeration systems as well as other devices that can be monitored remotely has heightened concerns about government-backed hybrid attacks.
The EU's food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the bloc was taking the incidents very seriously and warned of further disruption in the future.
Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier was careful not to attribute blame, but said: "These incidents of course show once again how cyber-attacks can disrupt essential services and affect citizens' daily lives."
"These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents."
In Italy, Giorgia Meloni's government called a meeting with intelligence chiefs, but said the impact was "currently very limited" and most of the food distribution chain had up-to-date security systems able to fend off such attacks.
At least four Co-op supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to the national cybersecurity agency.
Meloni's office said those businesses affected were "mostly still equipped with obsolete security systems, with interfaces directly exposed to the internet and inadequate authentication mechanisms".
Belgian supermarkets were among those hardest-hit, with dozens of stores reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.
Mathieu Tilman, a manager at a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, said he was shocked by this kind of attack: "I don't even understand how anyone could do this... How can we end up throwing away so much food? I find it truly distressing. In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."
In Ireland, 13 SuperValu stores were impacted by what the chain's owner, Musgrave Group, called a cyber-incident. "Replenishment of chilled and frozen ranges in the affected stores is well under way," a spokesman said on Monday.
A small number of corner shops in the Netherlands also suffered disruption. Last month, supermarket chain Albert Heijn had to take several services offline because of a separate cyber-attack.
There was disruption to refrigeration systems at the Rewe Büsken supermarket in western Germany after a cyber-attack on system provider Danfoss, the company told the BBC. Its systems have been back in operation since Monday afternoon.
In Portugal, the Mosqueteiros group said that incidents at seven Intermarché stores had been linked to a cyberattack, which "appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems".
Swedish chain ICA also said "a limited number" of its stores had experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyber-attack, and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
In Finland, irregular temperatures were detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group, which said it was investigating the issue.
In Estonia, at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50C, public broadcaster ERR reported.
In the UK, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned British retailers to update the software on fridge temperature controls.
The agency said the country was likely to suffer an AI-powered cyber-attack on critical national infrastructure within two years.
Richard Horne, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme there were a couple of instances in the UK where "vulnerable technology has been exploited" after the cyber-attacks.
"We don't know the full impact, but we do know there are a couple of instances where vulnerable technology has been exploited and we're working with those organisations."
Asked if there was any evidence that supermarkets in Britain or freezers of the same make or model had been targeted, Horne said: "It's not just supermarkets, it's through the whole food supply chain, and we've been working through the night alerting organisations where we can see they've got exposed technology that's vulnerable in this way."

Many forms of ear infections strike children and adults alike, but among the most common is acute otitis externa, also known as swimmer’s ear.
About 10% of Americans will experience swimmer’s ear during their lifetimes. Adults are affected more commonly, and children only rarely, generally ages 5 to 12.
But you don’t have to be swimming to get swimmer’s ear. Go out jogging or walking, or do yardwork on a hot day, and moisture from perspiration can drip in your ear. However, the occurrence increases fivefold in swimmers – thus the reason the condition came to be called “swimmer’s ear.” It also occurs more frequently in tropical climates because of humidity and higher temperatures.
As doctors who specialise in ear problems, we are actively involved in research and clinical treatment for children and adults struggling with ear, nose and throat problems. Practicing in the state of Florida, we’ve certainly seen our share of patients with swimmer’s ear.
Causes and symptoms of swimmer’s ear
Swimmer’s ear is an infection in the external ear canal, the tube leading from the ear opening to the eardrum. Typically, swimmer’s ear occurs only in one ear, and sometimes the eardrum itself is affected. Moisture trapped in the canal leads to a break in the skin barrier and creates an opening for certain bacteria types to enter or existing ones to overgrow.
One of these culprits is the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is present in soil and water throughout the world. These bacteria favor moist areas, such as sinks, toilets, inadequately chlorinated swimming pools and hot tubs, as well as outdated or inactivated antiseptic solutions.
If you have the infection, you’ll know it. Symptoms generally appear a few days after infection. The main symptom of swimmer’s ear is severe pain and discomfort. It’s particularly noticeable when the outer ear is tugged, or by touching the tragus – that’s the small bump at the front of your ear. Other symptoms include itchiness inside the ear, redness, swelling and drainage. A feeling of fullness, or the perception of a plugged ear, may also occur, along with disturbed balance and temporary hearing loss.
Predisposition to swimmer’s ear
Numerous factors can predispose someone to swimmer’s ear. They include a narrow ear canal, and skin diseases such as eczema or psoriasis. In addition, individuals wearing ear plugs, ear buds or hearing aids may be at an increased risk. Diabetics may also be more prone to the infection.
Swimmer’s ear can also come from something getting stuck inside the ear, excessive ear cleaning or contact with chemicals in hair dye or hairspray.
Diagnosis and treatment
Swimmer’s ear is diagnosed after a health care provider has gathered a thorough history and examined the inside of the ear. The ear canal will typically look red, swollen and moist. There is also a possibility of fluid drainage or the appearance of scaly, shedding skin. Depending on the degree of swelling, the eardrum may be hard to see. A sample of fluid may be removed from the ear and sent to a lab to look for bacteria or fungus.
Eardrops are commonly used to treat swimmer’s ear. These drops often contain antibiotics to kill the infection and steroids to stop the swelling.
One such eardrop is Ciprodex. It contains ciprofloxacin, an antibiotic, and dexamethasone, a powerful steroid. Patients will need to place about four to five drops in the infected ear canal twice a day for seven to 10 days.
Another commonly prescribed drop is Floxin, which contains an antibiotic but not a steroid. It is commonly prescribed in less swollen but still infected ears.
Other drop preparations include Cortisporin, which contains a commonly used combination of neomycin and polymyxin B, as well as hydrocortisone. However, neomycin is also damaging to the inner ear, so doctors nowadays often turn to Ciprodex or Floxin.
In some cases, the ear canal is too swollen for drops to reach the infected area, so the physician may place a wick or stent in the ear canal to keep it open. This will usually be left in place for three to five days until removed by the doctor, although occasionally the wick falls out once the swelling subsides. Usually, after 10 days the infection is resolved and the ear canal skin returns to normal.
Managing a persistent infection
Sometimes swimmer’s ear may not resolve after seven to 10 days of treatment with eardrops. Oral antibiotics are typically recommended if the infection has spread beyond the ear canal or in patients with poorly controlled diabetes. Hospitalization for swimmer’s ear is rarely necessary; however, complications that can occasionally lead to hospitalization include fever, worsening discharge, extensive narrowing of the ear canal or failure of previous treatments.
Among the precautions you can take to prevent swimmer’s ear: Keep the ear canal dry. Tip your head to one side to help the water drain. Use a soft towel or cloth, or gently use a hair dryer near it. If the self-cleansing mechanism of the ear canal is impaired, then the ear canal should be cleansed by a physician.
Since most bacteria prefer a pH-neutral environment, reducing the pH in the ear canal can prevent bacterial overgrowth. A homemade liquid tincture can be mixed from a solution of half rubbing alcohol and half distilled white vinegar. The alcohol combines with the water in the ear and then evaporates. This removes the water while the acidity of the vinegar keeps bacteria from growing.
Two to three drops are usually sufficient and can be applied as a preventive measure soon after the ear has been exposed to moisture. This liquid solution is not a replacement for medical treatment of an actual ear infection and is meant to be used only in people who are prone to such infections because of prolonged or frequent exposure to moisture.
Also, it is important to differentiate swimmer’s ear from a middle ear infection, the most frequent reason for the use of antibiotics in children under age 5. Middle ear infections are usually associated with a viral upper respiratory infection, and they are more often seen during fall and winter, when influenza and cold viruses are more prevalent.
(Thomas Schrepfer, Assistant Professor of Pediatric Otolaryngology, University of Florida; Rex Haberman Associate Clinical Professor of Otology and Neurotology, University of Florida)

Taking serious note of as many as 14 State-run universities functioning without Vice-Chancellors/Syndicates for the last three to four years, the Madras High Court on Tuesday called for an explanation from Tamil Nadu government as to when normalcy would be restored in all those educational institutions.
Justice N. Anand Venkatesh requested Advocate General Vijay Narayan to appear on behalf of the Higher Education Secretary, whom the judge impleaded suo motu in a batch of applications pending before him, and explain the reason for the absence of Vice-Chancellors/Syndicates on November 17, 2026.
The judge was seized of a batch of eight sub applications filed by the retired employees of Annamalai University to reopen their contempt of court petitions filed against the university Registrar since their pension had not been disbursed yet. In response, the Registrar said, the process was under way and sought time.
Senior counsel R. Singaravelan, representing the applicants, told the court that the Registrar was facing practical difficulties in administering the institution since it did not have a Vice-Chancellor or a Syndicate and was being run by a Convenor Committee headed by the Higher Education Secretary.
After recording his submission, the judge said, he dealt with yet another major issue where the retirement benefits of 500 former employees of the University of Madras got settled after a prolonged pressure exerted by the court. Anna University too was facing a similar issue.
“The common thread that runs through these Universities is the functioning of the Universities without Vice-Chancellors and properly-constituted Syndicate and their present functioning with the assistance of temporary Registrars and Convenor Committees,” the judge highlighted.
He went on to state: “The Convenor Committee headed by the IAS Officer, at the best can only be a temporary arrangement and it is virtually impossible for this Committee to run the Universities and administer the Colleges falling under the purview of those Universities.”
Lamenting that this status was continuing for three to four years, the judge said: “It has a direct impact on the functioning of the educational institutions. If the State government does not take immediate steps to set right this anomaly, it will directly impact the higher education in Tamil Nadu.”
Wanting to find a solution to the problem, the judge suo motu impleaded the Higher Education Secretary as one of the respondents and directed the officer to apprise the court of the steps taken by the government so far to restore normalcy in all the 14 State universities which were suffering without a regular administrative setup.

The leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital.
Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in central Delhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag.
The Cockroach movement initially emerged back in May as online satire, but has since grown into one of the most substantial challenges to the powerful Modi government over its 12-year rule.
Alongside student groups and opposition parties, its supporters have in the past month been out on the streets across India’s biggest cities calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of India’s electoral rolls that allegedly favours the ruling Narendra Modi government with the deletion of 130m names. The election commission and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) deny the claims.
The authorities, particularly in Delhi, have met the recent protests with a draconian crackdown, including bans on public gatherings, the deployment of tens of thousands of police, and detentions of thousands last weekend.
Friday’s protest was called by Dipke after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. They were sentenced to five days in jail this week for jumping police barricades and holding a brief protest – including waving the Indian flag – at a site recently restricted by police for demonstrations in Delhi.
At a press conference on Thursday, Dipke condemned the “repressive” attempts to silence the CJP movement and called on supporters to come out and show Narendra Modi “that we are not afraid”. He added: “If waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready.”
Delhi police had once again taken extreme measures to try to prevent Friday’s demonstration, due to be held at a park in a busy commercial centre in the heart of Delhi, from going ahead. Police were deployed en masse to the area and a police notice was sent to Dipke instructing him to call off the protest. The Delhi local authority also shut down the park where the protest was due to take place.
When Dipke refused to call it off, police detained him en route, just as people began to assemble for the protest. In videos captured of his arrest, the CJP leader was seen holding an Indian flag aloft and saying: “I have not broken any law right now … how can you detain me?” as he was led away by dozens of police officers.
In a post after his detention, the CJP posted on social media: “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”
Neha Bora, a student leader who has become a figurehead of the protests, was also detained on Friday as she began a march in the centre of the capital.
Despite Dipke’s detention, about 2,000 protesters still gathered and unfurled flags at the protest around Delhi’s Connaught Place. Among them was 23-year-old Sanna, who said the brutal police crackdown on peaceful protests over recent weeks demonstrated that India was “on a pathway to dictatorship under the Modi government”.
“We are only out here to peacefully hold up the Indian flag and they treat us as if we are criminals, not citizens exercising our democratic rights,” she said. “Gyanesh Kumar must resign, and no matter what the police do, detaining us or crushing our skulls, we still won’t stop protesting until he is gone.”
Smaller protests also took place in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna on Friday.
The BJP has claimed that the Cockroach movement and the political opposition alliance have been holding protests to cause “anarchy” in the country. “Their sole intention is to stage a coup in the country,” said the BJP’s national spokesperson, Sambit Patra.
The authorities have also gone to unusual lengths to punish figures who have been seen at the recent protests calling for Kumar’s resignation.
In Mumbai, the Bollywood actor Imran Khan was given a notice to leave the country after he was detained by police while attending a demonstration last weekend. Khan, who holds a US passport, was told to leave the country by the end of the month, an order he is now challenging in the courts.

What to know about the crisis around Poland's Constitutional Tribunal
Judges at Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal are meeting to decide its future after the court president was suspended in a dispute with the government
WARSAW, Poland -- Judges at Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal are meeting Tuesday to decide its future, following the suspension of the court president in a dispute with the government and a battle over the future of the rule of law.
Protesters have gathered daily outside the court in Warsaw since the suspension of the tribunal’s top judge, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the nationalist-conservative PiS party when it was in power 2015-2023.
The pro-European government of Donald Tusk accuses Poland’s President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, of blocking judges elected by the parliamentary majority from taking up their posts at the tribunal.
Święczkowski has called his suspension a “coup d’etat.”
On Friday, riot police encircled the building while the most senior of the newly elected judges announced Święczkowski's suspension from inside.
Nawrocki, who was on a visit to Senegal, turned his plane around to return to Warsaw, joining the protesters outside the tribunal.
Here's what to know.
The current crisis around the Constitutional Tribunal is the latest round in a long-term battle between the pro-European government led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and the main opposition party, Law and Justice (PiS), which seeks to return to power in elections next year.
Critics in Poland and the European Union accuse PiS, which led the country between 2015 and 2023, of imposing political control over key judicial institutions, including the Constitutional Tribunal. The European Union fined Poland for undermining the rule of law.
Tusk’s government came to power in 2023 promising to restore the independence of the judiciary, but its efforts have been blocked by two successive PiS-aligned presidents, including Nawrocki.
After repeated failed attempts to wrest control of the tribunal from PiS, the government decided to take a less orthodox path, one that Tusk himself said might not be to everyone’s liking.
Judges on the Constitutional Tribunal are elected by Parliament and sworn in by the president. In mid-October, parliament elected another judge, meaning judges not friendly to PiS would have a majority, but Nawrocki refused to swear in the new appointment.
The judges elected this year took an oath anyway during a ceremony in parliament, a move recognized by the government camp but rejected by PiS. On Friday, the new appointees entered the tribunal premises while riot police guarded the building.
One of the new judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, published the notice of suspension for Święczkowski, the tribunal president, on the court's website. She argued that she had the authority to do so because she is the most senior judge on the court and that he had allegedly committed irregularities while in office.
Many legal experts, as well as the European Commission and the EU's top court, agree that reforms to the justice system introduced by PiS while in power were highly problematic. In 2023 the EU Court of Justice ruled that the Polish Constitutional Tribunal was no longer an impartial court after PiS appointments.
Tusk’s camp and PiS accuse each other of breaking Polish law, including the Constitution.
“Restoring the rule of law is our obligation,” Tusk wrote on X on Friday evening. “After years of lawlessness under PiS this is a difficult process, sometimes painful and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.”
“This is a blatant, criminal attack on the constitutional order,” former PiS Justice Minister Zbigniew Ziobro, the architect of the reforms criticized by the European Union, wrote on X Friday evening. “That is why I call for resistance that will be loud, firm, united and fearless.”
But while human rights campaigners back the principle of reversing the PiS changes, some have criticized the methods.
“The legal basis for the suspension are doubtful and the presence of the police on the tribunal grounds caused a strong escalation of political emotions on both sides,” said Maciej Nowicki of the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights in Poland. “Those emotions might bury any hope for finding a solution to the crisis.”
A complete “reset” of the Constitutional Tribunal, involving the appointment of an entirely new bench under revised rules, could be necessary, he said.
Anna Korwin-Piotrowska called a general assembly of the Constitutional Tribunal judges for Nov. 3, to decide on the future of the court but also potentially on Święczkowski's immunity. That could potentially pave the way for the court president's criminal prosecution.
But it is unlikely the assembly will reach decisions that all sides accept. Judges chosen by the post-2023 parliamentary majority do not recognize the legitimacy of some judges appointed under PiS, while PiS takes the opposite view.
Decisions require a quorum, but the government and PiS disagree over which judges are eligible to vote and what constitutes a quorum. Some judges appointed under PiS may not even show up for the meeting on Tuesday in protest.
The current crisis is unlikely to be resolved on Tuesday
The functioning of the Constitutional Tribunal had already been impaired for years. Trust in judicial institutions has been eroded both by political conflicts around the courts and the daily inefficiencies of an overburdened judiciary.
In that sense, the current crisis will not suddenly make things worse for regular Poles.
But the Constitutional Tribunal makes decisions that are consequential. A ruling by this court in 2020 led to further restrictions on Polish women's access to legal abortions. The tribunal is needed to curb potentially illegal government decisions, Nowicki said.
Ensuring the Constitutional Tribunal operates well and independently of political power remains a key objective for Polish society.
The current crisis will also intensify the already high political polarization in Poland, one year ahead of general elections. In turn, that will make it much harder to achieve the kind of consensus needed to really fix the court.

Voting had only been underway in the US for a few hours and polls still hadn’t even opened in some parts of the country, but Republican strategist and pro-Trump influencer Joey Mannarino had apparently seen enough.
“MASSIVE AMOUNTS OF VOTER FRAUD BEING REPORTED ALL OVER THE COUNTRY!” Mannarino asserted on X at 9:02 am EST, offering no evidence to support his declaration. “The Democrats are stealing our country right out from under us!”
As in any other election year, as polling places opened, people began showing up to vote, and voting machines started whirring into action, some jurisdictions ran into problems.
Severe flooding along Florida’s Space Coast meant about 20 polling places had to be moved. Bad storms over the weekend likely caused brief power outages in Arizona’s Maricopa County, forcing the temporary closure of several polling places. Pennsylvania’s Luzerne County was missing a scanner box. And in Westchester County, New York, voting in the hotly contested House race between incumbent Republican representative Mike Lawler and Democrat Cait Conley hit a roadblock early on Tuesday morning when machines stopped accepting paper ballots.
Voting machine malfunctions—much like bad weather and power outages—are fairly common during elections. While typically attributable to some mundane problem like ageing components, these malfunctions are often the source of rumors or conspiracy theories.
And like other election years in recent memory, there’s a network of MAGA influencers, Republican lawmakers, pro-Trump trolls and administration officials with enormous online audiences who are waiting for anything—literally anything—that they can claim is evidence of voter fraud. The Trump administration has also been laying the groundwork, priming their electorate to believe that the American voting system is rigged against them.
Within minutes of reports that ballot scanners in Westchester weren’t working, some of the biggest proponents of election conspiracy theories seized on the county-wide glitch to claim that Democrats were sabotaging equipment to prevent Lawler from winning.
The Westchester County board of elections initially blamed the fault on “the thickness of the paper ballots” in a statement issued two hours after polls opened. But 20 minutes later, county officials updated the statement, removing the reference to the thickness of the paper and instead blaming a general “issue involving paper ballots.”
In a separate statement published online, Westchester county executive Ken Jenkins said that once the issues with the ballot machines are resolved, he’ll “convene a bipartisan team to conduct a thorough review of the decisions and failures that led to this debacle, determine where accountability lies and ensure that this never happens again. “I want to be absolutely clear,” Jenkins wrote. “This situation is unacceptable.” Later in the day, New York State officials put out an additional statement, saying that the problem was that most machines in the county had outdated programming, which meant they could not recognize and process Election Day ballots.
“The immediate priority is to restore scanning capability to at least one voting machine at every polling location, with additional machines being brought online as the day progresses,” officials said. They added that the programming issue had only caused ballots to be rejected, not tabulated incorrectly, so voters should have full confidence that “every valid vote will be counted.”
In a post on X, the Republican National Committee wrote that together with Democrats it is “seeking a joint court order to require central tabulation of ballots at the County Board of Elections.”
New York representative Claudia Tenney—who has backed efforts to challenge the results of the 2020 election—also jumped into the fray. “No surprise,” Tenney wrote. “The Democrats in NY will do anything and everything to cheat.” Conservative broadcaster Mark Levin shared Tenney’s post to his 5 million followers.
All manner of MAGA-world influencers have also weighed in. “This is how the Left steals elections,” wrote Katie Miller, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser Stephen Miller.
“Ban voting machines and prosecute those who’ve used them to cheat,” wrote president Donald Trump’s former spokesperson Liz Harrington.
“Democrats are already trying to steal the election in New York today,” wrote MAGA influencer Laura Loomer. Loomer also weighed in on polling location problems elsewhere. “The Democrats are already cheating” she wrote on her Loomer Unleashed account, in response to a post about power outages forcing closure of voting centers in Maricopa County.
The Center for an Informed Public at the University of Washington, which tracks online rumors about elections, found that posts on X about the malfunctioning machines—“often with a conspiratorial framing”—were coming about 150 times a minute just after 10:00am EST.
While Lawler urged voters to “stay in line” and cast their ballots despite the issues with the scanners, pro-Trump influencer Phillip Buchanan, known as Catturd, shared Lawler’s post writing: “Every. Single. Election. It's always somthing [sic]”. Catturd also boosted conspiracies about “Democrat shenanigans” in Florida’s Broward County, which suffered technical difficulties which were quickly resolved. MJ Ultra, a prominent pro-Trump QAnon account on X, added: “Broward County Florida is corrupted as hell.”
Rogan O’Handley, known online as DC Draino, called what was happening in Westchester the “the Maricopa Method of stealing” while also boosting conspiracy theories about Broward County. Meanwhile Trump’s nominee for ambassador to Jamaica, Kari Lake, also shared conspiracy theories about the issues in Westchester, as well as calling out so-called liberal “shenanigans” in Maricopa County. Lake has baselessly claimed her 2022 Arizona gubernatorial race and her 2024 Senate race were rigged.
While all of this has been unfolding on X, Trump has been largely preoccupied with other matters. He spent the better part of the morning complaining on Truth Social that people had taken him seriously when he announced—jokingly, he says—on Tuesday his plans to rename the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to “The Trump Reflecting Pool.” He eventually got around to posting about Lawler’s race, but didn’t mention the issues with the ballot scanners.
