Canva is cutting or relocating more than 1,200 jobs, representing 22% of its global workforce, as part of a major restructure that includes laying off staff who helped build the Australian-founded design platform.
The changes mirror a trend across the technology sector, where software companies are fighting to stay competitive against cheaper artificial intelligence disrupters while aggressively embedding AI tools themselves.
Canva’s chief executive, Melanie Perkins, said in an email to staff on Wednesday that the restructure was “without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history”.
“For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs,” she said. “Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today.”
The restructure will affect 1,271 people, according to the company, as it focuses on “collapsing layers” and bringing “more teams together in person”.
“We know relocating is a big decision for those being asked to consider it, and we’re committed to making the process as smooth as possible with comprehensive support,” said Perkins, who did not specify the exact number of job losses.
Those leaving Canva will receive at least six months of salary and retain healthcare coverage for a further 12 months in countries where workers receive that benefit. They can also keep their laptops.
Those leaving can also apply for US$10,000 (A$14,000) grants to start their own ventures.
The graphic design company is one of Australia’s most successful startups and has long been touted as a candidate for a blockbuster listing on the Nasdaq.
But it has now added to a wave of restructures in the technology sector, which has included 1,600 redundancies at the software company Atlassian, and job losses at Afterpay’s owner, Block, and at WiseTech Global, another software company.
While established software companies have rejected the threat of a “SaaS-pocalypse”, a term used to describe the idea that AI becomes so advanced that specialised software becomes redundant, many have overhauled their business models in response or aggressively adopted AI tools.
Unlike Atlassian, Block and WiseTech, Canva did not mention AI in its restructure announcement.

Vallari Sheel wishes she could carry a camera or a pair of binoculars without being asked what her father does for a living. Once, looking at a tree in her south Delhi neighbourhood, about 50 metres away from her home, a man in a car screamed at her: “You have been clicking photos here for 10 days. What are you going to do with them?”
Sheel, an urban ecologist, spends hours observing trees of all types in all seasons. She often travels by car for her own safety, worries about the impact of her work on her family, and has clear guidance for her female interns when they are, inevitably, approached: don’t engage, don’t respond.
“It’s the men who ask such intrusive questions: Who are you? Where are you from? What does your father do?” she says.
Sheel was recounting these experiences atop Delhi’s oldest fort inside Sanjay Van, a sprawling city forest overlooking a 12th-century minaret. She was one of about 20 women who had gathered on a crisp Sunday morning in October to enjoy nature, safely. Many had never experienced a forest before.
Among the group were a scientist who had stopped birding since she moved to Delhi, a psychiatrist who can’t find a safe place to run, and an environmental planner who cycles everywhere. For many women, simple pleasures such as enjoying nature have become beset by gender crimes.
“The city feels designed to crush any form of freedom, any form of exploration,” says Neha Sinha, who organised the walk. Author of My Wild City: Finding Nature, Meaning, and Hope in India’s Capital, Sinha has been organising these walks for two years.
During her own walks around the city’s forts, forests and wetlands to observe the diminishing number of fireflies, flying foxes, howling jackals, leopards and hyenas, civets and owls, and groves of 350-year-old trees, she has faced the wrath of men. She has changed her route countless times to mislead stalkers, and been asked by men on the street how much she would charge for sex.
“As has everybody else,” she says. “Nearly every woman I know has called a cop saying ‘I have a stalker.’ In a culture that tells you not to go out … how do you make nature your own?”
Two weeks before the women gathered on the walking trails of Sanjay Van, dotted with ruellias, vajradantis and jaal trees, hundreds of people had joined a protest in Delhi over the gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park.
Their demand was to make public spaces safer for women. The government’s response was to ban entry to public parks after sunset.
For Alankrita Narayan, a wildlife conservation student who often needs to work alone at night, that rule was unhelpful. During an internship, she recalls, her organisation trained her for worst-case scenarios in the jungle: What if something happens to your partner? What if you encounter a man carrying a weapon? What if you encounter a forest officer asking for sexual favours?
“And I was like, where did the animal come in here? What if I’m caught alone and a leopard comes in front of me? And they were like, ‘Oh, don’t worry about the leopard. It’s a man you don’t want to run into,” she says. Sinha agrees: “Animals have rules.”
Paroma Mukherjee, a photographer, recalls the advice she once got from a well-known photographer: be inconspicuous, wear clothes that blend in, keep your equipment small. “But then, he was a man. So he could blend in,” she adds.
“Men can pee on the road and we can’t even carry a camera,” another woman says. “You know, we had to take a detour today to avoid a lonely stretch on our way here,” says another. “I carry a pepper spray,” another adds.
On group walks, the women pick up and drop off each other at their homes, wait outside the forest gate until everyone has arrived, and stick together in isolated areas. “I always tell women, ‘Don’t go alone’,” Sinha says.
“We started the walk at 7am today, which is late for birdwatching, but everybody could not leave home while it was still dark,” she says.
However, the group agree that many of these measures might not work for women from less privileged backgrounds, who then miss out.
“No woman in the city is fully free,” Sinha says.
Walking as a woman is an act of resistance, as is observing nature. “Because you’re actually slowing down when you do that,” she says. “It’s so different from the instant gratification culture that we have today. It is more of an immersion, rather than conquering. Both are very political acts.”
In the heart of New Delhi, where India’s senior officials and dignitaries live, there are thousands of fruit bats that swarm out of their roosts every evening to feast on mahua trees.
“And on very clear wintry nights, when everything is silent, I even hear jackals crying and laughing from my home. It’s almost like a parallel city,” Sinha says.
Over three hours, the women collect cuttings, peer and marvel at speckle-like flowers through a pocket microscope, discuss the colonial concepts of wild plants labelled as weeds, chat about the drongo, black kite and tailorbird they spotted, and the next walk.
“Can we do it at night?” someone asks. “What would the forest look like at night?”
Sinha describes a previous night walk experience when frogs had put up an orchestral noise, fireflies lit the bushes and jackals were laughing. “It was the most eerie, magical, bewitching atmosphere I have ever experienced,” she says.
Men, she points out, can simply go ahead and enjoy such experiences, but women have to create an ecosystem around them to be able to.
But, she promises her enthusiastic group, she will try to arrange a night walk.

Carney says U.S. 'asking less and offering more' with 'more intense' trade talks underway
Some of Canada's red lines now seen by U.S. as off the table: PM
Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada and the U.S. have made progress on reaching a trade deal, but stressed more work is needed before any agreement is finalized.
"They're asking less and they're offering more, but we're not quite there," Carney said of the state of negotiations while on the sidelines of meeting with other Commonwealth leaders in Antigua on Tuesday.
After trade talks collapsed dramatically in August, Carney said "more intense negotiations" have since begun.
The prime minister attributed that to the White House's position shifting on some of Canada's "red lines."
When talks fell apart over the summer, the Canadian side said U.S. negotiators took issue with rules that ensure French-language content is easy to find on streaming platforms, such as Netflix, and that the Americans tried to restrict Canada's ability to strike trade deals with other countries.
"Those are now off the table. That's very welcome," said Carney.
The progress, as the prime minister described it, on the trade file comes as Trump's Republican Party faces what could be a tough midterm showing.
Pollsters have been expecting a blue wave as American voters increasingly voice frustrations about the cost of living, driven in part by the war in Iran and tariffs, in the lead up to Tuesday's vote.
In an interview Tuesday morning, Trump told Fox News that his administration was nearing a trade agreement with Canada.
While Carney didn't outline what issues remain, autos are expected to be a key sticking point, as they were in August before talks collapsed — triggering new tariffs on both sides.
Carney said he'll meet Trump in China later this month at the APEC summit.

Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good physical and mental health but is living in near-complete isolation, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years.
“She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong,” Kim Aris said. “I don’t think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she’s been held in solitary confinement from what I gather.”
After being deposed in a 2021 military coup, the Nobel Peace prize laureate has been moved to an unspecified location in the capital. “I’m still not entirely sure where she is,” said Aris. “I think it’s a residence in Naypyidaw, which is fenced off and it has a scrubby bit of land around it.”
Aris, who has lived in the UK most of his life and whose late father was a British historian, was allowed to speak to his mother on Thursday at the Myanmar embassy in London. While he welcomed the chance to talk, he said the invitation was part of a “public relations” campaign by the country’s military leaders.
The former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild international diplomatic ties, and in April switched his military fatigues for civilian clothes after elections that were widely condemned as a sham.
Activists have long demanded “proof of life” for Aung San Suu Kyi, as well as scores of other political prisoners. In August, she was finally photographed during a Red Cross visit. Last week, a government spokesperson published images of her smiling in a wood-panelled room as officials delivered two gardening books given to her as gifts by Britain’s King Charles. A paper calendar on the wall behind her showed the date.
Aris said these photo-ops were well-known stunts that the regime had used before to pretend his mother, a national icon, was being treated fairly. The daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San has spent much of her life since the late 1980s in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements.
“She remains completely shut off from the rest of the world. I think she’s unaware of what’s happening outside of where she is because she’s not allowed any newspapers or radio or television,” Aris said. “She’s been locked up for five years on trumped-up, politically motivated charges and she should be free.”
Ruled for decades by generals and suffering from western sanctions, Myanmar experienced a brief democratic moment after Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to run in a 2015 election that her party overwhelmingly won. She took up the role of “state counsellor” under a civilian-military power-sharing agreement.
Her international reputation was soon tarnished after the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims. Aung San Suu Kyi flew to the international court of justice in The Hague, where she said she acknowledged military units might have used “disproportionate force”, but defended the government against accusations of genocide.
Aris said that his mother was never “silent” on the Rohingya crisis and what she said on the issue “could fill volumes”. Under her leadership, Myanmar launched a domestic inquiry and appointed the former UN chief Kofi Annan to head a commission.
He added that as state counsellor, Aung San Suu Kyi was “always walking on a tightrope”, knowing the military could strip her of her fragile power at any moment.
“The very hard-won nascent democracy that she was trying to lead was holding on to things by a thread,” he said. “The military could have taken over at any point, and they were doing their best to make my mother’s situation a lot more difficult and to undermine her position. And I think in that respect they did a pretty good job.”
The 2021 power grab by the military triggered a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitors.
Aris said the level of public global support for his mother had “dwindled incredibly” since the Rohingya crisis and that the whole country was now suffering from a lack of international attention. While many governments have called for Aung San Suu Kyi’s release, she is not treated as the beloved international figure that she once was.
“Never mind my mother, the fact that people ignore what’s happening in Burma shouldn’t be down to what was being done to the Rohingya,” he said, using the country’s former name. “And that seems to be the case sometimes, that people say: ‘Oh, well, look how the Rohingya were treated. We can ignore what’s happening in Burma.’”

"Do you want to see a Rahul Gandhi vs Narendra Modi open debate?" Congress leader wrote on X.
NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi doubled down on his call for a debate with Prime Minister Narendra Modi over allegations of "foreign backing" levelled by both rival parties. His Congress and the BJP."Do you want to see a Rahul Gandhi vs Narendra Modi open debate?" the Congress leader wrote on X while posting a poll that contained two tricky options: "Yes, Modi Ji, Daro Mat" and "No, Modi Ji, Dar Gaye".The Congress leader, in a quirky note, also asked BJP's top brass, which includes some of PM Modi's colleagues in the Cabinet, to convince the Prime Minister to agree to a debate."Rajnath Singh Ji, Nitin Gadkari Ji, Shivraj Singh Chouhan Ji, Yogi Adityanath Ji, you you always have the PM’s best interest in mind, please convince him to come," the Congress scion quipped in the post.
The Rae Bareli Lok Sabha MP posted the poll hours after he renewed his challenge to PM Modi to face him in an open debate, saying 24 hours had passed since he dared the PM.In a video shared on X, Rahul said, “24 hours have passed, Modi ji. I challenged you. You say that the opposition is anti-national. Pick any stage, any venue, and debate me.”“Who is the anti-national? Who has connections with foreign forces? And what kind of connections are they? Do it as soon as possible, don't be afraid,” he said.
On Monday, Rahul had challenged the Prime Minister to an open debate on allegations of him becoming Prime Minister with "foreign help", saying the latter would not dare to accept it.The whole showdown began after Rahul retorted to Modi's 'Ekta Diwas' speech, in which the PM accused the opposition of turning into an "obstructionist force" (avrodh paksh).The Prime Minister also warned against forces "engaged in conspiracies to divide" the country, saying social media was "being weaponised, rumours being spread, and attempts being made to tarnish India's image"."When the country was seeking solutions to external challenges, some forces within the country were also creating instability by spreading lies and rumours. But the countrymen stood shoulder to shoulder with the nation," PM Modi said.“It is our misfortune that at this time in the country, the opposition has turned into an Avrodh Paksh rather than Virodh Paksh. In their frustration, these people are standing as obstacles in the way of the country’s development.
This is not opposition; this is obstruction,” he added.In a veiled reference to Rahul's foreign trips, he said, “Due to the frustration of more than a decade, these people have now come out in the open. Who is secretly meeting whom abroad? Whom are the anti-India forces supporting? Who is speaking the language of India’s enemies? We will have to recognise all these patterns.”

Midterms, midterms, midterms

First U.S. bird flu death of the year after cattle exposure
A person in Washington state has died from complications of the bird flu, the AP reported yesterday. It’s the first such death this year in the U.S., and the third overall since bird flu became a major public health concern in 2024. (The first two deaths were from the H5N1 strain of the virus. The Washington case stemmed from a rarer version, H5N5.)
It’s another day I wish Helen Branswell was still here. She reported extensively on bird flu over her career at STAT, and her most recent reporting offers a reminder: Cases over the past few years have largely been milder than expected, leaving scientists relieved and puzzled. (Also: Drinking raw milk is always a bad idea, Helen wrote, but especially when bird flu is circulating.)
Read more on the Washington case. And in more solemn infectious disease news: New York saw its first measles-related death in 30 years, the state’s governor announced yesterday.
FDA approves generic HIV prevention shot
The FDA has taken a key step to improve access to a groundbreaking HIV prevention medication for dozens of low- and middle-income countries. The injectable drug, lenacapavir, offers virtually complete protection against the virus with one administration every six months. More than a year after approving the brand name version, sold by Gilead Sciences, the agency gave tentative approval to Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories to make a generic version.
The move comes two years after Gilead reached licensing deals with six generic drugmakers, including Dr. Reddy’s, to produce and distribute a lower-cost version to 120 mostly low- and middle-income countries. Read more from STAT’s Ed Silverman on who the generic can help and how much it will ultimately cost.
Scientists are re-thinking ‘three-parent IVF’
I hope you took some time yesterday to read Megan Molteni’s incredible reporting on IVF clinics around the world pitching older women on a reproductive technique known as “three-parent IVF” as a way for them to have biological children, despite scant evidence that it works. Go read that story if you haven’t yet. Today, Megan and STAT contributor Edward Chen bring us a follow-up on the thorny ethical questions about developing the procedure.
The technique, formally known as mitochondrial replacement technology, was developed to reduce the risk of children inheriting sometimes fatal mitochondrial diseases from their mothers. Pushback against it has mainly focused on its expanding use as an infertility treatment, as Megan wrote. But now, some scientists are rethinking the entire approach due to questions around ethics, safety, and efficacy.
“The general public may have the idea that it is very safe and low risk and that’s just not the case,” said Bert Smeets, a clinical genomics professor who serves on the committee that reviews applications from patients to receive MRT at the sole U.K. clinic that has a license to perform it. Read more on why some of the data is worrying experts.
10%
That’s the proportion of minors who went to the ER after an electric bike accident that ultimately had brain injuries, according to an analysis of emergency room data published yesterday in JAMA. That’s double the rate of brain injuries caused by non-motorized bikes.
Researchers assessed data from six medical institutions between 2023 and early 2026, finding that injury rates for e-bikes and e-scooters increased much faster than harms from traditional, non-motorized bikes and scooters over those years. And while kids who get hurt on these motorized vehicles are generally older, 24% of e-bike injuries and 44% of e-scooter trauma occurred in kids younger than 12.
How one doctor got better at his job, overnight
Last fall, ophthalmologist Robert Kinast attended a meditation retreat in the Santa Cruz Mountains, hoping for a respite from his busy medical practice. But when he and the other attendees were asked to stay awake and meditate through dawn, Kinast found himself revisiting the most devastating injuries he’d witnessed as a doctor: Eyes ruptured by knives, fireworks, bungee cords, windshields, beer bottles, sticks, rocks, fish hooks, and more.
“That night taught me how the inner work of meditation and self-inquiry can support the outer work of patient care,” Kinast writes in a new First Opinion essay. Read more on how he’s changed his behavior in clinic to stay grounded and better serve patients.

Trillions of bacteria living in the human gut may play a role in Parkinson’s disease, a brain disorder that causes tremors, stiffness, and slowed movement, according to a new study involving patients from Keralam.
Researchers from the Cochin University of Science and Technology (CUSAT) and the Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST), Thiruvananthapuram, found significant differences between the gut bacteria of Parkinson’s patients and those of healthy individuals. The findings were published online in npj Parkinson’s Disease, an international scientific journal.
Parkinson’s disease occurs when nerve cells in the brain that produce dopamine, a chemical that helps control movement, gradually die. Scientists have long suspected that the gut and brain communicate continuously, and that an imbalance in gut bacteria could contribute to inflammation affecting the brain. Studies have shown that non-motor symptoms, including constipation and other gastrointestinal problems, can appear years before the tremors begin in Parkinson’s patients.
The study involved 65 Parkinson’s patients attending SCTIMST’s Comprehensive Care Centre for Movement Disorders and 65 healthy individuals, most of whom were the patients’ spouses. Spouses were included as healthy individuals for comparison, as they were more likely to share similar diets and living conditions.
Metagenomic sequencing
Researchers analysed stool samples using metagenomic sequencing (16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing), a technique that identifies the bacteria present and helps assess their potential functions in the gut. They found higher levels of bacteria potentially associated with inflammation and lower levels of beneficial bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids, which help maintain the gut lining healthy and regulate the immune system, in Parkinson’s patients.
The researchers suggest that the shift in bacterial communities could weaken the gut barrier and allow inflammation to spread.
“The study found that differences in the abundances of these bacteria were strongly associated with disease severity and other clinical features of Parkinson’s disease,” said Baby Chakrapani P. S., director of the Centre for Neuroscience and assistant professor in the Department of Biotechnology at CUSAT. “The findings also suggest that gut bacteria may be linked to disease progression through their influence on processes involving dopamine, glutamate, and GABA, chemicals that play important roles in brain function.”
Funded by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), the study was conducted by Aneesa P. A., a research associate at CUSAT, under the supervision of Mr. Chakrapani and Dr. Syam Krishnan of SCTIMST.
Gut bacterial composition is influenced by factors such as diet, age, sex, and lifestyle. Differences in these factors, as well as genetics, could explain why studies in different populations have reported inconsistent associations between particular bacteria and Parkinson’s disease.
According to the researchers, this is the first study in an Indian population to integrate gut microbiome composition with its functional role in Parkinson’s disease. The findings could help future research into simple tests for early diagnosis of the disease and treatments aimed at restoring gut health.

It could be the opening of a Jurassic Park rip-off: scientists examining ancient dinosaur bones find what appear to be fossilised red blood cells, and traces of the molecule that gives the beast’s blood its distinctive crimson hue.
But that is what researchers are claiming to have discovered after analysing the hind leg bones of a small, meat-eating dinosaur called an Aratasaurus that lived and died in what is now north-eastern Brazil 115m years ago.
Electron microscope images of the dinosaur bones revealed small, round structures that resemble red blood cells in fine channels where blood vessels once ran, while chemical tests identified the presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around the body.
Such claims are controversial because biological tissues and molecules can break down fast, leaving little or no trace in ancient fossils. But if confirmed, it would open up entirely new avenues for scientists, allowing them to investigate dinosaur blood, metabolism and even their activity levels.
“We are seeing a mineral and molecular echo of the dinosaur’s original biology,” said Prof Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Western Australia who led the research team. “Fossilised red blood cells with distinct chemistry related to heme have never been found in situ in any fossil, let alone a dinosaur. This is a world first.”
The fossilised remnants of the Aratasaurus were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil, where researchers continue to study them. While analysing the dinosaur’s hind leg bones, Grice spotted the structures that resembled red blood cells.
The scientists’ suspicions that they were looking at red blood cells were bolstered when chemical tests came back positive for heme and its breakdown products. Tests also found traces of the amino acid building blocks for collagen, a key protein in connective and other tissues.
If the structures really are fossilised red blood cells, as the researchers contend, it raises the question of how they were preserved. According to Grice, a manganese compound called hausmannite, which formed in and around the blood cells, may have lent a helping hand by stabilising them prior to fossilisation. The same process might have helped preserve the amino acids, she added. The study appears in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
The work is already stoking debate. Prof Mary Schweitzer at North Carolina State University in the US, who has discovered remnants of blood vessels and soft tissues in dinosaur fossils, is not convinced Grice and her colleagues have found red blood cells. One reason for her doubt is that the dinosaur’s red blood cells should have a “nuclear bulge” making them appear dome-like on both sides. The structures Grice found are concave, suggesting they might be something else.
Schweitzer was more persuaded by the discovery of heme and collagen amino acids in the bone and said there was so much more to learn from exceptionally well-preserved fossils. Schweitzer added: “The conventional wisdom in palaeontology that all endogenous organics would disappear in a million years or less is being routinely challenged, and will continue to be as technological approaches to palaeontological specimens are more routinely applied.”
Another question the research raises is what other biological material might lurk in fossils collections around the world. On this, Grice urges extreme caution, adding that her work does not imply that large biological molecules such as proteins or DNA live on in ancient fossils. “Any extraordinary claim needs extraordinary analytical evidence,” she said. “The aim isn’t to find Jurassic Park DNA, it’s to determine how much genuine molecular information deep time can preserve.”
“The really exciting implication is that extraordinary molecular information may already be sitting in museum collections around the world, waiting for us to ask new questions of old fossils,” she added.

US President Donald Trump has joked about moving to Israel and becoming its prime minister if Americans ever get tired of him, making the remark during a Fox News interview on Election Day.
Speaking to Fox News on Tuesday, the POTUS claimed he had a 99 per cent approval rating in Israel and suggested he could pursue a political career there if his popularity in the United States declined.
"In fact, if people ever got tired of me in the US, I'll move to Israel, become prime minister," Trump said.
According to TMZ, Trump made the remark while discussing the relationship between the United States and Israel. He also claimed to have the "highest approval rating of anybody in history", but did not provide any polling evidence to support the statement.
US Midterm Election Results 2026
His reported popularity in Israel stands in contrast to his approval rating at home. TMZ reported that Trump's US approval rating was 32 per cent, although it did not identify the poll behind the figure.
Trump praises Israel, announces end to US aid
During the Fox News interview, Trump also praised Israel as an important American ally and spoke about his administration's actions against Iran.
He announced that US would stop providing around $4 billion in annual assistance to Israel by the end of 2026. 
Fox News reported that Trump said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had raised the idea of ending the assistance and that the two leaders had discussed it for several years.
Trump argued that Israel no longer needed the financial support because of its economic strength. However, the announcement raises questions about the future of the existing US-Israel military assistance agreement, which provides around $3.8 billion annually through 2028, according to Fox News.
Trump had made a similar remark earlier
This is not the first time Trump has joked about becoming Israel's prime minister. According to TMZ, he made a similar remark in May, when he also claimed to enjoy 99 per cent support among Israelis.
His latest comments came as Americans voted in the 2026 midterm elections on November 3. The elections will determine which party controls the US Congress, including the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Trump's Republicans are defending their congressional majorities against the opposition Democrats. The results could shape the remainder of his presidency, including his domestic and foreign policy agenda.
The 2026 US midterm elections will determine control of all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats. Republicans are entering the elections with a narrow 219-214 advantage in the House, while holding 53 of the Senate's 100 seats. Democrats need to gain just four net seats in the House and four in the Senate to take control of both chambers. The party that wins the House needs at least 218 seats, while a Senate majority requires 51 seats, or 50 if the vice-president can break a tie. The elections are crucial for Trump, as a Democratic takeover of either chamber could make it harder for him to pass legislation, while giving the opposition greater power to investigate his administration and challenge his policies.

- Bethesda has confirmed that Elder Scrolls 6 is named Sentinel.
- The game is expected to take place in Hammerfell, as the teaser showcased a desert area and finished with a quote from Hammerfell's Moth Priest.
- There is still no official release window for Elder Scrolls 6 Sentinel.
After 15 years of waiting, Bethesda has finally announced the highly anticipated name for its sixth installment of The Elder Scrolls. Elder Scrolls 6 name is confirmed to be Sentinel, and with the name reveal comes a slight teaser. A one-minute video where we see dunes with sand flowing around in the wind, and on the surface of the dune is what appears to be a scroll.
Elder Scrolls 6 Sentinel Teaser and Name Reveal
This might hint that Elder Scrolls 6 will take place in a desert. The last game of the franchise, Skyrim, was inspired by Norse mythology and took place among the mountains. Does that mean Elder Scrolls Sentinel would be inspired by Egyptian mythology? We don’t know yet, but the upcoming games in 2026 will definitely give it a good fight in the future.
According to Elder Scrolls lore, the only location that comes with an arid desert is Hammerfell. At the end of the teaser, we also get a quote from Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell, and this is what it says:
The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate.
This further hints that Sentinel will take place in Hammerfell. Previous leaks about Elder Scrolls 6’s location had also suggested Hammerfell as the main location. There is a good chance of it being true, as the Elder Scrolls 6 title leak also ended up being correct.
If that does come true, then it won’t just be deserts that players will get to enjoy. Hammerfell has an incredibly diverse landscape, from vast jungles, wooded mountain ranges, subtropical grasslands, humid swamps, and the famous arid deserts. It’s the perfect landscape for creating the next big Elder Scrolls title.
Bethesda has not had that much success with their last couple of titles. Both Fallout 76 and Starfield, although successful, never reached their expected potential. However, Elder Scrolls has always been the biggest franchise for Bethesda, even larger than Fallout. The Elder Scrolls Sentinel has been in development for years, but it still doesn’t have a release window yet.
With the game having nearly as much hype as GTA 6, we can only hope that today’s name reveal means that things are progressing faster. So, are you excited for Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel? Tell us in the comments section below.

Quick Answer
To stop Google from using your Gmail, Drive, and Photos data for personalized ads, visit google.com/search-personalization, open Connected Content Apps, and disconnect Google Workspace and Photos. Then turn off personalized ads at myadcenter.google.com. You can also delete past activity at activity.google.com.
It’s not hyperbole to say AI agents are genuinely helpful. The big tech companies aren’t stupid to be investing billions of dollars to build these AI agents, but they need more than your money to help you – your data. Google is best placed to play this smart answers game considering it owns some of the most widely used services in the world – Search, Gmail, Chrome, Photos, and Android.
If you’ve let Google’s AI look at your Gmail or Google Photos for smarter answers, there’s a catch. As of October 16, 2026, Google’s privacy policy says data from those apps can also help personalize ads. Google is also testing ads in AI Mode for people who have connected their apps.
Here’s what changed, what it does and doesn’t mean, and how to turn it off.
Table of Contents
What changed
Since 2021, Google’s privacy policy has said that it doesn’t use your Gmail, Drive, or Photos content for personalized ads. According to Ars Technica and Google’s own archive, the old line read: “We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos.”
The current policy, effective October 16, 2026, adds a condition:
We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos, unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.
A new passage in the same section spells out how this happens:
You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive… For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.
You “choose” this through Personal Intelligence, the opt-in feature that lets AI Mode and other Search tools draw on your Gmail, Calendar, and Photos. Calendar is US and English only for now, Photos isn’t available in every region, and Drive, though named in the policy, isn’t currently one of the apps you can connect to Search.
The ads side is already live as a test.
What it means for you
It’s easy to overstate this, so here’s what Google actually says.
What Google says won’t happen:
- In its Search help page, Google says: “Ads will not be based directly on your Gmail inbox or your Google Photos library.“
- Advertisers don’t get access to your connected apps, and Google doesn’t share your name or email with them.
- Google says it won’t personalize ads on sensitive categories such as race, religion, sexual orientation or health.
What can happen:
The same help page says Search “may reference summaries, excerpts and inferences” from your connected apps, and “that same info may be used to show you ads.” The policy gives an example of personalizing answers: ask Search about a recent hotel booking, and it may use booking details from an email. The ads link comes from the help page: that same kind of info may now be used to show you ads.
Search vs. Gemini:
The ad test is in AI Mode in Search. Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub says “Your Gemini Apps chats are not being used to show you ads.” The policy still lists “Gemini Apps” among services you can connect your data to.
Beyond AI Mode:
When you connect your apps, Google says all Search services can access them, including Search, Discover, Maps, Shopping, Flights, Hotels, Translate, and News. The same page says human reviewers may see some of that data.
Where this applies:
Connecting content apps to Search is available to adults in a long list of countries, including the US and India. The UK and EU countries don’t appear on that list. Personal Intelligence in Gemini is not available in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, Nigeria, or the UK. Google hasn’t said where the ads test is running, and the policy wording is global. What we think is, since Google doesn’t offer either feature in the UK yet, UK readers look largely unaffected for now.
How to opt out of Search Personalization
Disconnect Gmail and Photos from Search (web, Android, iPhone)
As per Google’s help pages, the steps are the same on the web, Android, and iPhone:
- Open your Google Account and go to Data & privacy > Personalization settings > Personalized Recommendations in Search services. Or you can click this if you are already signed in: google.com/search-personalization.
- Under Additional Personal Intelligence, open Connected Content Apps.
- Disconnect Google Workspace and Google Photos.
To go further, turn off Personalized Recommendations on the same page. Google says it’s updating these settings, so labels may differ.
Disconnect apps in Gemini
- Gemini mobile app (Android/iPhone): tap Menu > your profile picture > Personal Intelligence > Connected Apps.
- Web (gemini.google.com): select Menu > Settings & help > Personal Intelligence > Connected Apps.
Turn off Google Workspace and Google Photos, plus any other apps you don’t want connected.
Turn off personalized ads in My Ad Center
Go to My Ad Center, select On or Off next to Personalized ads, choose Off, and confirm.
Google says it will then stop using your saved account info and activity for ads, and will show ads based on general factors like the topic you’re viewing. You’ll still see ads; they just won’t be tailored to you. This doesn’t stop connected-app data from being used for AI answers.
Clean up what’s already saved
Disconnecting doesn’t delete your Search Services History, which can still be used for product improvement. Review and delete it at activity.google.com. In Gemini, disconnecting doesn’t delete your Gemini Apps Activity either.
Should you disconnect?
Personal Intelligence is genuinely useful: asking about your trip without pasting in your booking is the whole point, and Google says advertisers don’t get access to your connected apps.
But helping you and choosing your ads are different uses, and the ads part was added after Personal Intelligence launched. If that bothers you, disconnect. A middle path is to keep Personal Intelligence on and turn off personalized ads in My Ad Center. Your data still feeds Google’s AI answers, and Search Services History can be used for product improvement, including AI model training.
The bottom line
While you’d see a lot of noise around these changes on social media, know that this change doesn’t touch everyone’s inbox, because it’s opt-in. But if you connected Gmail or Photos to its AI, what that AI learns can now help pick your ads, starting with a test in AI Mode. If that trade isn’t for you, the switches above take minutes.
FAQs about Search Personalization
1. Is Google reading my emails to target ads?
Not directly, according to Google. It says ads aren’t based “directly” on your inbox, but summaries, excerpts, and inferences Search draws from connected apps can be used for ads.
2. I never turned on Personal Intelligence. Am I affected?
As per the policy, Gmail, Drive, and Photos content isn’t used for ads unless you make it available to other services. It’s opt-in, but worth checking the settings above in case you connected and forgot.
3. Does this apply to Gemini chats?
Google says Gemini chats aren’t used to show you ads right now. The ad test is in AI Mode in Search.
4. Does disconnecting erase what Google already has?
No. Delete your Search Services History at activity.google.com and your Gemini Apps Activity separately, as we described earlier in this article.

The ‘Chalo Delhi’ march led by Congress leader Rahul Gandhi concluded with a rally at Ramlila Maidan on 01 November 2026, protesting Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and alleged voter roll anomalies. Amidst the demonstration, two videos (here & here) went viral on social media with claims that Delhi Police fired upon Congress workers, allegedly killing four people and injuring ten. Let’s verify the authenticity of these claims.
Claim: Visuals of Delhi Police opening fire on Congress workers during the ‘Delhi Chalo’ rally on 01 November 2026, allegedly killing four people and injuring ten.
Fact: These videos depict clashes between garment workers and security forces in Dhaka, Bangladesh. There were no credible reports of any such violence occurring at the Delhi rally. Delhi Police have officially refuted the rumours, warning of legal action against those spreading the misinformation. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
First, we reviewed media reports to understand whether any such firing on Congress workers happened in Delhi during the rally, but we could not find any evidence. Furthermore, we found no statements or allegations from the Congress party on their official social media handles (here & here) regarding such an incident.
Next, we investigated the first video, which shows clashes between police and civilians, and observed that the language on the signboards is Bengali. A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to an extended version (here, here & here) uploaded by Bangladeshi media outlets. These reports identified the footage as an incident from the Mirpur-10 area of Dhaka, Bangladesh.
Furthermore, Google Street View confirms that the location seen in the viral video is in Dhaka, not Delhi.
According to Bangladeshi media reports (here, here & here), severe clashes erupted in Dhaka’s Mirpur area in early November 2026 as thousands of garment workers protested to demand a minimum wage increase from 12,500 to 30,000 BDT. The unrest saw workers blocking major roads, including the Mirpur-10 intersection, and vandalising police vehicles. In response to the vandalism and roadblocks, security forces deployed tear gas, sound grenades, and baton charges to disperse the crowds.
We then investigated the second video, which shows a group of people climbing on and vandalising a police vehicle. According to Bangladeshi media reports (here & here), this video also depicts the same garment workers’ protest, specifically showing individuals attacking a police vehicle under the Mirpur-11 metro station in Dhaka. Additionally, the Dhaka Metropolitan Police logo can be seen on the vehicle.
Moreover, the Delhi Police and PIB Fact Check issued a statement clarifying that these viral videos originate from Bangladesh and have no connection to Delhi. They also warned that appropriate legal action will be taken against those spreading this misinformation.
To sum it up, unrelated videos from a protest in Bangladesh are being shared as footage of Delhi Police firing on Congress workers.

Judoka determined to prove refugees belong at Dakar 2026
- Published
Arno Yafunga Botay was six when his family fled the Democratic Republic of Congo after threats to his father's life culminated in an attack on their home which claimed the life of his seven-month-old sibling.
Following a spell living in the Kakuma refugee camp in north-west Kenya, the family settled in Nairobi. There, Arno used to watch his father Arnold practising judo and eventually asked him to teach him the sport.
Now, having coming through trials in East Africa, he will compete for the Refugee Olympic Team in the under-55kg category at the Dakar 2026 Youth Games.
"I didn't expect to be selected," the 15-year-old told BBC Sport Africa.
"I was so excited. I was crying tears of joy."
This is the first time that a team of refugees will appear at a Youth Games.
"It [means] a lot to me to represent other refugees, represent my community," Yafunga Botay added.
The family have been in Kenya since they were forced to leave DR Congo in 2017.
"There were people who wanted to kill me," Arnold said.
"At the time, I was detained somewhere when people came to our house and attacked my family. The situation led to the death of my child."
- All you need to know about the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics 
  - Published5 days ago
- Africa prepares for historic Olympic moment at Dakar 2026 
  - Published23 July
After finding safety, Yafunga Botay and his elder brother Christian would watch their father training before he headed out to work as a labourer.
Yafunga Botay began receiving instructions in judo rules and techniques at the age of seven.
However, life in their adopted East African nation provided its own challenges.
"I [did] not have the judogi clothes or transport fees for local competitions," he explained.
"It's been difficult going to school. There's no money for school fees.
"My father has no work. He needs to go to work and give us money to go and pay the school fees.
"And here we don't have support. As a refugee, to stay in Kenya, you need to have documents.
"[Thankfully] the IOC (International Olympic Committee) came with this programme of helping refugees achieve their dreams."
An Olympic first for refugees
The Refugee Olympic Team was first introduced at the Rio 2016 Olympics and Cameroon-born boxer Cindy Ngamba won the team's first ever medal at Paris 2024 when she claimed bronze in the women's 75kg category.
In a double first, the team will now make its Youth Olympics debut at Dakar 2026, which is the first Olympic event hosted on African soil.
"As a refugee, we have a right to compete," Yafunga Botay said.
"A refugee is a human being like other people."
Father Arnold says the team serves as a message of hope to people around the world who have been displaced.
"Being a refugee does not mean your life is over," he said.
"Refugees can also do things that surprise people.
"My message to fellow refugees is don't give up. Keep pushing until the end."
The six-strong team competing in Senegal is being mentored by two-time Olympic marathon champion Eliud Kipchoge.
"He teaches us [to] respect the coach, focus on what you are doing," Yafunga Botay said.
"I promised him I'll bring the gold medal [back] so he can see [what] I achieved."
Discipline and respect
Judo has become a central part of life for the family.
Arnold still coaches Yafunga Botay and Christian, now 17, occasionally serves as his younger brother's sparring partner.
The teenager describes his father as "strict" even at home, with a firm focus on the importance of discipline.
"Maintaining his weight is not easy. He [Arno] has to keep training consistently," Arnold said.
"Judo teaches him respect and helps him interact with others, whether at school or at home.
"Those lessons follow him everywhere. In judo, every time you fall you gain the strength to keep going."
The owner of the dojo in the Kenyan capital where Yafunga Botay has trained since 2020 says his selection for Dakar 2026 has "changed perceptions" of judo in the community.
"It is helping parents understand that judo is not just a fighting sport - it has real value," Lawrence Karisa Nyundo told the BBC.
"I have received calls from parents who want to enrol their children.
"It is a big achievement for this club that one of our athletes is going to compete at the Olympics. We are praying that he performs well."
After Dakar, Yafunga Botay hopes other refugees can benefit from his experience in the future.
"In Kakuma, there are good judokas.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins on Friday, with the opening ceremony a day later and judo events running from 1-3 November.

Diljit Dosanjh has performed in front of packed audiences across India and abroad, but there is one state where he has not been able to take his live show: Bihar. The singer recently revealed that he wanted to perform in the state but the plans fell through because of disagreements over who would be responsible for managing the crowd. Speaking during an Instagram Live session after his Delhi concert on 30 October, Diljit recalled that efforts had been made to organise a show in Bihar last year as well. However, the discussions did not move forward after crowd management became a major concern. Explaining what happened, the singer said in Punjabi, "We tried to go to Bihar; we had attempted to go to Bihar last time as well. But they said it was difficult to manage the crowd. They asked if we would take responsibility for it. I said that we couldn't; they would have to take that responsibility. Since they didn't, we couldn't go."s His comments suggest that the issue was not a lack of interest from the singer or his team, but the arrangements required to handle the audience expected at such a large concert. Diljit also explained why he was unwilling to take responsibility for managing the crowd at the proposed event. According to him, his concerts attract large audiences and require much more than a venue and a stage. "You see, it's difficult to manage the crowd. It's not just a small gathering; it's a massive crowd. I had to consider the logistics. It's like organising an event in Delhi," he said. A concert involving thousands of people requires proper arrangements for security, entry and exit points, traffic movement, parking and emergency response. These arrangements also need coordination between the event organisers, venue management, local administration and police. Diljit's concern was that crowd management could not be treated as the responsibility of the artist alone. While the singer and his team could organise the performance, managing a large gathering and ensuring public safety would require support from the authorities. The singer did not name the officials involved in the discussions or identify the proposed venue. There has also been no publicly confirmed announcement of a new Bihar concert date. Interestingly, this is not the first time Diljit's India tour plans have faced hurdles. His Delhi concert at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium on 30 October also ran into trouble before it received clearance. Diljit began the India leg of his AURA Tour 2026 with the Delhi performance. However, the show faced uncertainty after Delhi Police initially withheld permission, citing security concerns and festive-season law-and-order arrangements. The organisers subsequently submitted additional plans covering security, traffic and crowd management. The concert eventually went ahead, with Diljit later thanking the Delhi Police and the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) for their support. Speaking about the difficulties during his Instagram Live session, the singer said that several people had tried to stop the Delhi concert, but the show eventually took place. He also pointed out that organising concerts in India often came with challenges despite his experience of performing internationally. The Bihar situation highlights a larger issue facing India's growing live entertainment industry. As major artists attract increasingly large audiences, organising concerts requires close coordination between private event companies and government agencies. Following the Delhi concert, Diljit is scheduled to take his AURA India Tour 2026 to several other cities. His announced stops include Indore, Ahmedabad, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Lucknow, Chandigarh and Kolkata. Bihar, however, is not part of the announced schedule. The singer has not confirmed whether another attempt to organise a concert in the state is being planned. The Ebola outbreak in Congo passed a grim milestone this week — 10,000 confirmed cases — and spurred questions about whether health authorities are losing their ability to contain it.
Nearly half the infected people in this outbreak have died, and some experts say there are reasons to worry this could grow into the worst Ebola outbreak in history. Others don't think it will reach that level. Researchers are currently working on updated projections.
Current circumstances suggest it's unlikely to spark significant problems in most other countries, some researchers said. But about 30 confirmed cases have already popped up in other nations. And the risk that more will appear outside Congo will grow if the outbreak isn't tamed, said Justin Lessler, a University of North Carolina researcher who studies the dynamics of infectious disease outbreaks.
Experts also are hopeful that a vaccine will become available next year that could help control it.
At a virtual summit of African health ministers on Wednesday, Africa CDC Director-General Dr. Jean Kaseya said the continent is “not winning” the fight against Ebola and needs to do more after it spread to multiple African countries. “Together, we agreed to prepare every country, coordinate across our borders and keep those borders open while watching them closely,” Kaseya wrote on X.
Steady case numbers raise concerns about spread beyond Congo
About 400 to 500 new confirmed cases have been reported in Congo each week, and that number seems to be holding steady. It's good news that “cases are not rising exponentially,” at least for the moment, said Dr. Boghuma Titanji, an Emory University infectious disease specialist.
“But they're not coming down, either," she said. "It's at a plateau. And the plateau is at a very, very high set point."
A major challenge in Congo is limited contact tracing and collaboration with affected communities; health workers sometimes spend more time trying to convince locals to work with them than giving care.
Fewer than a quarter of new cases are coming from people known to have been in contact with an infected person, showing there are ongoing chains of transmission that health authorities are not aware of.
As cases mount, the likelihood grows that more infected people travel to other countries, Titanji and other experts said. France, Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda also have reported cases tied to the Congo outbreak.
Travel restrictions, like those imposed by the US, can make it harder for the virus to leave Africa. And in many places where a traveller's infection may surface, health officials should be able to quickly isolate an infected person and find any contacts, experts say.
“The direct risk it poses to the US at this point, I'd say, is very close to zero,” Lessler said.
But Ebola could flare in poor and conflict-stricken places with weakened health systems — like South Sudan, for example, Lessler said.
Viruses that cause Ebola disease spread through contact with bodily fluids such as vomit, blood and semen.
Second largest outbreak
Dozens of Ebola outbreaks have been reported since the disease was first discovered in 1976. The largest and deadliest occurred in West Africa in 2014 to 2016, with 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.
The current outbreak already ranks second, and has had at least three times the number of cases and deaths in the time since it was declared compared with the West Africa outbreak. Health officials declared the outbreak in May, but medical evidence suggests infections were occurring months earlier.
One reason is that past outbreaks were almost all caused by the Ebola virus. Initial testing was geared toward that virus — not the related, but different, Bundibugyo virus that was actually causing illnesses.
A series of other challenges have hurt the response, including armed conflict in some outbreak areas, gaps in the health system, mistrust and misinformation, and global aid cuts, experts say.
Conditions vary in Congo, which explains why cases can be stable or falling in some places but can be trending up in others, researchers and response workers say.
“Testing, care and contact tracing only work if we work with communities, going door to door, village by village to break the chain of transmission and stop this deadly escalation,” said Katie Thomas-Canfield, the International Rescue Committee's Ebola response director, in a statement.
Dr. Wendy Armstrong, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, said she thinks the situation is going to get worse.
“This is very far from being controlled,” she said.
Updating projections
Experts expect the outbreak will continue through the end of the year, but Titanji is hopeful about 2027. That's because vaccines are being tested against the Bundibugyo virus, and she is optimistic an effective shot will become available in the next 12 months.
She noted no vaccines were available early in the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak.
Forecasting the outbreak is difficult, of course, but scientists have been trying.
In May, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention published a range of scenarios generated by computer models. At the time, the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention was reporting 400 confirmed cases. The US CDC models estimated the growth in cases over three months could run from 10,000 to more than 20,000.
The CDC is updating its modeling work. But the agency declined to let The Associated Press interview staff scientists about how the outbreak is trending.
Alessandro Vespignani, a Northeastern University disease modeler, has been monitoring trends with US and international health officials.
There's not been the kind of “decay in the number of cases weekly that we need to see the light at the end of the tunnel,” he said.

If you've interacted with the likes of Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini, you've noticed that in addition to everything else they do, these AI chatbots can search the web for you. Depending on what you’re looking for, it can be easier to find more relevant results through a chatbot, which may explain why Google is so keen to push AI Mode for its own search engine.
When asked to search the web, the latest versions of these bots are combining elements of traditional web search (they're essentially just googling on your behalf) with knowledge they are able to pull out of their training data. Everything is then packaged and formatted in the now-familiar, polished generative AI style.
It's the added AI elements on top of the traditional googling where the differences come in, and that means AI-powered search may not always be the best option.
When to Use AI for Web Search
If you're looking up something simple and widely known—like the height of the Empire State Building—then AI search is a pretty safe bet. Not only is information like this easy to access online, the “autocorrect” probability patterns favored by large language models mean there's a near-certain chance that the results you see will include the right information.
If you just need a quick look-up, AI is OK. The more obscure the question, though, the closer you need to look at the answer. If you've asked something less well known, like the fifth-billed actor in an obscure television show, there might only be one or two references to it on the web, and an AI might choose the wrong one.
One of the takeaways from recent Stanford University research is that when AI finds an accurate source, it's very good at pulling the right information out of it. Where it tends to fall down is in not finding accurate sources (either because there aren't any or because the query has been misinterpreted) and presenting a confident answer anyway.
AI search is also helpful when you have a complex query that a standard Google search wouldn't be able to parse: "I need to know the best restaurants in San Francisco for a family of five who want to spend no more than $200." AI is able to query and collate multiple sources in response to a search like this, and then present a well-synthesized answer. A traditional web search would give you a list of blue links that most probably just rank San Francisco restaurants by more basic criteria.
Again though, sources are crucial. AI bots have never been to San Francisco or eaten there. They are relying on public accounts on the web, written by people who have. Where there are no exact page matches, they'll look for related words (like "affordable" or "family") and generate an answer.
For queries where there's lots of information online, like San Francisco restaurants, AI web search can feel incredibly useful. For less popular destinations and more specific requests ("dining tables shaped like stars"), you need to be more careful with the results, as the way that AI joins the dots then becomes less reliable.
So, with the caveat that you should always do some kind of double-check, AI web search works best for common queries that are likely to lead to a lot of accurate, up-to-date information online. In both the way they process search queries, and package together and synthesize answers, AI chatbots are a significant upgrade on googling.
When Not to Use AI for Web Search
The way generative AI bots and LLMs are put together means they work best when paraphrasing, synthesizing, and summarizing. But these processes can also introduce mistakes. If your search needs precise details (like a celebrity quotation, a report stat, or a device specification), a traditional Google search may work best.
Heading to Google and searching the old way is also likely to be better if you want full control over the sources used. Offloading web searches to AI is convenient, but you're relying on them to interpret your search correctly, find the right sources, and then extract accurate information from those sources. It saves time, but it's more opaque.
If you know the websites you trust most for technology news, for example, you can prioritize them in a traditional web search in a way that AI might not be able to. Researchers from UC San Diego have found that AI web searches will sometimes pick sources because they're more relevant to the query, rather than because they're ranked as more authoritative.
That means a personal blog might get chosen above a professional health care site if the AI deems it to be a closer match to what the user is actually searching for. This is a choice that you would be much less likely to make when scanning a traditional list of results, as you'd typically pick the one you trusted the most.
Other areas where traditional searching still wins out are for breaking news (there can sometimes be a lag in the timeliness of the data AI pulls up) and for high-stakes searches where you absolutely cannot make a mistake—searches related to health, the law, or your finances, for instance.
If you do feel like an AI approach is needed, be sure to double- and triple-check the sources the chatbot has used, which should be linked inside the answer. If you're in any doubt, you can ask the AI for clarification on where something was sourced from, to make sure it isn't an LLM invention.
Classic Google searches can still turn up false information on the web, of course, but you're in a much better position to discern what's true and accurate and what isn't without a chatbot in the middle. For queries where that's more important than convenience and speed, there's still a place for the old way of searching the web.

Beginning one day before voters headed to the polls for the 2026 midterm elections, posts claimed that an FBI field office incorrectly told voters that Election Day would be on Wednesday. Election Day always takes place the Tuesday immediately after the first Monday in November in accordance with federal law.
For example, one Threads user claimed (archived) that they received many messages about a deleted X post from the FBI's New Haven field office. The Threads post included a screenshot of the purported FBI New Haven post, which began, "Election day is Wednesday and the #FBI is working around the clock to ensure the midterms are safe."
Other posts claiming the FBI's New Haven field office erroneously posted that Election Day would be on Wednesday spread on Instagram (archived). Some posts on X (archived) and Reddit (archived) claimed that the broader FBI posted the wrong Election Day date, without noting any individual field office.
While the original post has since been deleted, an FBI New Haven X post incorrectly identifying Wednesday as Election Day was saved to the Internet Archive. Therefore, we've rated this claim true.
According to the archived version of the post, the FBI New Haven field office shared the post around 10 p.m. on Monday, Nov. 2. Since the Internet Archive uses Greenwich Mean Time, which is five hours ahead of Eastern Standard Time, that means FBI New Haven likely posted the incorrect information around 5 p.m. EST, which is the time zone where New Haven is located.
The archived post reads:
Election day is Wednesday and the #FBI is working around the clock to ensure the midterms are safe. Special Agent in Charge P. J. O'Brien and Public Affairs Specialist Christine Jeltema sat down with @thevoiceofct to discuss how the FBI protects the integrity of elections, including threats, voter intimidation, and ballot fraud. Listen in on their conversation here: ow.ly/2FOZ5102Zwb.
The Internet Archive's snapshot is from approximately 9 a.m. GMT on Tuesday, Nov. 3, which would mean the post hadn't been taken down or corrected by 4 a.m. EST on Election Day. The post was deleted at some point later in the morning, though we couldn't confirm exactly when that happened.
Snopes sent an email to the FBI's national press office asking if the mistake made by the New Haven press office originated from the national FBI. The FBI redirected us to the New Haven office, which stated, "The post was removed once the typo was identified." The New Haven office did not provide further clarification.
There's no evidence the wider FBI also told people Wednesday was Election Day, as some people claimed. The Department of Justice, which the FBI operates under, correctly shared on Facebook (archived) that Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.
Before its deletion, the Connecticut secretary of state's office addressed the FBI field office's inaccurate post in a news release (New Haven is a city in Connecticut). It read:
We are aware of misinformation circulating on social media, posted by the FBI's New Haven office, incorrectly stating that Election Day is Wednesday.
Do not believe it. Election Day is today, Tuesday, November 3.
Polls across Connecticut are open until 8 p.m., and anyone in line by 8 p.m. will be allowed to vote.
Don't let incorrect information or confusion keep you from making your voice heard today.
For further reading, Snopes is live fact-checking midterm election rumors.

Keralam Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan’s recent remarks questioning “unnecessary” angioplasty procedures have drawn objections from medical organisations concerned that it could undermine public confidence in doctors. But the Chief Minister’s remarks demand more than a reflex response; it requires a thoughtful, honest response built on up-to-date evidence based on clinical and research studies.
Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI), by balloon angioplasty and stent placement, has transformed cardiovascular care. During an acute heart attack caused by a suddenly blocked coronary artery, prompt angioplasty and stents can restore blood flow, save heart muscle and improve survival. There is no debate about this approach and second opinions are unnecessary as time is of essence in such an emergency. Stents also offer substantial relief to selected patients with persistent activity-limiting angina (chest pain caused by lack of oxygen-rich blood).
There is a crucial distinction between stenting as a life-saving measure in the above situations to medical treatment via stenting because a narrowing of blood vessels is seen on an angiogram. A coronary angiogram shows the anatomy of the arteries; it does not, by itself, establish that a narrowing requires intervention. The decision to intervene and how to intervene must take account of the patient’s symptoms, the severity of the blockage, its effect on blood flow, the overall pattern of coronary disease and the expected benefit of intervention.
The landmark ISCHEMIA trial, published in The New England Journal of Medicine in 2020, enrolled 5,179 patients at 320 sites in 37 countries with stable coronary artery disease and moderate to severe ischemia (restricted blood flow to the heart). The patients were assigned either to an initial invasive strategy — angiography followed by angioplasty or coronary bypass surgery — or to a conservative strategy of optimal medical treatment, with revascularisation reserved for those who had an acute event or angina. After a median follow-up of 3.2 years, there was no significant difference between the two groups in composite outcomes (cardiac arrests, hospitalisation for unstable angina or heart failure) and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality were similar. After a follow-up of 5 years, there was still no significant difference between the two groups in composite outcome or mortality. The core lesson is that most patients with stable coronary artery disease with ischemia on optimal medical treatment would do as well as those who undergo stenting or bypass surgery.
Concerning scale
The growing scale of PCI in India deserves careful examination. National Interventional Council figures show that annual PCI procedures rose from approximately 1,13,000 in 2008 to more than 7,26,000 in 2024 — an increase of more than six-fold. In contrast, PCI procedures in the U.S. fell by about 40% between 2003 and 2016, reflecting progress in prevention and treatment.
These figures do not by themselves prove that stents are overused in India considering its large population, the substantial burden of premature coronary disease, the socio-economic progress in the past decades and the improved access to cardiac care centres. Nevertheless, the divergence in trends between the two countries raises an important question: how much of the increase in PCI is a reflection of fulfilling a genuine clinical need, and how much of it is a reflection of differences in practice patterns, financial incentives and gaps in knowledge on the efficacy of optimal medical treatment?
Optimal medical therapy, based on evidence-based guidelines, is the foundation of care for all coronary artery disease patients. The elements of optimal therapy include LDL-cholesterol lowering, appropriate anti-platelet treatment, blood-pressure control, evidence-based diabetes management and lifestyle changes. A coronary stent treats a specific narrowing; it does not cure the underlying disease of atherosclerosis or eliminate the risk of future heart attacks. Patients remain vulnerable to disease elsewhere in the coronary arteries and must continue preventive treatment.
The way forward is neither condemnation of cardiologists nor unquestioning acceptance of every recommendation for angioplasty. Most doctors strive to act in their patients’ best interests, but no profession is immune to inappropriate practice. The ultimate test of healthcare is not how many procedures are performed, but how many lives are saved and whether patients receive the right treatment at the right time at an affordable cost.
Dr. Enas A. Enas is Preventive Cardiologist and Physician-Scientist, Founding President of the CADI Research Foundation USA; Dr. Basil Varkey is Professor Emeritus of medicine

EC: Previously enrolled voters can submit form 6 for inclusion
The Election Commission on Tuesday said previously enrolled voters can submit Form 6 for inclusion as electors if their names are missing from draft Special Intensive Revision (SIR) rolls.
The clarification came days after the Supreme Court asked ECI not to make nearly 4.3 million Delhi residents – whose names were removed from the electoral rolls after they could not be found at their last known addresses – reapply as new voters through Form 6 provided they were on the 2026 rolls. Instead, it suggested that such voters be permitted to restore their names through Form 8, which is intended for address-related changes, or through the enumeration process.
In a letter to all state chief electoral officers, ECI said that it was brought to its notice that certain people whose names did not figure in the draft electoral roll published during the ongoing SIR were hesitant to submit Form 6 as they were also required to furnish a declaration to the effect that their name was being included in the electoral rolls for the first time.
“Therefore, such electors believe that submission of Form 6, in view of their previous enrolment, would amount to making a false declaration and render them liable for prosecution under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950,” it said.
ECI clarified that voters whose names did not figure in the draft SIR rolls could submit Form 6 to seek fresh inclusion in the final voters’ list, even if they were enrolled previously. Citing a Delhi high court’s October 14 judgment, ECI said the apprehension of making a false declaration was misplaced.
A senior official in the Delhi CEO’s office said the machinery on the ground had received no guidance on the Form8 route. “We haven’t received any SOPs or instructions from the ECI to get people placed under ASDD categories to fill Form8,” the official said. Activists Anjali Bhardwaj and Amrita Johri also wrote to ECI and Delhi CEO, seeking “immediate compliance”.
