Your iPhone Duo can do more than multitask! These 10 quirky apps turn the foldable into a retro computer, cassette player, Nintendo DS, accordion, instant camera, virtual fridge, and even a grilled cheese toaster. Some are free, others paid, but all make clever, fun use of its folding design.
The iPhone Duo is perhaps the most radically different iPhone since the original iPhone. While its arrival was rumored for over a year, Apple finally launched it this September. The phone can fold in half to become nearly passport-sized and can be unfolded to shape-shift into a bigger, tablet-ish smartphone. Ever since its launch, we have been constantly hearing about its multitasking prowess, its computer-like processing abilities, how well it handles productivity apps, yada yada yada…
But all this is pretty basic, something we expect with all new iPhones, or rather flagship smartphones at this point. With the kind of price and specs these high-end smartphones come with, it hardly is a surprise that they can handle power-hungry tasks with ease. The foldable form-factor and the added display real estate make it a different experience, surely. But surely there is way more to the device than the same old tasks and apps? So, we are on a mission to make your iPhone Duo fun, using all that processing and multitasking magic that it possesses.
The result is these ten apps.
They are not at all useful. But they make the Duo a-not-just-another-serious (read: boring) device out there. They add an element to it that we all so need to survive – they make it fun. Got an iPhone Duo? Download! (Note: relax, all of these are optimized for the iPhone Duo)
Table of Contents
Top 10 Wacky and Fun iPhone Duo Apps
| Sl No | App | Price | What it does | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Tiny Computer | $3.99 | Turns the Duo into a retro PC with vintage keyboards, games, and interfaces. | 
| 2 | Deck Man | $4.99 | Recreates a cassette Walkman with realistic tape controls and sounds. | 
| 3 | MD Vinyl | Free | Turns the screen into a vinyl turntable with spinning records and music controls. | 
| 4 | Fold Accordion | $2.99 | Uses the folding hinge as accordion bellows to create music. | 
| 5 | Delta | Free | Recreates the Nintendo DS gaming experience with dual-screen controls. | 
| 6 | Toastie | $2.99 | Turns the Duo into a virtual grilled cheese maker that works when folded shut. | 
| 7 | TypeDraw | $4.99 | Recreates a paper notebook with handwriting, page turns, and paper effects. | 
| 8 | Snapshots | $1.99 | Turns the Duo into a Polaroid-style instant camera with developing photos. | 
| 9 | Phridge | Free | Creates a virtual fridge you can decorate, stock, and mess around with. | 
| 10 | ChompDuo | Free | Adds six animated monsters whose jaws open and close as you fold the phone. | 
Tiny Computer (USD 3.99): Unfolding Retro computer feels
Imagine getting a vintage PC feel on something as new and pristine as the iPhone Duo? That is exactly what the app Tiny Computer can deliver. Using the half-fold setting of the iPhone Duo, the app turns your phone into a proper vintage computer. The upper half of the screen becomes the display while the lower half becomes the keyboard. You get to choose from ten different computers in total, including the Apple Macintosh, IBM PC, iMac G3, IBM ThinkPad, Windows XP, Amiga 500, and more.
It is not just all show; you can actually use some retro paint apps, run old command-line interfaces, play games like Solitaire, and even type on clicky keyboards. Each machine also hides secret commands and files paired with occasional crashes to make the whole experience even more believable.
Deck Man (USD 4.99): Go cassette crazy!
Another app that brings retro feels to the Duo is the Deck Man. It is one of the most visually appealing apps for the Duo because it essentially turns your iPhone Duo into a 1980s cassette Walkman player. The app uses the unfolded version of the phone as the collection of cassettes in your music library that you can browse. You then “insert” the cassette of your choice into the deck, and once you fold it, the secondary screen mimics the look of a cassette Walkman player.
The app has realistic mechanical clicks, background tape static, and if you fast-forward or rewind it too aggressively, the virtual tape inside can get all tangled and then would have to be untangled manually, just like a retro cassette player. “Tape” this one to your Duo!
MD Vinyl (Free): Spin those discs!
If cassettes are “too” modern for you, then you can go even further back in the music era with the iPhone Duo by installing MD Vinyl. This essentially turns the Duo into a virtual turntable with spinning records and album art. The record design determines the aesthetics of the app. The app allows you to pick and drop the needle to play or pause the tracks. It can pair with music apps like Apple Music and Spotify. It is not a new app and has existed for years, but it attains a whole new dimension on the Duo, adding a vintage touch to the modern audio experience.
Fold Accordion (USD 2.99): Fold and unfold to create music
If there is one app that makes the most use of the iPhone Duo’s form factor, it is the Fold Accordion. It literally turns the hinge of the iPhone Duo into working accordion bellows. When you launch the app, it places the keys on the display, which you can press with your right hand while opening and closing the Duo with the left hand to create music of your own. The app comes with a learning mode which highlights keys you have to press to create something pleasant, instead of getting straight to the chaos of keys. A great way to test that folding mechanism too.
Delta (Nintendo DS) (free): Double screen gaming magic, DS style!
Popular Retro Game emulator Delta has launched an updated version of its app, specifically for the iPhone Duo. The app brings specially designed skins for the iPhone Duo, and the most interesting one of the lot is the Nintendo DS portable gaming console, which interestingly was the world’s first mainstream foldable device. The app uses the inner display of the iPhone Duo to bring a DS-style layout and controls across the displays. The game even enters sleep state when the device is folded, similar to the Nintendo DS. Trust the Duo to bring back the magic of double-screen gaming.
Toastie (USD 2.99): Smartest thing since sliced bread!
Unleash the inner chef in you with the absolutely useless but equally fun app called Toastie. This app turns the iPhone Duo into a – wait for it – virtual grilled cheese toaster. You get 15 seconds to assemble your sandwich, and once you are done, you have to hit the ‘grill’ button and physically close the iPhone Duo shut. You then have to wait, listen to the sizzle, or get a slight peek to ensure your toastie is grilling well. If you open the phone too soon, the cheese won’t be melted; if you wait too long, it might end up getting burned. Once you are done with it, you serve it, and you get a star based on your accuracy, recipe, timing, and so on. Useful? Not. But definitely the smartest thing since sliced bread. Actually, the smartest thing done to sliced bread!
TypeDraw (USD 4.99): Paper-like Moleskine
The iPhone Duo looks like a handy pocket notebook or a passport, and TypeDraw literally converts it into a handy little Moleskine-like notebook. It even comes with a digital thread, just like you find on a notebook, which you have to move or swipe aside to open the notebook (or just open the Duo). You can write anywhere on a page using an Apple Pencil or your finger and can even fiddle and curl up paper corners, as well as choose fonts (you can convert your handwriting into one, if you wish), types of paper, and even plain, ruled, dotted, or grid patterns on paper. And the page turns on the internal display are absolutely paper-like. It is like carrying a real notebook.
Snapshots ($1.99): Unfold to Polaroid
Snapshots is an app that helps your Duo morph into an instant camera. It is one of the very first community-developed apps optimized specifically for the iPhone Duo. When bent in half (90 degrees), the top half of the primary display becomes the viewfinder while the bottom half holds the controls. Once you hit the shutter, the photo captured on the upper half of the viewfinder is virtually printed on the lower half with the same mechanical sound and effect as on an instant camera. Just like with a real instant camera, the photo does not appear right away but takes a few seconds to develop, giving us those Polaroid feels.
Phridge (free): Chill…literally!
This is perhaps the most quirky and our personal favorite app in the list. It turns the iPhone Duo into a – wait for it – refrigerator. When folded, you can decorate the ‘door’ of this fridge with magnets, to-do lists, photographs. And when you open it, you can see groceries and food and drink inside and arrange them. This is when the real fun happens, because you can topple something over, drop a fizzy drink, or break a glass jar or bottle. You can also place your hand in a slingshot to shoot stones at the shelves, or get a sword to slice things in half, if you feel like some chaos. You can only close the fridge when you fold the phone shut, making the hinge integral to its operation. How cool is that? Just chillin…
Chompduo (Free): Jaw-dropping (and closing) stuff!
We all need an app that adds six hungry monsters to your iPhone Duo. Well, we do, anyway. That is exactly what ChompDuo does. When installed, it unleashes six hungry monsters on your Duo that open their huge mouths when the device is unfolded, making the inner display a giant mouth. You can tap on the open mouth to make it bite or drag it to squeeze it shut. When you fold the phone, the jaws close shut with a chomp sound, and a pair of googly eyes appear on the outer display, which can jump when you tap on them. What more does one need on a foldable?

Donald Trump has said that the US will no longer provide funding to Israel at the end of this year after striking a new deal with Benjamin Netanyahu.
“Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping,” Trump told Fox News' Fox and Friends.
“We've already agreed that by the end of this year we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it,” he said, arguing that Israel no longer requires Washington’s support.
The US president pointed out that some politicians on the Left were using funding for Israel as a talking point to bash Republicans.
There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu's office on Trump's remarks.
It was not clear which exact funding Trump meant. An Obama-era memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8 billion annual US military aid to Israel is approaching its expiration date in 2028 and conversations have been under way on how funding would continue.
“They can buy whatever they want. They can buy whatever they want. So can Europe. We make the greatest weapons in the world,” Trump added on Tuesday.
Netanyahu said in a May interview with CBS that he hoped to wean Israel off US military support within a decade. In a June letter to a US congressman he wrote that the time had come for Israel “to move from aid recipient to partner”.
Israel has been the largest cumulative recipient of US aid since its founding, receiving more than $300bn, adjusted for inflation, in economic and military aid since 1948, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.
At least $21.7bn in military aid was transferred in the first two years from the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attacks, which led to the war in Gaza and preceded US-Israeli strikes against Iran.
The US and Israel are yet to resolve the eight-month conflict with the Islamic Republic, and Washington carried out renewed strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island overnight even as Qatari mediators stepped up efforts to avoid another escalation.
Israel’s Netanyahu is fighting to remain in office after failing to hold his majority in last week’s elections, despite having received a glowing endorsement from president Trump, who said the US would have to “finish the job” against Iran alone if Israel has “the wrong leader”.
US public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of voters and 66% of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20% in 2017.
Trump is now under pressure to end the unpopular war and recoup some popularity as voting begins in the US midterm elections. The vote will decide who will control Congress for the last two years of the Trump presidency.

The Indian Council of Medical Research has funded a four-year study to investigate the genetic and immunological mechanisms underlying autoimmune diseases by studying families with multiple affected members, AIIMS doctors said on Thursday, appealing to SLE patients to get enrolled in the study.
The project titled ‘Genomic Profiling and Identification of Targetable Shared Immunopathogenic Events in Multiplex Families with Autoimmune Diseases’ has been awarded to Dipyaman Ganguly of Ashoka University, Sonipat, Haryana, and Ranjan Gupta, additional professor in the Department of Rheumatology, AIIMS, Delhi.
The study aims to build a nationwide cohort of 200 families in which multiple members are affected by autoimmune diseases. Each participating family must have at least one member diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), commonly known as lupus, Gupta said.
The researchers will conduct genetic and immunological assessments of the enrolled patients and their family members to identify shared biological mechanisms that contribute to the development of these conditions.
The findings could help scientists better understand the disease processes involved and identify potential targets for developing new therapies, he said.
Autoimmune diseases occur when the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own tissues. A family history of such conditions is associated with an increased risk of developing them, highlighting the importance of investigating genetic and shared immunological factors, Gupta said.
The four-year project will involve clinical centres at AIIMS Delhi; AIIMS Bibinagar, Telangana; Sanjay Gandhi Postgraduate Institute of Medical Sciences (SGPGIMS), Lucknow; St John's Hospital, Bengaluru; Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences, Hyderabad; and the Kolkata Medical College. These centres will contribute clinical data and biological samples for the study.
Patients diagnosed with lupus and residing in Delhi-NCR can contact the centre at AIIMS Delhi to check their eligibility for participation, Gupta said.
Participation will be subject to eligibility assessment and the study's enrolment requirements.

(Bloomberg) -- Parts of the private jet that crashed in Florida on Sunday killing nine people were found miles from the impact site, suggesting they broke off before the plane hit the ground, according to US air safety investigators. 
Most of the Learjet 60’s left elevator was located in three pieces within a range of about 1.3 to 3.8 miles from the crash site, US National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman told reporters Tuesday. The elevator is located on the tail of the aircraft and controls whether the nose is pointed up or down.
“Knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us towards other things to investigate,” Chapman said. The distance suggests it broke off before impact but the NTSB is still trying to determine if losing the piece contributed to the accident or if it was the result of forces on the plane when it began plummeting toward the ground. 
Investigators have been digging into what caused the fatal crash in Palm Beach County, Florida. In communications with air traffic controllers, one of the pilots of the Learjet 60 reported moderate turbulence, ice and precipitation. The aircraft briefly climbed before nosediving at a high speed. The crash created a large crater on a roadway. 
The NTSB previously said weather conditions are a major focus of its investigation. 
A public relations firm for the families of the crash victims said technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson was on the flight with his wife, Helen Sharp, and their two children. The children’s caretaker, Anita Maria Cetina, as well as Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, were also among the passengers, the joint statement said. 
News outlets have reported that the pilots of the aircraft were 55-year-old Jeff Gregory and 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras. 
Authorities haven’t publicly confirmed the victims’ identities, but Chapman said Tuesday that NTSB was aware of the names of the victims and “keeping them in our thoughts.”

- In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections, the Alaska Senate race was embroiled in controversy as a claim circulated that Democrats engaged in ballot-stacking, referring to an election tactic where political parties recruit additional candidates to draw votes away from an opponent
- Alaska Democrats allegedly pushed a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan to run for Senate in order to confuse voters and direct votes away from Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent. Snopes readers asked us to determine the veracity of this claim and the legality of such a tactic.
- The rumor stems from a New York Times investigation based on the claims of an ex-employee of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, interviews with dozens of people involved and a review of communications and documents. We have no reason to doubt the veracity of the Times' reporting. However, because we were unable to view the evidence or obtain additional confirmation from people involved, we cannot confirm its claims as of this writing.
- Snopes concluded that even if Peltola's team engaged in ballot-stacking, it's not unprecedented. Republicans have also employed the tactic during elections. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche also said that such actions "should be" illegal but stopped short of saying they are. The Alaska Supreme Court has permitted the independent candidate Sullivan to run on Nov. 3.
- Election expert John Fortier told Snopes that while people have been prosecuted for deceiving voters, there is no specific law related to the process of ballot-stacking.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Peltola's and incumbent senator's campaigns, as well as independent candidate Sullivan and members of the team allegedly involved in the stacking plan, and await responses.
In an investigation published Oct. 28, The New York Times reported that staffers for Alaska Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola spent months recruiting candidates named Dan Sullivan in order to peel votes from incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
Political parties often employ the election tactic, referred to as "ballot-stacking," to confuse voters by deliberately recruiting additional candidates to run with the goal of drawing votes away from an opponent.
In Alaska, a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan, whom a Democratic operative associated with Peltola's team allegedly recruited, is on the ballot, alongside Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan. President Donald Trump has called Peltola's alleged actions a "fraud on the American public." Additionally, the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit to block or delay the election certification if the incumbent were to lose the senate race.
Snopes readers asked us to look into the legality of ballot-stacking as an election tactic, as well as the veracity of the claim that Peltola's staffers tried to recruit multiple Dan Sullivans to join the Senate race. Readers also wanted to know whether the DOJ could block the election from being certified if the Republican candidate lost.
Below we break down everything we know about the controversy and ballot-stacking during elections:
Did Peltola's team carry out ballot-stacking?
The New York Times spoke to Elisa Rios, a former staffer and campaign manager for Peltola who was recently fired. Rios claimed top campaign aides instructed her to find as many people named "Dan Sullivan" as they could in Alaska and convince them to run for Senate, causing confusion among voters and possibly costing the incumbent senator crucial votes.
The Times reported that it reviewed text messages and conducted numerous interviews with Rios and 12 people who participated in the alleged plan, knew about the plan or were would-be candidates. Shortly before the story was published, Rios attempted to retract her statements to the Times, the newspaper reported. She was planning to file a wrongful-termination lawsuit against the Peltola campaign. The Times kept her statements in the story.
The Peltola campaign denied being involved in Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy. Jim Lottsfeldt, a local political consultant aligned with super PACs supporting Peltola, said Rios was a source of "disgruntled, anti-Mary Peltola stuff that I think is often not true." The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee also denied participating in such a project, but the Times said it had reviewed texts and documents showing otherwise.
Rios claimed a Democrat operative named Jerid Kurtz — who reportedly posed as a man named "Zane" and approached people to attempt to convince them to run in or to drop out of the race — made contact with Dan J. Sullivan and described him as amenable to running if it would help Peltola.  Kurtz is an Ohio native, according to the Times, and would reach out to people under the alias with an email that included the word "buckeye." Ohio is known as the Buckeye State.  
Rios also alleged that Jacquelyn Lopez, an attorney for the Peltola campaign, was involved in efforts to create a "right-wing state party" that could challenge the incumbent Republican senator.
We have no reason to doubt the veracity of the Times' reporting. However, because we were unable to view the evidence or obtain additional confirmation from people involved, we cannot confirm its claims as of this writing.
Snopes reached out to an individual we believe to be Rios via Facebook and will update this story if we receive a response We have also reached out to Lopez but did not receive a response by the time of publication. We were unable to contact Kurtz, who has removed his social media pages.
Additionally, we contacted Peltola's campaign to learn more and will update this story accordingly.
Ultimately, Dan J. Sullivan is allowed to run in the Senate election,
Who is Dan J. Sullivan and is he allowed to run?
Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, lives in the small fishing community of Petersburg, according to the Times. He is contesting the Nov. 3 senate election with no party affiliation, though he initially registered to run as a Republican. Sullivan has maintained publicly that he entered the Senate race of his own volition, though Rios contended that he was contacted by Kurtz and expressed a desire to help Peltola's campaign.
We reached out to Sullivan to learn more about the motivations behind his candidacy. We will update this story if we receive a response.
As of June 26, Sullivan is legally permitted to run in the election — something that the Peltola campaign and its affiliates celebrated, according to the Times' report — though the election board initially attempted to block him.
On June 15, the Alaska Division of Elections announced that Sullivan was ineligible to participate and would be removed from the ballot because his filing was "for the purpose of confusing or misleading voters." Carol Beecher, the elections division director, wrote in a letter (emphasis ours):
You requested to access the ballot under the name "Dan Sullivan" even though it appears from Division records that you have never registered to vote or sought ballot access under this name. Our records indicate that you are registered to vote under the name "Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr." That you chose the occasion of your declaration of candidacy for U.S. Senate to seek ballot access under a name you have not used in your interactions with the Division suggests—and in combination with the additional facts I outline in this letter leads me to conclude—that you are seeking to confuse yourself with another candidate in the race, the incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan, rather than distinguish yourself from him. Indeed, you yourself appeared to be confused when you initially emailed the Division asking to be listed on the ballot as "Dan S. Sullivan." "S" is Senator Sullivan's middle initial, not yours.
She added, in a likely reference to Kurtz:
A political consultant you have admitted is working with your campaign is a known longtime supporter of Democratic candidates including the primary Democratic challenger to Senator Sullivan. This consultant's work on your behalf is, in isolation, innocuous. Alongside the other facts I have catalogued in this letter, however, it suggests a determined effort and a deliberate attempt to use the similarity of your name to confuse Alaska voters in the upcoming primary election.
Upon appeal, on June 26, the Alaska Supreme Court permitted Sullivan to appear on the ballot, though it did not give its reasoning. Alaskan Republican officials made the decision about how Sullivan was to appear on the ballot, and determined he would be listed without a party affiliation while the incumbent senator would be listed as a Republican. Alaskan voters can vote for both men if they are confused between the two, as the election employs a ranked-choice system. 
Is ballot-stacking illegal?
Generally, ballot-stacking as an election tactic is not illegal. In a Fox News interview, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche called the practice fraud. When asked whether the practice was illegal, Blanche said "it should be" but stopped short of saying it actually was.
The Times investigation also noted that "ballot-stacking tactics are common in politics and generally considered legal."
For example, in 2024, according to an Alaska News Source report, a registered Democrat named Eric Hafner ran for Alaska's U.S. House seat, even though he was incarcerated in a federal prison in New York and did not even live in Alaska. (Hafner had been sentenced to 20 years in prison for making death threats to judges, police officers and others.)
The Alaska Beacon noted that while the Democratic Party sued to keep Hafner off the ballot, the Republican Party sought to keep him on it. The Alaska Supreme Court ruled in Hafner's favor and the Republican candidate defeated Peltola for the House seat. Hafner's campaign advertising was also reportedly backed by a Republican campaign group.
Also in 2024, a pro-Peltola PAC ran ads for a third-party candidate after Democratic strategists saw the tactic as favorable to Peltola.
John Fortier, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a right-leaning think tank, told Snopes over the phone that there is no specific law against adding similar-sounding names to ballots as an election tactic. However, there have been cases where people were prosecuted on grounds of deceiving voters, Fortier said, like cases filed against groups accused of making deceptive "robocalls" to voters to spread false information about election dates.
For example, in 2011, a campaign manager for Republican former Maryland Gov. Robert Ehrlich was convicted of two counts of conspiracy to violate election laws and two counts of election fraud. He orchestrated a scheme of robocalls targeting Black Democratic voters by informing them that Democratic Gov. Martin O' Malley had already won the election as of 6 p.m. on Election Day 2010, and thus attempted to deter them from going to the polls.
We also found a 2020 case in Florida where a local Republican Party chairman was found guilty of a misdemeanor campaign finance violation through a scheme in which he planned to use a so-called ghost candidate to siphon votes away from the Republican candidates' competitor.
Can DOJ delay or block election certification process?
On Oct. 22, the DOJ filed a complaint against the state of Alaska, Beecher, the state election board and the state ballot counting review board, saying the sole purpose of Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy was to "benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan." The lawsuit sought to delay or block Alaska from certifying its election results if the Republican candidate lost.
Fortier told Snopes that the DOJ complaint did not have a "real leg to stand on [as] the grounds were not really clear." He said, generally speaking, it is uncommon for election certification to be delayed or overturned, and even more uncommon for federal actions to be imposed on a state's election. The DOJ complaint appeared to be geared towards "broadly raising the issue [of ballot-stacking] and putting it back into people's minds," he added.
The U.S. Constitution allows states to control their own elections, so the DOJ lawsuit may have little merit in the long run. Additionally, Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means it could take weeks to finalize a result.
The state argued thst the DOJ lawsuit had "no legal basis," adding that "delaying certification of Alaska's election results—but only if a particular candidate does not win—would interfere with state election administration and threaten election integrity." The state also noted that the ballots now clearly distinguish the two candidates, who are now listed as "Daniel J. Sullivan Jr." with no party affiliation, while the incumbent is listed as "Dan S. Sullivan."
The state's response said:
If any voter remains confused, Alaska law allows voters to receive assistance from others. And if the voter is still uncertain, he can rank both Sullivans as his first and second choices under Alaska's ranked-choice voting system so that his vote will count for either Sullivan over any other candidate.
Will it affect the election?
Some Alaskans say such political tactics will do little to change their views. An Alaska Public Media report featured interviews with Alaskans on both sides of the aisle. One registered Republican said he was still voting for Peltola and that Rios' claims were likely because she was a disgruntled former employee.
Another voter said, "Voters are intelligent and can figure out how to rank and can figure out which Dan Sullivan is their person."
Some Petersburg locals also described Dan J. Sullivan as a man of "high character" and did not believe the Times' account of him working with Democrats behind the scenes.
In sum …
While The New York Times' reporting indicates Democrats in Alaska may have engaged in political skullduggery, ballot-stacking appears to be a common tactic employed many times by both sides over the years with minor repercussions. Even the U.S. attorney general said such a practice "should be" illegal but did not assert it was.
As of this writing, both Sullivans are on the ballot for the Nov. 3 Senate election in Alaska.

Tonya Azevedo says she has lost $155,000 and her family of four can no longer live in their home of 20 years after a contractor who told them he was licensed did work that turned out to be unsafe.
Azevedo said she discovered dirt used to fill concrete blocks in the foundation of the home's addition, live electrical wiring under drywall and a sewer pipe that was ruptured.
The Town of Amherstburg even ordered a stop to construction because the work didn't match approved drawings and "multiple deficiencies" were found, according to documents obtained by CBC News.
"I'm absolutely heartbroken," said Azevedo. "Every time I come here and see what's left of a home that I raised my two children in and all of the happy memories … it's just gone."
She remortgaged her Alma Street home to get $200,000 from the bank for an addition and new garage.
There were plans to build onto the rear of the home, expand the family kitchen and the master bedroom, and add an en suite bathroom and a third bedroom upstairs.
Azevedo said she just finished spending the remainder of the loan undoing and fixing the contractor's work.
In the meantime, the family is living with a relative. Azevedo and her husband are sleeping in that home's laundry room.
"We don't have a home," said Azevedo. "This is just the level of destruction that we're left with."
Police looking to charge contractor
Windsor police said Tuesday that there's now a warrant out for the arrest of contractor Jessie Flaricee after Azevedo filed a report with Windsor police's Amherstburg detachment.
Flaricee is wanted on fraud over $5,000, uttering a forged document and obtaining more than $5,000 under false pretenses.
His company, MBS Home Solutions, was dissolved for non-compliance in November 2024, according to Windsor police.
During a conversation with CBC News on Monday, Flaricee said he offered to fix the issues, has made attempts to reach out to the family and there's been a communication breakdown.
"They pretty much fired me and didn't give me the opportunity to fix any issues."
Jessie Flaricee is the owner of MBS Building Solutions and did work on Azevedo's home from March to August. (Facebook)
Flaricee said he also hired subcontractors, but didn't specify who did the problematic work.
"There is more to the story than portraying it as a contractor trying to take somebody's money. That's not even close to the case," said Flaricee. "There are a lot of layers to this situation that are far more complex than what is being portrayed."
When asked if there's any remaining money that could be returned to Azevedo, Flaricee said "that'll be between me and her."
"There's no intent to take anything from anybody," said Flaricee.
Azevedo said Flaricee told her he was a fully licensed contractor, something she says is not true.
"I guess it expired, so I had to renew it, but I'm insured. My bank account is under my business name and my name," he said.
"People have now touched that project and started working and undoing or doing [work]."
'We trusted this person'
Azevedo said her husband knew Flaricee from the local youth football community and he quickly became a family friend.
"We trusted this person," said Azevedo. "Maybe we shouldn't have listened to him and had just done some more research. I was just too trusting of him."
The Better Business Bureau (BBB) said every contractor should provide the type of licence they have, what agency it's registered with and when it expires.
"So if you want to dig into the broader term of validating licensing, check directly with the issuing authority, which is easy to do online as well," said Jennifer Matthews, CEO of the BBB in southwestern Ontario.
Some tips for consumer protection
Matthews said people should also ask for three references.
The BBB's website allows the public to check the experience and reputation of companies, which Matthews also recommends doing.
"You can look at are their complaints against that business, how have they been resolved."
Demolition and construction first began in March, when she first gave Flaricee $45,000 to get started. That's when the family packed up all of their things and moved out while the work was being done.
They moved back in by June and then the work stopped in August.
Azevedo said Flaricee asked for more money, but she refused.
She remembers telling him that she doesn't "feel comfortable giving you any more money until there is close to $155,000 worth of work here and a home that we can live in safely."
Tonya Azevedo, left, is seen with her husband, Joel Charron, right, her son, Bradley Azevedo and her daughter, Jocelyn Azevedo. (Tonya Azevedo)
In Azevedo's case, there was an attempt to figure out where the money went. She said she asked for invoices and receipts, and never received them.
But Flaricee insisted he was fired and not given the opportunity to fix the problems.
Son's 'safe space and sanctuary' is now gone
Either way, Azevedo said, there's been a lot of "stress and trauma" put on her family throughout this process.
Her 16-year-old son, who has autism, just wants his bedroom back. She calls it his "safe space and sanctuary" and said it's taken a toll on his mental health.
"To have everything stripped away from them and as a mom, not being able to fix that," said Azevedo.
The town's building department noted that the foundation mortar joints didn't comply with the Ontario Building Code and new part of the foundation was not connected to the existing foundation.
After the contractor's demolition, Azevedo said, there's been no heat in the home, the family is without a washroom and there isn't power to much of the house.
"We're not asking for our home to be finished. We're just asking for our home back."

Chennai-based stroke medicine expert Sivarajan Thandeswaran has called for certification of Indian hospitals to distinguish them as ‘stroke-ready’ so that people do not waste time in seeking treatment.
“Hospitals in India have to apply for and obtain NABH or JCI certification; instead, a proper government legislation making it mandatory for patients to be taken to and treated at comprehensive stroke centres, as done in the West, will improve stroke care,” said a senior consultant in Stroke Medicine, General Internal Medicine and Gerontology, at Kauvery Hospital in Alwarpet on Wednesday.
He was speaking at a webinar on ‘The Golden Hour: Every Minute Matters, Every Life Counts’, presented by Kauvery Hospital in association with The Hindu to mark World Stroke Day, observed annually on October 29.
He was joined by Harish R. Kamath, consultant neurologist, Kauvery Hosur. The experts stressed on the need for timely access to care as time is the most crucial factor to salvage the brain. Stroke is the second leading cause of death and, therefore, treatment in the window period of 4.5 hours is critical.
Treatment of stroke has transformed tremendously, and families need to be aware, Dr. Thandeswaran added.
In his presentation, Dr. Kamath explained the symptoms of stroke, including loss of balance, blurring vision, facial asymmetry, weakness in arms, and slurring speech. He said 1.8 million new stroke cases are added every year and 7.25 million deaths due to stroke occur every year.
Dr. Thandeswaran said that while big city hospitals have facilities for scanning, imaging, and treatment, including thrombolysis (dissolving blood clots with medicine) and thrombectomy (removing clot through surgery), in remote areas, telemedicine and video calls were being used in identifying stroke patients and transferring them to Comprehensive Stroke Centres, where advanced services and specialist teams are available.
The doctors discussed lifestyle-related risks, including poor dietary habits, physical inactivity, and inadequate sleep.
“People should take ownership of their health through routine check-ups for better treatment outcomes,” Dr. Thandeswaran suggested.

Afcon to return to two-year cycle after Caf U-turn
- Published
The Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) will return to its traditional two-year cycle after a U-turn from the Confederation of African Football (Caf).
In December, Caf announced that the tournament would be held every four years instead, but that decision has been reversed after a review.
Under the new plans, the governing body was planning an African Nations League to replace Afcon as its biennial tournament, but acknowledged that it would take several years to generate the revenue required to become self-sufficient.
"The decision by the Executive Committee to reinstate the organisation of the Afcon every two years aims to advance, protect and promote the interests of African football and the 54 Caf Member Associations, as well as those of African players playing for clubs outside the continent," Caf president Patrice Motsepe said in a statement.
The biennial hosting of Afcon has long caused issues with the football calendar, with the vast majority of recent tournaments held midway through the European club season.
Fifa's expanded 32-team Club World Cup was held in June and July last year, which also forced Caf to opt for mid-season dates.
The next Afcon will take place in 2027, with Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda jointly hosting the tournament, followed by editions in 2028, 2031 and 2033. There will be no tournament in 2030 because of the World Cup.
The dramatic 2025 Afcon final saw Senegal crowned champions before they were stripped of their title three months later in favour of Morocco.

iPad mini OLED vs. iPad mini: What's new?
Apple's new iPad mini gets a bunch of upgrades, but they come at a cost.
Apple doesn't update its iPad mini every year, which is why each new generation usually gets a huge performance boost. The new iPad mini is powered by the 5-core, 2nm A20 Pro SoC, which Apple says is up to 2.7 times faster in graphics performance and up to 4.5 times faster in AI workloads than the A17 Pro in its predecessor. It comes in the same three storage configurations as last time, and the 512GB model features an extra CPU core and a dual 16-core Neural Engine.
While both models support Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, the A20 Pro should be more suited to demanding on-device AI tasks. The outgoing iPad mini offered 8GB of RAM, and while Apple doesn't officially list how much memory its phones and tablets have, the new iPad mini likely has 12GB of RAM. Battery life claims haven't changed, but the new iPad mini charges faster (capable of hitting 50 percent in 30 minutes) with a compatible adapter.
Unfortunately, color options have been reduced to just Midnight and Starlight. The price has also increased: the new iPad mini costs $200 more, starting at $699 for the 128GB model. If spec'd with cellular connectivity and a nano-texture glass finish, the 512GB iPad mini will set you back a whopping $1,249 — that's iPad Pro money. We'll let you decide if it's worth it; for now, let's look at the changes Apple has made to its compact tablet offering this year.
The iPad mini is finally OLED
The big iPad mini upgrade this time is the OLED panel. That makes it the only other iPad in Apple's lineup with an OLED display aside from the iPad Pro. It's roughly the same resolution as last time, but can get much brighter at up to 1,200 nits of peak HDR brightness. OLED also brings other benefits: the new iPad mini is the same height and nearly the same width, but is thinner at 5.4mm and lighter at 255 grams — likely thanks to the thinner OLED panel. In comparison, the A17 Pro iPad mini maxes out at 500 nits of SDR brightness, weighs 293 grams and is almost an entire millimeter thicker at 6.3mm.
The new iPad mini also features a slightly larger 8.5-inch display, owing to the bezels that are now 24 percent thinner. The only major letdown is the lack of ProMotion. Plenty of users on X have understandably expressed disappointment about Apple sticking with a 60Hz display on a $700 product in 2026. However, in an interview with Christopher Lawley, Apple's vice president of Hardware Engineering, Dave Pakula, said that the "display experience is about more than just a single spec" and that OLED's faster pixel response time "makes everything really smooth."
If you're coming from an older iPad mini, the display on the new one will be a huge upgrade, especially for creative workflows involving HDR content. Apple Pencil Pro support is still present, too, making the new iPad mini a compact, color-accurate canvas for artists and designers.
A handful of other changes
Despite its nearly identical design, the new iPad mini is Apple's first water-resistant iPad. One of the ways it has achieved an IP67 rating is by replacing the speaker grilles with its new Acoustic Display system. This involves tweeters placed between the glass and aluminum body, with woofers firing through the display. The result, apparently, is punchier bass, clearer treble and more volume. It's similar to the Huawei P30 Pro's acoustic display, though that particular setup was largely designed to replace the earpiece speaker for phone calls rather than deliver a full stereo speaker experience like the iPad mini.
Connectivity upgrades are also present, including Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Apple's new C2 cellular modem system, which it claims should deliver up to 50 percent faster cellular data speeds. Authentication is still handled by the Touch ID-enabled power button, and while the iPad mini's optics seem largely unchanged, the front-facing camera is now positioned along the tablet's longer edge, making it better suited for video calls in landscape orientation.
The new iPad mini runs iPadOS 27 and supports Apple's most powerful on-device AI model with improved dictation and the option to adjust Siri's pace and expressiveness. While only the 512GB variant gets the extra CPU and Neural Engine cores, the 5-core A20 Pro SoC in the lower-end storage variants still delivers a substantial performance boost over the A17 Pro. With so many good AAA titles like Control and Death Stranding now available natively on the App Store, the new iPad mini is shaping up to be a portable powerhouse for gamers.

Stay rattled: Aga Ruhullah fires back at NC after moral bankruptcy jibe
Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi hit back at the National Conference after it accused him of moral bankruptcy following his resignation. Ruhullah questioned Omar Abdullah's commitment to Article 370, reservation reforms and election promises, accusing the leadership of political arrogance.
Srinagar MP Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi on hit back at the Jammu and Kashmir National Conference (NC) leadership after the party accused him of “mental and moral bankruptcy” and “self-obsession” following his resignation from the party and parliamentary seat. In a sharp response posted on X by his office, Ruhullah accused the NC leadership of abandoning its electoral commitments and questioned Chief Minister Omar Abdullah's stance on the restoration of Article 370.
Calling the NC's statement “shameless”, Ruhullah said the party leadership appeared more angered by a man questioning its promises than by those who stripped Jammu and Kashmir of its constitutional rights.
“You have more anger for a man holding you to your promises than for those who stripped Jammu and Kashmir of its rights. Your courage appears only when the questions are directed at you,” the statement said.
Ruhullah also responded to the NC's criticism of his reference to the 2010 political events in Jammu and Kashmir, saying he had been part of the government at the time and had acknowledged his responsibility. He questioned whether Omar Abdullah, who was the chief minister then, had similarly acknowledged his role.
“He was part of that government. He owes answers for that, and leaving the party does not erase that responsibility. He has acknowledged it. Where is the same acknowledgment from the man who was Chief Minister?” the statement said.
The NC had accused Ruhullah of conveniently remembering the 2010 events after 16 years, alleging that he had continued as a minister until a general reshuffle and contested the 2014 Assembly elections on the party's ticket.
RUHULLAH QUESTIONS NC'S ARTICLE 370 STAND
Ruhullah challenged the NC leadership to explain its position on the restoration of Article 370, questioning why the party had sought votes on the promise despite knowing that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) was in power at the Centre.
“Why did you ask people to vote for the restoration of Article 370 if your answer after winning was that those who took it away would not return it?” the statement asked.
He also questioned what had changed after the Assembly elections, apart from the NC gaining access to government office.
The NC, in its statement, had questioned Ruhullah's parliamentary efforts towards restoring special status, asking whether he had attempted to gather support among MPs or introduce a resolution or bill on the issue.
Ruhullah also defended his protest against the reservation policy, saying he had stood alongside students outside the chief minister's residence in December 2024. He accused the NC government of failing to provide transparency on its proposed reservation reforms.
“You promised to correct the injustice. Now you want applause for a committee and sympathy for a stalled file,” the statement said, demanding that the government publish the decision, relevant dates and details of what remained pending.
'VOTES BELONGED TO THE PEOPLE'
Ruhullah further rejected the NC's assertion that he owed his political existence to the party, saying the mandate belonged to the people of Jammu and Kashmir.
“Stop telling people that he owes his political existence to you. The votes belonged to the people. The seats belonged to the people,” the statement said.
He accused the NC leadership of treating public office as an inheritance and portraying those questioning its decisions as ungrateful.
The exchange comes amid growing political tensions within the ruling NC after Ruhullah announced his resignation from the party and parliamentary seat at a gathering in Budgam on Tuesday.
Ruhullah said he could no longer stand by the party as it allegedly moved away from its campaign promises on Article 370, constitutional rights, reservation reforms and the release of political prisoners.
The NC had termed his resignation “too late”, accusing him of undermining the party and contributing to its defeat in the Budgam Assembly by-election.
Ruhullah ended his response with a direct attack on the NC leadership, saying his resignation had returned the parliamentary seat that the party had repeatedly used against him.
“Today, he returned the seat you kept throwing in his face,” the statement said, adding, “Stay rattled.”

Keralam Health Minister K. Muraleedharan on Friday said the government would take further action after receiving a report from an expert committee probing the allegations that expired doses of Remdesivir were administered to Nipah patients in previous years.
However, critical care specialist Dr A S Anoop Kumar, who treated several Nipah patients at a private hospital, said that patients who died due to Nipah were not administered doses of Remdesivir.
Former Health Minister Veena George said that allegations raised by Mr. Muraleedharan are suspicious as the medicine has an expiry period of 2.5 to 5 years.
In a reply to a submission by Congress MLA Mathew Kuzhalnadan in the Assembly on Thursday, Mr. Muraleedharan said that Remdesivir procured in 2021 had an expiry date of May 2023 but might have been administered to patients admitted to Kozhikode Medical College till 2025.
Speaking to reporters in Kozhikode, Mr. Muraleedharan said the information presented to the Assembly was based on reports from responsible officials of the Health Department and that he would not make further comments until the expert committee submitted its findings.
The government would investigate whether the deaths of Nipah patients were linked to the administration of expired medicine and whether other patients who received the drug had suffered any adverse effects, Mr Muraleedharan said.
“There are several doubts regarding the medicine, including whether it was administered after its expiry date. We will investigate and take a decision,” he said.
The Minister clarified that there were no concerns about the quality or efficacy of Remdesivir itself and that the issue under investigation was whether expired doses had been administered to patients.
Recalling the procurement of the drug during the Nipah outbreak after the UDF government came to power, he said efforts to source it from different parts of the country had failed as the available stocks in Mumbai had expired.
Subsequently, the Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) informed the government that the medicine was available in Bahrain, following which it was procured within 48 hours, he said.
He said patients who received the medicine within its validity period had recovered and asserted that the controversy concerned its expiry date rather than the drug’s efficacy.
Mr. Muraleedharan said the expert committee headed by Dr R Aravind, head of the Infectious Diseases department at Thiruvananthapuram Medical College, would conduct an impartial examination without any preconceived conclusions.
The probe would also examine how the medicine was procured and supplied, the role of intermediaries and the functioning of KMSCL.
The government would investigate whether any agents were involved in the procurement process, he said.
The Minister also said the Kozhikode Medical College superintendent had informed him that the packaging of the Remdesivir medicine listed an expiry date but did not mention its manufacturing date. Both details are normally required on medicine packaging, and the discrepancy would be examined, he said.
“Further decisions on the issues would be taken after receiving the expert committee’s findings,” he said.

Asian Cup postponed in wake of attacks on Saudi Arabia
- Published
The 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia has been postponed because of a series of deadly attacks on the host country.
The 24-team tournament was scheduled to take place from 7 January to 5 February but has been rescheduled to run from 23 December, 2027 to 21 January, 2028.
In October, a missile attack by Yemen's Houthi movement on Riyadh's airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
A statement from the the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), external said the decision to reschedule had been taken "in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions".
It added: "The new dates of the tournament will be presented to Fifa for approval."
The Saudi Pro League has postponed this week's round of fixtures following the rescheduling of the Asian Cup.
It says the rescheduling creates "additional flexibility" in the calendar to allow for a "more balanced distribution of fixtures" across the rest of the season.
A number of events in Saudi Arabia have been cancelled recently, including the Six Kings Slam tennis exhibition event, which was scheduled to be in Riyadh.
The Asian Tour has also indefinitely postponed it's season-ending golf tournament, which was scheduled to take place from 18-21 November.
This is the second successive Asian Cup to be postponed after the 2023 tournament was moved to 2024 and to Qatar from China because of the Covid pandemic.

The decision to postpone the 2027 Asian Cup means a number of Premier League players will not have to miss part of the current season.
Some of the players that would have been expected to be called up were Japan's Zion Suzuki of Aston Villa, Wataru Endo, who plays for Liverpool, and Daizen Maeda of Ipswich Town.
Leeds United's Ao Tanaka, Crystal Palace duo Takehiro Tomiyasu and Daichi Kamada, and Hull City's Hidemasa Morita also play for Japan.
Japan would have been one of the favourites for the tournament and Villa, who are in the Champions League, might have had to do without Suzuki for at least seven games if his country had reached the final.
Liverpool are also in the Champions League but Endo has yet to play for the Reds this season.
Brighton winger Kaoru Mitoma is currently injured but is expected to be back later this year and is also likely to have been called up by Japan.
Manchester City defender Abdukodir Khusanov, of Uzbekistan, and Hull City and Australia defender Lucas Herrington would also have expected international call-ups for the Asian Cup.

A mother’s knowledge, attitude and feeding practices can significantly influence a child’s willingness to try new foods, which highlights the need for stronger nutrition counselling for caregivers during early childhood, according to a new study by researchers at the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN).
Reluctance to try unfamiliar or diverse foods studied
The study, published in the Journal of Nutritional Science, examined food neophobia, a condition in which children are reluctant to try unfamiliar or diverse foods. Such behaviour can limit dietary variety and potentially affect nutritional health during crucial years of growth.
Researchers assessed 150 mother-child pairs from Addagutta in Hyderabad between August and October 2025 focusing on children aged two- seven years and explored how maternal feeding practices were associated with food neophobia and children’s nutritional status.
Findings
The findings revealed that nearly 77% of children showed moderate levels of food neophobia, while 11.3% displayed high levels and 12% had low levels. Boys recorded slightly higher food neophobia scores than girls, although the differences were not statistically significant.
Nutritional status-food acceptance link
The study also found a link between nutritional status and food acceptance. Children suffering from wasting were more likely to exhibit higher food neophobia scores than those with normal nutritional status, suggesting that reluctance to try new foods may be associated with poorer dietary outcomes.
Nutrition knowledge an important factor
Researchers observed that maternal knowledge, attitudes and practices played an important role. Children whose mothers demonstrated moderate levels of nutrition-related knowledge and positive feeding practices had lower food neophobia scores than those whose mothers had lower scores.
Karthikeyan Ramanujam, Scientist-C at ICMR-NIN and lead author of the study, said the findings underscore the importance of everyday feeding behaviours. He suggested that caregivers should repeatedly offer a variety of foods without pressure, create positive mealtime experiences and respond supportively when children reject unfamiliar foods.
ICMR-NIN Director Bharati Kulkarni said the findings offer an opportunity to strengthen behavioural feeding counselling through existing government programmes such as the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) and POSHAN Abhiyaan.
Researchers cautioned that the study was limited to a single urban low-income community and a relatively small sample size. They noted that, as a cross-sectional study, it identifies associations but cannot establish direct cause-and-effect relationships, as per a press release.

East Bengal’s profligacy in front of goal proved costly as Omani side Al Seeb scored twice in the closing stages to register a 2-0 victory in their Group D fixture of the AFC Champions League Two at the Salt Lake Stadium on Tuesday.
Despite dominating possession and creating several clear-cut opportunities, the Red and Gold Brigade failed to find the breakthrough, with Axel Meye and Zahir Sulaiman striking late to secure all three points for the visitor.
East Bengal started on the front foot, dictating the tempo with its passing game. Dani Ramirez came close in the 10th minute after Edmund flicked the ball through to Rashid, who picked out the Spaniard on the edge of the box. Ramirez’s left-footed effort narrowly missed the right post.
The host threatened again in the 20th minute when Al Seeb goalkeeper Ibrahim Al Mukhaini saved Edmund’s effort from close range. Bipin Singh collected the rebound and returned the ball into the danger area, but captain Rashid headed it wide.
Ramirez tested Ibrahim once more in the 33rd minute, but Ibrahim produced an excellent diving save to his right. East Bengal also suffered an early setback when defensive leader Anwar Ali sustained an injury and was replaced by Sandip Mandi in the 18th minute.
AS IT HAPPENED | EAST BENGAL VS AL SEEB HIGHLIGHTS
Despite its attacking superiority, East Bengal went into the break goalless. Al Seeb threatened after the restart, with Meye heading over from close range following a corner in the 48th minute. East Bengal responded in the 61st minute when Ramirez attempted to poke home after a move involving Jay Gupta and substitute Ake Loba, but Ibrahim produced another outstanding save.
At the other end, East Bengal goalkeeper Phurba Lachenpa denied Al Seeb midfielder Omer Almalki with a sharp reflex save in the 76th minute after a cross from substitute Zahir. East Bengal’s inability to convert its chances eventually proved decisive. Meye broke the deadlock in the 85th minute, controlling Hassan Al-Ajmi’s cross before getting past Mandi and firing home.
Al Seeb sealed the victory in stoppage time when Meye turned provider, releasing Zahir down the left. The substitute raced into the penalty area before calmly slotting the ball into the bottom-right corner in the 90+1 minute.
East Bengal head coach Antonio Habas’ team selection also raised questions, with three of the six registered foreign players initially left on the bench. Foreign forwards Loba and Lukasz Zwolinski were introduced midway through the second half, but their inclusion failed to change the outcome as the hosts continued to struggle in the attacking third.
The defeat left East Bengal bottom of Group D with two points, while Al Seeb climbed to third with four.
The result was particularly disappointing for East Bengal, which had earlier secured creditable ‘away’ draws against Jordan’s Al Hussein SC (2-2) and Al-Seeb (0-0).
However, consecutive home defeats against Iraq’s Al Shorta SC (3-2) and Al Seeb have exposed its inability to translate attacking promise into results. East Bengal’s lack of clinical finishing remains a major concern as its continental campaign falters.

A half-time speech, a retaken penalty - and a win to save Carrick's job?
- Published
We cannot know how important Bryan Cristante's foot touching the Roma penalty area as Bruno Fernandes took his initial spot-kick at Old Trafford will prove to be for Michael Carrick.
In the moment, as the Roma fans celebrated, and Manchester United trailed 2-0, it seemed catastrophic for the club and terminal for Carrick's position as head coach.
But the video assistant referee (VAR) Carlos del Cerro Grande stepped in, advised a retake was required - and at the very least changed the course of the night.
Fernandes kept his nerve to drive home his second attempt and then, in a frenzied atmosphere, Matheus Cunha scored twice in the final seven minutes. Even without the context of everything that came before the game, it was the most improbable of comebacks.
Even Cunha's sending off soon after, which ensured a nervy ending, would not deny United a first win in 10, bringing some respite after a dreadful few weeks.
How did Carrick feel when the penalty was saved? And what did he say at half-time in response to a desperate first-half display that brought condemnation from legendary United figures Wayne Rooney and Nicky Butt, who were covering the game for Amazon Prime?
In that moment, there was even a sense of deja vu.
"I knew at half-time against Watford," recalled Ole Gunnar Solskjaer in September 2023 of his own dismissal as United boss a couple of years earlier. "At half-time, I told the players it was probably going to be the last time we worked together."
United were two goals down at Vicarage Road at half-time that day. Carrick was on the bench as one of Solskjaer's coaches. They went on to lose 4-1.
Not this time.
Despite the bleakness of the situation, Carrick clearly has a more positive mindset.
"At half-time, I was wanting them to be more positive if anything, and not get too disappointed and frustrated," said Carrick.
"The easiest thing is when you keep trying to do something is feeling sorry for yourself. If something goes wrong, you get disappointed. That's not going to help anybody. We might as well all go home if that's the case. We've got to keep looking for the next moment, the next solution.
"I don't like to keep talking to the lads about what this place can do and the history and what's gone before too much, but it's there.
"This place does magical things, it's done it before and it'll do it over and over again at some point in the future. There's just something in this place that when we do have these types of nights, we do it the hard way.
"But one moment can flip the whole place in a different direction. I spoke about that with the boys. Let's have one moment that can trigger it. And we had that."
Rooney, who was almost pleading with United's players to "show some passion and desire" after a "nothing" first half, could only praise Carrick at the end.
"I think Michael Carrick deserves a lot of credit," said Rooney, "because if you were in his shoes you are thinking how can I change this around?
"Whatever he said to the team at half-time, that got them on the front foot and got that belief in them that they could win the game."
Carrick refused to be downcast - even when Fernandes missed that first penalty.
"I didn't chuckle, I didn't smile, I wasn't happy about it," he said. "But it felt almost like 'there's another moment'.
"But at the same time, I was quite calm because I had a feeling the boys were in a place leaving the changing room that they felt something could happen.
"I have to say, for Bruno to double take that penalty - to have the mentality and finish like that - he deserves a lot of credit."
One great comeback - but what happens now?
While United's victory was certainly well received, it will not mask wider issues.
'Green and gold' protests against the ownership took place before kick-off and during a first-half when the home side were abysmal.
Chants against the Glazer family, minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and director of football Jason Wilcox will not stop just because of this victory, no matter how thrilling.
The sober assessment should also recall United came from behind to beat Atalanta 3-2 at Old Trafford during Solskjaer's time. They lost 5-0 at home to Liverpool four days later. Within a month, the Norwegian had been sacked.
In October 2018, Jose Mourinho was on the brink of dismissal before a Premier League encounter with Newcastle. United trailed 2-0 after 10 minutes but fought back to win. Mourinho lasted 13 more games.
No-one can know how much time Carrick has bought himself with this victory.
"I don't have a crystal ball to know what happens next," he told Amazon Prime. "We move on to the weekend. We've got a really important game here against Aston Villa, which we need to prepare for."
Chief executive Omar Berrada and Wilcox certainly looked much happier at the final whistle than they had done midway through the first half.
Suddenly United look like they can qualify for the next phase of the Champions League. For the first time since September, Carrick's players are enjoying the winning feeling.
But it will mean little unless they can maintain the momentum against Villa, who were getting beaten heavily by Barcelona as Old Trafford was in tumult.
Asked if he will sleep better thanks to the win, Carrick was honest enough to admit that would not be the case.
"Genuinely, no. I don't. Really, I don't," he said. "Whether that's right or wrong, or normal or not, I don't know, but I didn't feel relief. It was more I was genuinely pleased for the players.
"I know how much they care, I know what they're giving. Sometimes it looks like that, sometimes it doesn't, sometimes we play well, sometimes we haven't, and I understand that.
"But I could feel their willingness to do well, and so for them to have to dig really deep, and to see everybody having that feeling that we all crave, that's why we're all here."
'Perfect night' or just 'papering over cracks'?
While the pundits were unanimous in their dismay at United's first-half performance, there was plenty of praise for the second-half revival.
"I said at half-time if you're going to go down, go down fighting. You can accept losing if you've given absolutely everything," said former Denmark goalkeeper Kasper Schmeichel. "They didn't do that in the first half, but they did in the second half.
"Things look a little bit better. Don't get me wrong, the second half is papering over the cracks from the first half, so now it's a case of using this as a benchmark and now having even more of those conversations.
"You have to put your differences aside because you aren't able to change your players now, so you need everyone on side. Everyone has to be on the same page right now."
Being on the same page has seemed like a challenge for Carrick and his players. Lisandro Martinez and Fernandes have both been publicly critical in recent weeks, the targets ranging from the club's hierarchy to the head coach's tactics.
Ex-England defender Stephen Warnock, however, says the narrative set from the win over Roma is "absolutely perfect" for Carrick.
"What's happened is Manchester United have gone in, a vulnerable team, a team lacking in confidence, they've gone 2-0 down - now what's the reaction?
"Now we've just seen the reaction, so we know it's in there. The team are fighting for the manager and they're fighting to turn results around. You've got to fight and show something. When you show fight and start to run for each other, you get more confident in each other and you start to believe that you can do something.
"The Old Trafford fans and that crowd will have turned it up a notch in the second half as soon as that first goal went in and helped the team believe that they could get something out of it.
"It's a perfect night for Michael Carrick."
