Quick Answer
Samsung’s latest Galaxy Z Fold 8 ad mocks Apple’s iPhone Duo at a difficult time. Reports of cracked displays, long delivery delays, and missing features have raised concerns about Apple’s first foldable. With its reputation for hardware excellence at stake, Apple needs more than silence to restore confidence.
Believe it or not, Samsung might finally have landed an ad glove on Apple. While the two brands have been taking digs at each other for years, Apple has kept things subtle, while Samsung has never been shy about being more direct. So when Apple finally decided to join the foldable race with the iPhone Duo, it was hardly surprising to see Samsung going all out against its rival – from Apple’s late arrival to the foldable party, the Duo name, the features, the price, you name it, and Samsung probably has tried to make fun of it. But as in the past, these attempts seemed just that… attempts to ruffle a leading brand on a perceived weakness, and to reassure their own fanbase. But very recently, we think Samsung struck a bit of a serious nerve in the Apple nervous system.
The Samsung Z Fold 8 slices up an apple (no, really!)
Samsung released a 32-second video on Instagram that shows an apple (duh) with a “new” sticker on the open screen of the Galaxy Z Fold8. The phone folds, and the apple gets sliced. This slice rolls down the floor, through all the old versions of the Z Fold in the past to show how many foldables Samsung launched before Apple made its first.
The video also boasts about the Z Fold 8 being thinner and lighter than the iPhone Duo, all while comparing it to a slice of apple. This is not the most clever or cinematic Apple attack we have ever seen, but it is entertaining and thankfully is not over the top (unlike some others). What it also is, is a direct jab at something that Apple rarely has had to face – a perceived hardware problem with the iPhone.
iPhone Duo: from potential elixir to possible albatross
When Apple announced the iPhone Duo, we thought it would be just the thing the foldables needed. Foldables have been a regular part of tech news and product portfolios since pre-COVID times (the first Galaxy Z Fold came in 2019), but even after years of iterations and multiple devices from multiple brands, the foldable segment was actually running out of steam.
So, when Apple launched the iPhone Duo, we thought that foldables would finally get some serious momentum. After all, once Apple launches something (even if it has been in the market for some time), it usually becomes more desirable and eminently “inspirational” for the competition: we have seen new features, specs, and design get picked up by the competition from Apple products, and become mainstream. From accepting touch to rejecting 3.5 mm audio jacks, it has all happened. So you could hardly blame many for thinking that Apple would launch a foldable phone, and voila! All foldable phones would start selling like hotcakes.
That scenario, however, does not seem to be playing out.
When Apple launched the iPhone Duo, the tech world went abuzz, which is business as usual when a new iPhone launches. But when the iPhone Duo became available for purchase, all the news that came in was not good. In many markets, due to supply and production issues, consumers had to wait for two months or more to get a device even after paying an advance. The brand’s decision to limit sales to two devices per person was also not well-received in some markets. It would have been understandable in the case of a new brand launching its first product, but from the first trillion-dollar company in the world, it just seemed unusually odd. The fact that it came with a super premium price tag did not help matters.
All those who have got their hands on Apple’s first foldable phone have not been thoroughly impressed with it either. There has been talk of users missing the speed and convenience of Face ID, the lack of app optimization, the new placement of the status bar, and more. And as if that were not enough, there was news that landed Apple in perhaps the hottest soup it has been in a very long time – reports have started coming in of the internal display cracking at the hinge, and a line of dead pixels appearing on it.
Often coming late to the party and rocking it…but perhaps not this time!
Once again, such problems from a new brand’s first product might have been treated with more patience. But imagine spending Rs. 2,99,900 and getting a device whose display has hardware issues. Imagine also being a person who has booked the device and is waiting for their unit, which is two months away. While Apple has acknowledged the issue, insisted that the issues exist in a small number of devices, and has assured users that all devices facing the issue will be replaced, a lot of damage has been done.
Apple’s reputation has, in some ways, worked against it. With Apple, the tech world has become accustomed to waiting for features, functions, and form factors that were seen on other devices. Android users have mocked Apple fans for getting the features that were on Android after years. But while Apple has delayed the addition of a feature or an entry into a segment, it has generally delivered an excellent performance. And that has been the defense of many Apple fans – Apple might not be the first to make a certain kind of device or bring a certain feature, but its implementation (whether it was capacitive touchscreens, Touch ID, App Store, and more) has been excellent and often an industry benchmark.
With Duo, that belief is being rocked. The brand has stepped into the foldable zone almost seven years after others, and launched a device with what seems to be a hardware flaw– not a software bug that can be fixed with an update, but a problem that can only be fixed with replacement.
Is silence golden for the communication wizard?
Apple’s handling of the issue so far has been a little unusual. The brand has found itself in trouble in the past as well with issues such as Antennagate and Bendgate, both of which generated a storm of criticism. But Apple officially addressed those issues publicly – Steve Jobs himself came out with an explanation in the case of the iPhone 4 when its stainless steel band interfered with the phone’s cellular performance, and the company also issued a very detailed statement on BendGate, famously pointing out that the issue had occurred with only nine users.
While there has not been radio silence from Apple with regard to Duo’s screen, no major management figure has come out to explain the issue or build back confidence – even in his first earnings call, new Apple CEO John Ternus limited himself to saying that while the issue existed, it affected a very small percentage of units. This relative silence could be (mis)interpreted by many in the public. To many, it does not seem as if the brand is working out solutions, as it has actually been launching devices left, right, and center since the Duo was launched.
To see management showcasing new products and talking of record earnings, even while complaints trickle in about a high-profile flagship does not make for great optics. We hope that changes soon, or alternatively, Apple comes out with a strong defense of its first foldable – it needs it. The longer it keeps silent, the more space it gives to its competitors to score points off its perceived weakness. And Apple cannot really afford to let cracks develop not just on the Duo, but in its own reputation for hardware excellence. As Samsung has shown, its competitors will not hang back in taking potshots at it. And unless credibly explained, these shots will start to hurt.
Given its potential and the hype around it, the Duo could still prove to be the elixir the foldable sector needs, but Apple needs to address the issues around it swiftly and effectively. This is a challenge unlike any other the brand has faced in recent times. Even the relative failure of the Vision Pro was more about a product being too futuristic (almost a prototype of sorts for an elite audience). The Duo, however, is supposed to redefine how we use foldables in particular and even smartphones in general. Many have even called it Apple’s most radical iPhone since the OG iPhone. How John Ternus tackles the issues surrounding the Duo could well define the tone of his tenure.

Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.
In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).
Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.
“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.
Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.
South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.
However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally.
Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.
Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.
South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.
In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song.
The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.
Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.
Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.
The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.
For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed.
The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.
However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated.
Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.
“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.
“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.”
Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.
“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”
In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.
While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

Two government-backed startups release sovereign AI models that can run in airgapped environment
India AI Mission-backed startups Soket AI and ZenteiQ unveiled sovereign, offline models for secure use in coding, maths, science and research.
Two startups backed by the government’s India AI Mission - Soket AI and ZenteiQ - on Tuesday released their sovereign AI models that can work in air-gapped environments, meaning systems fully cut off from the internet and outside networks. The models were unveiled at a press briefing in New Delhi in the presence of IT Ministry secretary S Krishnan and India AI Mission COO Sudeep Shrivastava.
Soket AI launched EKA-1, a 26.3 billion parameter model built for maths and coding. It was trained on about 7.5 trillion tokens covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages and English. ZenteiQ released two open-source models, Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B. These are multilingual assistants that support English and 10 Indian languages. They are designed for secure, on-premise and offline use in critical sectors.
ZenteiQ’s Sashikumar Ganesan explained the difference of airgapped systems from popular chatbots. With a service like ChatGPT, he said, the “inferencing”, the step where the model produces an answer, happens in a server at a remote location. In an air-gapped setup, it happens locally.
“No data will go outside,” he said, adding that the model needs no network connection. It can also run on a mobile phone with at least 6 GB of memory. He named defence and cybersecurity as possible users.
Krishnan said smaller models have many uses, including cybersecurity, and can be deployed in air-gapped environments. He said the two models have different strengths - Soket’s is aimed at maths and coding, while ZenteiQ’s is aimed at science and research.
Ganesan said ZenteiQ trained on Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) because of the scarcity of GPUs. He said TPUs are not inferior to GPUs, and that getting GPUs would have meant waiting another three to four months
Soket founder Abhishek Upperwal said safeguards are in place, including protections against content on suicide and self-harm.

Concert tickets that surge to $1,650, an airline pocketing $75m of unused flight credits and a washer/dryer cycle that takes 25 hours have all made the dishonour roll in consumer advocacy group Choice’s annual Shonky awards.
Now in their 21st year, the Shonkys spotlight Australia’s worst products and services as decided by Choice.
Choice awarded Virgin a Shonky gong for imposing strict deadlines on customers to use credits issued for cancelled flights between 2020 and 2022, amid Covid-19 travel restrictions. Customers had to book their trips by 30 June this year, and had to use the credits for flights taking off before 27 May 2027. This resulted in $75m of credits going unused and then being returned to Virgin’s bottom line, according to Choice.
A spokesperson for Virgin Australia said: “More than 93% of Covid credits were redeemed by guests, supported by strong bookings over the past four years.
“Following a number of extensions between 2023 and 2025, we regularly communicated the expiry date and later extended the fly-by date to 27 May 2027, giving guests almost another year to travel.”
Ticketmaster and Ticketek received Shonky awards for using what Choice deemed “sneaky” tactics – dynamic pricing and “in demand” seats – to unfairly inflate prices for live events amid the broader cost-of-living crisis.
Dynamic pricing – common in transport and hotel sectors, but a more recent phenomenon for live events – describes products whose prices fluctuate based on demand.
For example, when a popular concert goes on sale, ticket prices may go up as more customers join the online queue.
Choice said John Farnham fans who logged on to Ticketek looking to secure tickets to a tribute concert earlier this year found themselves facing variable prices. “Ultimate” tickets – the most premium option available, which were not subject to variable pricing – cost $1,650.
Similarly, NRL supporters who bought tickets to some matches in 2026 through Ticketmaster reported “in demand” seats selling for $50 more than regular seats, even though they were only one row and one bay apart.
A spokesperson for Ticketmaster said it did not use surge pricing or algorithms that automatically increase prices in response to real-time demand, and that prices were set by event organisers.
“For ‘in demand’ tickets, event organisers set the prices of sought-after seats closer to market value and may review these over the sales period,” they said. “These prices do not automatically increase because more fans join a queue.”
Guardian Australia contacted Ticketek for comment.
The Albanese government promised to restrict dynamic pricing in 2024, but did not include any prohibitions against the practice in its new laws designed to limit unfair trading practices, due to come into effect in 2027.
Choice’s chief executive officer, Monique Perry, said the organisation wanted to see expanded price-gouging laws to protect consumers.
“With Virgin, we’d love to see consumers get the $75m back or have unlimited time to [use] those flight credits,” she said.
Perry said Choice decided which products to consider for Shonky awards based on consumer feedback.
“Some of these are really serious for consumers and where we really have a call to action and sometimes it’s more about buyer beware,” she said.
Perry said calling out companies sometimes resulted in tangible actions, such as Commonwealth Bank pledging to refund $68m of fees after Choice gave it a Shonky in 2025 for charging $270m in excessive fees to low-income customers.
This year, Hisense got a Shonky for advertising a washer/dryer model as “super energy efficient”.
However, Choice says the energy rating can only be achieved on the 2025 Series 8i heat pump combo washer/dryer (HCF8I1215HB) if one uses its 13.5-hour “eco” dry cycle, and 728-minute wash cycle – more than 25 hours combined for a wash and dry.
A spokesperson for Hisense said: “The energy rating displayed on our product is determined in accordance with the Australian government’s regulated Energy Rating Scheme and the applicable Greenhouse and Energy Minimum Standards (GEMS) requirements. Energy ratings are calculated using prescribed Australian testing standards, established performance criteria and defined assessment methodologies.”
Perry described Hisense’s ratings as “gaming a broken system”. Manufacturers get to nominate which program will be assessed for energy ratings “and it’s usually one that produces the best energy-efficiency outcome, rather than one households would actually use”.
Choice scolded Petcover for its “economy” insurance policy, saying the insurer sold customers an entirely new policy every 12 months, which classifies all conditions their pet has previously experienced as pre-existing, thus excluding them from cover.
Quest received an award for selling its “protein chips” at a huge mark-up compared with similar, non-protein options. For example, at more than $20 per 100g, the Quest nacho cheese protein chips were 886% more expensive than nacho cheese flavour Doritos, which cost $2.06 per 100g.
Although the Quest chips contain 56g of protein per 100g, compared with 7.5g for Doritos, Perry said there were much cheaper and simpler ways to get additional protein.
PlayStation owner Sony received a Shonky for revealing customers did not actually own the movies and games they’d paid for, and instead had only bought a licence to access the content, which can be revoked at any time without a refund.
Choice said the problems with this kind of licensing arrangement became apparent in June, when Sony announced an end to its licensing agreement with Studio Canal in the UK and Europe. This resulted in 500 movies paid for and stored in customer’s digital libraries being removed, without any kind of refund, Choice said.
Guardian Australia contacted Quest, Petcover and Sony Entertainment for comment.

Filmmaker Madhumita is set to return to the big screen with John Doe, a Tamil psychological thriller starring Arjun Das, Sachana Natrajan and Srishti Singh. Ahead of its theatrical release on November 13, the director has opened up about the film’s casting, the performance she sought from Arjun and her approach to creating a story that balances mystery with human emotions.
Director Madhumita explains why Arjun Das was the right fit for psychological thriller John Doe: “The film needed an actor who could hold complexity without over-explaining it”
Explaining why Arjun was the right choice for the psychological thriller, Madhumita said the character required an actor capable of conveying complexity through restraint rather than lengthy explanations. She said, “Arjun was right for 'John Doe' because the film needed an actor who could hold complexity without over-explaining it. The character requires restraint, vulnerability, and an underlying intensity—and Arjun naturally brings all three.”
The filmmaker also revealed that Arjun’s recognisable voice became an important part of the film’s storytelling. Instead of relying on it merely as a familiar characteristic, the team incorporated it into the narrative to add another dimension to the mystery. Madhumita explained, “Voice also became an important part of the film’s design. Arjun is always associated with a very distinct, powerful voice, and rather than treating that as just a familiar trait, we used it as an element of the story. In a psychological thriller, voice can create intimacy, unease, authority, or doubt depending on how it is placed in a scene. His voice adds a layer to the character’s presence and to the audience’s experience of the mystery.”
Madhumita further spoke about discovering a different side of the actor during the shoot, particularly in scenes that demanded controlled expressions and emotional restraint. She said, “Yes, working with him revealed a quieter, more internal side of him. People associate Arjun with a certain commanding screen presence, but in 'JOHN DOE' he had to be controlled, fragile at times, and deeply human.” She added, “Some of his best moments in the film came from silence and small shifts in expression, not loud dramatic beats.”
The director’s approach to John Doe also connects with her recent work on the Tamil web series Love Always, which premiered on JioHotstar on October 30. Adapted from the Korean webtoon Here We Go Again, the series explores marriage, relationships and second chances. Madhumita described her approach to both projects, saying, “I aspire to be a genre-agnostic filmmaker. For me, genre is only the wrapper; the starting point is always people and emotion. Love Always uses fantasy and comedy to explore a marriage, while John Doe uses tension and mystery to explore fear and truth. The emotional questions may differ, but the process is similar: understand the characters, find their contradictions, and serve the story honestly.”
Madhumita previously made her Bollywood debut with Kaalidhar Laapataa, an adaptation of her Tamil film K.D. With John Doe, she returns to theatrical cinema through a psychological thriller, which is scheduled to release on November 13.

The Best Space Heaters for Portable Warmth
Featured in this article
The Best space heaters are winter’s rear guard, the last line of defense against goose bumps and cold feet. Though not a great way to heat a whole home, space heaters can be indispensable for a late-evening movie night, a workbench in a chilly garage, or the home’s odd corners that refuse to stay warm. And if you live in an apartment building where you don’t control the heat, they may be your only way to feel OK in January.
Even so, these little machines do bring about serious safety and reliability concerns, along with a need to be able to parse dodgy and opaque marketing claims. (For example, no matter what the marketing specifies, large space heaters usually aren’t more powerful or more effective than small ones.) So we turned down the thermostat and tested dozens of space heaters to find the ones that’ll warm you up as quickly, quietly, and safely as possible.
Alongside naming the top pick overall—the blessedly balanced and quiet Dreo Whole Room Heater 714—we also pinpointed which heaters are best poised to suit specific needs, from the best bathroom heater and a space heater that doubles as an air purifier to an option that’ll warm your towels. For those on a tight budget, the bare-bones Honeywell 360 Surround often goes on sale.
Looking for more ways to tailor your air? Check out our guide to all things that improve your indoor air quality, as well as our specialized guides to the Best Air Purifiers, Best Humidifiers, Best Fans, and Best Dehumidifiers.
Updated November 2026: We’ve added a new Honeywell model (HHF365) as a pick, heaters from Lasko and Amazon Basics to Honorable Mentions, and information about a Dreo recall. We’ve also updated links and prices.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Frequently Asked Questions
Are Large Space Heaters More Powerful Than Smaller Ones?
Nope! It may seem counterintuitive, but large space heaters don’t necessarily heat any better than smaller options. In fact, most space heaters in the US and Canada deliver about the same amount of heat, regardless of size. Space heaters top out at 1,500 watts, which is the highest safe operating load for a 15-amp household circuit. And aside from some low-power personal heaters here and there, most space heaters available are capable of 1,500 watts.
What’s more, electric space heaters are all pretty much 100 percent efficient at converting that electricity to heat. Whether directly or indirectly, nearly all of that energy eventually becomes heat.
So if space heaters share basically the same power and efficiency capacity, why are some 1,500-watt heaters advertised for small rooms and others for large rooms? This likely has as much to do with marketing as science. Pretty much every ceramic, electric-coil, and positive-temperature-coefficient (PTC) heater has about the same amount of juice and, thus, the same ability to heat a room … at least eventually.
What differs among heaters is how and where the heat gets distributed and how quickly. All other things being equal, a heater's efficiency mostly focuses on whether it puts the heat where you want it to go.
What Are the Different Types of Space Heaters?
All electric space heaters essentially do the same thing: They take electricity off the grid, usually 1,500 watts of it, if you're in the United States, and turn that power into heat.
The vast majority of space heaters, including ceramic heaters and PTC heaters, are electric-resistance heaters. This means they run an electrical current through something that creates resistance: maybe an electric coil or maybe a specially designed ceramic. This quickly turns electricity into heat.
Most space heaters use a fan to disperse this heat out into the world, where we all live. These forced-air convection heaters tend to be the fastest at quickly raising the temperature of the surrounding air. The air then heats you. While this variety heats quickly, it can take quite a bit of electricity to warm an entire room.
Oil-filled radiators, in contrast, heat oil that circulates inside the device, which then emits heat to the surrounding room. These tend to heat up more slowly than electric-resistance heaters, but they offer even, lasting heat and are very quiet. These radiators operate on the same principle as steam radiators in buildings with a boiler room. And just like steam radiators, they can get hot to the touch.
Radiant heaters, such as infrared heaters, operate much like the sun or a campfire: Rather than heat the air, they directly heat objects or people by radiating energy in their direction. Infrared devices heat the air only indirectly, via the objects they heat. The glow is immediately palpable as warmth, but you’ll need to be in the path of the radiation to feel it, much like the feeling of being in direct sunlight versus the shade. Likewise, the thermometer might not immediately register the warmth you perceive. Infrared heaters tend to be superior for providing warmth without expending much energy, making this type common in large, lofty spaces or outside on a patio.
Though they deliver heat differently, both infrared and oil-filled heaters are subject to the same wattage limitations as electrical-resistance heaters and share efficiencies.
The same is not true of heat pumps, a newer technology that’s expected to provide the next generation of household heat. Heat pumps don’t use energy to create heat. Instead, they move heat energy from one place to another. Accordingly, they require far less energy than other space heater types. But household systems are costly to install, and while more affordable window and portable heat pumps are ramping up, they’re not yet broadly available.
Are Space Heaters Safe?
Yes, but also definitely no.
Space heaters are much safer than they used to be. Modern space heaters are heavily regulated, especially regarding exposed heating elements and automatic shutoff switches to prevent overheating. But all heating devices require caution, and so do all devices that pull a lot of energy over long periods.
The vast majority of residential heating fires start with actual fire—specifically in fireplaces and fuel burners. But portable heaters, including electric space heaters, accounted for more than an average of 1,600 fires per year in the US between 2020 and 2022, according to the United States Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC). These fires were associated with an average of 70 deaths and 150 injuries annually during that time period.
So, treat your space heater with the caution and wild skepticism that it deserves. See WIRED's Guide to Space Heater Safety for a full rundown of how not to start fires or cause other hazards with the machines. That guide follows recommendations from federal experts at the U.S. Fire Administration (USFA) and the CPSC, as well as the Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers (AHAM).
But for the short version:
Don’t leave a space heater unattended. "Unattended” includes sleeping, y’all! Might we suggest a wonderful down comforter instead? When possible, safety experts also recommend you don't leave a portable heater running unattended in a room with a baby, nor a person with mobility issues.
Plug your heater directly into the outlet. Don't use extension cords or power strips with space heaters, lest you build up too much electrical load and risk a fire.
Don’t plug another appliance into the same outlet or circuit as the space heater.
Place a space heater only on the floor or on a level surface. Heat rises. You don't need to prop up a heater on an unstable chair or table. The exception is the rare heater designed to be mounted on a wall.
Keep your heater at least 3 feet from flammable objects. This includes bedding, drapes, furniture, clothes, papers, and books.
Keep space heaters away from water and dampness, whether in bathrooms or in moist basements prone to dripping or flooding.
Read the manual. Manufacturers have good advice.
How We Tested and What We Tested
Testing space heaters involves answering a few key questions: How safe is it? How loud is it? How quickly and evenly can it heat a room?
During intensive testing of dozens of space heaters, I lived for weeks in a home with the thermostat set to a chilly 65 degrees Fahrenheit.
I tested how well and quickly each device heated a medium-size room (14 by 14 feet), and also how well it heated a small seating area in a larger, open-format space. To test each heater’s thermostat and also measure the evenness of heating, I placed thermometers at three or more locations in each room, including behind the heater.
I gauged the loudness of each device with a decibel meter at 3 feet away and verified power usage with a wattmeter. To understand whether the heater’s exhaust put out painful levels of heat, I used an infrared thermometer to collect precise surface temperatures. When in doubt, I put my own fingers on the line.
Finally, I tested safety features and basic durability. I looked at independent safety certifications, of course. But I also rudely knocked over each device to verify how its tip-over protections functioned and confirmed that the heater started working again when set back upright.
To test overheat protection, I smothered each device with an old sheet to see whether the device shut itself off or adjusted its power output to keep internal temperature low. In the event that the heater turned off, I then checked how soon it could turn back on, if it ever did. (Some heaters gave up, in permanent complaint!)
If any device fails the tip-over or overheat tests, I don’t recommend it. If it’s significantly louder than 50 decibels at 3 feet, I don’t recommend it. If the heater breaks during routine operation, I don’t recommend it. Maddening rattles and squeaks are also disqualifying.
I continually test my favorite models to track how they hold up over time and subject new heaters to this testing regimen to see if they can oust the current top picks.
More Space Heaters We Recommend
Amazon Basics Ceramic Space Heater for $21: This was the least expensive heater we tested, and for the same price, you can choose a model that oscillates. It has tip-over protection and auto shutoff if it senses a temperature spike. Dials are analog, though this heater does have a light that glows when it's plugged in. At about 48 decibels on high, it was loud but not as loud as some other heaters we tested. It seemed to take ages to heat the 100-square-foot room it's designed for, so I felt like I always had it turned on. But if that doesn't bother you, it's a great value. —Kat Merck
Vornado AVH10 for $100: Vornado has an unholy variety of models that look quite similar but have different levels of loudness and feature sets. Some are built in America, some in China. In general, the models I’ve liked best are the ones that advertise “vortex action,” a fancy name for spinning a fan into a spiral grate oriented opposite to the action of the fan. This leads to a mostly quiet and nigh-undetectable column of warm air, directed out to the back of the room, where it scatters. The TAVH10, which is basically this model but with a timer and remote, is my current favorite, though if you need neither, you can save $30 and get this instead. —Matthew Korfhage
Vornado MVH for $75 and Vornado VH240+ for $65: These two devices are very nearly identical. The MVH is among the most silent, even in its heat, and reasonably priced space heaters available. However, the TAVH10 is a bit quieter, and its included remote and timer make it more attractive. This said, there are reasons to favor analog devices like these. For instance, you can regulate them with a temperature-controlled power outlet in order to get the most accurate version of a thermostat. —Matthew Korfhage
Lasko Ellipse Ceramic Tabletop Heater for $70: This little ceramic number from Lasko was the space heater I kept reaching for while testing dozens of other space heaters last year. It’s not the most obvious choice: It doesn’t heat a room evenly, its grill surface gets wackily hot, and the thermostat is an inside joke. I’m not sure I’d run it near babies or small dogs. And yet I still kept voting for it with my cold, cold feet. Why? Because this little thing can radically change my whole experience of life within about 15 seconds of turning on. It brings the heat, as they say, though mostly within an 8-foot radius. Within that manifold, it’s like living inside a hair dryer, which is more pleasant than it sounds. This previous pick for best foot warmer is still good, but it’s just not as versatile as our new top pick for personal heater from Vornado. —Matthew Korfhage
Shark TurboBlade Cool + Heat for $400: WIRED reviewer Kat Merck enjoyed the customizable airflow of Shark’s original TurboBlade cooling fan (7/10, WIRED Recommends), which you can angle every which way. On cooling fan settings, these virtues remain true of the Cool + Heat version. True to its name, the Cool + Heat model also adds a 1,400-watt heater to the equation, with emphasis on “little.” The TurboBlade does not push air through its blade-like “wings” for heating as it does for cooling. Rather, it blows hot air only out of the small vent at the center of the device, whose aperture is only somewhat larger than some hair dryers. The versatility of heating and cooling is nice, and I especially love that the thermostat is accurate. Shark also automatically modulates its energy output to maintain temperature in a room, which helps to avoid the wild on-off swings of some less sophisticated heaters. But for such a small heater, the TurboBlade is quite big and loud. Even on low settings, the high-pitched jet engine whir never stops. Standing in front of it on high settings, my phone registers 70 decibels. So I’d recommend this for someone who predominantly wants to use the device as a fan. The heater is more of a secondary function. —Matthew Korfhage
De’Longhi Slim-Style Portable Panel Heater for $210: This electric panel heater is an interesting hybrid, with dual heat exhausts on each side but also a broad radiant heat panel. This makes for a middle ground between radiators and resistive fan heaters—heating a room much faster than a classic radiator would, but still maintaining warm radiant heat over time. That said, it shares a radiator’s main fault, which is that it’s painfully hot to the touch across a large surface. It still issues the same amount of fan noise as a fan heater, also. But it may be your choice if you need to heat up a space quickly and evenly and maintain that heat over time. —Matthew Korfhage
Dreo MC706 Fan and Heater for $170: Dreo’s innovative 2-in-1 fan-heater combination uses auto-shift positive temperature coefficient (PTC) technology, which moves the heater’s ceramic element aside to allow full fan airflow. Its 1,700 ft/m wind speed is a rarity among tower fans, let alone tower fan/heater combos. It’s not the strongest space heater, but it is sufficient, with five settings, 120-degree oscillation, and tip-over protection. Note that though it includes a remote, it has no smart features, and it does not work with Dreo’s app. —Matthew Korfhage
Dreo Bathroom Heater for $55: Like Dreo’s smart wall-mounted model I far prefer, this ceramic heater comes with an ALCI plug for safe use near water. I prefer to keep bathroom heaters away from the floor, but not all bathrooms have mountable wall space. This remains a possible, though not ideal, alternative, with a somewhat janky thermostat. —Matthew Korfhage
Vornado VC-02 Ceramic Heater for $130: Vornado put out two new ceramic heaters at the tail end of 2025. The less expensive, smaller, horizontally oriented VC-01 ($80) is WIRED’s top personal heater pick. The VC-02 is a bit like the 01 turned on its end and made into a tower heater. The VC-02 is, in most ways, a premium model, with more options in terms of power and fan settings. It’s even quieter than its sister model—in fact, it’s one of the quietest heaters I’ve tested, period. It has a thermostat that’s reasonably accurate. It’s also got a remote and the ability to swivel from side to side for full-room coverage. (It does not pivot up and down, though, the way the VC-01 does.) But while I like all these features, its tower-heater shape makes it less optimized than the VC-01 for up-close heating, which is what ceramic heaters do best. —Matthew Korfhage
Not Recommended
Heatbit Maxi Pro: The Heatbit Maxi Pro (5/10, WIRED Review) is a cool-looking, luxury-styled air purifier and heater with a twist: It offsets its energy use by mining Bitcoin. At the high energy rates and lagging Bitcoin price of 2026, the Bitcoin mining certainly wasn’t profitable. But it did offset the cost of heating with the device by about a third, and made onboarding quite easy for Bitcoin novices. The app and safety features are admirable enough. But the Heatbit is neither a quiet heater nor a great air purifier, and its Bitcoin mining might take most of a decade to make up the $1,500 to $2,000 price tag of the device. In the end, the Heatbit is a conversation item, something to show off to houseguests. But I couldn’t find a way to make it practical. It's also currently out of stock. —Matthew Korfhage
Lasko Design Series 16" Ceramic Space Heater: It's a fact that short space heaters work just as well as tall space heaters to heat a room. However, most of them aren’t much to look at. This little ribbed cylinder, however, sits on a plastic faux-wood tripod base and looks more like a speaker or modern air purifier than a heater. I quite liked having it in my office during testing, and it includes all the trimmings—oscillation, digital thermostat, remote, digital display (which can be snoozed for bedrooms), and a timer. However, its plastic grate got extremely hot during testing, rendering it a burn hazard for kids and pets. —Kat Merck
Boldr Kelvin (Gen 2): The Kelvin is a much different heater than the others on this list: It is a silent white or black panel that slowly heats up over the course of an hour, emitting what the company attests is far-infrared radiation, similar to those mail-order saunas you can find on Wayfair. The standard model tops out at just 450 watts, so the sell isn’t really that it emits a lot of heat. Rather, far-infrared feels warmer if you stand in front of it. It operates on the same principle as heat from the sun, warming surfaces (including people) directly rather than heating up the air. In the ideal case, this means you can feel more warmth while using less energy than a traditional heater. Its makers recommend it for those stubborn cold spots in a house. But I struggled with this heater. A wall-anchored heater offers less flexibility, and, in the shorter term, a radiant heater provides warmth only directly in the path of the panel, meaning it must be positioned with quite a bit of care to be useful. The Kelvin also uses up quite a bit of wall space, and must be located near an outlet. By design, its front gets quite hot to the touch—near boiling, in fact—and the device projects quite a bit of heat backward into the wall even after a second-generation upgrade to its insulation. It’s an interesting concept, with a smart app to track energy use, but the caveats add up. At $400, it’s hard to make it pencil. —Matthew Korfhage
Pelonis 16-Inch Space Heater and Pelonis 23-Inch Space Heater: Both of these towers heated up quite quickly. Both were also incredibly hot at the surface of their vents, with relatively little shielding from the visible heating elements. The 23-inch was significantly quieter than the 16-inch, however. —Matthew Korfhage
Vornado Velocity Cube 5S: This cube’s outer housing stayed quite cool, and the fan functionality is welcome. But its surface vent got a little hot, and the fan was a bit on the noisy side compared to other Vornados. —Matthew Korfhage
Vornado Velocity 5R Whole Room Heater and Vornado VHEAT: The MVH and TAVH line from Vornado are among the quietest space heaters I’ve tested. These were two of the loudest. The 5R topped 70 decibels, and while the vintage-looking VHEAT is quite lovely visually, it’s also a bit of a noisemaker. —Matthew Korfhage
Lasko MyHeat Mini: This little thing looked cute, and I thought it would be a nice desktop or under-table personal heater. But even with its low output at 400 watts, the vent got way too hot to want it anywhere near your laptop or papers. —Matthew Korfhage
Lasko 22-inch Oscillating Tower With Remote: This one failed our tip-over test when I knocked it over, blasting heat endlessly into the rug until it overheated and sent a burnt-plastic smell into the air. It did restart hours later, meaning this shutoff was a safety feature. But this tower’s a bit too tall and tippable to risk repeating these events often. —Matthew Korfhage
Honeywell 2-Position Heater: This compact, simple, analog heater was a nice enough idea, able to rest vertically or on its side. Lord, it’s loud when its fan is in operation, though. As of February 2026, this device is out of stock, but I’ll monitor restocks. —Matthew Korfhage
Honeywell Compact Ceramic Tower: This Honeywell performed well in terms of fast heat and safe surface temperature. Its fan wasn’t too loud, either. But the one I received had a maddening squeak each time the tower oscillated fully counterclockwise. —Matthew Korfhage
Gone but Not Forgotten
Vornado Sensa Cribside Heater: I loved the idea behind this Vornado Sensa Cribside Heater when I tested it: A space heater with an external temperature sensor, with, therefore, accurate temperature management (which is hard to find among space heaters!) But it’s disappeared from Vornado’s website, and has dwindled on retail sites. It’s no longer available on Amazon, but if you see it on sale at another site, I still like it. —Matthew Korfhage
Also tested but discontinued: Vornado VMHi600, Morento 26-cm Heater, Morento 40-cm Heater, Dyson HP07, many other models of Vornado before the brand’s late-2025 refresh. —Matthew Korfhage

Pocognoli focus on Scotland tidy-up as Euros loom
- Published
When Sebastien Pocognoli's disjointed Scotland trudged off at a two-thirds-full Hampden after being well beaten by Slovenia, the intrigue that came with the start of the new boss' extended maiden camp had turned to a sense of deflation.
A dominant display in a Nations League draw away to the Slovenians 10 days prior, plus another in a 2-0 victory at North Macedonia, had built optimism.
A 3-0 defeat at home to Switzerland was written off after Jack Hendry's early red card was quickly followed by an opening goal for the 12th-ranked Fifa nation.
A second straight Hampden loss under the Belgian felt different, though. Pocognoli's side were "outfought" and simply "not good enough", said captain Andy Robertson.
Cut open defensively throughout by Slovenia, placed nine spots below Scotland in the world rankings, a sobering second-half showing led to questions about approach, systems and squad make-up.
However, heading into a double-header against North Macedonia and Switzerland this month, which will conclude the Scots' Nations League campaign, Pocognoli insists this is more of a clean-up job rather than one that requires any radical change.
"We want to continue what we produced in the first camp," the 39-year-old said after naming his latest squad, which marks the returns of Scott McTominay, Che Adams and Kieran Tierney, while James Penrice has received a first call-up as reward for an impressive run of form with Rangers.
"There's no reason to change everything because I was happy with the camp. The main word is continuity [after the first camp].
"It's important to get some good results for sure. I was clear we need to find the right balance between changing things, experimenting and also being successful."
- McTominay returns as Penrice earns first Scotland call 
  - Published5 hours ago
- Honeymoon over as Pocognoli's Scotland suffer domestic disharmony 
  - Published6 October
Pocognoli seeks mood-shifting result
In football's savage, reactive world, a deserved defeat at home to a team ranked outside the world's top 50 is bound to attract scrutiny.
Given it was the final match of a four-game run before a six-week wait to attempt to put things right, that criticism only becomes prolonged.
Pocognoli shared the Tartan Army's disappointment, but after a few days the "real feeling" came after a debut camp packed with new faces and "strong decisions".
"When the disappointment was gone, the first feeling was positive," he said. "We did a lot of good things.
"But we need a good result to give something to the supporters and give confidence to the players that we are winning games - that's the main factor in qualifying for tournaments.
"We want to just continue the good things we showed in Slovenia and North Macedonia in a very short period of time, to keep the fragment of these games and to try to clean some situations."
The 'big job' coming up
Despite the positivity Pocognoli is harbouring, he is not oblivious to the fact Scotland need to improve this month.
His side are third in Nations League Group B1 and require a minimum of four points to have any chance of finishing second and featuring in the promotion play-offs, while one point would stave off any threat of relegation.
Then comes qualification for Euro 2028, coined "the big job" by Pocognoli.
Scotland will have to qualify for the tournament they are co-hosting along with England, Wales and the Republic of Ireland - but two places will be reserved at the finals should any of the host nations fail to qualify.
The qualifying draw takes place in Belfast on 6 December, with group fixtures starting in March next year.
Any time Pocognoli therefore has with his players is critical, and he hopes Napoli star McTominay, Torino striker Adams and Celtic's Tierney will help bring consistency to a squad that has had the refresh button hit on it since Steve Clarke's shock summer exit.
"If you accumulate their caps, we have some experience that will be useful for this camp," the head coach said of the returning trio.
"All I want to do now is make the most of this time to know my squad as deeply as possible, to see the body language, the attitude of the players in some situations and to have most of the information to start the big job [of qualifying for the Euros]."
Penrice 'deserves' chance - but what about Miller?
After an autumn camp full of fresh faces, including Pocognoli and much of his backroom team, the Belgian will greet another with the call-up of Penrice.
The left-back has excelled since joining Rangers on loan from AEK Athens in August, particularly in recent weeks, with Derek McInnes occasionally utilising the versatile 27-year-old in midfield.
"We have some missing players around the left side and, combined with his quality and what we are looking for on the pitch, it's a logical choice," Pocognoli said of Penrice's inclusion.
"He can be very useful for the system we want to play, and I think he deserves it."
There was more disappointment for Lennon Miller, though. Having returned to the squad following his World Cup exclusion, the Udinese midfielder has been dropped again.
Despite Pocognoli playing down the decision to leave out the 20-year-old as "not a big topic", his international career remains a curious case.
After delivering a standout performance in his only start for Scotland, a 4-0 victory in Liechtenstein in June 2025, Miller was expected to follow an upward trajectory but has since played just three minutes for the national side.
Pocognoli suggests Miller is a victim of playing in the area of the team's "most competitive" field and wants to deploy him in a more advanced midfield role.
"We've offered him the opportunity to play for the Under-21s, maybe in the position and shape from the first team," the Scotland boss revealed. "For Udinese he plays as a number six. I want to see him higher on the pitch.
"Like with Findlay [Curtis], if he's doing well with the Under-21s, for us it's like a massive scouting report for the future because we can see him in his best position in the shape we want to see."

An underground activist group says it plans to start openly doxing billionaires as part of a phased campaign against what it calls the American oligarchy—beginning this month with a release that maps the homes of Elon Musk, his brother Kimbal, and Tesla’s board, alongside investors and suppliers that keep the corporation afloat.
Two of its members, interviewed by WIRED on the condition of anonymity, say they spent the past year constructing dossiers on billionaires—and one trillionaire—and the people they consider their top lieutenants, using nearly every method available to a private investigator, and some that are not.
The pair say the group is international and includes grassroots activists, researchers, journalists, and artists, including some who received top honors in print, television, and digital media in their former careers. For security, many work in “silos” and do not know each other’s names. Through its connections, the group says it has raised more than $1.2 million from “a heartening number of wealthy class traitors” who share in the view that concentrations of extreme wealth and political power pose an “existential threat.”
In a press release Monday, the group says it intends to publish in coming releases more than 150 home addresses, most of them previously unreported. It also promises more than 3,500 records on people with a combined wealth of about $1.4 trillion, plus reporting on what the group alleges are “criminal exploits and security lapses.”
Members of the organization call themselves Capytistas, a play on Zapatistas, the Indigenous insurgents of southern Mexico.
The capybara, a placid rodent famous for getting along with almost any other animal, became the group’s avatar during the early days of Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency, as a secret rival to the Shiba Inu—the Doge meme Musk used to brand the agency. (The meme has since been reclaimed by pro-Ukranian activists who post as cartoon dogs to mock Russian propaganda and raise money for the war.)
Americans have long used the term “oligarch” to refer almost exclusively to Russian tycoons who carved up state industries after the Soviet collapse. But it entered mainstream American politics decisively in January 2025, when President Joe Biden used his farewell address to warn that an “oligarchy is taking shape in America.” No one typifies the “extreme wealth, power, and influence” Biden described more than the trillionaire Musk, who held an unpaid job as a special government employee for much of 2025 and has thrown more than $700 million into federal elections since 2023; the equivalent of roughly 15 million typical donations online.
Doxing—the Capytistas’ chosen tactic—has meanwhile become a favored weapon of political guerrillas and self-appointed state informants: In March 2025, as protesters gathered outside Tesla dealerships, an anonymous site called DOGEQuest posted what it claims were the addresses of Tesla owners and DOGE staff. Months later, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement official testified that his unit drew more than three-quarters of its deportation referrals from Canary Mission—a site with similarly nebulous funding but radically different goals: building dossiers on pro-Palestinian students and professors.
Few have done more to expand doxing than the Department of Homeland Security itself, which simply broadened the term to include, effectively, any “videotaping” of law enforcement. Its aggressive stance on keeping officers’ faces hidden, and its refusal to identify those credibly accused of crimes, has all but ensured public campaigns to unmask its employees. Last week, hackers published the names and work contacts of more than 40,000 DHS employees and contractors, citing its practice of collecting data on the public while hiding who its officers are.
Pressed on whether its strategy amounted to doxing, the Capytistas members agree that it does, saying they have no qualms with describing their efforts that way. The group has even taken as its creed an adapted quote from the late folk singer and labor organizer Utah Phillips: “Democracy is not dying, it’s being killed,” they say, “and those who are killing it have names and addresses.”
Most of the Capytistas’ work involves digging up property records, court filings, and the LLCs and trusts that wealthy people use to buy real estate. The activists say they turn occasionally, but far less often, to physical surveillance, human infiltration, and advertising intelligence, the location and profile data bought and sold through online ad markets.
To remain profitable, one of the Capytistas argued, the businesses billionaires operate need to continuously collect people’s personal information, often nonconsensually, even as their owners and executives enjoy relatively private lives—entire fortunes built around “doxmaxxing.”
A copy of the Musk dossier seen by WIRED sorts its subjects into tiers and contains 32 home addresses tied to Musk and his executives. Musk is the “primary target.” Tesla’s board members and top executives—among them board chair Robyn Denholm and Kimbal Musk—are “secondary targets.” Each profile pairs a critical biography, drawn from court rulings, labor board decisions, and securities filings, with a home address. Investors such as Vanguard and BlackRock and nearly 40 suppliers are considered “tertiary targets,” listed only by corporate office, factory, or mine.
Tesla’s press office and investor relations team did not respond to requests for comment.
The Capytistas see Musk as effectively a gateway for normies who have yet to join its class war. Its file on him is among the smallest it has prepared, and he ranks among its “least important” targets, members say. But he was chosen first because no other person draws as much public anger, and the group hopes to harness that and release it upon others whose fortunes rely on forever wars, omnipresent surveillance, and carceral expansion.
Law enforcement records obtained by WIRED show how quickly that anger spread across the country last year. Within months of Musk’s arrival in Washington, attacks on Tesla vehicles and dealerships had hit at least nine states, according to a joint FBI-DHS bulletin released under public records law. Other documents show intelligence analysts warning cops across the country that calls to boycott Tesla and protest Musk were multiplying alongside the attacks. Hundreds of demonstrations were planned barely two months after Trump took office for the second time.
In Nevada, analysts were forced to issue formal first responder guides to fighting electric-vehicle battery fires, which they said can take up to 8,000 gallons of water to extinguish. “As a high-profile tech company tied to immense wealth and business culture, Tesla can potentially represent those grievances,” one bulletin said of vandals who had “expressed anti-corporate or anti-capitalist views.” Musk’s role at DOGE in particular, a Northern California agency wrote, had made Tesla dealerships “symbolically larger targets.”
The Capytistas say doxing gives them one thing above all: a sense among those targeted that someone is watching. Some, they hope, will simply fold under the sheer weight of that attention. For the rest, the group wants the public to make its displeasure well known, hoping for protests outside homes and on golf courses—confrontations with those who buy their way into government in the very places they go to escape all the outrage.
Privacy is the one thing that the group believes billionaires, and now trillionaires, value that activists can take away. “The Capytistas intend to level the playing field,” it says, “by giving oligarchs a taste of the invasions of privacy they commit, and monetize, every day.”
Tech executives’ homes have already become targets. In April, San Francisco police arrested a 20-year-old man they say threw an incendiary device at the home of OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, setting fire to an exterior gate. The man returned less than an hour later to threaten to burn down the company’s headquarters. No one was hurt.
In the interview with WIRED ahead of the release, one member pointed to the killing of UnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson in December 2024, arguing that what the group is doing is trying to prevent such bloodshed—a sentiment echoed in a statement released by the Capytistas on Monday: “While Elon Musk and the other individuals we target will undoubtedly try to frame our work as extreme and stochastic, what we’re doing is using radical accountability to build an off-ramp that might prevent the inevitable violent and tragic outcomes the oligarch class has been steering us toward.”
“In the end,” they said, “we may be doing them a favor.”

A lot of Floridians lost their healthcare this year. Now, they're heading to the polls
📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App
WELLINGTON, Fla. – The insurance agent called Bianca in January. Bianca's health insurance premium had at least doubled from its previous rate, the agent said, wondering if the registered nurse who works a 40-hour week could still afford access to health care.
"I talked to my husband about the new rate," said Bianca, 32, who asked NPR to withhold her last name, as political activists in her community have faced harassment. "It was not something we were able to afford."
She cancelled a lineup of asthma and mental health related doctors' visits. Since then, she's had to take loans to pay out of pocket for a visit to the emergency room and for prescriptions to treat pneumonia.
The rise in Bianca's insurance premium is not isolated to her, or even to Collier County in South Florida. In December 2025, the Trump administration let enhanced subsidies that the Biden administration had announced for Affordable Care Act coverage during the Covid-19 pandemic expire. In the Senate, most Democrats had voted to extend the subsidies; most Republicans opposed them.
The expiration caused a spike in premiums for millions of people across the country, but it hit Floridians especially hard because of its large number of ACA enrollments and expansive gig economy. In 2025, 4.3 million people in Florida were enrolled in ACA plans. Nearly 443,000 fewer people had healthcare in Florida in 2026 according to federal enrollment data. Florida is also one of the states that opted out of expanding coverage to Medicaid.
This November, as open enrollment begins, premiums are expected to rise again, at the same time voters head to the polls. In some of Florida's newly drawn, competitive districts, such as the area encompassing Tampa and parts of South Florida, access to healthcare appears to be on the ballot for this election.
Bianca said she will be voting for the Democratic nominee in her district, Pia Dandiya.
"Pia is trying to expand the Affordable Care Act," said Bianca. "Which I think is really important, especially for families like mine."
Dandiya, running in Florida's 22nd Congressional District, is campaigning on bringing back the subsidies, reversing the cuts the Trump administration has made to Medicaid and lowering drug prices.
"We know that we need to all work together to introduce [health insurance] legislation at the House level, and get some bipartisan support," she said in her campaign office in Wellington. "Health care is not a blue issue or a red issue. It's a red, white and blue issue. It's something that is impacting all of us."
Dandiya's Republican opponent, Casey Askar, wants to eliminate the ACA altogether and crack down on fraud to preserve Medicare and Medicaid. His campaign did not reply to interview requests.
The district Dandiya and Askar are running in consists of the Everglades, stretching from the Gulf coast on one end, to suburbs of Palm Beach County on the other. But lack of access to health insurance spans even wider. More than 10 percent of Floridians are uninsured according to United Health data from 2024. The passing of the One Big Beautiful Bill tax cut and spending bill —which affected ACA subsidies and reduced federal Medicaid funding — exacerbated the situation.
Prices are expected to rise even further this November, said Katie Roders Turner, the Executive Director of the Family Healthcare Foundation, a Tampa-based nonprofit that connects families in West Central Florida with health insurance.
"We've already seen the projection of higher maximum out of pockets and higher deductibles," she said. "Changes to the availability of subsidies based on people's immigration status is creating more of a burden for people."
Mixed feelings about healthcare
Back in the 22nd District, many retirees and others on Medicare and private insurance said their vote is not related to health insurance.
Fred Gleim recently retired after working with the city's water department for more than 30 years. He's conservative and will be voting Republican.
"I'm 76, I've got Medicare," he said while walking his dogs in Naples. "It's been working great."
For those struggling to find affordable health care, Jerson Dulis, the Executive Director of the Florida Health Justice Project, a non profit which focuses on health equity and access to care, says a big problem is the confusion that comes with changing laws and policies.
"A lot of people don't know if they even belong in the system or not, or if they deserve access to health care," he said. "Often when people receive a notice saying there's been a change in their ACA or Medicaid policy, they miss their appointments or just abandon their care."
Deyanah Johnson, 24, used to have insurance but she fell off and for a while, she didn't even realize when, why or how that happened, she said.
Johnson used to live in West Palm Beach with her family. As rent got too expensive, they moved inland and are still struggling to pay for housing.
She's working as a receptionist at Palm Beach State College, while also studying to be a dental hygienist, and isn't sure if she qualifies for Medicaid. At the same time, she can't afford any of the plans she's been looking at on the healthcare Marketplace.
"It's like we basically can't afford to live," she said. "I hope we get free health care. In other countries, they get free health care."
Johnson has previously voted for Republicans, but this time she's considering voting for Democrats, "to get our country back in order," she said.

As U.S. citizens headed to the polls to vote in the midterm elections on Nov. 3, people shared a rumor alleging the FBI uncovered more than 20,000 fraudulent Democratic ballots in a raid of a storage facility in Texas.
For example, on Election Day, a user named Jonathan Gregory posted on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and X (archived) a headline reading, "OVER TWENTY THOUSAND FRAUDULENT BALLOTS UNCOVERED IN FBI RAID OF HOUSTON STORAGE LOCKER WAREHOUSE ALL FOR DEMOCRATS." That post, along with others on Facebook and X, displayed three images and said the alleged raid happened in Houston:
An FBI raid of a storage locker warehouse in Houston Texas last night uncovered over twenty thousand fraudulent ballots all marked in favor of Democratic candidates. Agents seized the massive stash during the operation after tips led them to the facility where the ballots had been stored and prepared for distribution. The discovery has sent shockwaves through the election system as officials scramble to determine how many of these illegal ballots may have already been cast or were ready to be injected into the count.
Every single one of the fraudulent ballots was filled out for Democratic candidates which points to a coordinated effort to tip races across the state. Investigators are now examining the origin of the ballots the people who controlled the storage units and any connections to political operatives or campaigns. This is not an isolated incident but clear evidence of organized ballot fraud designed to overwhelm legitimate votes.
The American people deserve immediate answers and full transparency about who was behind this warehouse full of fake ballots. Texas and the nation cannot allow such brazen attempts to steal elections to go unpunished. Law enforcement must pursue every lead and ensure these fraudulent votes never count.
People who left comments under the Facebook and X posts appeared to believe the FBI truly conducted a raid uncovering many thousands of fraudulent ballots. Snopes readers emailed us and searched this website to find more information.
In sum, our research quickly found this rumor was false and may have originated as satire. Gregory displays his Facebook page category as being a comedian. His Instagram and X accounts don't display such a label. None of Gregory's profiles specifically mention the word "satire," though he has previously used the term near the very end of some of his posts — potentially as a way of hinting at the truth about his content. (Because the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" and "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' own descriptions of their work.)
Rosio Torres-Segura, a spokesperson for the Harris County Clerk's Office in Houston, confirmed Snopes' conclusion: "The information circulating on social media is false."
We also reached out to Gregory via Messenger to ask if he wished to speak about social media users appearing to believe the claim that the FBI found thousands of fraudulent ballots in Houston and will update this article if we receive a response.
The bogus story spread in the aftermath of a reported incident involving the same number of ballots. On Monday, the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's request to set aside 20,000 ballots the FBI alleged may have been issued to noncitizens.
Further research
Reverse image searches for the post's three images found photos pertaining to unrelated matters in Atlanta and San Francisco, as well as the picture of a building matching that of a Houston storage company.
(@TrumpNews_Baby via X)
A scan of the text in Gregory's posts with the Pangram artificial intelligence detection tool returned the results "100% of this text is AI," as well as "We believe that this entire text is AI."
Snopes doesn't entirely lean on the purported accuracy of such tools for fact-check ratings. Rather, we consider scan results as one of at least several data points necessary to make a rating determination.
In the past, we've published fact-check articles about other matters originating from Gregory's social media accounts, all of which involved false claims.
For more about the midterm elections, look to our live updates blog for all of Snopes' Election Day coverage.

Heavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and Turkey over the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150 mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.
Travelling eastwards towards South Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85 mph (140 km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of over 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.
Heading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150 mph (240 km/h), with winds gusting over 185 mph (296 km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered by Typhoon Champi earlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which have already been battered by four super typhoons this year alone.
Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of western Mexico. Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100 mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150 mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.

If there’s one thing WIRED staffers love almost as much as tech gear, it’s caffeine. We take our coffee so seriously that we don't suffer fools when it comes to travel mugs. Through painstaking testing that's yielded spilled lattes, lukewarm brews, and dented thermoses, WIRED testers have pinpointed the very best travel mugs available. Whether you need a sturdy option that can survive the chaos of an NYC morning commute or a self-heating tumbler for all-day sipping, consider yourself covered.
Want more help leveling up your morning brew? Be sure to check out our guides to the Best Coffee Subscriptions, Best Coffee Grinders, Best Espresso Machines, Best French Presses, Best Portable Coffee Makers, Best AeroPress Coffee Makers, and How to Make Better Coffee at Home.
Updated November 2026: We've added the BrüMate Strova and Ember Tumbler 2, and information on what to look for in a travel mug. We've also updated links and prices throughout.
The Best Travel Coffee Mug
The Hydro Flask Coffee with Flex Sip Lid is my go-to travel mug. It’s low-maintenance and built like a tank, making it a forgiving choice for the clumsiest of sippers. The brand's powder coating can handle clammy hands, and the 16-ounce tumbler fits into most car cup holders.
It's also a multipurpose mug that isn't limited to housing just your steaming morning brew. Because Hydro Flask wide-mouth lids are conveniently interchangeable, you can swap in a straw lid for cold beverages (or anything else you'd like to drink). And if you purchase the travel mug directly from Hydro Flask, you can get it engraved with text or a graphic, in addition to picking from the 10-plus available color options.
A Mug That Can Handle Your Mornings
Imagine sitting by a campfire under the stars, sipping hot cocoa, then waking up at sunrise to a cup of coffee by the lake. A handleless mug just doesn't do that scene justice. Hydro Flask's travel coffee mug brings that camp aesthetic to life. It also just feels great to hold in any setting—including for morning dog walks or while you get yourself ready for your day at home. The slider lid keeps out curious bugs and helps to slow the release of heat, but it’s not leakproof.
I also appreciate the mug's stainless steel rim that's smooth to sip from sans lid. Just note that it’s not TPU powder-coated like most Hydro Flask bottles, so it's a bit less grippy and you’ll have to hand wash it.
Best Value
If you’re a fan of the Owala FreeSip’s spout, then the lightweight SmoothSip Slider will not disappoint. Its triple-layer insulation helps to keep drinks hot for around six hours or cold for 24. The slider lid works fine for everyday use and didn't leak when I flipped it upside down. But I still wouldn’t toss it into a bag because of how easy it is to unlock. Alongside being available in fun colors, Owala also releases limited-edition designs you can shop. Also notable is that Owala bottles are lead-, BPA-, and phthalate-free.
Best Flippable
After an unfortunate entanglement with a coffee mug and my computer, there was a period of time when the only bar where everybody knew my name was the Genius Bar. Now, lid security is my top priority for any liquid I tote around. For that singular concern, BrüMate's cupholder-friendly Strova gets a W from me. The brand claims its patented BevLock lid is fully leakproof, and after putting the mug through its paces—flipping, shaking, and dropping it—before I even considered placing it in my purse to intermingle with my water-sensitive electronics, I came to trust the promise: I couldn't make a single drop of coffee slip through the closed-mouthpiece edges or perimeter of the lid. Further, the mug's ceramic-lined interior both protects the temperature and taste of whatever you're drinking, and it comes in more than a dozen colors and designs any aesthete would be happy to show off.
The compromise you'll have to make is that the Strova is a bit awkward to sip. The mouth opening is quite small, running in a thin, tight line, like an expressionless face, as opposed to larger, easier-to-sip options that might conjure more of an open-mouthed cackle. The construction means you have to tip the mug up past your nose to sip when it's half full or less. This may look a bit aggro while you're drinking, but it’s frankly a small price to pay for confidently avoiding spillage. —Alexis Berger

A long morning commute can be a slog. Add in successive underwhelming sips of tepid coffee, and you're less and less likely to walk into work bright-eyed and bushy-tailed. This travel tumbler, from the brand that normalized spendy warming mugs, holds a generous 16 ounces, fits into a car cupholder, and—most importantly—keeps your beverage hot. It claims to have a battery life of three-plus hours, but I noticed my brew losing its steam after about two. You can control the temperature on the tumbler itself by pressing a button on the bottom that toggles between five heat levels, or you can choose a precise temp via the Bluetooth-connected app. But if you're driving, you'll probably just want to default to the hottest temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit before you depart.
