The Delhi Police had posted a video on their X handle on October 25, which urged citizens to not burn crackers this Diwali. Along with a meme video, the post was captioned: “This festive season, let tails wag, not tuck. Say NO to crackers, YES to a greener Diwali.”
Soon after the post was made, social media users had predicted that it would be removed soon. Incidentally, just within a few hours of the post being made, the Delhi Police removed it from X.
While Delhi Police did not issue any clarification as to why the post was taken down, several X users wondered whether the reason behind the post being taken down was perhaps the purported pressure from the BJP-led central government.
Alt News co-founder Mohammad Zubair had also remarked on Delhi Police’s post, before it was taken down, with the caption: “This tweet will soon be deleted due to political pressure.”
Another X user, Jeevansh Arya, shared a screen grab of the Delhi Police’s post and questioned whether it would be deleted.
@zoo_bear @DelhiPolice Tweet Deleted Now ?
Daro Mat 😂😂 https://t.co/q51PIYEFZG
— 𝐉𝐄𝐄𝐕𝐀𝐍𝐒𝐇 𝐀𝐑𝐘𝐀 🇮🇳 (@jeevansharya) October 25, 2026
After the post was deleted, many social media users posted that they expected something like this to happen.
Like most of us predicted, tweet deleted by @DelhiPolice
— Piyush Rai (@Benarasiyaa) October 25, 2026
The official handle of Indian Youth Congress also questioned the logic behind the retreat of the Delhi Police.
Administrative Indecision in The Past
This is, however, not the first time that the Delhi administration retracted its position during Diwali regarding firecrackers. Over the past two years, Delhi’s authorities and the courts have attempted to take a strong stance against firecrackers due to the city’s severe air pollution, but they have often backtracked on their decisions.
Ahead of Diwali 2024, the Delhi government imposed a complete ban on the manufacture, sale, storage and bursting of all firecrackers until January 1, 2025. The Supreme Court later criticised the poor enforcement of the ban and suggested that the government consider making it permanent. In December 2024, the Delhi government told the court that it had imposed a year-round ban on firecrackers.
However, the position changed soon. In April 2025, the Supreme Court refused to relax the ban, but in October it allowed green crackers to be sold and used in Delhi-NCR for a limited period during Diwali. The court said these crackers had to meet standards set by the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI), and allowed their use only during specified hours. The Delhi government and the Centre supported the relaxation.
In effect, the authorities moved from a complete ban on firecrackers to allowing a limited category of green crackers, despite earlier court observations that even green crackers could not be considered a comprehensive solution to Delhi’s pollution problem.
Delhi Pays The Price
Delhi’s air quality worsened sharply during Diwali 2025, with the city’s AQI (Air Quality Index) reaching almost 500, falling under the hazardous category. Firecracker bursting was followed by a dramatic rise in PM2.5 and PM10 levels.
According to a Times of India report, between 9 pm and 10 pm on Diwali 2025, the PM 2.5 concentration of Delhi’s Nehru Nagar region saw a spike from 679 micrograms per cubic metre to 1,763µg/m³. The report also mentioned that the peak PM2.5 concentration was more than 29 times the national daily limit of 60 µg/m³ and around 118 times the World Health Organization’s recommended daily guideline.
Pollution Concerns Framed as Anti-Hindu
Following Diwali last year, Alt News had written about the Right-wing supporters in the country interpreting complaints on the detrimental environmental effects of bursting firecrackers as an “attack against Hindutva” itself.
YouTuber Dhruv Rathee had posted a video on his X page asking his audience to desist from burning firecrackers. Right-wing social media users immediately began sharing images of firecrackers that they had apparently hoarded. While some questioned Rathee’s stake in it, others indulged in whataboutery and asked whether he had shown environmental concerns on Bakrid. Certain users went to the extent of mockingly comparing the extreme pollution levels in India to the genocide in Gaza.
Similarly, when BJP leader Subramaniam Swamy wrote on X, “Exploding fire crackers after 10 pm today is a criminal offence. Police should crackdown on them”, Right-wing influencer Chandan Sharma (Hindutva Knight/@HPhobiaWatch) targeted Swamy’s daughter, The Hindu’s Diplomatic Editor, Suhasini Haidar, using obscene language for being married to a Muslim man.
Several Right-wing accounts, such as @NamitaBalyan, @AchAnkurArya, and @JaipurDialogues, posted photos showing the firecrackers and the knight sky shrouded in smog, ultimately dismissing grave environmental concerns under the garb of protecting Hindu festivals.

Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting are among the most distressing side effects of cancer treatment in children. Preventing them is essential not only to improve quality of life, but also to help patients complete treatment. Yet the medicines used to prevent vomiting can themselves cause adverse effects, making the search for safe alternatives an important challenge in paediatric oncology.
An Indian multicentre clinical trial suggests that olanzapine may offer an alternative to dexamethasone, a corticosteroid routinely used to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in children receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy — treatment with a high risk of inducing vomiting. The current regimen using dexamethasone is a guideline that is used regularly, but dexamethasone is a corticosteroid. The study was aimed at finding a comparable, non-corticosteroid option.

Bangladeshi author Taslima Nasrin, who is currently living in Kolkata, on October 20, Tuesday, wrote on Facebook that although Leftists in West Bengal organise bookstalls during Durga Puja, such stalls are absent during other ‘religious’ festivals such as Christmas and Eid. She questioned why Leftists choose not to sell books promoting ‘atheism’ during other religious festivals, but instead promote them only during a Hindu festival.
In her post, she wrote (translated from Bengali), “Someone asked, “Have you ever seen Leftists selling books on atheism to Muslims near an Eidgah on Eid? Have you ever seen them selling books by Richard Dawkins or Christopher Hitchens to people attending Christmas prayers on Christmas Day? Then, quite naturally, the question arises: why do they want to sell books on atheism specifically at Hindu Durga Puja pandals?” What answer do the Leftists of Kolkata have to this question?”
This post has garnered over 7,000 likes and 1,300 reshares, and garnered significant traction, although she had disabled the comment section of the Facebook post.
Nasrin, who has been in exile since leaving Bangladesh in 1994 amid death threats and protests over her writings critical of the ‘dogmas’ of Islam, was forced to leave Kolkata in 2007 following violent protests against her autobiography ‘Dwikhandito’ and pressure on the then CPI(M)-led Left Front government.
She remained unable to return to West Bengal for nearly 19 years, with successive CPI(M) and Trinamool Congress (TMC) governments in power. However, in July 2026, following the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) coming to power in the state, Nasrin returned to Kolkata and was publicly welcomed and celebrated by sections of the Right-wing BJP-RSS ecosystem.
Against this backdrop, her recent Facebook post questioned what she portrayed as the Left’s selective promotion of atheism. Moreover, her statement comes on the heels of state authorities demolishing and damaging certain bookstalls set up by Left parties near Jadavpur’s 8b bus stand on October 17.
Fact Check
Alt News found several social media posts and news reports that refute Nasrin’s claim that the bookstalls are exclusively set up during Durga Puja.
The Students’ Federation of India (SFI) and the Democratic Youth Federation of India (DYFI) have been organising a bookstall near Park Street, where Christmas is celebrated in Kolkata, for at least 10 years. Prominent Left leader Biman Bose has also visited the stall. The bookstall has been featured on the social media handles of SFI, DYFI, CPI(M) and other affliated organisations, and has also been covered by the media. The Telegraph reported the setting up of the bookstall at Park Street for the first time in 2016, Alt News also founds images of stalls from 2017, 2022, 2024.

Below are images of a bookstall set up during Christmas in 2024:
Similarly, the SFI-DYFI local committee in the Khidderpore area of Kolkata organised a bookstall during Eid this year. Khidderpore has historically been home to a significant Muslim population. The bookstall was organised for two days and was featured on the Facebook page of the CPI(M) Kolkata Port Assembly Committee.
Below are glimpses of the stall set up on Eid at Khidderpore:
Further, Nasrin claimed that the Leftist bookstalls only sell books promoting atheism. However, the images on social media, posted by people who bought books from hundreds of these stalls, clearly show a vast array of books from across genres being sold in these stalls.
An Alt News correspondent visited the CPI(M) bookstall set up near Jadavpur 8B bus stand and encountered a diverse section of books, ranging from Bengali classics, poetry, history among others. Books on Ramkrishna and Vivekananda were also available at the stall.
CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh made a video, interviewing a woman who visited the stall and described herself as a devotee of spiritual leader Lalon Fakir. In the video, she shared her book haul which comprised books on Lalon Fakir, and other Hindu spiritual leaders like Nityananda Mahaprabhu, and even a cook book.
CPI(M) leader Sudip Sengupta, who is in charge of the 8B bookstall regularly posted pictures of the stall on his Facebook page. In one such image, physician Dr. Arjun Dasgupta was seen holding a book on Swami Vivekananda, along with a book on the Second World War.
According to Dasgupta, apart from Leftist books, the stall also contains books such as Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’s Anandamath. “I was looking at some old pictures my family took at the Jadavpur 8B stall, and I could see Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’s books behind me. His books include ‘Anandamath’, which has the song ‘Vande Mataram’. So it is simply not true that these stalls only sell books promoting atheism. These stalls are part of Bengal’s culture, and anyone who loves books should stand against efforts to shut them down,” said Dasgupta.
“We Bengalis feel that a book is a book, whether it is sold at an ISKCON stall or a CPI(M) stall. We love books and naturally gather around any stall that sells them. When we were children, these stalls introduced many of us to great books from around the world. I vividly remember my father buying me a copy of ‘Ispat’, the Bengali translation of Nikolai Ostrovsky’s ‘How the Steel Was Tempered’. I think thousands of people like me have similar memories,” he added.
Similarly, the Rashbehari-1 area committee of the CPI(M) set up a book stall near the Kalighat temple during Durga Puja. Images of the stall show stacks of books ranging from Bengali children’s classics such as Thakurmar Jhuli to literary works including ‘Ichhamati’ by Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyay, ‘Kapalkundala’ by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, ‘Grihadaha’ and ‘Devdas’ by Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay, among others. Books on Maa Sarada, and books written by Rabindranath Tagore were also visible at the stall.
Thus, the findings above show that Nasrin’s claim that Leftists organise bookstalls only during Hindu festivals such as Durga Puja is false, as there is documented evidence of Left organisations organising bookstalls during both Eid and Christmas. Her claim that books exclusively on atheism are sold at the stalls is also false, as there is documented evidence of books of various genres being sold across Left bookstalls.

With crowds thronging Sadar Bazar for festive shopping ahead of Deepavali, the North District police have stepped up security arrangements, deploying face recognition system vans, drones and additional personnel to prevent crime and manage the rush.
The police also conducted a flag march with paramilitary forces in the wholesale market on Tuesday to reassure shoppers and deter criminal activity. Sadar Bazar, one of Old Delhi’s busiest wholesale markets, witnesses a significant surge in footfall in the days leading up to Deepavali, as traders and customers from across Delhi-NCR and neighbouring States visit to purchase festive goods in bulk. The market is currently bustling with shoppers looking for decorations, lights, firecrackers, clothes, footwear and other festive essentials.
“This flag march was conducted in view of the Deepavali festival and for the security of people coming to the market for shopping. It is also meant to instil confidence among them. We conduct such marches regularly so that shoppers feel assured that they are safe,” said Sonu Kumar, Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP), Sadar Bazar.
Alongside routine patrolling, public announcement systems have been installed at key points in the market to caution shoppers against crowding and gathering at one place. The police have also deployed Facial Recognition System (FRS) vans, including those under the Delhi Police’s Dynamic Real-time Identification and Surveillance for Human Tracking Initiative (DRISHTI) and Ikshana surveillance systems, at major intersections and busy junctions.
The systems scan faces in real time and match them against police databases to identify known offenders, pickpockets and wanted criminals. Police said the deployment is aimed at curbing seasonal offences such as theft, pickpocketing and chain-snatching, which become a concern in the densely packed market during the festive rush.
Police personnel have also been stationed on elevated watchtowers, or machans, along busy market lanes. Equipped with binoculars, officials monitor crowd movement and keep an eye out for suspicious activity. Drone surveillance is also being carried out to monitor congestion and movement across the market.
North District DCP Niharika Bhatt said crowd management remained a priority in busy markets such as Sadar Bazar, particularly during the pre-festival rush. Police personnel are being deployed on the ground round the clock to regulate the movement of shoppers, prevent overcrowding and avert any stampede-like situation.

As Americans go to the polls today, many will have had their decision about who to vote for informed by an artificial intelligence-powered chatbot.
Around 50 percent of recently surveyed US adults have at one time used an AI chatbot, and 8 percent say they have used these tools ahead of the midterms to find information on candidates and policies, according to Pew Research.
But a lot of information from these chatbots is out of date and has been hallucinated or sourced from partisan websites.
Even supposedly non-partisan chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s Gemini have been found wanting when it comes to questions about the midterms.
Just last week, Google’s AI Mode refused to provide the results of the 2020 elections and the company’s Gemini chatbot said the deadline to request a mail-in ballot in Pennsylvania was November 3, rather than the real deadline of October 27, according to research by Forum AI.
According to the Forum AI research, almost 40 percent of election answers given by all the mainstream chatbots contained at least one factual error. In August, when Forum AI’s researchers asked why someone should vote for North Carolina congressman Don Davis, Claude gave a response that confused the lawmaker with a “former school superintendent” of the same name.
Google and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment. Open AI directed WIRED to a blog outlining the company’s approach to elections in 2026.
Part of the problem is that chatbots are reliant on an increasingly problematic pool of online information. Research by NewsGuard found that mainstream chatbots cite so-called “pink slime” websites nearly 50 percent of the time when asked about candidates and policies related to the midterms. “Pink slime” sites present as mainstream news websites, but are in fact funded by political or ideological groups and individuals.
Ahead of the midterms, many more of these sites have sprung up, and chatbots are paying attention. The worst offender, according to NewsGuard, was OpenAI’s ChatGPT, which cited the “pink slime” sites in more than 70 percent of searches, while xAI’s Grok chatbot performed best, citing “pink slime” sites in 30 percent of cases.
“I don't think that most Americans are prepared to navigate an election in the age of consumer AI,” Nina Jankowicz, executive director of the American Sunlight Project and a former disinformation czar during the Biden administration, tells WIRED. “One of the problems is that executives and companies have really overpromised on what AI is capable of. It has to ingest this information from somewhere, and often those sources are not very good. And it's predictive, so if it doesn't know the answer, it does frequently make things up.”

The AI race has largely revolved around frontier labs and models that can write, code, analyse documents and reason through prompts. But as companies move from chatbots to AI agents, another part of the stack is gaining attention: models that make a specific decision and return an answer that another system can act on. Decision models gained momentum with the arrival of Jev, the first public model from TypeSafe AI, founded by Diogo Almeida, who helped develop research behind ChatGPT at OpenAI. Released in September, Jev focuses on decision-oriented outputs, including scores and yes-or-no probabilities, rather than conventional text generation. Other companies have since explored similar capabilities, though their products differ in architecture and intended use. Cloudflare has introduced Clef and Clef-flash, while Microsoft has released Decision-1, a model based on Alibaba’s Qwen family that has been post-trained for decision tasks. AWS has introduced Strands Decider 2B for agent workflows, and OpenAI has launched a Decisions API. Perplexity has also explored decision-oriented APIs. Under this approach, an agent handling a customer complaint, for instance, may need to decide whether to escalate it, route it to a particular team or resolve it automatically. It does not necessarily need a long, generated response to make that decision. The same applies to systems classifying transactions, checking whether an action should proceed or routing requests across software tools. These decisions can be handled by general-purpose large language models (LLMs), but using them for every step can add latency, cost and complexity. Decision models are designed to handle narrower tasks, returning a label, score, probability or confidence level instead of a paragraph of text. The idea is to give software a more direct way to make a bounded judgement without requiring a general-purpose model to generate a full response at every stage. In agentic systems, where multiple tools and models work together, this could make routine decisions easier to integrate into a workflow. They are not necessarily replacements for LLMs. Rather, they can become specialised components within larger AI systems, handling defined decisions while general-purpose models take on tasks that require broader reasoning or language generation. Enterprises Seek Reliability For enterprises, the opportunity extends beyond reducing token consumption and cost savings. Companies need AI systems that can work with internal data, understand domain-specific context and make decisions that can be reviewed and governed. General purpose models are probabilistic by design. Their responses can vary, even when prompts appear similar. That flexibility is useful for open-ended tasks, but enterprise workflows in sectors such as manufacturing, energy, finance and aerospace often require defined outputs, traceability and tighter controls. Articul8 AI, an enterprise AI company spun out of Intel in 2024, is building a platform around what it calls a “correctness stack”. According to Ananthanarayanan S, the company’s managing director for India, enterprises need more than access to a capable model. They need a system that connects their data and domain knowledge with models that can deliver outputs suited to specific workflows. The platform is designed to work across cloud environments, on-premises deployments and air-gapped systems. Its data perception layer brings information from different enterprise sources into a unified view, helping AI systems work with the context and relationships within an organisation’s data. Articul8 has developed around 28 domain models spanning areas such as energy, finance, aerospace and manufacturing. Its platform can select models depending on the task and combine specialised models with customers’ preferred frontier or reasoning models. The company says its approach can reduce token usage by more than 50% in relevant workflows, although the savings will depend on the application and deployment. In October, Articul8 announced Bivia, a multimodal decision model designed to process inputs such as text, images, video frames, tables and charts, and return structured decisions. Ananthanarayanan said the differentiation lies less in any single model than in the platform’s ability to connect models and solve difficult customer problems. He cited an engineering company with around 10,000 documents that were ingested in roughly 10 hours before an application was made available for use. Articul8 has also said the American Society of Mechanical Engineers selected it for work related to standards. These examples point to the company’s focus on applying AI within existing enterprise workflows rather than selling a standalone model alone. PurpleTalk is approaching the opportunity through Sthānika, its applied AI research lab, and the Sieve family of decision models. Sieve-31Bv3 is designed to be called by AI agents as one component in a larger system. It returns a defined answer with a confidence score, allowing the agent to decide what to do next. The company claimed at the time of launch that Sieve-31Bv3 ranked first on the full Jev Decision Index, a collection of 43 private and public benchmarks hosted on Hugging Face. The company reported a score of 71.1 on the full index and 71.7 on the public test, where it ranked third. Sieve builds on earlier compact, confidence-aware decision models used within PurpleTalk products Ello and Mina. The company sees potential applications in voice, customer experience and robotics, where routine decisions need to be made quickly and predictably. “Sieve-31B shows that a focused model fine-tuned in India can perform among the best in the world at this work. The private tests matter most to us. They come from domains outside the public suite, and Sieve generalised better than most of the field. It learned the task, not the test,” said Sridhar Muppidi, cofounder of PurpleTalk. Bharat Lingam, CEO of PurpleTalk, believes decision models will open up a new category of agentic systems: more reliable, more controllable, and fast enough for voice, customer experience and robotics. “We are publishing everything needed to reproduce our results, and we invite the research community to test it, challenge it and build on it,” Lingam added. The approaches illustrate two sides of the enterprise opportunity. Articul8 is building a broader platform around enterprise data, models and governance, while PurpleTalk’s Sthānika is a specialised model that agents can call for particular decisions. In both cases, the commercial test will be whether these systems improve real workflows, not simply whether their models perform well on benchmarks. A Decision Model For Every Workflow The decision model opportunity is not limited to enterprise platforms in India. Smaller AI startups and researchers are also exploring models that can be adapted, deployed locally and used by developers building their own applications. Kerala-based ConvAI Innovations has developed Laya, an open-weight decision model intended to run locally on devices such as laptops and mobile phones and be adapted by developers. Founder Nandakishore Mukkunnoth said the initial focus was on building small, fast models that did not always require cloud access. Interest in a general-purpose, open-source decision model grew after Jev’s release. The startup has discussed plans for Laya Max, with image and audio capabilities, alongside APIs, software development kits and a commercial enterprise offering. It has also suggested that Laya could deliver substantial cost savings compared with Jev. These claims will need to be tested against comparable workloads, as performance and cost depend on the task, model configuration and deployment. Laya’s significance lies in the possibility of giving developers an adaptable model that can run closer to where decisions need to be made. Local execution could be useful where latency, connectivity, data control or inference costs matter. But open weights alone will not establish a durable advantage. The model will still need to perform reliably on real tasks and be straightforward to integrate into applications. For investors, the opportunity may be less about backing another general-purpose model and more about identifying where decision-making can become a product in its own right. “Decision models are one of the most important shifts in AI this year. What can’t be copied is a company’s own record of decisions and outcomes. For startups, the real test is how fast the model improves on a specific, high-volume workflow,” said Shubham Gupta, founding general partner at Together Fund. That points to a potential advantage for startups that can pair models with proprietary data, feedback from actual outcomes and a clearly defined customer problem. A model may be accessible to competitors, but the data and workflow knowledge used to improve its decisions can be harder to replicate. In the Indian context, this creates several possible entry points: developing specialised models, building infrastructure that routes tasks to the right model, and creating applications around high-volume enterprise workflows. The challenge is to demonstrate measurable improvements in accuracy, cost or speed, rather than compete on benchmark scores alone. As the global industry moves towards more specialised AI systems, the question is whether Indian builders can turn their models into products that enterprises repeatedly use. The next advantage may not belong to the model that can do the most things, but to the system that can make a particular decision reliably, cheaply and at scale.

ANC for all models. Improved noise cancellation. Rated IP57. Wireless charging model gets a battery boost. Pocket-friendly case.
TIRED
Battery life could be better. Can get slippery with sweat. No heart-rate sensing. No hearing aid features.
I’ve owned AirPods since the original pair launched in 2016. Over the years, I’ve tested earbuds from many brands, but I always come back to my trusty AirPods. They’re easy to pair, they integrate well with the Apple ecosystem, and they deliver some of the best-sounding active noise cancellation (ANC) on the market. The latest AirPods 5 continue the trend and deliver more of Apple’s best audio features at a lower price than their predecessor.
The AirPods 5 come in two models: $129 with a standard case and $149 with a wireless charging case that works with Apple Watch chargers, Qi-compatible chargers, and USB-C. Both include ANC, which is a welcome change from the AirPods 4, where you had to pay extra ($179) for the privilege of a feature that’s increasingly standard on most wireless earbuds.
For $149, the AirPods 5 (with a wireless charging case) are an easy recommendation. But after a month of testing, I’d still pay extra to get the AirPods Pro 3. The difference comes down to noise cancellation, fit, and controls.
ANC for All
First and foremost, if you’re buying the AirPods 5, spend the extra $20 on the version with a wireless charging case. You’ll get an extra hour of battery life (up to five hours) on the earbuds and an extra two (up to 22 hours) with the charging case compared to the $129 model. That's the same battery life as the AirPods 4 without ANC, so you’re actually getting more listening time even with noise cancellation.
Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz
The inclusion of ANC in both AirPods 5 models is the biggest upgrade here. You no longer have to pay extra just to get noise cancellation, and even the $129 model is a better deal than the standard AirPods 4 were at launch. Both versions also support Conversation Awareness, Live Translation, and Spatial Audio, along with Apple’s Siri features.
And, for semi-open earbuds, the AirPods 5 have exceptional ANC. Apple says the noise cancellation removes up to 50 percent more external noise than the AirPods 4 with ANC, due to a redesigned multi-port acoustic architecture and improved audio processing. I can’t verify that percentage, but the improvement was noticeable during my testing.
I was especially impressed on a domestic flight, where the AirPods 5 did a stellar job at suppressing the sound of the airplane engines. They didn’t make the cabin totally disappear, and the AirPods Pro 3 still deliver stronger isolation, but it was a huge improvement compared to the AirPods 4 with ANC.
Transparency mode sounds even more natural. I found this especially useful with Adaptive Audio, which automatically balances ANC with Transparency mode based on your surroundings. On a run, for example, footsteps approaching from behind prompted the earbuds to lower my music and let more environmental sound through. The transition felt smooth enough that the outside noise almost blended into the song. I could stay aware of my surroundings without getting distracted by every little thing happening around me.
For people who run outdoors or commute, the open-ear design can be more appealing than the tighter seal of the Pros. You sacrifice some isolation, but you get a more natural sense of what’s happening around you.
The Open-Ear Trade-Off
Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz
The notable improvements can't overcome the simple fact that I generally prefer the silicone tips of the AirPods Pro 3 to the semi-open fit of the AirPods 5. The AirPods Pro 3 create a snug seal without making my ears feel clogged, and the interchangeable sizes let me tailor the fit. That seal also makes a noticeable difference when I’m working out. During longer runs, I found the AirPods 5 could start slipping as sweat built up. The Pros stayed put. Their more secure fit also naturally improves noise cancellation.
The AirPods 5 inherit the Pro 3’s volume controls, which let you adjust the volume by swiping up or down on the stem, but I’ve found the feature tricky to use across AirPods models because the stems are so short and slim that I struggle to get the right touch with my long nails. I generally prefer the volume controls on Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds, which offer more surface area to work with.
I find the Pro 3’s controls are easier to use than the AirPods 5’s, especially while running. The stem protrudes a little more where it meets the earbud, giving me a more accessible spot to press. With AirPods 5, I’ve had to take an earbud out just to locate the right control spot, which is not ideal mid-run. A few days ago, I nearly sacrificed one to Lake Michigan after fumbling with it. The upgraded IP57 rating means the earbuds can withstand brief immersion in water, but I wouldn’t recommend testing that claim in a lake.
I’d Still Buy the Pros
While the AirPods 5 offer a lot for the money, the pinpoint controls and a few missing features make the Pro 3 worth the splurge in my mind. The Pros have integrated heart-rate sensing for workouts, hearing aid features, and longer battery life with ANC enabled.
The $100 price difference between the two is significant, though. For casual listeners, tweens, and teens, the AirPods 5 are great. You still get solid noise cancellation, Apple’s seamless ecosystem integration, and an open-ear design that’s more comfortable for people who don’t like silicone eartips. The smaller charging case is another perk—it slips more naturally into a pocket or the waistband of leggings.
But as an iPhone owner who works out daily and travels frequently, I’d still spend $249 on the AirPods Pro 3. Their secure fit, stronger noise cancellation, and more accessible controls make them the better all-around earbuds for me.
The AirPods 5 are the better value. The AirPods Pro 3 are the better earbuds.

The New York Times and other newspaper companies sued Brave Software yesterday, alleging that the browser maker illegally bypasses paywalls and sells stolen news content to AI companies.
“Brave is the supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content for its own users and many of the most prominent GenAI companies, including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere,” the NYT alleged in a lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Southern District of New York. Citing third-party revenue estimates, the suit claimed that “Brave has made more than $100 million by copying and reselling publishers’ work without consent or permission,” while “publishers have received nothing.”
The lawsuit said, “AI companies pay Brave to provide them with real-time online content from the Brave search index,” and use content from the Brave index “to train their own AI models” and “to respond to specific user queries.” The NYT lawsuit points to Brave’s website, which says the Brave Search API is “used by some of the biggest names in AI, including Cohere, Mistral, Perplexity, and You.com.”
The lawsuit accused Brave of all the major types of copyright infringement: direct infringement, contributory infringement, and vicarious infringement. The lawsuit claims Brave infringes copyrights directly by scraping articles for its search index, for its “Ask Brave” AI search feature, and for the Brave API that “serves as an illicit source of unlicensed copyrighted material, including Times journalism, to other AI companies.”
The NYT accused Brave of being “a contributory and vicarious infringer when it deliberately induces, facilitates, controls, and profits from its users’ and GenAI customers’ copying of the copyrighted content.” Finally, the lawsuit said Brave violated the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) by circumventing technological measures the NYT and other content owners use to restrict access to their articles.
“The Brave Browser includes a default setting that, when activated, causes the browser to go behind website paywalls and provide the paywalled content to the user,” the lawsuit said. The browser “blocks advertising that would otherwise appear on The Times’s website, and instead shows its own ads, offering its users a cut of the revenue even as it deprives The Times of digital advertising revenue that helps it fund the expensive effort of producing journalism,” the lawsuit said.

Update | November 3, 2026, 21:45 IST EV maker Ola Electric has allotted 37.03 Cr partly paid-up equity shares under its rights issue, through which it will raise about ₹999.7 Cr once the shares are fully paid. The shares carry an issue price of ₹27 apiece. Of the issue price, shareholders have paid ₹16.2 per share on application, amounting to ₹599.8 Cr. The remaining ₹10.8 per share, totalling ₹399.9 Cr, will be payable on the first and final call under the terms of the letter of offer. Ola Electric’s rights issue committee approved the allotment following the finalisation of the basis of allotment in consultation with NSE, the designated stock exchange. Original | October 7, 2026, 20:08 IST Ola Electric’s ₹1,000 Cr rights issue is set to open for subscription onOctober 22 and close on October 30, its board of directors finalised today. The last date for on-market renunciation of rights entitlements has been set at October 26. At an issue price of ₹27 per share, the company expects to raise ₹999.74 Cr, assuming full subscription and payment of call monies. To note, the issue price is set at a discount of over 5% to Ola Electric's closing price today (₹36.30). The rights issue will comprise 37.03 Cr partly paid-up equity shares with a face value of ₹10 each. Shareholders will be entitled to two rights shares for every 25 fully paid-up equity shares held as of the record date of October 13. The ₹27 issue price includes a ₹17 premium. Shareholders will have to pay ₹16.20 per share, or 60% of the issue price, on application. The remaining ₹10.80 per share will be payable through a first and final call. The company's board approved the rights issue on September 28. Following that, founder and CMD Bhavish Aggarwal pledged a 4.32% stake in the electric two-wheeler maker to fund his participation in the rights issue. Ola Electric plans to split the proceeds between debt reduction, business expansion and general corporate requirements. The company has earmarked ₹350 Cr for repaying or prepaying borrowings at Ola Electric and its material subsidiaries. The allocation will also cover accrued interest and any applicable prepayment penalties. A larger ₹400 Cr will be directed towards organic growth, with the company planning to invest across its electric mobility and energy storage businesses. The spending will include manufacturing, R&D, stores and dealerships, service infrastructure, as well as sales and marketing. The balance of the proceeds will be available for general corporate purposes. Ola Electric expects to utilise the funds during FY27 and FY28. This would be the second fundraise for Ola Electric within 2026. The company raised ₹780.24 Cr via a qualified institutional placement (QIP) earlier in June. Meanwhile, on the financial front, Ola Electric managed to trim its net loss for the June quarter (Q1 FY27) by 22% to ₹336 Cr from ₹428 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Operating revenue declined 45% to ₹455 Cr from ₹828 Cr in Q1 FY26.

The US midterm elections are on us, and this time America will once again vote for which party will control the US Congress, but as usual the results of these elections might take some days to arrive at.
Control of the House of Representatives will depend on which party can reach the count of 218 seats. The Republicans are currently the majority in the House, but with the slimmest possible margin of one. There are currently two vacancies.
On the other hand, in the Senate, bar is 51 seats for the Democrats or 50 for the Republicans, since Vice President JD Vance will have the opportunity to cast his tiebreaking vote. Here also the Republican majority, 53-47, is pretty slim.
Quick answers to key questions
Mail-in ballots, close contests, recounts and state-specific counting rules can delay final results. In California, ballots may arrive and be counted after Election Day.
If no candidate receives more than 50% of first-choice votes, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and their ballots are redistributed according to voters’ next choices. This process can take longer to complete.
The Senate battlegrounds highlighted in the articles are Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas. Results in these contests could help determine which party controls the Senate.
A party needs 218 seats for a House majority. Democrats need a net gain of four Senate seats to take control; a 50–50 Senate would leave Republicans with the tie-breaking vote of Vice President JD Vance.
The first polling stations are scheduled to close at 4:30 am IST on Wednesday, November 4, and initial projections may follow within hours. Final results in close races could take several days or longer.
Some states often take days to count their ballots. The most populous state in the US, California itself has seen thousands of mail-in ballots dropped off on Election Day. Half of the votes cast in California in 2022 were counted after Election Day, the Associated Press said.
Moreover, there are states like Alaska and Maine, which have key senatorial races this year, and these states use ranked choice voting.
Even if a candidate wins more than 50% of the votes in the first round, if no one reaches that threshold then the candidate who has the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated, and their votes are redistributed to the second choice of the voter. This is a process that can significantly delay results.
All eyes will be on Senate elections in n Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas, while battlegrounds for the House race are scattered across the United States.
The Republican Party has had a financial advantage over the Democrats. Combined, the Republican National Committee, its related congressional committees, as well as its corresponding super PACs have raised more than $2.2 billion.
On the other hand, the Democratic National Committee and its aligned committees and groups have been able to raise $1.3 billion.
However, when it comes to individual races, Democratic candidates have outperformed their GOP counterparts, raising more than $2.3 billion to about $1.6 billion.
For the first time since 2006, the Democrats are aiming to capture a majority of governors' officers. 36 states will be electing a governor on 3 November (local time), as they head into elections. Among the 50 US states, Republicans currently hold a 26-24 majority. If the Dems manage to pick up two more seats, they will be able to secure a majority, which had last happened for them in 2006.

The Indian Patent Office has rejected a patent application filed by the U.S.-based Global Alliance for TB Drug Development (TB Alliance) for the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL), a six-month, all-oral treatment regimen for drug-resistant tuberculosis.
The Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust and Third World Network (TWN) welcomed the development.
Recommended by the WHO for eligible people, BPaL offers a shorter course of treatment than older, longer regimens, reducing the burden of treatment on patients and their families.
“Only those who have been treated for TB know what it feels like to go through more than a year of antibiotics with painful injections. Access to a shorter, oral and effective treatment can mean returning to work, caring for their families and rebuilding their lives”, explained Loon Gangte of DNP+.
The decision follows two pre-grant oppositions filed in 2020—one by Eldred Tellis (Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust) and Ganesh Acharya, with support from the Lawyers’ Collective and Médécins Sans Frontières Access Campaign, and the other by the Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), with support from TWN.
The opponents challenged the patent application on the grounds that the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid, as well as its use in a shorter treatment regimen, had already been disclosed in scientific research and clinical trials dating back to 2015. They argued that combining these known medicines did not constitute an inventive step warranting a new patent monopoly.
The Opposition invoked key safeguards under India’s Patents Act, including Section 3(d), which restricts patents on new uses of known substances, Section 3(e), which excludes mere admixtures, and Section 3(i), which excludes methods of medical treatment. The opponents further argued that the application failed to sufficiently disclose the claimed invention. All four grounds were upheld by the Indian Patent Office.
India has the world’s largest tuberculosis burden. According to WHO estimates, approximately 2.71 million people developed TB in the country in 2024, accounting for a quarter of global cases, with an incidence rate of 187 per 1,00,000 people. Civil society groups are also demanding that the TB Alliance stop the pursuit of proprietary rights over BPaL in other countries.
“Having received public and philanthropic support to develop pretomanid, one of BPaL’s components, they should not be applying for a patent, let alone over frivolous secondary patents on its combination with the other two known medicines,” said Mr. Tellis.
In light of the weak claims by the TB Alliance, Prathibha Sivasubramanian, senior researcher at TWN, endorsed the call for the waiving of patents. “The Indian Patent Office’s decision should serve as a clear signal to the TB Alliance to voluntarily surrender granted patents and to withdraw all corresponding pending applications in other jurisdictions. TB Alliance should also publish its pretomanid licence agreements,” she said.
Patents on the BPaL combination have been granted in 11 countries and are set to expire in 2036: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Bulgaria, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, South Africa, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.

Gritty knocks from captain Akshay Wadkar (100, 212b, 9x4) and Nachiket Bhute (97, 111, 6x4, 5x6) hauled Vidarbha to a first-innings lead on the second day of its Ranji Trophy Elite Group A match against Madhya Pradesh at the VCA Jamtha Stadium in Nagpur.
After losing four overnight, Vidarbha needed to show resolve to see out the morning session. Dhruv Shorey provided an early stamp of his intentions with a pair of classy straight drives, but it proved a false dawn as he was beaten through the gate by Avesh Khan.
Kumar Kartikeya Singh ran proceedings on the first evening, but perhaps looking to make a statement, Harsh Dubey launched him for a six over mid-on early on. However, his attempt to do the same to Saransh Jain was less successful, as he holed out.
With Vidarbha six down early, MP looked to go for the kill, packing close catchers around the bat. However, those catchers were soon forced back by Wadkar and Bhute’s counter-attack.
Bhute was the earlier aggressor, launching Saransh for a maximum on just his fifth ball of the innings, while Kartikeya was sent to the fence with equal disdain.
Fearing a leakage of runs, MP brought its field back, leaving space for the duo to continue knocking runs around at a healthy rate. Wadkar was prolific in manipulating angles to find gaps in the field with ease.
The duo soon brought the deficit below 100, and Nachiket launched Saransh for another straight six to bring up his half-century in 56 balls in the final over before Lunch. Post-resumption, the pair maintained a quick tempo against seamers Avesh and Ravi Kiran, capitalising on errant line and length.

However, Nachiket was fortunate to survive a pair of squandered opportunities. He first miscued a pull off Avesh up into the air, only for Rajat Patidar to shell a tough chance diving backwards, before wicketkeeper Saksham Purohit let slip a stumping chance off Kartikeya.
The efficient Wadkar notched his second consecutive fifty from 122 balls before Bhute thrashed Kiran through the covers to confirm the host’s first-innings lead. As the second session progressed, the Vidarbha captain began taking more of the strike, sending several glorious backfoot punches and drives to the fence.
Bhute moved past his highest First-Class score with a continuation of his attack on Saransh, but with three figures closing in, MP brought Arshad back into the attack, and the 26-year-old fiddled behind into the outstretched left glove of Saksham.
Wadkar, too, seemed to suffer a case of the nervous 90s, attempting to manufacture shots in a way that was incongruous with the assuredness of the rest of his innings. He went into the Tea break stranded on 98, and though he reached his century after the resumption, it came at a heavy personal cost.
The Vidarbha skipper punched Avesh into the offside and set off for a tight single, diving at full stretch to make his ground. He managed to do so successfully, but was in visible pain afterwards and unable to get up.
A stretcher was brought out, and he was taken to an ambulance for further treatment.
Darshan Nalkande was able to land a few further blows before skewing up a caught-and-bowled off Saransh, leaving Parth Rekhade and Rajneesh Gurbani to navigate the final hour. The duo pushed the lead past 100 before Rekhade holed out.
The visitor faced six overs of the new ball and got off to the worst possible start as Yash Dubey picked out cover on the second delivery, leaving it facing a tall task again tomorrow.

TOI Correspondent From Washington:
 Donald Trump made an unlikely political breakthrough in 2024, prising away a slice of Indian-American voters from a community that had reliably backed Democrats for decades. Two years later, the romance appears to have soured.
A new survey by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace finds that the Republican gains have largely evaporated, with Indian-Americans swinging back towards Democrats ahead of the November 2026 midterms. According to the Indian American Attitudes Survey conducted in October, 62 per cent of Ind-Am citizens intend to vote Democratic in their congressional district, against just 19 per cent backing Republicans, whittled down from nearly 30 per cent who voted for Trump in 2024. Another 12 per cent are undecided. Senate voting intentions show a similar pattern: 63 per cent favour Democrats and 21 per cent Republicans.
The nationally representative survey of 1,000 Indian-American adults, conducted with YouGov between October 7 and 27, has a margin of error of 3.87 percent.
The reversal is striking: In 2020, 68 per cent intended to vote for Joe Biden against 22 per cent for Trump. In 2024, Kamala Harris retained 62 per cent support, but Trump improved his showing to 30 per cent. 
Democratic support subsequently slipped to 57 per cent in January 2026 before recovering to 62 per cent, still short of the years they leaned heavily Democratic but a distinct uptick.
The community's return to traditional Democratic preference appears to reflect its immigrant and minority experience, support for legal immigration and social welfare, and discomfort with the MAGA Republican Party's association with Christian evangelicalism and perceived intolerance of minorities.
Previously, their economic success, entrepreneurship, lower-tax preferences and concerns about illegal immigration made some desis receptive to Republican arguments. Trump's cultivation of PM Modi, including their high-profile Howdy Modi rally in Houston in 2019, also improved his standing.
The subsequent Trump second term presidency, however, has exposed the limits of that appeal. Immigration crackdown, including efforts to restrict birthright citizenship and the hex on H1B visas and workplace raids have struck particularly close to home in a community with extensive family and professional connections to India. Carnegie found that two-thirds opposed the new H-1B fee and 74 per cent opposed deporting immigrants to third countries.
Racial hostility has compounded the alienation, with the September controversy involving Bo French, the Republican nominee for the Texas Railroad Commission, a grating example. After the University of Texas football team defeated Ohio State, French posted a photograph of brown students celebrating in the stands, suggesting their presence illustrated how Americans had been displaced by foreigners. The implication that students who looked Indian were somehow not American provoked outrage, inviting criticism from moderate Republicans like Senator John Cornyn, who has been sidelined by Trump, who has made little effort to contain the rampant racism of his nativist MAGA flock.
Yet the Democratic resurgence is not necessarily an ideological conversion, with 35 per cent of those intending to vote Democratic say opposition to Republicans, rather than enthusiasm for Dems, is their primary motivation. Meanwhile, 26 per cent identify as independents, underscoring the community's political fluidity.
With more than 5.2 million people of Indian origin, roughly 1.5 per cent of the US population, Indian-Americans cannot determine a national election by themselves. But their concentration in California, New Jersey, Texas, Georgia, Michigan, Illinois and the Washington metropolitan area gives them influence in closely contested races.
The message for Republicans clearly is that economic conservatism and affinity with Modi cannot indefinitely outweigh anxieties about immigration and belonging. For Democrats, the lesson is not to take the community's support for granted. The 2024 Republican breakthrough showed that Indian-American voters are persuadable. The 2026 survey suggests they are now heading back to the Dem fortress.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Chinese space officials confirmed this weekend that the Asian nation plans to land its astronauts on the Moon within three years.
At the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, officials, including Wang Xiang, chief designer for the lunar exploration program, laid out the country’s most publicly detailed plans yet for a series of missions leading up to a crewed lunar landing “before 2030.”
China’s lunar landings will involve a lunar-orbit rendezvous similar to what NASA did in the 1960s and early 1970s with the Apollo program. However, lacking a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V vehicle, the crew and lunar lander will launch separately to the Moon.
According to slides shared on social media, the current plan involves:
- An uncrewed test of the Long March 10A rocket (a single-stick variant, with no boosters) and the Mengzhou spacecraft to low-Earth orbit. Target: early 2027
- An uncrewed test of the larger Long March 10 rocket (a core stage with two boosters) and the Lanyue lunar lander, including descent/ascent from Moon’s surface. Target: 2028
- A concurrent launch of two Long March 10 rockets, one carrying uncrewed Mengzhou and the other the Lanyue vehicle; they will dock in lunar orbit. Target: 2029
- Dual launch of Long March 10 rockets, this time with crew on the Mengzhou spacecraft, leading to crewed landing mission. Target: “Before 2030”
The public release of this new information provides a timeline for gauging China’s technical progress in its efforts to land humans on the Moon before 2030 and beat NASA and the United States back to the lunar surface.
Notably, the plan (for now, at least) omits a mission similar to Apollo 8 or Artemis II, which involved a crew flying out to the Moon and either entering orbit or passing close by before returning to Earth. The Mengzhou vehicle should still get a workout closer to Earth with humans on board as part of missions carrying astronauts to Tiangong, China’s space station in low-Earth orbit.
China’s program has been largely opaque
NASA has set a target of landing humans on the Moon by 2028, a year or so ahead of China. The United States, which has been working on the Space Launch System rocket for 15 years and the Orion spacecraft even longer, has a more established rocket and crew vehicle.

Don’t expect Apple to offer a sale on the iPhone Duo. The company almost never discounts its products, especially new ones that are selling like hotcakes. (It’s back-ordered.) With the Duo starting at $2,000, it’s very expensive for most people to buy Apple’s first foldable, and the best way to get a deal may be through a carrier.
Of course, there are stipulations, but if you qualify, you could “save” significantly on an iPhone Duo—as much as $1,200, knocking the price to $800. (Keep reading, there’s a catch.) Here are some of the potential deals we found.
Shipping times are stretching into January, so it may be a while before you can get your hands on an iPhone Duo, even with one of these offers.
Save $1,200 on an iPhone Duo at T-Mobile
If you sign up for an Experience Beyond plan, T-Mobile will credit you $1,200. To qualify, you need to purchase the iPhone Duo and sign up for the Experience Beyond 2.0 plan for 36 months if you’re a new customer, or sign up for the Experience Beyond 2.0, Experience Beyond, or Go5G Next plans if you’re an existing T-Mobile customer and not already enrolled in another payment plan.
Here’s how the deal works.
You don’t get $1,200 upfront. Instead, T-Mobile spreads that amount across 36 monthly credits on your bill. For the 256-GB base model, for example, you’ll pay $22.22 a month for the phone on top of the monthly plan; those payments total about $800 over three years, plus the Experience Beyond 2.0 plan is $100 a month, excluding taxes and fees. The deal doesn’t apply when you pay in full or choose a cheaper plan. If you hate expensive contracts, this isn’t for you.
T-Mobile offers several other incentives for the iPhone Duo, including $1,200 off with trade-in or $1,000 off for seniors, military personnel, students, and first responders. To see what you might qualify for, click on the “see promotions” link on the T-Mobile iPhone Duo purchase page.
If you’re not clamoring for the iPhone Duo, T-Mobile’s incentives also apply to the new iPhone 18 Pro and other models.
Verizon and AT&T Have Similar Incentives on iPhone Duo
AT&T and Verizon are also offering incentives on the iPhone Duo. AT&T has a trade-in plan similar to T-Mobile’s: You’ll pay $22.23 a month for the phone for 36 months, which is equivalent to $1,200 off after you’ve fulfilled your contract. AT&T also has a “contract-breaking” deal that will get you an $800 reward card when you switch to AT&T, but you’d still have to pay the full price of the iPhone Duo.
The same goes for Verizon. You can get $1,200 off a 36-month Unlimited Ultimate plan, with or without a trade-in, as a new or existing customer. As an extra incentive, Verizon is including your choice of an Apple Watch Series 12 or iPad.
Whichever company’s deal you pursue, you’re entering into what is essentially a contract. The phone will also be locked to the carrier until you’ve made your final payment. You’ll also pay more after fees and taxes are added, although there’s no monthly interest. When you factor everything—the cost of a particular plan and the discounted phone—it could be what you're currently paying for a premium plan, or possibly much more.
We usually don’t recommend cell phone contracts; it’s best to get a phone unlocked, even if it means paying full price. However, if you plan to stay with a carrier long-term and want to lower the cost of the iPhone Duo, it’s still worth considering. But do the math before committing.

Chennai man killed in chopper crash was based in Canada, had visited India before ill-fated Nepal trip
Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu was from North Chennai and was married to Anila Chauhan, who is from Gujarat.
A 47-year-old man from Chennai was killed in a collision between two helicopters in Nepal's Solukhumbu district on Tuesday. Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu had moved to Canada for work a few years ago, officials from the Commissionerate of Rehabilitation and Welfare of Non-Resident Tamils said.
He was travelling in a Fishtail Air helicopter when it collided with an Air Dynasty chopper at around 8:11 am while landing at Pheriche in Ward 4 of Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality, according to a statement by the District Police Office.
An official from the Commissionerate said Balaramudu was from North Chennai and had relocated to Canada due to work. He was married to Anila Chauhan, who is from Gujarat. The couple have a son. The official said the couple had visited Nepal during a brief trip to India.
Deep Dive
ALSO READ | Indian tourist killed, three injured as two helicopters collide in Nepal's Mount Everest region
Helicopters carrying Everest trekkers collide
The two helicopters were ferrying trekkers who had been hiking towards Everest Base Camp during Nepal's popular trekking season, the Associated Press reported.
The collision took place at Pheriche village, located at an altitude of around 4,200 metres (13,780 feet). The incident left Balaramudu dead, while three others, including a passenger and the pilots of the two helicopters, sustained injuries.
Shailesh Krishna Patel, a New Zealand citizen of Indian origin who was travelling in the Fishtail Air helicopter, was injured. He was airlifted to Medicity Hospital in Kathmandu aboard a Prabhu Air helicopter after receiving initial assistance in Lukla, according to police.
The pilots, Prajjwal KC of Fishtail Air and Rabindra Prajapati of Air Dynasty, also sustained minor injuries, Nepali media reported.
Fishtail Air, in a statement on its website, said Balaramudu's mortal remains had been taken to Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu for an autopsy. It added that the injured passenger and the Fishtail Air pilot were admitted to Medicity Hospital and were out of danger.
What caused the helicopter collision
Preliminary reports suggest that miscommunication between the pilots may have led to the collision. The area is outside the coverage of the Lukla Airport air traffic control tower, requiring pilots to communicate with one another, Mukesh Dangol, director general of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, was quoted as saying by The Kathmandu Post.
The number of passengers aboard the two helicopters at the time of the collision is yet to be confirmed.
Indian Embassy coordinates repatriation
The Embassy of India in Kathmandu expressed its condolences over the death of the Indian national and said it was coordinating with Nepalese authorities for the early repatriation of his mortal remains.
In a statement shared on social media, the embassy said it was in close contact with the concerned authorities following the helicopter collision in Solukhumbu district.

Logistics unicorn Porter has appointed former Amazon executive Gaurav Jain as its CFO, while elevating Shubham Gupta and Mohit Rathi to CTO and CMO roles, respectively. Jain’s appointment comes nearly six months after the exit of his predecessor, Anurag Jalori. He joins after over 11 years at Amazon, where he most recently served as director and head of finance for India operations and supply chain. A chartered accountant, Jain previously held finance and strategy leadership roles at Shalimar Paints and financial services company Religare. Meanwhile, Gupta, who joined Porter in 2015, will lead technology across the startup. Previously VP of engineering, he oversaw the engineering function during its expansion, modernising the core technology stack, enabling self-service infrastructure access, strengthening security, optimising technology costs, and adopting AI. Rathi, who has spent over 11 years at Porter, will lead growth and marketing. As VP of customer growth and engagement since 2023, he worked on customer retention and insights, scaling Porter Enterprise, rebuilding the customer rewards programme, and refining the go-to-market strategy for newer services. “Shubham and Mohit have been pillars of this company, the core of how we work. Their new roles recognise the ownership they have shown, the impact it has created, and the trust we place in them to take Porter forward. We are also delighted to welcome Gaurav as our CFO. His experience in scaling businesses will be a strong addition as we enter our next phase of growth,” said Porter cofounder and CEO Uttam Digga. Founded in 2014 by Digga and Pranav Goel, Porter offers B2C and B2B logistic services, including enterprise-level goods movements and management, packers and movers service for relocation, and intercity courier services. It claims to serve over 30 Lakh customers, including 20 lakh MSMEs and 3 lakh driver-partners every month across 35 cities in India. The startup joined the unicorn club last year after raising $200 Mn at a valuation of around $1.1 Bn to $1.2 Bn in a round led by Kedaara Capital and Wellington Management. Overall, Porter has raised over $330 Mn to date from investors like Peak XV Partners, Elev8 Ventures, Tiger Global, Lightrock, among others. On the financial front, Porter’s net profit more than quadrupled to ₹229 Cr in FY26 from ₹55.3 Cr in FY25. Revenue grew 54% to ₹6,650 Cr from ₹4,306 Cr in the previous fiscal year.

A stroke is an urgent situation where either the flow of blood to the brain is cut off, or there is a rupture of the blood vessels in the brain. Oxygen and glucose are the two elements essential for brain activity. Interruption of their supply results in impairment of brain activity and eventual damage of brain tissues -- and this damage occurs in minutes. The first few hours of a stroke, therefore, determine how damaged the brain can become.
Types of strokes
Strokes can be categorised into ischemic strokes and haemorrhagic strokes. In ischemic strokes, the stroke occurs due to the blocking of an artery by a blood clot. In haemorrhagic strokes, there is a rupture of the blood vessel, which leads to blood in the brain tissue. Regardless of the type of stroke, the result is damage to the brain tissue, which can result in vital body functions including speaking, movement, vision, memory and coordination becoming impaired.
An ischemic stroke is accompanied by oxygen starvation of the affected brain tissue. Due to insufficient energy resources, brain cells cannot function normally. The chemical composition of the brain cells, therefore, changes, which results in the accumulation of toxic substances that harm brain cells and other structures. With continued oxygen starvation, cells continue to deteriorate. The damage, however, does not occur uniformly. In the central area of the brain (core) where oxygen starvation is critical, damage can occur rapidly and irreversibly. Around this area, there is a zone called the ischemic penumbra. Here, even if blood flow is low, brain cells can survive for a certain period of time. They can be saved if blood flow is restored promptly.
The effect of bleeding in a haemorrhagic stroke is brought about by the leaking of blood into the brain when there is a rupture of a blood vessel. This may lead to injury of brain cells, and also interfere with proper blood and cerebral spinal fluid flow in the brain.
The first few hours
There are only so many minutes that the brain can withstand interrupted blood flow. Brain cells (neurons) begins to undergo irreversible damage within 3 to 5 minutes of interrupted blood flow. With each minute that goes by, 1.9 million neurons, i.e. 32 neurons per second, die due to lack of oxygenation, which is why we emphasise that ‘time is brain’. The first few hours are critical since at this point, one needs to assess what kind of stroke it is and start appropriate treatment.
In some cases of ischemic stroke, intravenous thrombolysis, the administration of drugs that dissolve the clot within the blood vessels, might be given in the first 4.5 hours after symptoms develop. In some patients with large vessel blockage, there might be indications for mechanical thrombectomy. In simple terms, a mechanical thrombectomy involves the removal of the clot using special equipment, and it might be done up to 24 hours after the patient was last seen without symptoms. In cases of haemorrhagic strokes, others strategies must be employed: this includes blood pressure control, correction of the consequences of taking blood thinners, management of intracranial pressure, and surgical procedures, where necessary.
Not all patients automatically qualify for all interventions. There are other issues that have to be taken into account, including the patient’s medical status, imaging studies, timing of stroke symptoms, and dangers involved in the therapy. Even some of those who come after these time windows, can still be eligible for certain treatment procedures after imaging is done.
How brain function is affected
The effects of a stroke vary, depending on the site and degree of damage within the brain. Movement centres can be damaged leading to weakness or paralysis that usually affects one side of the body. Speech centres could be damaged causing speech problems and comprehension difficulties or trouble reading and writing. A stroke involving the visual pathways leads to a sudden loss of vision or partial visual fields. If the cerebellum or the brainstem is involved, there could be a problem with dizziness, poor coordination, problems swallowing, double vision or loss of balance. There could also be memory, attention and decision-making problems and problems with emotional regulation.
It is important to know and understand these symptoms since sometimes a stroke occurs without the characteristic facial drooping or arm weakness of the disease.
Recognising warning signs
The BE FAST method is an effective means of identifying the symptoms of a stroke:
- B – Balance: Sudden loss of balance, dizziness or difficulty walking
- E – Eyes: Sudden blurred vision, double vision or loss of vision
- F – Face: One side of the face is drooping or numb
- A – Arms: One arm is weak or dropping down
- S – Speech: Slurred speech
- T – Time: Call for help immediately
Sudden changes in vision, lack of balance, confusion or even a severe headache without apparent reason might be symptoms of a stroke as well. Disappearing symptoms within a minute or two shouldn’t be considered harmless and require immediate medical examination.
After the golden hour
The ‘golden hour’ is significant to preserve as much of brain function as possible and to ensure best possible outcomes, but this does not mean medical professionals cease working after this window is over. Medical teams will continue monitoring the condition of the patient, controlling blood pressure and preventing additional harm to him or her. In case the condition of the patient becomes satisfactory, it is likely that he or she will be offered physiotherapy, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy and cognitive therapy.
It is worth noting that every stroke patient has his or her own path to recovery, which depends greatly on the level of injuries, the affected area of the brain, timely assistance and the patient’s health in general. For all individuals, however, it is important to understand how the brain functions, remember the signs of a stroke and seek timely help for oneself or a loved one.
(Dr. B. K. Madhusudhan is lead consultant – neurology, Aster RV Hospital, Bengaluru. madhusudhan.bk@asterhospital.in)

By the time the three hikers called for help from a rocky face on Mount Shasta in Northern California, they’d made a series of bad decisions. They didn’t bring enough food, and they’d overestimated their fitness. Instead of turning back in late afternoon when they hadn’t yet reached the top, they summited at 7:30 pm and had to descend in the dark. Their lack of preparation and poor planning, as they admitted later, came partly from relying on Google’s artificial intelligence chatbot Gemini. By morning, they were lost on a gnarly part of the mountain, and one hiker had banged up his knee.
“We get plenty of people who come unprepared or don’t do any research at all. To these guys’ credit, they did try,” said Nick Meyers, US Forest Service program manager of the Mount Shasta Wilderness Climbing and Avalanche Center, which responded to the call. “But I think they kind of turned their brains off.”
The three 20-year-olds aren’t the only ones making missteps in wild spaces with the help of artificial intelligence. Another Mount Shasta visitor pitched her tent near a “No Camping” sign, insisting she had a right to do so because AI told her she could, Meyers said. His team also encountered a man wandering around at a trailhead with an AI-generated map that showed prominent features on the wrong side of a nearby mountain. In British Columbia, a helicopter crew rescued a 16-year-old hiker from a ledge in the Widowmaker Arete on the back of Crown Mountain. The teen had used Anthropic’s chatbot Claude to help him plan his trip. News stories focused on that fact went viral across Canada and the US, though the hiker said later that he also consulted Google Maps and the popular hiking app, AllTrails.
Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming has also seen a marked uptick over the past year in the percentage of visitors who report using AI for travel information, said Park Superintendent Chip Jenkins. “It went from zero to 26 percent. And I’m guessing that curve is not going to flatten.”
It remains to be seen whether increasing AI use will lead to an increase in backcountry accidents and search and rescues, Meyers said. His office, which oversees a massive wilderness area in Northern California, averages a dozen rescues each year, and 2026 is shaping up to be an average year. Calls to search and rescue in Wyoming have actually gone down compared to 2025, with only 312 calls so far in 2026 compared to a total of 466 in 2025 and 377 in 2024.
Some search and rescue veterans say that AI chatbots are just the latest tools giving people new ways to get into trouble. Roughly a decade ago, when hikers, backpackers, climbers and other outdoor enthusiasts began to source their destinations, inspiration, and information from Instagram and other social media sites, they faced sometimes deadly consequences. Before that, hikers and other recreationists were led astray by their reliance on Google Maps or smartphone connectivity.
“Over the last two decades, there’s been a phenomenal push in the media to get more people outdoors, and consequently we have more people outdoors and recreating,” said Jim Moss, a Colorado-based recreation attorney and search and rescue volunteer. It’s still unclear how questionable advice from a robot will influence all those people, he added.
Turning to an AI chatbot for guidance does come with unique risks. Chatbots can “hallucinate” persuasively presenting misinformation as real, and their use can lead to a phenomenon called “cognitive surrender,” said Chris Flathmann, a human-centered computing professor at Clemson University in South Carolina who has studied AI and search and rescue.
“When humans work with AI systems, they can get so deep into it they give up thinking critically for themselves,” he explained. When AI pretends to be an expert on an unfamiliar topic, “you can’t call BS on that because you don’t have the expertise.” And once you stop thinking critically, it can be hard to start again, especially in a stressful backcountry situation.
Chatbots also tend to tell users what they want to hear and to do so with authority regardless of whether the sources they’re consulting are reliable, Flathmann and others said. Claude or ChatGPT might answer a query with extensive directions and advice that sound credible but are actually scraped from Reddit threads and out-of-date YouTube videos—and might even be entirely fabricated.
TikTok and Instagram may offer a viewer inspiration, but AI tends to offer instructions—right or wrong—as well as encouragement, Flathmann said. “AI isn’t trying to trick people into going up mountains, but I think it’s the natural evolution of what happens when you get a tool like this.”
Regardless of the resources recreators use, experts have the same advice: When you’re headed to a new place, make sure you double-check your information against reliable, authoritative sources like up-to-date public-land agency maps and websites, trail association websites, or guidebooks. Even better, talk to a real-live guide, a national forest official, or a park ranger.
“If you’re going to go into places that will kill you,” Meyers said, “you should take your planning seriously.”
