Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

Do you know signs of a stroke? BE FAST are the words to remember
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., suffered a stroke on Saturday. His prognosis is excellent, according to his office. His case illustrates the importance of knowing the warning signs of a stroke.
The American Stroke Association says following the six letters in the acronym BE FAST — can help save stroke victims and prevent permanent brain damage.
Murphy, 53, had the "A" for "arm weakness" — he felt numbness in his arm while he was at his son's hockey game, according to a statement from his staff. And they said he acted quickly to get care — that's the "T" for "time."
Being seen by medical professionals as soon as possible — be fast! — gives people the best shot at survival and full recovery.
Here are all six of the stroke-spotting signs in the BE FAST acronym, according to the American Stroke Association:
B – BALANCE loss
Dizzyness, trouble walking or a sudden loss of balance are all signs that a stroke may be occurring.
E – EYE changes
Is the person having trouble with their vision? Blurred vision, double vision or loss of sight in one eye are important symptoms.
F – FACE drooping
Ask the person to smile. Is their smile uneven? Numbness or drooping on one side of the face is a symptom.
A – ARM weakness
Numbness in one arm, as Murphy had, is a symptom. Weakness is too. Ask the person to raise both arms. Does one arm drift down?
S – SPEECH difficulty
Trouble talking is another common symptom. Can the person repeat a simple sentence? Is their speech slurred or hard to understand?
T – TIME to call 911
If you or someone you are with is experiencing these symptoms, call 911 as soon as you can. Getting care quickly is very important for survival and to minimize long-term effects.
A stroke happens when blood flow to or within the brain is interrupted. It can happen when an artery is blocked or when a blood vessel in the brain bursts. Brain tissue that is deprived of oxygen can be permanently damaged, resulting in long-term disability or death.
Other important symptoms of a stroke are a severe headache, confusion and numbness on one side of the body.
Stroke is the #4 leading cause of death in the U.S., killing more than 162,000 people in 2023, according to the American Heart Association.

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday (November 4) said Washington would stop providing $4 billion in annual funding to Israel after the end of this year, claiming he had reached an agreement with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to end the financial assistance.
Trump said Israel no longer needed the money and argued that continued US funding had become a political talking point for Democrats and left-wing politicians criticising Republicans.
"Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping," Trump said speaking to Fox News' Fox & Friends.
"We've already agreed that by the end of this year we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it," he added.
Trump also suggested that Israel could continue purchasing American military equipment.
"They can buy whatever they want. They can buy whatever they want. So can Europe. We make the greatest weapons in the world," he said.
There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu's office on Trump's remarks.
Also Read | Trump surprises Republicans with election eve speech about reflecting pool
Why is Trump stopping US funding to Israel?
Explaining the decision, Trump said Israel no longer required the financial assistance and argued that the funding was being used by political opponents to question the fairness of American support for the country.
"The left uses the $4 billion payment that everybody knows about, well it's no secret, as a signal of unfairness, and we can't allow that to happen," Trump said.
"We were giving them 4 billion, we are, but it gets cut off at the end of the year. Why? Because they don't need it," he added.
Trump's remarks come amid growing debate over Washington's financial and military backing of Israel, particularly following the Gaza war that began in 2023.
What is the existing US military aid agreement with Israel?
Under a memorandum of understanding (MoU), the US currently provides Israel with $3.8 billion in annual military assistance. The agreement is approaching its expiration in 2028, with discussions already under way on how Washington's assistance to Israel could evolve beyond that date.
Trump's reference to $4 billion does not precisely match the $3.8 billion annual military aid commitment under the existing MoU.
Trump indicated that Washington could still help Israel if required.

Office space provider DevX’s consolidated net profit zoomed 213.5% to ₹5.5 Cr in the second quarter (Q2) of fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27) as against ₹1.7 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Sequentially, the bottom line also surged 265.4% from ₹1.5 Cr in Q1 FY27. Meanwhile, operating revenue also jumped 54.8% to ₹80.2 Cr in the quarter under review compared to ₹51.8 Cr in Q2 FY26. On a quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) basis, the top line rose nearly 50% from ₹53.8 Cr in Q1 FY27. Including other income of ₹2.2 Cr, the listed company’s total income stood at ₹82.4 Cr in Q2 FY27. Nevertheless, expenses continued to bite and surged nearly 43% to ₹75.6 Cr in the quarter ended September 2026 compared to ₹52.8 Cr in Q2 FY26. DevX also reported a loss of ₹55.4 Lakh from an associate in the quarter, while its tax expenses stood at ₹82.7 Lakh. Alongside its Q2 FY27 financial results, the company’s board also approved a proposal to raise ₹300 Cr via issuance of non-convertible debentures (NCDs) to certain investors on a private placement basis. “The board… approved the proposal for raising funds through Issuance of Non-Convertible Debentures, in dematerialised form, in one or more series or tranches on a private placement basis for an aggregate amount up to ₹300 cr to eligible investors…,” said the company. The board also approved the allotment of 33.3 Lakh shares at ₹45 apiece to cofounders and promoters Parth Shah, Rushit Shah, and Umesh Uttamchandani for a sum of nearly ₹15 Cr. This comes five months after the company allotted 33.3 Lakh convertible warrants to the trio in June this year. At the time, the founders had paid ₹3.7 Cr (25% of the total) as initial subscription amount. The remaining 75% of the shares (pursuant to the conversion of the aforementioned warrants) will be allotted once the founders pay the remaining ₹11.3 Cr. Once the allotment materialises, the promoter shareholding will rise to 37.29% of the total issued capital from 35.09% currently Founded in 2017 by Parth Shah, Rushit Shah, and Umesh Uttamchandani, DevX is a flexible workspace provider that offers managed office spaces, individual coworking spaces, office designing solutions, and facility management services. It competes with the likes of Awfis, WeWork, Smartworks and IndiQube, which are also listed on the bourses. DevX operates in cities such as Ahmedabad, Vadodara, Pune, Hyderabad and Noida. Shares of DevX closed Tuesday’s trading session 1.83% higher at ₹43.86 apiece on BSE.

Exclusive-Japan fund JIC plans to sell JSR to Mitsui Chemicals, sources say
TOKYO, Nov 4 : Japan Investment Corp (JIC), a state-backed fund, plans to sell chipmaking materials maker JSR to Mitsui Chemicals in a deal that could exceed 1.3 trillion yen ($8.20 billion), two people familiar with the matter said.
A decision could come as soon as within the month, one of the people said. Both people declined to be identified as the information is not public.
JIC, JSR and Mitsui Chemicals did not reply to a request for comment.
Reuters, which previously reported JIC is considering selling JSR, is reporting the final buyer for the first time.
JIC acquired JSR for some 900 billion yen two years ago and had said it planned to use the business to drive consolidation in the semiconductor materials sector.
The fund will instead sell JSR to a domestic chemical major as it takes advantage of a lift in the valuation of chip-related firms due to a boom in AI investment.
JSR, established in 1957, is a leading manufacturer of photoresists which are used to transfer circuit patterns onto semiconductor wafers.
Mitsui Chemicals, which is also expanding its chip materials business, has a market capitalisation of about 800 billion yen.
The deal could be among the largest in Japan's chemicals sector, exceeding the 2020 acquisition of Hitachi Chemical by Showa Denko which created Resonac Holdings.
Mitsui Chemicals had 217.8 billion yen in cash and cash equivalents and 876.4 billion yen in interest-bearing debt as at the end of June.
Its debt-to-equity ratio, a measure of financial soundness, stood at 0.75.
JIC, which is overseen by the trade ministry, was set up in 2018 to invest in companies with the goal of boosting Japan's competitiveness.
Its investments include medical equipment maker Topcon alongside private equity firm KKR.

A person in Washington state has died from bird flu after exposure at an infected dairy farm, state health officials reported Sunday. It marks the third human bird flu death in the US since a strain of highly pathogenic (H5) avian influenza (HPAI) made the unprecedented jump from wild, migratory birds to dairy cows, which was first reported in the US in March 2024.
The person who died was a Yakima County resident and was said to have had underlying health conditions, which could have made the person more vulnerable to the infection. On Friday, county officials reported that the person was severely ill and hospitalized. In the subsequent announcement of the person’s death, officials said they would not be releasing further information about the person, including their name, gender, or age, out of respect for the family’s privacy.
“Our hearts go out to the individual’s family and loved ones during this difficult time,” Dave Atteberry, health officer for the Yakima Health District, said in a statement. “Avian influenza can cause severe illness, particularly among people who have underlying health conditions. While this is a serious and heartbreaking outcome, the risk to the general public remains low.”
Continued threat
In all, three people have tested positive for bird flu in Washington since the virus was reported in dairy cattle in the state on October 8. All three have been in Yakima County. While announcing the death on Sunday, officials also reported the third case. That case, like the first case, was in a person who had exposure to an infected dairy herd in the county. Both people have reportedly not experienced severe illness nor been hospitalized.

World champion Jepchirchir fails drugs test
- Published
Olympic and World Championships marathon gold medallist Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for EPO.
Kenyan Jepchirchir provided the sample prior to winning the Sydney Marathon on 30 August 2026.
The 33-year-old clocked a time of two hours, 18 minutes and 31 seconds to win in Sydney.
EPO, or erythropoietin, is a natural substance produced within the kidneys that stimulates the creation of new red blood cells.
If injected, it is only detectable in the urine or blood for a short window of time, and increases the amount of red blood cells, which carry oxygen to the muscles, in the blood stream.
Jepchirchir became the Olympic women's marathon champion at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics and returned to the Japanese capital to win the World Championships in September 2025.
She broke the women's half-marathon world record in 2017 and on three occasions in 2020.
In addition to Sydney, her other major wins came at the New York Marathon in 2021, the Boston Marathon in 2022 and the London Marathon in 2024.
Jepchirchir won the Sydney race, which became the seventh world major in 2025, by more than three minutes from compatriot Irene Chepet Cheptai.
She provided the sample which tested positive for EPO while in Kenya prior to the race.

Over the past decade, Sanofi and Regeneron’s Dupixent has become the top-selling drug in immunology, bringing in tens of billions in revenue while transforming outcomes for the 1.4 million patients currently on the therapy for conditions including eczema, asthma, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. But investors and doctors are intensely following an experimental therapy positioned to rival the pharma blockbuster, with results from a key study fast approaching.
Massachusetts biotech Kymera Therapeutics plans to announce data from a mid-stage clinical trial of its lead asset, KT-621, in eczema before the end of the year. Market analysts for the investment bank Jefferies, using common shorthand for immunology and inflammatory disorders, have called the upcoming results “one of the most impactful I&I readouts this year.”
Success (or failure) could have major consequences for Kymera, its growing list of competitors, and the millions of people who live with eczema in the United States. The results could also bolster or dampen the biotech’s aspirations to treat a broader class of immunological diseases with its drug, including chronic spontaneous urticaria and asthma. Analysts forecast that the drug’s sales could reach nearly $4 billion by 2035, including more than $3 billion in eczema revenue, according to Visible Alpha.

Five arrested after South African farmer shot and tortured
- Published
Warning: This article contains graphic details that some people may find distressing
South African police have arrested five people in connection with a brutal attack on a cattle farmer, who was assaulted and tortured in what has been described as a "senseless and barbaric" act.
Donovan Marx, 50, was attacked during a house robbery on his farm in Ventersdorp, a small town in South Africa's North West province, last Wednesday.
Marx was ambushed as he returned home, shot and stabbed and had his ears cut off in the horrific ordeal, police said.
All five of his alleged attackers were arrested over the weekend, a move welcomed by Marx's wife and family.
They added that the "legal process must [now] take its course".
The horrific attack has caused widespread outrage in a country which is used to high levels of violence.
Police last week explained how the attack on Mark happened.
A group of masked men armed with guns approached a worker at Mark's house as he was mowing the lawn, they said in a statement.
The attackers then demanded to know where Marx was before tying the worker's hands and feet with cable ties.
When Marx returned home, police said two of the suspects allegedly approached him and shot him in the upper body.
"They [then] dragged him inside the house, tied his hands and feet with cable ties, and allegedly stabbed him."
The suspects then ransacked the house and took three firearms from a safe before escaping with Marx's van.
The ordeal ended after the farm worker managed to free himself and call for assistance.
Marx was rushed to hospital, where he remains, but may need prosthetic ears after surgeons were unable to save his own, local news site IOL reported.
South Africa's Agriculture Minister Willie Aucamp condemned the attack on Marx, adding there was no "place in our country for such senseless and barbaric acts".
The chair of parliament's police committee, Ian Cameron, praised police for the swift arrests and called for a "strong, properly investigated case" to follow.
The five suspects, aged between 26 and 56, will appear in local courts on Tuesday and face house robbery, attempted murder and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition charges.
Some right-wing groups have used such attacks on white farmers, who are often from the Afrikaner community, to say there is a genocide against white people in the country - a claim that has been widely discredited.
Although the claims have been dismissed by every political party in the country, including those representing Afrikaners, US President Donald Trump has repeated them and has offered white Afrikaners asylum in the US.
South Africa's latest crime statistics, covering the period between April and June 2026, do not specify how many attacks took place on farms and only recorded one robbery in a rural area.
However, police data show most victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black.

Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.
A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.
During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.
The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.
Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.
Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.
Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.
A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.
A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”
During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.
The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

There are advantages to all this real estate. The advanced thermal design, with multiple heatsinks and channels for airflow, allows the router to operate at top performance reliably over the long term without a noisy fan. It remained silent and cool to the touch throughout my month of testing. There’s also space for a generous array of ports, including a 10Gbps WAN/LAN, a 10 Gbps LAN, four 2.5Gbps (one WAN/LAN), one 1Gbps LAN, a USB 3.2 Gen1, and a USB 2.0 port. You can even use link aggregation on the two 10 Gbps ports (y’know, just in case you need a 20 Gbps conduit).
Inside, you’ll find Broadcom’s BCM 6718 Wi-Fi chip, featuring a 2.6GHz quad-core processor, 256 MB of Flash memory, and 2 GB of DDR4 RAM. This is a quad-band router, so you have the usual 2.4 and 5 GHz bands, alongside two 6 GHz bands. I don’t want to drown you in spec soup here, but these are all 4 x 4 with OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access), 4096-QAM, and maximum-width channels, so we’re talking theoretical top speeds of 1.3 Gbps for the 2.4 GHz band, 5.6 Gbps for the 5 GHz band, and 11.5 Gbps for each of the 6 GHz bands. If you need explanations of the jargon and why each of these specs matter, you’ll find them in my detailed guide to how to buy a router. Just know that this router is at the top of the game.
Further and Faster
Of course, you never get maximum speeds in real life, but the speed of the Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro does not disappoint. You can reasonably expect up to 3 Gbps in the same room, around 1 Gbps through a wall, and I was still able to pull 350 Mbps at the bottom of my thick-walled old home’s garden. Comparing my upgrade pick of the best Wi-Fi routers, the tri-band Wi-Fi 7 Asus RT-BE96U, the GT-BN98 Pro proved slightly faster at all distances and longer-range across the board on every band. It also has an extra 6 GHz band, perfect for wireless backhaul if you want to use AiMesh (Asus’s mesh networking functionality) to create a mesh with another Asus router.
Multi-Link Operation (MLO), enabling you to connect devices on multiple bands simultaneously, seems to be maturing since its buggy debut with Wi-Fi 7. It enabled close-range speeds close to 5 Gbps in my tests, but that's using a second Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro as a client (most Wi-Fi 8 devices, when they arrive, won't manage that).
Bear in mind that I can’t test the Automated Frequency Coordination (AFC) support yet, which cross-checks with licensed services in the area so your router can boost power for increased range and coverage on the 6 GHz band. It is available in the US and will be in the UK soon, but not every country allows it, and your mileage will vary depending on your local licensees.
Wi-Fi 8 isn’t primarily about higher speeds. It aims to improve stability and reliability with a raft of features that compensate for local interference and reduce latency for important tasks like gaming. The Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro boasts adaptive Quality of Experience and device optimization, automatically recognizing gaming devices and streams and giving them priority.

Get better at: Showing leadership potential
Today's move
If you want to get promoted, don't just bring your boss problems — come to them with possible solutions when something goes wrong.
Jason Kidd, the chief operating officer at Chipotle, visits roughly a dozen restaurants every week and he uses team dinners in every location as a way to scout talent for promotions. He said he looks for four qualities in the people he promotes, including how they respond when things go wrong.
Why it works
At any company, including a fast-moving restaurant like Chipotle, problems are bound to arise. Kidd looks for leaders who can anticipate issues, take ownership, and find a solution.
Those employees show they aren't waiting around for problems to land in their lap. They're actively taking initiative to improve the workplace.
Try it today
The next time an issue comes up at work, take a few minutes to brainstorm possible solutions.
When you approach your manager, tell them what went wrong, a couple of possible solutions, and your recommendation for what to do next. That demonstrates leadership and initiative.
The bottom line
You aren't directly responsible for every problem that comes up at work. However, by showing your boss that you're actively working to avoid adding another task to their to-do list, you're helping make their job easier and showing them that you can handle more responsibility.
Source
This insight is based on Business Insider's reporting about how Chipotle's COO Jason Kidd promotes workers, and the qualities he looks for. Read the full story from Ana Altchek on Business Insider.

Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?
- Published
Kenya is grappling with its first ever outbreak of Ebola, a disease which neighbouring countries, such as Uganda and Democratic Republic of Congo, are used to dealing with.
Nine cases have now been confirmed including its first patient, who travelled from DR Congo and died two weeks ago.
Four relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner have now tested positive, meaning they are all linked to him.
But concerns are rising that the virus could start spreading further, even as the government has sought to assure citizens.
The US has warned it citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Should Kenyans be concerned?
Kenyans have been expressing their concerns that the disease could spread more widely.
More than 4,000 people have died since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
The latest outbreak has been caused by the Bundibugyo species, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Kenyans raised questions from the outset, about how the first patient was able to spend time in the region worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified. He died days after his arrival in Kenya.
As a regional transport hub, the risk of the outbreak spreading is a big concern.
The doctors' union in Kenya has expressed concerns at "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenya's main airport.
Dennis Miskellah, the union representative, told the BBC that border and port facilities were grossly understaffed.
However, Health Director-General Patrick Amoth on Tuesday evening sought to reassure people, saying that the eight patients were all improving and responding well to treatment.
What is being done to stop it spreading?
When the first case was announced, the authorities urged people not to panic, assuring them of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings.
Kenya has since introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from 10 countries it considers to be at high risk: DR Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.
The government has additionally designated treatment and isolation facilities across the country, and health workers have been trained to deal with the disease.
Amoth also said that a dedicated laboratory had been set up at the Kenyatta National Hospital Infectious Disease Unit to handle Ebola tests, to ensure that the hospital's laboratory was not contaminated.
In Kenya, 134 out of 135 people listed as contacts of the first patient remain in quarantine. That means about 99% of the contacts have been traced and isolated, in order to prevent Ebola from spreading to the wider population.
That all of those infected so far had links to the first victim shows Kenya's early response is working, according to the International Rescue Committee.
The government is also working with international partners, including Africa CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), to support its response, including surveillance, communication and community engagement.
A toll-free emergency hotline, 719, has been provided to the public to report suspected symptoms.
Is Kenya prepared in case it starts spreading further?
Amoth said that none of the contacts of the first patients had showed symptoms before going into quarantine "and therefore the potential to spread to another person is very minimal, literally non-existent".
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
Despite that, Kenya's health ministry says nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola at the national and local levels, besides the facilities that have been designated to handle the virus.
The ministry has urged people to remain calm and vigilant. It has also asked Kenyans not to stigmatise people identified as contacts of Ebola cases.
The ministry, along with the WHO, have produced posters to help people understand Ebola and support its containment. One message reads: "Stop stigma, choose support. Stigma can discourage people from reporting symptoms or cooperating with response teams."
In addition, the government has procured supplies of protective equipment.
Is enough being done to protect health workers?
Not according to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Union (KMPDU).
With three health workers and a hospital cleaner among those infected, questions have been asked as to whether the government could do more to protect workers.
Health workers and carers can face a higher risk of Ebola infection because caring for infected patients may bring them into contact with blood and other bodily fluids.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Dennis Miskellah, the KMPDU deputy secretary general, told the BBC that protective equipment must be provided to hospitals so that they are fully protected, especially in case patients with symptoms do not declare that they have been in areas with Ebola.
He suggests the government ought to conduct proper health education to destigmatise the virus, so that people do not seek to hide their symptoms.
The International Rescue Committee has also called for continued funding for contact tracing, border screening and training of frontline health workers in Kenya.
Will there be any restrictions, like a travel ban?
Kenya remains open with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings.
Despite confirming the eight cases, the authorities have explicitly ruled out a national lockdown or general travel ban for Kenyans.
The US on Monday issued an advisory asking citizens to reconsider travelling to the country over Ebola concerns. Other countries have issued health alerts, including the UK, which warned its citizens that they may encounter enhanced health screening, and Canada, which has asked citizens to monitor their health for 21 days.
No country has issued an outright ban against their nationals visiting Kenya, nor have Kenyans been blocked from entering other countries over Ebola fears.
Has business and tourism been affected?
Analysts have raised concerns over the potential impact of public health fears on international travel and tourism but there is no evidence this has happened yet.
But the situation could change if the outbreak were to spread into the wider population.
How many Kenyans are there in DR Congo?
The exact number of Kenyans living in the DR Congo is not clear.
A report authored last year by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think-tank put the number of Kenyans living in eastern DR Congo at about 2,500, including about 50 investors. It also noted that there were about four times as many Congolese living in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, alone.
The Kenyan embassy in the Congolese capital, Kinshasa, which represents Kenya's interests in four countries - DR Congo, Central African Republic, Congo-Brazzaville and Gabon - has in the past urged Kenyans living in the region to formally register so that it is able to serve them better.
How have neighbouring countries responded?
Several countries in the region have announced tightening of surveillance measures and enhanced screening for visitors.
One man who came into contact with the man who died in Kenya is under quarantine in Somalia and samples have been sent to Kenya for testing.
Somalia has also said it was taking precautionary measures, including enhancing surveillance measures at border points "given the evolving regional situation and the movement of people between countries".
The suspected case in Somalia had travelled through Ethiopia, which has also said it had tightened surveillance to prevent an outbreak
In Tanzania, visitors are expected to undergo daily health monitoring for 21 days, through an automated tracking system, which was announced after Kenya confirmed multiple cases of Ebola infections.
Uganda said after Kenya's first Ebola case that it was continuing to "maintain strong surveillance measures to protect public health".
The Kenyan businessman had travelled through Uganda on his way home from DR Congo.
Uganda had reported two Ebola deaths shortly after the outbreak was reported in DR Congo, but the WHO has since declared it to be free of the disease.
On Tuesday, Nigeria confirmed a case of Ebola in a female patient who travelled from Uganda to Abuja. Nigeria is the first West African state to report a case linked to the current Ebola crisis in East and Central Africa.
Ugandan health officials say the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business before passing through Uganda in early October.
The health ministry stressed she did not have symptoms while transiting through Uganda and only developed them after arriving in Abuja.

Do screens in cars represent luxury? Judging by the latest car interiors, the answer would seem to be an emphatic “yes.” Screens aren’t just getting larger; they are multiplying across the dashboard and morphing into different forms and concepts. Indeed, an interior’s screens are a pretty good indicator of what brand made the car—or at least how much the owner paid for it.
But is this actually what customers want? Are more screens really better? And even if they are, luxury car features inevitably trickle down to cheaper, more mainstream offerings, and screens can only get so big. That leaves luxury automakers with another question to answer: “What’s next?”
Mercedes-Benz is working on a new display alternative that could provide an answer. For now, it’s known as the holographic display. Forget the images from Star Trek and Star Wars that just popped into your head, though. It’s effectively a more advanced form of heads-up display, or HUD.
Eyes on the road, not the dash
Whereas a traditional HUD projects images onto the windshield glass, the holographic display has two main components. It still uses a projector, but its key element is a special transparent film laminated into the glass. The film uses holographic optical elements, or “super-small mirrors,” as Mercedes development engineer Lena Hees described them, that selectively reflect the light emitted by the projector, keeping the image visible even in direct sunlight while hiding it from the driver’s view.
Today, the passenger-side touchscreens in Mercedes and other luxury vehicles rely on driver-monitoring cameras or screen polarization to keep the driver from seeing what is playing on the passenger side.
Speaking of passenger screens, the holographic display is clearly being considered as a future alternative or replacement for this technology. Although screens in cars are increasingly ubiquitous, a recent JD Power study indicated that car owners classify passenger screens as “not necessary” and have generally negative opinions about them. Mercedes has clearly observed similar opinions but for slightly different reasons.
“We have customers who like the Hyperscreen,” said development engineer Maximilian Hilger of the pillar-to-pillar screen found in an increasing number of Mercedes models. “But there are others who want to maintain luxury materials.”
In other words, the massive screen design doesn’t seem as luxurious as the pillar-to-pillar bands of wood or other materials found in previous-generation models. And that’s not an opinion isolated to Mercedes’ customers.
New Mercedes chief design officer Bastian Baudy recently told German magazine Auto Motor Sport that “Materiality and haptics must remain tangible—with switches, buttons, and intuitive controls. Real materials are at the heart of Mercedes: metal, wood.”
Mercedes CEO Ola Källenius went further, grouping interior quality and materials among the brand’s “forever values,” along with safety and maintaining what a Mercedes is like to drive.
That presents conflicting priorities, however.
“Yes, you need to have all the [technology] that a customer could ever dream of and wants,” Källenius told Ars. “But you need to package it in an aesthetically pleasing way. That’s also part of it.”
That brings us back to the holographic display. Keep in mind that the photos in this article show early prototypes I saw at Mercedes’ research facilities in Sindelfingen, Germany. The prototype projector sits inside a rather crude, trapezoidal hole dug into the dash of a right-hand-drive, pre-2027 S-Class. It’s also loud, with a cooling fan whirring like a laptop visiting too many junk-filled websites.
The production version would have a much smaller projector opening than those of the prototype and existing heads-up displays. Manual Holstein, a manager working in Mercedes research for future displays, indicated that the projector could be small enough to be hidden behind wood or metal trim pieces. Holstein also said you won’t hear a fan in the production model and that the resolution would improve.
The resolution is certainly considerably better than any current head-up display, including Mercedes’ own, which features augmented reality elements. Full-color, commercial-like videos of the C-Class Electric played during the demonstration, and the display was sufficiently bright, even though Holstein said the prototype was operating at just 20 percent of its maximum brightness.
It’s not there yet
Issues remain, however. The resolution may be good compared to the arrows, script, and graphics of a current HUD, but it’s poor when compared to a passenger touchscreen. The video’s contrast was also too high, and as you can see in the photos, the picture was distorted into a narrow height due to the angle of the windshield. Frankly, no one would choose to watch anything on it over a phone, tablet, or conventional passenger screen. It needs to improve by orders of magnitude before becoming a viable alternative.
Again, though, this is just a prototype. Holstein said the holographic film size, or “eyebox,” can be made much bigger and be raised higher than the HUD-like height of the prototype. He also dismissed the distortion as a problem unique to the prototype.
Imagine nearly half the windshield transformed into a virtual screen that’s visible only to the passenger. Beyond videos or other entertainment, Mercedes envisions the holographic display highlighting points of interest in the view through the windshield. A similar display could be placed on the driver side, showing situational information, enabling video calls, or providing entertainment when parked. In the future, it could even let drivers watch things other than the road when Mercedes’ Level 3 autonomous driving system allows them to take their eyes off it. At the very least, the technology could replace today’s HUDs and their larger projector boxes.
Currently, it might work for a weather widget, but you won’t want to watch a video.
Credit:
Mercedes-Benz
Currently, it might work for a weather widget, but you won’t want to watch a video.
Credit:
Mercedes-Benz
Having experienced the prototype while the car was moving, I also think the holographic display could help prevent the motion sickness that can come from staring at a passenger screen while the car is moving. The higher screen angle and ability to see more of the outside world beyond created a notably different visual experience.
Of course, the question remains: “Is this what customers want?”
If the JD Power survey found that customers don’t care about passenger touchscreens, will they be any more enthusiastic about holographic video displays? That seems doubtful. But that’s just as much of an open question as whether the production version will actually live up to its promises.
There’s also another matter: What, exactly, defines luxury? Before Bastian Baudy took over as Mercedes’ chief design officer this year, his predecessor and former boss Gordon Wagener echoed Källenius’ thoughts about the direction of the brand’s interiors. He was considerably blunter, though.
“Screens are not luxury,” Wagener told ABC News. “You have a better—and bigger—TV at home, right? And every car has a big screen. So we have to create luxury beyond the screen. That’s why I talk about craftsmanship and sophistication.”
If the holographic display lets automakers emphasize traditional design and materials while still offering unique technology, it could be a promising way forward.

Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities.
Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals.
In a statement posted on Instagram late on Thursday, the organisers said: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.”
Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood.
Founded in 2001 by a group of Peking University students, the festival grew to become the only film festival in mainland China to offer a public forum for films and discussions exploring LGBTQ+ issues.
The Chinese authorities have grown increasingly intolerant of open discussion of feminist or LGBTQ+ issues. Film festivals in particular attract particular scrutiny because they provide an opportunity to platform narratives that sit outside the Communist party’s worldview.
Beijing Independent film festival, China’s most prominent independent film festival, was closed down in 2014 after the authorities detained the founders and shut off the electricity supply to the venue. Last year, an independent Chinese film festival that was due to be held in New York was cancelled after harassment from the Chinese authorities, an incident which raised concern about transnational repression.
Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director for Human Rights Watch, said: “The Chinese government under Xi has been relentlessly tightening social and ideological control, and so any activities outside of those sanctioned by the party-state are subjected to intensifying scrutiny and often also official harassment.
“The authorities have put more pressure on what little is left of China’s civil society, as well as the LGBT communities and independent film-makers. A queer film festival basically faces all of these overlapping pressures.”
Hongwei Bao, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of St Andrews who focuses on LGBT issues, said that the festival was “a beacon for LGBT resilience” in China.
“The shutdown of the Love Queer Cinema Week has a chilling affect on the Chinese queer community,” Bao said.
In June this year, screenings of films with LGBTQ+ themes that were scheduled to be held in Beijing during Pride month at the Institut Français, a French cultural centre, were cancelled because of police harassment.
Despite the increased pressure, Beijing Queer film festival remains a popular event. Several international film-makers whose work had been selected for the festival had travelled to China to participate. Last year, the festival received 200 volunteer applications, four times the number received in 2024.
Beijing’s public security bureau could not be reached for comment.

Mining giant joins fight to stop killer toad march across Australia
- Published
Rio Tinto is ploughing millions of dollars into stopping the poisonous cane toad reaching the Pilbara region of western Australia, where the mining giant has a vast iron ore operation.
The firm, alongside Curtin University in Perth and others, will spend A$28m (£14.5m) building a "toad containment zone" to prevent the pest travelling south.
While the cane toad is not a direct threat to Rio Tinto's business, it produces toxins lethal to native wildlife and poses a threat to Pilbara's ecosystem.
Rio Tinto has previously faced criticism for destroying two sacred Aboriginal rock shelters in Pilbara which sat above tonnes of iron ore.
The decision cost the former chief executive his job, provoked a widespread backlash and saw Rio Tinto commit to rebuilding trust with Indigenous communities.
Commenting on the proposed containment zone, Roberta Hunter, a ranger in Australia's Nyangumarta Warrarn Indigenous Protected Area, said: "Cane toads destroy the water and animals.
"When toads come close to our country, we want to be there to stop them because we don't want the country to be destroyed."
The plan is to cut off the toad's water supply by building a barrier across 7,500 sq km (2,895 sq m) of land between the Great Sandy Desert and the Indian Ocean.
In drier months, the cane toad needs water every few days to survive.
If there are no natural water sources, the toad relies on artificial water points normally used for cattle and irrigation.
The funding will be used to stop the toad accessing dams, storage tanks or other ground-level water sources. The five-year project will begin in 2027.
A number of native species are at risk if the toad gets into Pilbara. These include the northern quoll, whose numbers have been decreasing, the goanna lizard and the ghost bat.
The toads were introduced into Australia in 1935 to control beetles within the sugar cane industry.
Since then, they have been on a slow march west across the country's northern landscape, according to the Australian government, travelling between 40 km and 60 km a year.
There are no predators or diseases that control the toads, which defend themselves using poison.
Ben Phillips, a professor at Curtin University, said the toads would reach Pilbara within two decades without action.
He said: "The toad containment zone is a once in a lifetime opportunity to stop one of the world's worst invasive species in its tracks and protect the region's unique wildlife."

October was a month of contrasts for the Indian startup ecosystem. While AI, deeptech and advanced manufacturing continued to attract significant investor capital, a series of cybersecurity incidents and regulatory actions highlighted the risks and responsibilities that come with scaling digital businesses. The month saw India’s cybersecurity watchdog CERT-In flag unauthorised access to Indian organisations’ live systems by AI agents under evaluation, alongside the use of agentic tools in financially motivated cyberattacks. Digital trust company eMudhra faced a major security setback after researchers recovered eight weak private keys from publicly available certificates, prompting Google, Mozilla, Apple and Microsoft to distrust the affected certificates. Meanwhile, IRDAI’s proposed insurance commission caps raised concerns among distributors and brokers, with industry representatives warning of significant revenue and employment implications. Together, these developments underscored the mounting compliance, data security and governance challenges confronting India's digital businesses. Amid this, venture capital interest in the ecosystem took a slight hit. Indian startups raised over $686 Mn across 104 funding deals in October, down almost 10% MoM from September's $760.7 Mn. AI remained a major funding theme, while capital also flowed into spacetech, defence, semiconductors and industrial automation. The public markets remained active, with four new-age tech companies making their debuts during the month. Zetwerk, Tonbo Imaging, Moneyview and Snapdeal parent AceVector made their market debuts, while Cult.fit and Atomberg received SEBI's approval for their respective IPOs. Against this backdrop of funding momentum, public-market activity and growing regulatory scrutiny, Inc42 is back with the latest edition of its flagship ‘30 Startups To Watch’ series, spotlighting early-stage ventures that stood out to us in October. Founded in February 2025, Regenerix onboards village-level entrepreneurs (VLEs) who lease its patented Stubble Removal Machine (SRM) to clear farmers' fields after harvest. The company buys back the collected residue, processes it into pellets and briquettes, and supplies it to industrial buyers as a coal substitute. Its machine can clear and chop one acre in around 90 minutes, compared with five to seven days through conventional methods. The opportunity is backed by India's estimated 230 Mn tonnes of surplus agricultural biomass annually and a government mandate requiring coal-based thermal power plants to use biomass blends. Regenerix has touched ₹2.3 Cr in revenue and plans to expand its machine network and pelletising capacity. ________________________________________________________________________ Ressl AI | Testing AI Agents Before Deployment AI agents may look impressive in demos, but getting them to work reliably in real-world business environments is another story. Customised software, incomplete data and unexpected scenarios can throw even sophisticated agents off track. Bengaluru-based Ressl AI is looking to address this challenge by putting AI agents through realistic tests before they are deployed. Founded in 2025 by Arushi Gandhi and Abhishek Eswaran, the Y Combinator Winter 2026 startup builds simulated enterprise environments that replicate business software, data, policies and potential failure scenarios. Its platform allows developers to test agents across different workflows, compare AI models, identify weaknesses and evaluate performance without exposing live business systems to potential errors. It also offers customised benchmarks and evaluation services to enterprises and AI developers. Ressl AI is tapping into a global AI agent testing and validation market projected to reach $2.58 Bn by 2031. However, with established players such as LangSmith, Braintrust and Patronus AI already operating in the space, the startup will need to demonstrate how its simulated environments deliver more reliable results. ________________________________________________________________________ SCRUB Robotics | Building Robots To Keep India's Lakes Clean Cleaning a lake is one thing. Keeping it clean is another. Across Indian cities, floating waste keeps returning to urban water bodies, forcing authorities to rely on repeated, labour-intensive cleanup drives. Bengaluru-based SCRUB Robotics wants to make lake maintenance less dependent on manual labour by deploying autonomous robots to collect waste and monitor water quality. Founded by Krishna Purwar and Atharva Agarwal, the startup is developing a range of marine robots for different cleaning and monitoring needs. Its flagship product, V1, is a solar-assisted, twin-hull robot equipped with a conveyor to collect floating waste and aquatic vegetation. The V2 uses a simpler intake mechanism, while V4 focuses on water-quality monitoring and mapping. SCRUB is also developing a system to intercept waste in rivers and canals. Its prototypes have undergone trials at Bengaluru’s Kengeri and Madiwala lakes, with an early version collecting up to 5 kg of waste per cycle. Operating in India's clean technology market, projected to reach $152.5 Bn by 2030, the startup targets municipalities, campuses and industrial clients. It plans to generate revenue through robot sales, managed deployments and cleaning-as-a-service contracts. ________________________________________________________________________ SpectraGaze | Building India's Eyes In Space From monitoring Earth's surface to tracking objects in space, satellites depend on advanced imaging sensors to see what the human eye cannot. Yet, India continues to rely on imports for several critical optical and infrared components. Ahmedabad-based SpectraGaze Systems wants to reduce this dependence by developing indigenous imaging technologies for space, defence and scientific applications. Founded in 2023 by former ISRO scientist Arup Banerjee, the startup develops optical sensors and electro-optical payloads, including hyperspectral, multispectral, panchromatic and thermal imaging systems. SpectraGaze has worked with ISRO, the Physical Research Laboratory and Kaynes Technology. Its early projects include delivering an infrared detector to ISRO and securing an image-sensor development contract for the space agency's next-generation HRSAT programme alongside AMETEK. The startup is also developing an indigenous infrared detector assembly. Separately, it is developing a hyperspectral camera for a 3U satellite for Kaynes. However, building space-grade sensors is only half the battle. SpectraGaze must now demonstrate consistent reliability and performance while converting its early institutional projects into repeat orders. ________________________________________________________________________ Tecnod8.ai | Helping Industries Harness The Power Of GenAI When factory machinery breaks down, or production lines grind to a halt, finding the right technical expertise can be a challenge. As manufacturers increasingly embrace automation, access to specialised engineering knowledge is becoming more crucial than ever. Mandi-based Tecnod8.ai is looking to bridge this gap with a generative AI copilot that helps engineering, maintenance and production teams troubleshoot problems and develop automation solutions. Founded in 2024 by Ravinder Kumar and Akshar Singh, the startup aims to make industrial engineering as accessible as a DIY workflow. Its platform combines a customised LLM, AI-powered assistance, voice interaction and 3D simulations to help engineers diagnose machinery issues, access technical information and design automation systems. It is also exploring multilingual capabilities to make technical knowledge accessible to a wider workforce. Tecnod8.ai is entering a global AI-in-manufacturing market projected to grow from $7 Bn in 2025 to $35.8 Bn by 2030. However, the startup will need to demonstrate the accuracy of its AI-generated guidance, compatibility with diverse industrial systems and ability to convert initial pilots into recurring enterprise customers. _______________________________________________________________ TensrAI | Designing Self Learning Robots Robots may be transforming factory floors and warehouses, but making machines autonomous remains expensive. For many businesses, adopting automation means replacing existing equipment with costly new robots. Hyderabad-based TensrAI wants to change that by bringing autonomous capabilities to machines already in use. Founded in 2025 by Sai Nikhil Rao Gona, Venkata Sai Charan Chalamalasetty, Harshith Uppalapati and Vivek Datta, the startup is building an AI-powered autonomy platform for industrial and commercial equipment. Its technology combines computer vision, AI-based localisation and robotic manipulation to help machines navigate their surroundings and perform tasks with limited human intervention. TensrAI's retrofit-first approach aims to automate existing machines rather than replace them. Its potential applications span material handling and cleaning across factories, warehouses, airports and hospitals. The startup is also developing a mobile manipulator that combines autonomous movement with robotic arms. With India's robotics market projected to reach $4.6 Bn by 2030, TensrAI is entering a growing but competitive sector. As players such as Ati Motors, Addverb and Peppermint Robotics expand their offerings, TensrAI's challenge will be proving that retrofitting can make automation more accessible. ________________________________________________________________________ ULOOK | Mapping Radio Signals From Space Ships, aircraft and communication systems constantly emit radio-frequency (RF) signals that can reveal their location and activity. However, tracking these emissions across vast maritime and remote regions remains challenging, particularly when vessels switch off or manipulate conventional tracking systems. Bengaluru-based ULOOK is building a satellite-based intelligence network to detect and interpret these otherwise invisible signals. Founded in 2024 by Siddhesh Naik and Adheesh Boratkar, ULOOK is developing autonomous satellite swarms for RF sensing and spectrum awareness. Unlike conventional Earth-observation satellites that capture optical images, its technology picks up radio signals emitted by ships, aircraft and ground-based systems. Its proprietary PulseTrack payload suite is designed to identify, classify and geolocate these signals, with applications in maritime surveillance, defence intelligence and monitoring suspicious vessel movements. ULOOK aspires to capture a slice of India’s space economy, projected to reach $44 Bn by 2033. In November 2025, ULOOK raised ₹19 Cr, which it plans to use for hardware validation, payload development and its first satellite swarm. North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
- Published
North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".
Kim Yo-jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.
This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.
Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.
The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.
"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.
"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.
- Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far 
  - Published3 days ago
But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.
The country has consistently denied such claims.
Kim Yo-jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".
